title: ‘The greatest arms I’ve ever seen’: Matt Damon’s muscular female stunt double Devyn Dalton | The Odyssey | The Guardian
description: Canadian stuntwoman is only 4ft 6in and stood in for star to make the giant Laestrygonians appear even bigger
Author: Olivia Bowden
Headline: Canadian stuntwoman is only 4ft 6in and stood in for star to make the giant Laestrygonians appear even bigger
Content: ‘Apparently my biceps have their own fan club right now,’ said Dalton.Photograph: @devyn.dalton/InstagramView image in fullscreen‘Apparently my biceps have their own fan club right now,’ said Dalton.Photograph: @devyn.dalton/InstagramThe Odyssey‘The greatest arms I’ve ever seen’: Matt Damon’s muscular female stunt double Devyn DaltonCanadian stuntwoman is only 4ft 6in and stood in for star to make the giant Laestrygonians appear even biggerOlivia Bowdenin TorontoSun 2 Aug 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 19.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA35-year-old stuntwoman is one of the great unsung heroes of Christopher Nolan’s new blockbusterThe Odyssey– standing in for Matt Damon and displaying what the actor called “the greatest arms I’ve ever seen”.Canadian Devyn Dalton was the Hollywood star’s stunt double in a pivotal scene in the film where Odysseus (Damon) and his men are confronted by the Laestrygonians, giant armoured cannibals.In order to make Damon and his crew appear dwarfed by the group of goliaths, the actors doing stunts needed to be small. Dalton is 4ft 6in (137cm) and her rippling, muscular arms were perfect to represent Damon’s own biceps.View image in fullscreenMatt Damon – or Devyn Dalton – faces the giant Laestrygonians.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyDalton has “the greatest arms I’ve ever seen”, said Damon, speaking to podcaster Josh Horowitz on his show Happy Sad Confused.“Knowing my arms impressed Matt was honestly pretty special,” Dalton told the Guardian. “His shoutout in the press completely caught me by surprise … I’ll always appreciate that he did.”Dalton said she had known she wanted to tell stories since she was a child, inventing characters and costumes and putting on shows for her family.She started out acting professionally at nine years old, which gradually led her into stunt performing – a different way of telling those tales: through the body, through her own strength.“We celebrate men who build careers around being powerful … so why shouldn’t women be celebrated for that too?” she said.View image in fullscreenDalton (right) filming in Scotland.Photograph: @devyn.dalton/InstagramAfter Damon made the comments in his press tour for The Odyssey, the big-screen depiction of Homer’s epic Greek poem that has become a huge hit for Nolan and sparkedendless media coverage, Dalton said her phone “absolutely exploded”.She is currently filming a project in New Zealand and was not expecting to receive global attention.“Apparently my biceps have their own fanclub right now, which definitely wasn’t on my 2026 prediction,” she said.View image in fullscreenDevyn Dalto.Photograph: Scott HemenwayShe said she was cast in the role through the network of professional representatives and stunt coordinators rather than any open casting call.“When I found out I booked it, I was genuinely so excited and incredibly grateful. It’s one of those moments where years of hard work and persistence suddenly feels worthwhile,” she said.Daltonflew to Scotlandto film and she said it was a continuous reminder of just how many people it takes to put together a production like The Odyssey.“What audiences see for a few minutes often represents months of preparation,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘It reminded me of James Bond’: Guardian readers on The OdysseyRead moreDalton said she trained hard for the role, refining her regular regime of exercises, a combination of muay thai, jiu-jitsu, dance, yoga and strength-based workouts.“I took the responsibility very seriously,” she said. That’s why Damon’s shoutout made her feel the training truly paid off. Meeting him on set, Dalton said that “he’s every bit as genuine, kind and generous as you’d hope”.Stunt performing is actually an exercise in being extremely well rehearsed and prepared, rather than engaging in anything dangerous or scary, she said. “The best stunt performers are very aware of risk … so everything can be performed as safely as possible.”Some audiences have been vocal online that stuntwomen in particular should be celebrated more and recognised for their physical prowess and performance.“I’m proud to represent strong women … I’m passionate about encouraging more people, especially young women, to realise there isn’t just one path into this industry,” she said.“I hope more young girls grow up believing they never have to choose between being strong and being themselves.”As for what’s next, Dalton said she would love to lead in a film or series as a starring actor – who of course could do her own stunts.“Audiences are hungry for new faces … I’d love to show what I’m capable of,” she said.Explore more on these topicsThe OdysseyChristopher NolanMatt DamonScotlandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Richard E Grant’s Very Modern Odyssey review – far more thrilling than the Christopher Nolan borefest | Television | The Guardian
description: The actor gobbles up food, roars with glee and finds himself deeply moved in this four-part travelogue inspired by the journey of Homer’s hero. It’s a real success of a show
Author: Sarah Dempster
Headline: The actor gobbles up food, roars with glee and finds himself deeply moved in this four-part travelogue inspired by the journey of Homer’s hero. It’s a real success of a show
Content: Richard E Grant’s Very Modern Odyssey – the actor in Malta’s Grand Harbour.Photograph: Emporium ProductionsView image in fullscreenRichard E Grant’s Very Modern Odyssey – the actor in Malta’s Grand Harbour.Photograph: Emporium ProductionsTV reviewTelevisionReviewRichard E Grant’s Very Modern Odyssey review – far more thrilling than the Christopher Nolan borefestThe actor gobbles up food, roars with glee and finds himself deeply moved in this four-part travelogue inspired by the journey of Homer’s hero. It’s a real success of a showSarah DempsterSun 2 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere comesRichard E Grant, pounding towards us in his tiny leather jacket as he gesticulates wildly at his cobbled surrounds. “Wow,” he gasps. “Look at that.” We look at that. It’s Malta. Specifically, Malta’s Grand Harbour: a sobbingly beautiful gateway to the Mediterranean and the sun-blessed starting line for Richard E Grant’s Very Modern Odyssey, a four-part travelogue “inspired by Homer’s hero” in which the veteran actor traces Odysseus’s “incredible journey” while wearing a succession of increasingly voluminous linen trousers.Said tracing is not, however, an exact science. This is not one of those awful celebrity things in which our noble hero arms himself with set squares and a scholastic scowl before setting sail on a “voyage” to uncover “the truth”.The Odyssey review – Nolan goes god-tier with breathtaking epic of men, monsters and moral metamorphosisRead moreNor is it an attempt to contribute to the seemingly interminable Odyssey discourse – the ongoing hoo-ha overthe historical accuracyof the Christopher Nolan blockbuster that already feels as if it’s lasted longer than the Trojan war.Instead, it’s a loose-limbed, easygoing thing that attempts to separate Homeric myth from reality but appears equally “chill” with the fact that much of it remains fundamentally unknowable. “Essentially,” says Grant, grinning hugely, “we’re dealing with an act of the imagination.”So here we are in the Maltese capital of Valletta, which doesn’t appear to have featured on Odysseus’s itinerary, but does have a Michelin-starred restaurant that serves butter-basted pigeon with sage and rosemary. Grant is cock-a-hoop. “Mmm,” he shouts while frantically licking his plate, much as the Greeks “licked” the Trojans after the siege of Troy.This is followed by a brief stop at the luxurious Phoenecia hotel for a lime mocktail and some wistful reminiscing about Malta’s colonial past (“this was Queen Elizabeth’s favourite hangout!”), before it’s off for a gander at Valletta’s perfectly extraordinary St John’s Co-Cathedral.View image in fullscreenInto antiquity … Grant takes a boat trip from Valletta.Photograph: Emporium Productions“I’ve never seen anything like this in my life,” splutters our host, drifting through the nave open-mouthed as he takes in its baroque tumult of golden whorls and thunderstruck cherubim. “Honestly, it out-Sistines the Sistine Chapel.” And it does. Built by the Order of St John in the 16th century, it’s a frantic masterpiece of death and glory, its ornate marble floor housing the tombs of 400 “warrior knights”.“In Homer’s world,” says Grant, “heroes make a sacrifice to the gods every time they sail into danger. Here, the ritual was different, but the idea was the same: ask for help before you do something terrifying.”The actor is moved. “I’m not a religious man,” he tells us later, chin smushed into his enormous brown neckerchief. “But going inside that jewel of a church was one of the most beautiful experiences I’ve ever had.”Here, there are epiphanies around every corner. Valletta’s Lurpak-coloured stonework is “a revelation”. The cave on the Maltese island of Gozo that may or may not have been the inspiration for the home of the saucy nymph Calypso leaves him “nearly in tears”.“I’m utterly bewitched by every detail,” he roars at one point. He is a one-man brass section of patrician glee.These days, we note, there is a slight fuzziness to Grant’s barrel-aged boom, as if his vowels had rolled under a chaise longue and been left to gather a fine layer of fluff. When he reads extracts from Homer’s poem in the ruins of an amphitheatre, he sounds both wearily thrilled and knackered, like a kindly oak tree completing a particularly taxing parkrun.The opening episode concludes with a visit to the bronze age ruins of Troy. This was “almost certainly” the site of “a real, bloody war”.More vagueness. But it’s all to the good. Homer’s gargantuan tale of Mediterranean aggro remains powerfully relevant, says a local historian. “Refugees, climate change, political crisis – all of these things you find inThe Odyssey.”Another huge grin from Grant. “It seems Homer blurred fact and fiction into a story that has lasted over two and a half thousand years,” he trumpets. “A success by any measure.” As, indeed, is Grant’s own Very Modern Odyssey.Lime mocktails all round.Richard E Grant’s Very Modern Odyssey is on Channel 4 now.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewRichard E GrantThe OdysseyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: This is how we do it: ‘If I’m honest, the fact that Thomas was married made it more exciting’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Vivian and Thomas both left physically unfulfilling marriages and are rediscovering their sex drives in later life
Author: Olivia Ladanyi
Headline: Vivian and Thomas both left physically unfulfilling marriages and are rediscovering their sex drives in later life
Content: Illustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianThis is how we do itLife and styleThis is how we do it: ‘If I’m honest, the fact that Thomas was married made it more exciting’Vivian and Thomas both left physically unfulfilling marriages and are rediscovering their sex drives in later lifeHow do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymouslyAs told toOlivia LadanyiSun 2 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVivian, 61double quotation markSince menopause and being with Thomas, my interest in sex is much higher“If you don’t use it, you’ll lose it,” my sister told me a couple of years after my divorce. “Go and buy a vibrator or something.” It was then, in my mid-50s, that I started masturbating for the first time. I had a sexual awakening: I orgasmed for the first time in my life, started listening to podcasts about sex, and was hornier than I’d ever been. It was around that time that Thomas and I started flirting via texts.If I’m honest, the fact Thomas was still married made it more exciting. I justified it by telling myself that he and his wife hadn’t had sex in years. He told me he had feelings for me, but it was me who made the first move.double quotation markOur drives probably aren’t that different, but for me, sex is connection and reassuranceWe first had sex seven months before Thomas eventually separated from his wife. I thought it would be a one-off. I couldn’t imagine us as a couple, but I knew we’d have fun. I’d never been with someone who cared about my pleasure before.In my marriage, sex was boring and vanilla, something we did on a Saturday night. Since menopause and being with Thomas, my interest in sex is much higher. If it were up to me, we’d have sex every other day, but it’s more like twice a week. Once Thomas has had time to replenish, I’ll say: “It’s been a few days …” But my desire is responsive and I’m not used to being the initiator.Thomas’s libido has declined since we’ve been together, and I worry it will continue to. Our drives probably aren’t that different, but for me, sex is connection and reassurance. When he orgasms, I feel complete. If Thomas initiates, it reassures me that I’m not too old, that I’m still attractive, that he still desires me.Share your experienceIf you’re keen to talk to us about your sex lives you can get in touch by filling in the form below. It is very important that both sexual partners are happy to participate.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.First name of partner oneFirst name of partner twoLength of relationshipContact number or email address of partner onePlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Contact number or email address of partner twoPlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Do both parties agree to being contacted by a journalist from the Guardian?YesBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreThomas, 58double quotation markEven the way Vivian sinks into my hugs shows how she desires meFourteen years ago, I joined a swimming club after moving to a new area with my wife and kids. I remember walking out on the pool deck and noticing Vivian. She was physically fit, friendly and took care of people in a way I found attractive. After she mentioned that her husband had to be home at 8pm to watch his shows, I imagined that their sex life wasn’t great. I fantasised about going over to their house in the day while he was at work and having sex with her.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe first time we kissed – at Vivian’s door after I drove her home – I felt a warm tingling sensation. It was the most sexually intimate I’d been with someone in almost eight years. But the first time we had sex it didn’t go very well. It was May, and I suggested a swim in a lake, imagining there would be something sensual about that. We tried to warm up in the shower, and I loved the feeling of her wet, smooth, slippery skin, but then we moved to the bed and the sheets stuck to our damp bodies. I couldn’t maintain an erection. Despite being as limp as a noodle, it didn’t feel like a failure – we laughed about it.double quotation markI feel grief over the loss of libido – I miss my youth and how easy it was to get an erectionMy sex drive is lower than it once was. I struggle to stay hard and it takes me a couple of days to recharge after sex. Vivian thinks that means she’s lacking in some way, but it’s nothing to do with her – it’s because I’m tired.After my ex-wife stopped enjoying sex, I became embarrassed to express my sexuality. I’d wear pyjamas in bed and roll over with my back to her. But even the way Vivian sinks into my hugs shows how she desires me, which makes me feel comfortable expressing my sexuality.I feel grief over the loss of libido – I miss my youth and how easy it was to get an erection. But non-sexual intimacy has expanded into the space left by sex, so I don’t feel frustrated.Names have been changedExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThis is how we do itSexRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The monthly scourge of ‘period poop’ is real. Here’s why your gut acts up | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Menstrual and digestive discomfort often coincide, and a researcher who has been looking in to it for a decade tells us what she learned
Author: Keren Landman
Headline: Menstrual and digestive discomfort often coincide, and a researcher who has been looking in to it for a decade tells us what she learned
Content: Period-related GI symptoms are common enough to have their own moniker. The science, however, has barely kept up.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeriod-related GI symptoms are common enough to have their own moniker. The science, however, has barely kept up.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesCall the doctorWell actuallyThe monthly scourge of ‘period poop’ is real. Here’s why your gut acts upMenstrual and digestive discomfort often coincide, and a researcher who has been looking in to it for a decade tells us what she learnedKeren LandmanSun 2 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery period, right on schedule: the cramps arrive, and right behind them, the urgent need to poop.If this is your experience, you’re in good company: in one study,73%of healthy premenopausal women reported at least one significant gastrointestinal symptom in the days before or during their period. Abdominal pain and diarrhea were the most common complaints, but women reported nausea and constipation too.Menstrual and digestive discomfort often coincide: “If you ask women about ‘period poops’ they’ll tell you they’re having menstrual cramps and those GI cramps at the same time,” said Taylor Judkins, a nutrition researcher at the University of Florida who has spent more than a decade studying the phenomenon.Period-related GI symptoms are common enough to have their own moniker. The science, however, has barely kept up. Judkins has personal experience with the phenomenon; when she first went looking for research on the phenomenon as a university student, she found almost nothing. A decade later, she says, there’s still a lot to learn.Why do period poops happen?It all starts with the uterus. As your period approaches, levels of estrogen and progesterone fall sharply. That’s the signal for your body to start breaking down the uterine lining, which you start shedding on day one of your period.At the same time, cells in the uterus startmakinghormone-like compounds called prostaglandins. These cause contractions in the type of muscle cells that make up most of your uterus and digestive tract, among other effects.It’s unclear exactly what happens next. But the leading theory, said Judkins, is that some prostaglandins enter the bloodstream from the uterus and stimulate similar contractions in the neighboring gut. This would explain the intestinal cramping and diarrhea many experience alongside menstrual cramping, especially on thefirst day or twoof their periods.One other theory relates to thevagus nerve,which runs signals between the gut and the brain. This neural pathway is highly sensitive to stress signals and inflammation. When activated, itprovokesfluid release within the gut and increased contractions of its muscles, leading to diarrhea. This is why some experts believe many people get anupset stomachwhen they’re anxious. Judkins theorizes that menstruation may also trigger the pathway.Many women also note constipation one to two weeks before their periods start, says Judkins, which may be a consequence of highprogesteronelevels. However, the evidence is less clear on the prevalence and timing of that symptom.People withirritable bowel syndromeandinflammatory bowel diseasetend to have significantly worse symptoms around their periods, and those with endometriosis typically carry a higher burden of GI symptoms overall. But you don’t need an underlying diagnosis to have period poops.“It’s very common, and some will tell you that it’s normal,” she says, “but it doesn’t mean you should have to live with this drastic decrease in your quality of life.”Can anything reduce period gut symptoms?Options exist, but none are a clear fix.Judkins and her team ran the only randomized trial to date testing the effects of probiotics on menstrual GI symptoms. Probiotics improved indigestion – but not diarrhea, the symptom most people are actually trying to solve.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSome experts recommend oral contraceptives on a theoretical basis: they reduce the amount of endometrial tissue your body makes, which should lead to less prostaglandin production when that tissue gets shed. However, there’s no good evidence suggesting they are effective for GI symptoms; one of Judkins’ studies that exclusively enrolledwomen taking oral contraceptivesfound they also reported period poops.Do women’s periods actually sync up with each other?Read moreAnti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and naproxen reduce prostaglandin production, which can ease both uterine and digestive-tract cramps. The catch: they can irritate the gut lining and actually cause diarrhea, and for anyone with Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis, they can worsen symptoms and should generally be avoided.For now, diet is your most practical starting point. Judkins recommends staying hydrated and eating more fiber – fruit, vegetables, whole grains, legumes — and less greasy comfort foods, which tend to worsen diarrhea. Exercise helps some people; the data aren’t robust, but the risk is low. And if symptoms are severe enough to affect work or daily life, that’s worth raising with a doctor.Why isn’t there a solution for this common issue yet?Judkins began studying period gut over a decade ago. “When you search these keywords, it’s my name that comes up,” she says.That’s not a triumphant statement. It reflects a research culture that has treated menstrual health as a niche concern rather than an important issue affecting roughly half the population.When researchers don’t study something, clinicians are less likely to treat it. Patients are also less likely to raise it, because nobody has signaled that it’s worth mentioning or that anything can be done. Judkins hopes that changes. “Funding for women’s health research is ultimately a gain for everybody,” she says.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyCall the doctorMenstruationWomen's healthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Inside M&S’s swanky Oxford Street revamp, the blueprint for its £700m growth strategy | Marks & Spencer | The Guardian
description: As boss Stuart Machin unveils a new-look Pantheon the retailer has fashion and overseas challenges ahead
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: As boss Stuart Machin unveils a new-look Pantheon the retailer has fashion and overseas challenges ahead
Content: The M&S Pantheon store on Oxford Street first opened in the 1930s.Photograph: Marks & SpencerView image in fullscreenThe M&S Pantheon store on Oxford Street first opened in the 1930s.Photograph: Marks & SpencerMarks & SpencerInside M&S’s swanky Oxford Street revamp, the blueprint for its £700m growth strategyAs boss Stuart Machin unveils a new-look Pantheon the retailer has fashion and overseas challenges aheadSarah ButlerSun 2 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a hot summer’s evening on London’s busy Oxford Street, a crowd of fashion influencers, models, journalists and the odd City analyst gathered for a first look at the upmarket revamp of Marks & Spencer’s landmark Pantheon store.Some may have had to double-check they had the right address, such is the scale of the makeover at the 88-year-old outlet, which is intended as a blueprint for change across the retailer’s more than 200 large stores.“We know we’ve got a big job modernising the store experience and modernising the online experience as well,” M&S’s chief executive, Stuart Machin, told the crowd.He said a collection of “legacy old stores” – such as outlets in Newcastle or central London – had remained profitable so “most previous leadership just kept them open”.But Machin has a bigger vision. He is an exacting, obsessive leader who loves to wade into the detail of store operations and warehouse refurbishments. He once admitted to disliking “all this talk about work-life balance”. Four years into the job, he is keen to leave his mark on the 142-year-old retail group.View image in fullscreenStuart Machin, chief executive of M&S, says the coming year is ‘one of the most important in our history’.Photograph: Marks & SpencerAfter a tough year marred by a cyber-attack thatknocked out M&S’s online tradingfor almost seven weeks andhit profits by more than £300m, Machin told shareholders at its recent annual meeting that the year ahead was “one of the most important in our history”. He went on to say: “The next three years are critical for M&S as we invest for growth.”The Pantheon, which was built in the late 18th century, was an opera house and entertainment venue before its reconstruction for M&S in the 1930s. With the latest revamp now finished, the next big project for the retailer will be its Marble Arch store, at the other end of Oxford Street.Machin said the group’s most profitable but rather low-ceilinged and labyrinthine outlet would be knocked down next year, a plan which has prompted outrage over the potential environmental impact.Thenew, 10-storey buildingwon planning permission only after a legal challenge andapproval by the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, in 2024. It will include just two and a half floors of shop space – compared with five at present – topped by offices and a gym, and will stand at the eastern tip of the London mayor Sadiq Khan’spedestrianisation of Oxford Street, which is due to be in place next year. .The rebuild is expected to take four years, during which M&S will lease a temporary store across the road in the same block as Zara. Machin told those gathered at the Pantheon that “hopefully” he would still be chief executive when the Marble Arch rebuild was completed, adding: “So let’s see how we do.”It is a question many shoppers and analysts may well be asking as Machin, backed by his retail veteran chair,Archie Norman, attempt to lead a turnaround of M&S that actually sticks and extends beyond a few high-profile outlets.Several predecessors have come up with flashy, short-lived revival plans to combat competition from Primark, H&M, Zara and younger, online rivals. After losing momentum, M&S only briefly regained annual pre-tax profits of £1bn in 2008, having first reached that milestone in 1998.View image in fullscreenM&S took over the pit lane at Silverstone last month before the British Grand Prix go under way.Photograph: Mark Sutton/Formula 1/Getty ImagesDespite a global financial crisis, Brexit, the coronavirus pandemic and the cyber-attack, the retailer appears to be on the front foot – with strong food sales andfashion credentials to match.Underlying profitsfell to £671mlast year, and Machin told the Guardian that climbing back to £1bn was not the aim. “Profit will be what it will be,” he said. “Our plan is for a growth business.”While some shareholders may complain about lacklustre dividends, Machin said they would thank him in the long term. His plan involves £700m of investments in revitalising stores, modernising its supply chain and distribution system, and further improvements in products.The group, which employs more than 65,000 people, has 227 full-line stores – containing food, clothing, homewares and beauty – after closing dozens of old and out-of-place outlets. More will shut over the next two years and a handful of new outlets are opening. It aims to have 200 full-line stores in the UK.In contrast, M&S’s food arm is expanding, with 18 food-only stores opening this year as it heads for a target of 420, compared with 335 directly operated outlets now. Franchise partners run another 466 in the UK and more overseas.A wave of new food stores and some cheaper groceries may have brought a broader range of shopper into M&S, but Machin said the retailer was “just at the starting blocks” with changes in fashion, home and beauty.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenM&S is aiming to double food sales by becoming a ‘true shopping-list retailer’The Pantheon store is “where we’re testing how we make shopping our ranges easier, more curated and more inspiring”, he said.The fashion floors are now broken up into bright “rooms” for different brands and product types, – flanked by digital displays, green-tiled pillars and modern shelving.On food, M&S is aiming to become a “true shopping-list retailer” as it aims to double sales. It is already the fastest-growing food retailer in the UK, with sales up 16% in the latest three-month tally from Worldpanel by Numerator. This has kept its market share at an all-time high of 4.1%, or 4.6% if sales via its online partner Ocado are included.On clothing, Machin has said M&S had “finally dumped the frump” – grasping the No 1 spot on style perception from its Spanish rival Zara to add to its existing top position on value, according to Worldpanel.View image in fullscreenModern shelving at the revamped M&S storeM&S is regaining market share – now controlling more than 10% of the UK fashion (clothing and footwear) market – and driving for more. It has even had to buy inmore smaller-sized womenswear and lingerieas consumers in their 40s, 30s and even 20s reappraise the brand.With the help of its marketing director, Sharry Cramond, who is bringing the social media-fuelled interest to fashion that she first delivered on food, the brand is creating a buzz.Senior industry insiders believe M&S is now “in a solid place”. One said it had “re-established itself and its credentials”, and another that it had “a lot more self-confidence”. “Clothing has finally got its mojo back,” according to one former senior executive.But another former executive needled that despite Machin’s “quite high ego quotient”, massaged with appearances on social media with glamorous influencers such as the Chicken Shop Date comedian Amelia Dimoldenberg or the actor Gillian Anderson, there was more work to do.“It has lost a massive amount of market share on womenswear which it will never recover,” he said.Another industry insider said M&S, which once had a vast empire, was continuing to struggle overseas. Two decades afterquitting the US, it still has a presence in 70 countries – but many operations are small. He added that theacquisition of a 50% stakein Ocado’s retail arm in 2019 was largely unprofitable, even if it had brought in a younger audience.Machin said revamping the international business had been harder than he envisaged, but said its fashion revival was helping overseas too.Perhaps his biggest challenge lies behind the scenes, with big warehouse projects in the next few years in south-west England and the Midlands. “Deadlines are realistic. We are not going from zero to 10 overnight,” he said.Explore more on these topicsMarks & SpencerLondonRetail industryFashion industryFood & drink industryArchie NormanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dining across the divide: ‘He didn’t change my mind on anything – but he did give me a lift to my car’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: A prospective Restore Britain voter and a Green-supporting Chinese immigrant found some common ground over small-boat crossings, but where did they land on foxhunting?
Author: Sam Wollaston
Headline: A prospective Restore Britain voter and a Green-supporting Chinese immigrant found some common ground over small-boat crossings, but where did they land on foxhunting?
Content: Phill (on left) and Joe. All photographs: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhill (on left) and Joe. All photographs: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianDining across the divideLife and styleDining across the divide: ‘He didn’t change my mind on anything – but he did give me a lift to my car’A prospective Restore Britain voter and a Green-supporting Chinese immigrant found some common ground over small-boat crossings, but where did they land on foxhunting?Want to meet someone from across the divide? Clickhereto find out howSam WollastonSun 2 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenPhill, 58, HertfordshireOccupationStairlift surveyorVoting recordAlways Conservative. AlmostReform UKin the last general election.Restore Britainin the nextAmuse bouchePhill has auditioned for Britain’s Got Talent many times. Never successfully, he says, because “I haven’t got a sob story”View image in fullscreenJoe, 32, CambridgeOccupationAgricultural engineerVoting recordLabourwhenJeremy Corbynwas leader. More recently GreenAmuse boucheJoe is an expert at the Chinese strategy board game GoFor startersJoePhill was better dressed than I was. I’d been at an agricultural show, so I was dressed for being on a farm. We talked about our lives. I’m an immigrant from China, came to the UK when I was four, lived on a council estate. My dad worked in a takeaway. I have an eight-month-old daughter.PhillI’m about to celebrate my silver wedding anniversary. I’ve got two boys at university, both home for the summer, working on the punts in Cambridge. Joe’s a nice chap. I didn’t think, oh God, he’s a lefty – I don’t judge people like that.JoeWe asked them to surprise us and they delivered a beautiful sharing board with many of their signature dishes; dal, lamb and chicken curries.PhillThe food was really nice. Washed down with a pint of cider.View image in fullscreenThe big beefJoeI voted for theGreensbecause I was impressed by their manifesto. I liked their policy on housing – there are many vacant properties that could be converted in a cost-effective and environmentally friendly way.PhillI thinkZack Polanskiis a raving idiot, and a danger to the country. None of their policies have been costed – it just involves taxing companies and successful people more. I think Labour and the Tories are history. The next election will be Greens v Reform. I’m hoping [Restore Britain leader] Rupert Lowe might do a deal with Farage. I don’t trust Farage – he’s very establishment, a showman like Boris, but not as likable.JoeI disagree that the Greens’ economic policies are unrealistic. I have seen Rupert Lowe’s website – I wouldn’t call it a manifesto. It seems to talk about immigrants and non-British people almost exclusively, which in my mind is insufficient policy to run a country.PhillThe country is in a lot of trouble, particularly with immigration, but also with far too many people on benefits that shouldn’t be. There are genuine people, but there are a lot that aren’t.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSharing plateJoeWe talked a little about foxhunting. He was strongly in favour. I was more on the fence, but I can see the economic benefit of allowing it to occur. I do think, from the videos I’ve seen, that the intention isn’t to cruelly kill the fox.PhillIt should never have been banned; it was wildlife management. Generally, the foxes that were killed were the injured ones. Since the ban, there has been something like a third less foxes in the countryside. Trail hunting – following a scent – is still allowed. Very occasionally, a fox will run out when they’re on the chase, and the dogs will chase it, but not with our hunt – my wife is master of the hounds.JoeI asked Phill if I could come along and see what happens. I don’t have my own horse, or any dogs – perhaps he will lend me some.View image in fullscreenFor aftersPhillWe agreed immigration is necessary, but disagreed on the type of immigration. I think it should be stopped for the time being so we sit back and look what’s happening to the country; then, if needed, start opening it up again but with the right people who are going to do something for the country rather than take, take, take.JoeWe agreed it wasn’t good to have people coming on small boats, but for me it was more about danger and money going to people traffickers. They are a small minority, and I feel he generalised from those people to the larger immigrant population. I would agree there are some bad immigrants, and he agrees there are some good ones. We didn’t discuss whether I was a good immigrant.View image in fullscreenTakeawaysPhillJoe wasn’t how I was expecting a mad lefty to be – he’s well mannered, a family man, a decent chap.Dining across the divide: ‘I worry the England flag is seen as racist – even at the World Cup’Read moreJoePhill didn’t change my mind about anything, but he is a great person – interesting, personable, charming. Because I’d parked further away, he gave me a lift to my car.View image in fullscreenAdditional reporting: Kitty DrakeJoe and Phill ate atMitr in Royston, HertfordshireWant to meet someone from across the divide?Find out how to take partExplore more on these topicsLife and styleDining across the divideSocial trendsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Britain could face food shortages as drought continues, farmers warn | Farming | The Guardian
description: Farmers battle to salvage what they can of their crops as heatwave set to continue
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Farmers battle to salvage what they can of their crops as heatwave set to continue
Content: ‘Across much of the UK, combines have been rolling earlier than usual this year.’Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAView image in fullscreen‘Across much of the UK, combines have been rolling earlier than usual this year.’Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAFarmingBritain could face food shortages as drought continues, farmers warnFarmers battle to salvage what they can of their crops as heatwave set to continueHelena HortonSun 2 Aug 2026 12.54 EDTFirst published on Sun 2 Aug 2026 11.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain could face shortages of certain foods after punishing drought in parts of England, the National Farmers’ Union (NFU) has warned as a heatwave was forecast to continue into next week.The UK’s Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has issued heat health alerts for eight regions of England, with temperatures set to rise above 30C in parts of the country. UKHSA said rising temperatures may increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.Farms across the country were affected by floods over the winter, making planting extremely difficult, and now in many areas they do not have access to water as irrigation is being restricted due to drought.Drought mapIt is the third drought in five years and farming groups say this is the new normal for agriculture in Britain. Wheat farmers say their crop is half its normal height, and England is seeing its earliest ever harvest as farmers battle to salvage what they can of their produce.In some areas it has not rained for over a month, while multiple record-breaking heatwaves have hit the country since early summer, drying out the soil.Tom Bradshaw, the NFU president, said this could lead to food shortages and he had asked the prime minister to take action. He told BBC Radio 4 that farmers should be given tax breaks to build water storage systems on their land to prepare for the years ahead.“Those other countries around the world that we currently rely on to produce our food and vegetables, their climates are changing as well,” he said. “It does feel like there is going be some shortages of [food] products.”Climate breakdown is exacerbating extreme weather conditions such as droughts. This summer the Met Office has reported that England had just 8% of its average rainfall for July and it is likely to be confirmed as the driest July on record.About 23 million people across England and Wales areunder a hosepipe ban. The dry weather has fuelled devastating wildfires across the country,most recently in Suffolk.UKHSA has issued amber heat health alerts for the East Midlands, the east of England, the south-east and London regions from 9am on Monday to 9am on Wednesday. The north-west, Yorkshire and the Humber, West Midlands and the south-west regions will be under a yellow alert during the same period.Bradshaw said: “Let’s draw a line in the sand and make sure we prioritise domestic food production to deliver growth across the UK.”Cereals such as wheat and barley have been particularly affected, the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB) said.Its firstharvest report of 2026said the hot weather had resulted in the earliest harvest since records began in 2006, with many farmers across the south and east of England completing harvest two to three weeks ahead of the long-term average.Anthony Hopkins, the AHDB’s director of cereals and oilseeds, said: “Across much of the UK, combines have been rolling earlier than usual this year, with many farmers working through the night to avoid the most extreme daytime temperatures. Cereal yields have generally been below the 10-year average so far, with some farms experiencing significant reductions. Following successive years of difficult weather and rising costs, the financial pressures are becoming increasingly acute for those businesses hardest hit.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA combine harvester cuts corn in a field near Ashford in Kent.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAAnthony Speight, a senior analyst at the AHDB, said: “At this stage, the emerging picture points to disappointing cereal yields in many areas, but we’ll gain a clearer understanding as harvest continues.”Farming is becoming unprofitable as the government removes the EU-derived subsidies that once kept the industry afloat and the climate crisis causes extreme weather that can wipe out any profits from crops. A recent report found a third of British farmers were making a loss or only breaking even.Gavin Lane, the president of the Country, Land and Business Association, warned that for many farmers this could be their last harvest.He said: “Farmers are telling us this is the worst harvest in years. A sodden winter followed by drought has left wheat at half its usual height and some crops not worth harvesting.“This is the third drought in five years. What was once extraordinary is becoming part of farming in Britain, and government must start planning for it. We know that proper government investment in resilient farming systems, from reservoirs to wildfire prevention, could help farmers cope with these new extremes.“Farmers have shown again and again that they can adapt and deliver solutions, but resilience has limits. If we want them to keep feeding the country, they need proper support. Otherwise, this harvest could be their last.”Polly Ashmore, an acting consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said periods of hot weather could result in serious health outcomes, especially for older adults, and it was therefore important that everyone took sensible precautions while enjoying the sun.“We are urging health and social care services in affected regions to ensure they are prepared, and reminding people to look out for elderly relatives, neighbours and those with underlying health conditions, making sure they are aware of the forecast and following the necessary advice,” she said.“Simple steps such as staying hydrated, avoiding the sun during the hottest part of the day and keeping your home cool are some of the key ways to help keep yourself and others safe during periods of hot weather.”Explore more on these topicsFarmingFood & drink industryDroughtClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Chaos of border crossing gives way to limbo for Moroccans on Ceuta’s streets | Spain | The Guardian
description: People among the more than 50,000 who entered Spanish enclave this week describe the journey and their prospects
Author: Okba Mohammad
Headline: People among the more than 50,000 who entered Spanish enclave this week describe the journey and their prospects
Content: People rest on a beach under the supervision of Guardia Civil officers in Ceuta on Saturday.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople rest on a beach under the supervision of Guardia Civil officers in Ceuta on Saturday.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesSpainChaos of border crossing gives way to limbo for Moroccans on Ceuta’s streetsPeople among the more than 50,000 who entered Spanish enclave this week describe the journey and their prospectsOkba Mohammadand Javier Jennings Mozo in CeutaSun 2 Aug 2026 09.11 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour days ago, Youssef El Abbas saw an opportunity to reclaim the life he had lost seven years earlier. News was circulating that about 400 people had swum fromMoroccoto the neighbouring Spanish enclave of Ceuta on the north African coast, approximately 12 miles (19km) across the strait of Gibraltar from mainland Spain.Here was a chance for the 44-year-old Moroccan father of four to return toSpain, from which he had been deported when his residency expired after the loss of his job in Bilbao in 2019.El Abbas took a taxi and headed to the city of Tétouan, south of the enclave. While en route, he saw Facebook posts and news reports claiming that the Moroccan authorities were allowing people to pass through their side of the border. That meant that unlike those who had crossed the previous night, he could simply travel overland before swimming for just five minutes across the border from Moroccan to Spanish territory to avoid the Spanish border controls.View image in fullscreenPeople returning to Morocco on Sunday after crossing into Ceuta.Photograph: Reduan Dris/EPAHe reached Tétouan to find the city completely overwhelmed. “Young men were running through the streets, flooding every corner,” he said. By the time a second taxi took El Abbas to Fnideq, the town bordering Ceuta, he realised that the usual blockades and checkpoints preventing people without European documents from even approaching the frontier had been removed.View image in fullscreenYoussef El Abbas in Ceuta.Photograph: Okba Mohammad“The Moroccan police were shouting at us: ‘Go, go, go! Run now, run into Spain,’” he said. “The night before, they were beating people. But that morning they were letting us through. Nothing made sense.”Despite the crowds, El Abbas noticed the police were only letting Moroccans cross over. “All the sub-Saharan migrants were being pushed back by force.”He reached the border at 2.45pm on Wednesday. By 3pm, after a short swim, he was standing on Spanish soil. Not everyone was so lucky.“In just 10 minutes in the water, I saw four people floating dead in Moroccan waters,” he said. “People were pulling their bodies out.” They were among at least 72 people who drowned or were crushed trying to reach the Spanish territory.El Abbas is just one of the50,000 or so people to have crossed into Ceuta this week, in what Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, described as “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”.Map showing location of Ceuta between Morocco and Spain, and another map showing line of Morocco-Ceuta border and Tarajal breakwaterMadrid has attributed the latest influx to “human-trafficking mafias” that have taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta or Melilla – the other Spanish enclave on the north African coast – could not be summarily returned under special rules.double quotation markThe same hand that helped me out of the water was the one that later hit meYoussef El AbbasBut there has also been speculation that the Moroccan authorities may have opened the border to signal their displeasure at Sánchez’s recent visit to Algeria, which supports efforts to free the disputed territory of Western Sahara from Moroccan occupation.Morocco’s ambassador to Spain, Karima Benyaich Millán, said Rabat was not happy about the mass crossing, adding that it hoped those in Ceuta would return.Moroccan government sourcestold the Europa Press news agencythat the surge of people entering Ceuta was down to “criminal organisations” and insisted that Rabat’s cooperation with Spain remained “exemplary”.In May 2021, Rabat loosened border controls –allowing 10,000 people to cross into Ceuta over the course of two days– during a diplomatic standoff triggered after Madrid allowed a Western Sahara independence leader to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain.View image in fullscreenA man bends down to pick up a pair of shoes from debris washed up on Ceuta’s shore.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersEl Abbas said he had never stopped dreaming of returning to Spain, where he had worked mainly in the hospitality sector for 14 years. Since being deported to Morocco in 2019, he has lived apart from his wife and four daughters, who remain in the northern Spanish city of Bilbao, while scraping by with occasional work repairing mobile phones alongside his father.“I never stopped thinking about coming back,” he said. “In Morocco, I was alive, but I wasn’t really living.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhy is Ceuta a migration flashpoint and how were so many people able to cross from Morocco?Read moreThe return has been bittersweet. When he swam ashore in Ceuta, a Spanish Guardia Civil officer extended a hand to pull him from the sea. But that gesture of aid eventually gave way to one of violence. Three days after arriving, the group of people he was with were surrounded by a military patrol and beaten.“The same hand that helped me out of the water was the one that later hit me,” he said.El Abbas’s story is hardly unique. Although more than 48,000 people had crossed back into Morocco by Friday night, hundreds are still sleeping in parks, public squares and on pavements, waiting for a chance to move on or simply to find somewhere to rest. It appears to be virtually impossible for migrants to leave Ceuta for mainland Spain.Said, 17, from Casablanca, was sitting on a kerb a few hundred metres away. He, too, had joined the Ceuta-bound crowds when he heard that the border was open. But the jubilation had given way to reality and all he had was a bottle of water and the carton of yoghurt a local resident had given him.3:37Tens of thousands of migrants cross into Spanish enclave Ceuta from Morocco - videoThe teenager said he was taken to a centre for unaccompanied minors after he crossed, but there were no places available, so he ended up back on the streets. According to a soldier who asked to remain anonymous, the current protocol for the authorities – including the military, the police and the Guardia Civil – is to treat unaccompanied minors as regular migrants and return them to Morocco.Said and the other teenagers with him said no one would sell them food or allow them into shops and restaurants because they did not speak Spanish.Three days after the mass influx, Ceuta is slowly trying to recover a sense of normality. By early evening on Saturday, cafe terraces were beginning to fill again and some businesses had reopened their doors. Many of the remaining arrivals are being tended to by Ceuta locals, who walk the streets handing out bottles of water, sandwiches, blankets and clothes. Others stop to ask if they need help or to offer to call a relative.Such shows of solidarity have been threatened by the arrival of far-right politicians and a neo-Nazi group, all keen to use the humanitarian crisis for their own ends.“They’re going to exploit our feelings to claim the credit and say they defended Ceuta,” said a local woman called Malika. “We don’t want them here. If they want to defend something, they should go somewhere else.”View image in fullscreenPeople who crossed into Ceuta this week are escorted back to Morocco by the Spanish army on Saturday.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/APMalika, who was born in Ceuta to a soldier who served in the Spanish army, rejected the notion that the city should be defined solely by the political confrontation that followed this week’s mass arrival. But she also acknowledged the pressure on a city of just over 80,000 people. “It would have been an impossible situation for any city,” she said.Fatima Hamed Hossain, a member of Ceuta’s assembly, fears that the strain created by the crisis has deepened divisions within the city. “Everything we’ve lived through has created tensions between neighbours,” she said. “That’s exactly what feeds the far right.”As a caravan of people returned back over the border, Said’s mind was on the future. His goal is simple: get a place in a protection centre, spend the next year learning Spanish and, once he turns 18, find work as a barber. What he fears most is ending up without legal documentation and seeing that plan collapse before it has even begun.Leaving is not on his agenda, however. “All I need,” he said, “is a chance.”Explore more on these topicsSpainMoroccoMigrationAfricaEuropeMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: At least five Mohamed Al Fayed abuse survivors confirmed as human-trafficking victims | Mohamed Al Fayed | The Guardian
description: Decision comes after group of survivors claimed ex-Harrods owner’s associates must have helped facilitate his crimes
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Decision comes after group of survivors claimed ex-Harrods owner’s associates must have helped facilitate his crimes
Content: Officers are looking into who may have facilitated Fayed’s crimes, in an investigation known as Operation Cornpoppy.Photograph: Luke MacGregor/ReutersView image in fullscreenOfficers are looking into who may have facilitated Fayed’s crimes, in an investigation known as Operation Cornpoppy.Photograph: Luke MacGregor/ReutersMohamed Al FayedAt least five Mohamed Al Fayed abuse survivors confirmed as human-trafficking victimsDecision comes after group of survivors claimed ex-Harrods owner’s associates must have helped facilitate his crimesHelena HortonSun 2 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least five victims of the former Harrods ownerMohamed Al Fayedhave been confirmed by the Home Office as victims of human trafficking.A group of survivors of abuse by the deceased businessmanhad called forthe Metropolitan police to make trafficking the main focus of its investigation, arguing that Fayed could not have committed his offences without a steady stream of women sent to him by associates.The women were victims of international and domestic trafficking, and one survivor told the Press Association (PA) they were recruited to a false role withinHarrods. Two further victims were hired for a legitimate role and then selected from the shop floor for abuse. These cases stretch from the 1990s to the most recent, which took place after the 2010 sale of Harrods.Officers are looking into who may have facilitated Fayed’s crimes, in an investigation known as Operation Cornpoppy. Four people have been questioned to date, 21 months after the investigation opened.One survivor, known as Justine, told PA she felt “shellshocked” when she received the conclusive grounds decision in June that she had been a victim of modern slavery.She added: “But it’s a really significant thing, getting that decision, seeing it in writing that you were a victim of modern slavery and trafficking is very … it’s really shocking to read.”Another survivor, Isabella, who worked in the chair’s office at Harrods in 2001, told PA: “He couldn’t have done what he did without Harrods processing women to him and silencing them afterwards. It wasn’t just Harrods, obviously. It was any entity that Fayed owned or had control of. It was his yachts, his aviation business, the Ritz Paris, his properties all over France and Monaco. It went as far as the States and the UAE – anywhere that man touched.”More than 400 allegations of sexual misconduct have been made against Fayed for the period between 1977 and 2014 – including claims of rape, sexual assault, human trafficking, false imprisonment, drugging, physical violence and forced abortions. The Egyptian businessman died in 2023 aged 94, without facing any charges.A woman who said she was sexually assaulted by Fayed previously came forward to say she had been trafficked in Paris on his orders in 2008 before being sent to London to be sexually assaulted by him. Pelham Spong, 40, from South Carolina in the US, said Fayed, who owned the Ritz hotel in Paris, had forcibly kissed her and offered her a salary of€65,000 a year if she slept with him.Victims have previously complained of how theMetropolitan policehave handled the investigations into Fayed’s abuse. The Independent Office for Police Conduct is examining complaints about the force’s handling of allegations between 2018 and 2024.A Harrods spokesperson said: “Harrods supports all survivors in their pursuit of justice and continues to work closely with the Met police on its investigation”.Explore more on these topicsMohamed Al FayedHarrodsRape and sexual assaultSexual harassmentMetropolitan policenewsShareReuse this content

title: Artists, writers and scientists urge UK government to save Jodrell Bank Observatory | Astronomy | The Guardian
description: New Order and Simon Armitage among more than 100 signatories to criticise ‘foolish and shortsighted’ cuts
Author: Geneva Abdul
Headline: New Order and Simon Armitage among more than 100 signatories to criticise ‘foolish and shortsighted’ cuts
Content: Jodrell Bank Observatory includes the Grade I-listed Lovell radio telescope.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJodrell Bank Observatory includes the Grade I-listed Lovell radio telescope.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianAstronomyArtists, writers and scientists urge UK government to save Jodrell Bank ObservatoryNew Order and Simon Armitage among more than 100 signatories to criticise ‘foolish and shortsighted’ cutsGeneva AbdulSun 2 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 100 artists, writers and scientists have called for the UK government to save the “world’s clearest eyes on the sky”, afterfunding for thenetwork of radio telescopes at Jodrell Bank Observatorywas slashed.New Order, the Canadian astronaut Chris Hadfield and the poet laureate,Simon Armitage, are among those calling on the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, to save the deep space observatory which includes the Grade I-listed Lovell telescope, prized by astronomers who study galaxies, star formation and planets beyond the solar system.Last week the observatory’s funder, UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), said it would withdraw funding for the e-Merlin network, the UK’s national radio astronomy facility at Jodrell Bank, when the current agreement ends in March 2028.“We believe that to shut it down to save just £2.8m a year is foolish and shortsighted,” states the letter to Burnham as well as the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the head of UKRI.View image in fullscreenJodrell Bank Observatory in Cheshire is facing closure after government funding for the facility was slashed.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThe letter argues that to close down the home of e-Merlin would be to poke out “some of the world’s clearest eyes on the sky”. The Lovell telescope tracked the Sputnik launch in 1957 and is at the centre of a global project tasked with mapping the first billion years of the universe.Scientists have also called the decision a blow to UK astronomy, with observations at Jodrell Bank in Cheshire due to end completely unless other funding is found. The move threatens 28 jobs at the observatory and will affect nearly 3,000 researchers who work within the facility. Further cuts were announced for dozens of facilities, instruments and projects, which are expected to result in about 800 job losses.The UKRI has an annual budget of nearly £10bn. The drop in funding is the latest in a rolling package of cuts from the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), which it funds. The STFCneeds to make substantial savingsas a result of cost overruns, soaring electricity and staff costs, and high foreign exchange rates for international collaborations.The letter continues: “This beacon of science is more ambitious than ever, with exciting plans already under way that will ensure the UK’s relevance and leadership in the rapidly evolving domain of science exploration and utilisation.”It argues that continued funding of Jodrell Bank, a Unesco world heritage site and the UK’s largest radio telescope, would ensure vital contributions to global safety, including tracking space debris, destructive solar flares, satellites and asteroids.The observatory hosts the new headquarters of the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO), a global project tasked with mapping the first billion years of the universe withsister telescopes in South Africa and Western Australia.The Guardian view on the Lovell telescope: budget cuts to physics are bad science and worse politics | EditorialRead more“Do we really want SKAO discoveries to be announced from a HQ alongside what would be the world’s largest disused radio telescope?” the letter states. “We ask that you find funding for it immediately, so that the unique and essential services it provides can continue without interruption, and so that this important source of national pride and global scientific respect is saved.”Jodrell Bank was among dozens of facilities, instruments and projects hit by cuts last week. The Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began work only last month to capture the largest astronomical survey in history, faces a 20% cut to UK participation. Another telescope, the Next-Generation Transit Survey, which is searching for solar systems similar to Earth’s, received a 45% cut. The UK will also withdraw from the Event Horizon Telescope that allowed astronomers to image the black hole at the heart of the Milky Way.A spokesperson for the STFC previously said the body had “undertaken a rigorous prioritisation process to focus investment on the areas that will deliver the greatest long-term scientific capability, impact and value for the UK”.Explore more on these topicsAstronomySpaceNew OrderSimon ArmitagenewsShareReuse this content

title: Healey’s profiteering warning on food and fuel risks row with retailers | UK cost of living crisis | The Guardian
description: Chancellor says the government wants to prevent shoppers being ‘taken for a ride’ at the pump or till
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Chancellor says the government wants to prevent shoppers being ‘taken for a ride’ at the pump or till
Content: ‘Conflict and uncertainty increases inflation … pushes up costs for businesses and governments alike,’ Healey wrote.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Conflict and uncertainty increases inflation … pushes up costs for businesses and governments alike,’ Healey wrote.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersUK cost of living crisisHealey’s profiteering warning on food and fuel risks row with retailersChancellor says the government wants to prevent shoppers being ‘taken for a ride’ at the pump or tillSarah ButlerSun 2 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTFirst published on Sun 2 Aug 2026 13.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe chancellor,John Healey, has said the government is standing by to prevent the public from “being taken for a ride at the pump or the till” as the Iran war continues to hit prices.While he said there had been “no significant evidence of so-called price gouging” during the crisis, he used a weekend column to tell the big retailers that ministers were “watching closely” for any signs of profiteering.Healey faces a difficult economic balancing act as the energy price shock caused by themonths-long conflictin the Middle East reignites the cost of living crisis.Last week the Bank of Englandkept UK interest rates on holdas it warned that a further escalation in the Iran war could drive inflation above 4% next year, adding to financial pressures on households.Healey’s comments came as a new report warned that UK economy could fall into recession next year if the crucial Strait of Hormuz remains closed into 2027 amid a prolonged conflict.The latest EY economic outlook warned that gross domestic product (GDP) could slow sharply to 0.5% this year and contract by 0.2% next year if the conflict is not resolved and the vital waterway – through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas is normally carried – remains shut until early or mid-2027.On the other hand, if the strait reopens by the end of the third quarter of this year, EY’s base case forecast suggests growth will remain fairly resilient, at 0.9% in 2026 and 1.2% in 2027.“The conflict affects our national security, our UK bases, personnel and allies in the Middle East,” Healey wrote in the Sunday Telegraph. “But it also threatens our economic security: impacting the family finances of millions of British people.“And I know that many British businesses have been put under pressure by increasing costs too. Conflict and uncertainty increases inflation, threatens growth and pushes up costs for businesses and governments alike.”The comments about profiteering threaten a new war of words between the government and retailers. Amid ongoing public concern about the cost of living, it emerged earlier this year that Rachel Reeves, then the chancellor, had raised the prospect of acap on food pricesto limit inflation caused by the Middle East conflict.The proposals prompted a backlash from supermarket bosses, with Stuart Machin, the chief executive of Marks & Spencer, calling the plans“completely preposterous”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe British Retail Consortium suggested on Sunday that the new chancellor should instead be looking at the effect of tax increases, including employers’ national insurance and business rates, on inflation.Andrew Opie, of the British Retail Consortium, which represents big retailers including Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Asda, said: “Supermarkets operate in a highly competitive environment, delivering the most affordable food in western Europe.“The government’s independent competition regulator, the CMA [Competition and Markets Authority], has repeatedly found that fierce competition between retailers, not government action, has kept food prices as low as possible.”Explore more on these topicsUK cost of living crisisRetail industryPetrol pricesEnergy billsHousehold billsJohn HealeyLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Rupert Lowe urges Nigel Farage to work with Restore Britain | Restore Britain | The Guardian
description: Lowe says the two should put ‘personalities and our past disagreements aside for good of the country’
Author: Morgan Ofori
Headline: Lowe says the two should put ‘personalities and our past disagreements aside for good of the country’
Content: Rupert Lowe told Nigel Farage that if he was ‘prepared to work together around serious policies, serious reform and serious government, then so are we’.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAView image in fullscreenRupert Lowe told Nigel Farage that if he was ‘prepared to work together around serious policies, serious reform and serious government, then so are we’.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PARestore BritainRupert Lowe urges Nigel Farage to work with Restore BritainLowe says the two should put ‘personalities and our past disagreements aside for good of the country’Morgan OforiSun 2 Aug 2026 17.05 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe leader ofRestore Britain, Rupert Lowe, has extended an olive branch to Nigel Farage, saying the two should put “personalities and our past disagreements aside for the good of the country”.Lowe told theReform UKleader that if he was “prepared to work together around serious policies, serious reform and serious government, then so are we”.In a video posted on X, Lowe said: “I truly believe there could be sufficient common ground for our two movements to cooperate collectively, destroy the looming leftwing alliance that will finish off what hope remains for this country.‘Stench of sleaze’: Farage struck deal over political return months before 2024 election, reports sayRead more“In my view, failing to even try because of our own personal difficulties is simply not an option. Now is the time to put our differences aside and cooperate for the good of the country that we all love.”The offer comes after Restore Britain placed fourth in the Greater Manchester mayoral byelection, where its candidate, Marlon West, took 8.7% of the vote. Reform’s Sian Astley came second on 21%, behind Labour’s Andy Burnham’s successor, Bev Craig.Lowe was among five Reform MPs who entered parliament for the first time in the 2024 general election, representing the constituency of Great Yarmouth.The leader of Restore Britain was suspended in March 2025, whenaccusations emergedthat he had bullied staff and threatened chair Zia Yusuf, claims Lowe denied.Lowefounded Restore Britainin February with backing from Elon Musk.Lowe asked Farage to put “personalities and our past disagreements aside” and he set five conditions for cooperation:Mass deportation of illegal migrants “including women and children”.Tougher rules on legal migration, a ban on halal and kosher slaughter, the burqa, cousin marriage and sharia courts.A referendum on the death penalty.Welfare cuts to fund “self-sufficiency”.The exclusion of former Tory ministers from any future cabinet.“Mass deportations must become a political inevitability,” he said. “They must all go.”He cited Reform and Restore’s cooperation on Norfolk county council as proof cross-party working can succeed nationally.Farage framed the next election as “an existential fight to save the country” and said Reform would need support beyond its own ranks to win.The tangled financial web at the heart of Reform UKRead more“I understand Reform UK will need the support of people from other parties, as well as millions who have never voted before,” he wrote in a post on X. “That is the broad coalition I am building.”He added that Reform has “always been open to anyone” who shares its aims on borders, the economy and democracy, but added: “I will never turn my back on my team.”Farage is fighting a byelection after resigning his seat of Clacton. All other mainstream parties have declined to stand a candidate against him, though there are 34 independents on the ballot paper, including novelty candidates such as Count Binface.Explore more on these topicsRestore BritainReform UKNigel FarageRupert LowenewsShareReuse this content

title: Pressure on Gianni Infantino increases as Uefa members prepare to oppose re-election | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: European nations are to withdraw letters of support for Gianni Infantino, with an appetite to ensure the Fifa president is quickly removed from his post
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: European nations are to withdraw letters of support for Gianni Infantino, with an appetite to ensure the Fifa president is quickly removed from his post
Content: Gianni Infantino’s reign is in severe peril after the collapse of his privately backed scheme to sell off chunks of the World Cup.Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPAView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino’s reign is in severe peril after the collapse of his privately backed scheme to sell off chunks of the World Cup.Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPAGianni InfantinoPressure on Gianni Infantino increases as Uefa members prepare to oppose re-electionEuropean nations to withdraw letters of support for Fifa presidentAppetite to ensure Infantino is quickly removed from postExclusive byNick AmesandMatt HughesSun 2 Aug 2026 15.36 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEuropean countries are planning to increase the pressure onGianni Infantinowith a mass withdrawal of letters supporting his re-election as Fifa president.Infantino’s reign is in severe peril after the collapse of his privately backed scheme to sell off chunks of the World Cup, which was largely scuppered when Uefa member associationsthreatened to boycott future Fifa competitions. The mood remains febrile and there is a widespread appetite around Europe to ensure that he is quickly removed from his post.Gianni Infantino could face leadership challenge as Fifa council members rebelRead moreNow a groundswell of national governing bodies are discussing the formal withdrawal of their support for Infantino in a bid to hasten his resignation, with announcements likely in the coming days. Before last week’s crisis unfolded all of Uefa’s 55 members apart from Germany, Romania and Norway had written letters to endorse Infantino’s candidature next March, with a fourth term for the Swiss viewed as a fait accompli.A simultaneous withdrawal has been mooted but there is also the possibility member associations could remove their backing one by one. Doing so would effectively amount to a vote of no confidence and increase the pressure on Infantino to resign.Fifamust be notified by any country wishing to recall their letter.Discussions continue with countries in other confederations. Despite the failure of his Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, a number of countries in the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) publicly backed Infantino over the weekend. Sources within European football have questioned whether those federations have been made fully aware of the level of ­dissent facing Infantino.After the financial powerhouse of Qatar backed Infantino on Saturday, smaller Asian associations Sri Lanka and Kuwait offered their public ­support on Sunday. The AFC rarely votes en masse however, and it is possible that some associations unhappy with Infantino could rally to the European cause.As the Guardian revealed in July, more than 200 of Fifa’s 211 members have provided letters of endorsement for Infantino. Fifa is understood to have applied heavy pressure upon those wavering even though his tenure did not appear endangered at the time. Many backed him despite privately offering misgivings about his presidency but, in Europe and beyond, patience has run out.Efforts to identify a candidate to replace Infantino are being stepped up. Anyone put forward for the election would require significant levels of support outside Europe, particularly from the AFC and the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation, Concacaf. Gathering quickly around a suitable contender could be key to persuading Infantino that his position is untenable.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionInfantino appears determined to stay on, and is believed to be ­lobbying individual member associations across the globe to ensure he retains their support. Both the ­Confederation of African Football and the South American confederation, Conmebol, are fully behind Infantino however, leaving Asia and North America as the crucial battlegrounds as Uefa members seek a new leadership at Fifa.Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoFifaUefaWorld CupFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to be ‘relentless’ on small boat crossings after Ceuta crisis | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Prime minister says UK needs to ‘bring back that control’ and safe routes for refugees are necessary to tackle trafficking
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Prime minister says UK needs to ‘bring back that control’ and safe routes for refugees are necessary to tackle trafficking
Content: Andy Burnham promises to be relentless in tackling small boat crossings – videoImmigration and asylumBurnham to be ‘relentless’ on small boat crossings after Ceuta crisisPrime minister says UK needs to ‘bring back that control’ and safe routes for refugees are necessary to tackle traffickingAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentSun 2 Aug 2026 14.16 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has pledged to be “relentless” in tackling small boat crossings aftertens of thousands of migrants enteredthe Spanish territory of Ceuta, and he said “safe routes” for refugees were necessary to tackle trafficking gangs.Speaking during a visit to Dover, the prime minister said he had been assured by the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, that approximately 98% of the estimated 50,000 people who entered Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta last week had now been returned to Morocco.But while that dealt “substantially” with the immediate issue, “of course there’s a broader issue about the Schengen area and our relationship with it”, he said, adding: “I would want to be in regular dialogue with the EU on those issues”.Asked if he wanted to change the tone of the debate on the issue by stressing the need for safe routes, he said the UK had to “deal with the issue rather than play politics with the issue” and make changes that would reassure the public.“The public don’t like the idea that the border looks like it’s not controlled.
