We need to bring back that control, but also we need to offer support for people who genuinely need it,” he said. “It’s about changing the whole approach, and slowly but surely we are putting in place those building blocks of a very different approach to this issue.”Last Wednesday was the busiest day for small boat crossings across the Channel so far this year, with 752 people arriving in the UK. Official provisional figures suggest 14,526 have entered the UK so far this year. This is 43% lower than the number recorded by this time last year (25,436) and down 14% on the same period in 2024 (16,903).“Progress is being made but we’re not complacent,” Burnham said. He said the number of National Crime Agency officers tackling organised immigration crime had more than doubled since the start of 2025, from 376 to almost 800.On Sunday the latest figures showed that more than 2,000 people had crossed the Channel in small boats since Burnham became prime minister. Home Office numbers showed 326 people arrived on Saturday in four boats, bringing the number up to 2,057 since he took over from Keir Starmer on 20 July. There were 1,962 crossings in the same period last year.On a separate visit to the National Crime Agency headquarters in Stratford, Shabana Mahmood said the government’s work to tackle small boat crossings were beginning to “bear fruit”.The home secretary has faced fierce opposition within the ranks of the Labour party over proposedimmigration measuresincluding doubling the time it takes to qualify for indefinite leave to remain from five to 10 years. But she said reform was needed “to address the pull factors that draw people into boats in the Channel”, adding: “I want to change the calculus. I want them to change their mind about whether they get on the boat in the first place.”She rejected calls to copy Spain’s response to the influx into Ceuta, in which tens of thousands of people have been returned to Morocco without processing any asylum claims. That was possible because Morocco and Spain share a land border and have an agreement in place. Mahmood said people smuggling and the shared waters of the Channel made things “trickier in many ways”.At least 72 people died trying to reach Ceuta, some of them drowning and others being crushed when attempting to climb the border fence.Sánchezcalled the huge influx “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”. The surge of people, which took place over the course of just 24 hours from Thursday, overwhelmed the city of 85,000 people, triggered a political crisis for Madrid and led to an angry reaction from some EU countries, including calls forSpainto be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.On Saturday, Spanish police installed a 500-metre (1,640ft) floating barrier off its border ‌with Morocco to prevent others from making their way around the border. But Spain’s leftwing government has continued to come under pressure from right and centre-right governments already angry at its plan toregularise about 500,000 immigrants living in Spain.EU ministers haveconvened emergency talks for Tuesday. The leaders of 22 EU countries have demanded an emergency response, citing the need to prevent further uncontrolled crossings. The summit was called during a “sobering” meeting of officials representing EU member states and Frontex border agency experts on Saturday, as EU leaders sought to heal divisions in the bloc and restore a unified approach to migration.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumAndy BurnhamLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Tiger mum’ Lucy Powell on Labour’s vocational skills drive: ‘It’s about ambition for everybody’ | Lucy Powell | The Guardian
description: New education secretary says it is ‘false trade-off’ by critics to suggest schools cannot pursue academic excellence alongside technical skills
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: New education secretary says it is ‘false trade-off’ by critics to suggest schools cannot pursue academic excellence alongside technical skills
Content: Lucy Powell: ‘I absolutely don’t want schools to dumb down.’Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLucy Powell: ‘I absolutely don’t want schools to dumb down.’Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianLucy PowellInterview‘Tiger mum’ Lucy Powell on Labour’s vocational skills drive: ‘It’s about ambition for everybody’Pippa Crerar, political editorNew education secretary says it is ‘false trade-off’ by critics to suggest schools cannot pursue academic excellence alongside technical skillsSun 2 Aug 2026 09.58 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLucy Powell has said she wants to be an ambitious “tiger mum” for all young people, whatever their route through education, after the government was accused of dumbing down England’s schools with plans to create more vocational routes.The new education secretary said secondary pupils should be able to pursue academic excellence as well as high-quality vocational training, and it was a “false trade-off” to suggest schools could not provide both.In an interview with the Guardian, Powell said she did not have “lower ambition” for those children following technical routes, and her critics – includingMichael Gove, the former Tory education secretary – should recognise that their approach had left too many behind.Andy Burnhamtold schoolsacross England this week to adapt their curriculums to the needs of local businesses, as part of a drive to make technical and vocational skills as valued as academic qualifications and help tackle the jobs crisis for young people.Powell said: “I absolutely don’t want schools to dumb down. My kids might say I’m a tiger mum. You know, I’m a tiger mum for all our kids – every single child that’s in our education system achieving excellence, achieving what they can do.”Powell said those arguing against a focus on vocational education were making a “false trade-off” by framing Labour’s plans as a choice between knowledge and skills. “What I’m not going to oversee is some kind of lower ambition for some kids. It’s about ambition for everybody.”Most of the criticism of her approach has come from Tory politicians who oversaw the system for years. “They have to take some responsibility for creating … a system that has left over a million young people now not in education, training or employment. The current approach has left too many behind,” Powell said.However, she acknowledged that headteachers were concerned about extra pressure on their budgets to provide vocational routes, saying she was “very conscious” of school funding, which took a hit during the austerity years. She insisted any specific new proposals would be fully funded.With many teachers struggling, and strikes potentially looming, Powell said she wanted a constructive relationship with the unions, and the government was already making changes to help ease the pressure. “What I’ll say to teachers is ‘work with me’,” she said.Powell has been under pressure since she took over the brief to row back on plans made by her predecessor, Bridget Phillipson, to overhaul the special educational needs and disabilities system (Send), in particular limiting education, health and care plans (EHCP) to pupils with the “most complex needs”.Powell signalled that she would stick to the plans, while accepting that the issue was creating worry and anxiety for many parents. “We can reassure them, because this is about tilting the system so that you don’t have to fight tooth and nail. That you get much earlier help,” she said.Pressed on Labour’s election pledge to recruit 6,500 teachers, which has since been watered down, she suggested the government was doing well against a lower target, and that a sharp drop in primary numbers reflected falling rolls in schools.Asked about private schools, Powell took a less adversarial approach than her predecessor, saying it was up to parents to make their own decisions about where they sent their children. “I’m not here to worry about private schools. I’m here to worry about state schools,” she said.View image in fullscreenPowell sits next to Andy Burnham during his first cabinet meeting as prime minister.Photograph: Chris Ratcliffe/EPAPowell added that she would be spending a significant amount of time at the No 10 North outpost in her central Manchester constituency. The DfE’s third biggest office, housing 1,100 civil servants, is also based in the city.She batted away suggestions she was unhappy not to have been appointed deputy prime minister by Burnham, saying they had agreed she would continue to play a central role in Labour’s political direction as education secretary.There had been no purge of the Starmerites, she added, saying the new cabinet was representative of people from across the party, and that, in contrast, the last cabinet had been too narrow. “That was one of the issues for Keir towards the end. His government wasn’t necessarily one of all the traditions.”Powell also criticised Starmer’s government for focusing too much on the Reform threat rather than Labour’s own plan for the country. “What most people wanted to know was not what we thought about other political parties, but what were we doing? What were we about? What has been refreshing over the last week or two, is being on the front foot. Every day you’re on the front foot is a day you’re winning.”She insisted that despite multiple spending pledges in Burnham’s first fortnight in office, all policy announcements were funded, with the prime minister and his chancellor, John Healey, “quite prudent and careful” about this.Explore more on these topicsLucy PowellEducation policyDepartment for EducationSchoolsLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Kindness of strangers: When we were lost in the Thai rainforest, a fellow backpacker picked me up and carried me home | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: For hours we hobbled back, until we were close enough for him to place me down and run for help
Author: Katie Cunningham
Headline: For hours we hobbled back, until we were close enough for him to place me down and run for help
Content: ‘It was on the way back that things began to go wrong. Within minutes of setting off, I started tripping over my own feet.’Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian Design/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘It was on the way back that things began to go wrong. Within minutes of setting off, I started tripping over my own feet.’Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian Design/AlamyKindness of strangersAustralian lifestyleKindness of strangers: When we were lost in the Thai rainforest, a fellow backpacker picked me up and carried me homeFor hours we hobbled back, until we were close enough for him to place me down and run for helpRead more inthe kindness of strangers seriesAnkit Rao as told toKatie CunninghamSun 2 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 20.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe had heard there was an incredible waterfall somewhere deep in the Thai rainforest. Seeking it out almost killed me.In 2003 I was travelling solo through south-eastAsiawhen I met Paul, an American with an easy-going, natural warmth. We were the only two people bunking at a youth hostel somewhere in southern Thailand and got chatting one morning. When the staff told us about a beautiful waterfall not far from where we were staying, we made plans to hike there together.It was only meant to be an hour’s walk away. Thinking we would be back in time for lunch, we didn’t bother to take any food with us. Big mistake.For four hours we walked through dense foliage, even climbing down vines in search of this supposed waterfall. At many points it occurred to us that we might be lost, but the naivety of youth propelled us forward. Eventually, the forest opened up to reveal a glistening pool of water with a waterfall at one end. We jumped in and laughed at how the trek had taken us four times as long as expected.The kindness of strangers: When Mum was hospitalised on a family holiday, our hotel’s owners were heaven-sentRead moreIt was on the way back that things began to go wrong. Within minutes of setting off, I started tripping over my own feet. Then I became confused and unable to answer simple questions. In hindsight, I was clearly starving and dehydrated. But at the time I did not understand what was happening to me.That was when Paul did something unexpected. He put my arm over his shoulder, lifted me up and started to carry me back through the forest. When he could go on no longer, we stopped while he dug through my bag, found some old sugar and salt sachets, and whipped me up a makeshift rehydration elixir. It gave me enough strength to walk on my own.For hours we hobbled back, Paul leading the way and cheering me on. Close to the hostel, I slipped on a loose rock and badly twisted my ankle. Paul again picked me up and carried me until we were close enough for him to place me down and run for help. He returned a short while later on the back of a motorcycle, before I was transported the remaining distance home. Paul walked back alone.Paul left the next day and I never saw him again. But I’ll always remember how a kind young man I had met only a few hours earlier wrapped his arms around me, picked me up and quite literally carried me home. Did he save my life that day? I would say so.What is the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?Share your experienceWhat's the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.What is your name?Where do you live (city, state and country)?Tell us a bit about the kind act you've experienced?Where and when did this encounter take place?Can we publish your response?Yes, entirelyYes, but contact me firstYes, but please keep me anonymousNo, this is information onlyAre you comfortable with a journalist contacting you about this story for potential publication?YesNoWhat is your phone number?OptionalYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.What is your email addressYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.Would you be interested in speaking to our audio and/or video teams?Audio onlyVideo onlyAudio and videoNo, I'm not interestedBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreExplore more on these topicsAustralian lifestyleKindness of strangersThailand holidaysAsiaBackpacking holidaysWalkingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Attack of the birthdayzillas: the people turning their big days into epic events – at huge cost to their guests | Life and style | The Guardian
description: First it was weddings. Now, going overboard on birthdays, planning murder-mystery breaks or mini-festivals with dress codes and branded merch, is the norm for many. Is this driven by monster egos, or a search for connection in a fractured age?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: First it was weddings. Now, going overboard on birthdays, planning murder-mystery breaks or mini-festivals with dress codes and branded merch, is the norm for many. Is this driven by monster egos, or a search for connection in a fractured age?
Content: Illustration: Belicta CastelbarcoLife and styleAttack of the birthdayzillas: the people turning their big days into epic events – at huge cost to their guestsFirst it was weddings. Now, going overboard on birthdays, planning murder-mystery breaks or mini-festivals with dress codes and branded merch, is the norm for many. Is this driven by monster egos, or a search for connection in a fractured age?Meena AlexanderSun 2 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMikeFest takes place every year, over the August bank holiday weekend, in a large leafy garden on the Cornish coast. Birthday boy Michael’s nearest and dearest turn up in their sparkliest gear (as per the invitation) with tents tucked under their arms. Masks with his face printed on them are handed out, as are handheld fans and sippy cups branded with each guest’s name. Organised fun ensues, including a compulsory talent show. Michael always wins first place with his interpretive dance routine.Michael is not turning 10; he is about to be 44. And he accepts the title of “birthdayzilla”, admitting that he’s guilt-tripped friends who were unable to make it and barred those who miss two festivals in a row from future events. But he’s quick to defend his fellow birthday fanatics. “It doesn’t feel like there’s much to celebrate these days, and it’s harder than ever to get people together. So yes, I’m militant about my birthday,” he says. “I just think: I’ve managed to build a life I like and a network of people I love, why not make a fuss about it? I don’t think expecting them to show up for me once a year is such a big ask.”While you may still be on the waitlist for a ticket to MikeFest, I’m sure you’ve noticed the ballooning of birthday culture. Perhaps you were added to a group chat against your will, its title crowded with cake emojis. Maybe a save-the-date arrived on creamy card bearing only one name in cursive font. Adult birthday celebrations are getting bigger, splashier and heavier with meaning, now jostling with weddings for a place at the pinnacle of our social calendars. Since when did they become such a big deal?Where once a slice of cake sufficed to ring in a new age, today it’s not unusual to throw a fully catered party, rope your friends into a series of activities or organise a group holiday abroad. Lauren, a 29-year-old from Edinburgh, has already run through her annual leave allowance. “I’ve been to eight 30ths this year and the most low-key was a dinner in a private room that still set me back £100,” she says. “I’ve been to a castle in Scotland for a murder mystery weekend; a house party where we all took part in a quizshow about the birthday girl; a weekend of live music in Marseille; and a night out involving a salsa lesson and karaoke. It is draining my bank account, but once you say yes to one friend’s birthday it feels very loaded to say no to another. And you start to feel you deserve payback, so you plan your own huge thing and become part of the problem.”View image in fullscreenOyinda’s 30th birthday sippy cups, branded with each guest’s name and ‘Mykonos 2024’.Photograph: courtesy of OyindaLauren has witnessed first-hand how quickly a birthday can breed a tyrant. One of her friendships is hanging by a thread after an old schoolmate berated her for announcing she was pregnant during their “birthday month”. “There’s something to be said about the main-character energy of my generation – we are all the stars of our social profiles, and we all like a bit of attention – but I think we’re losing the plot,” she says. “Not all of these big birthdays are about optics, but a lot of them are, and that’s when the time and expense of being a guest starts to grate.”Birthdays are highly emotive because they act as mirrors. As American historian Howard P Chudacoff wrote in his 1989 book How Old Are You?, they “provide a milestone by which individuals can compare their status, accomplishment and appearance with other people who are the same age. It’s kind of like a train: are you ahead of time, on time or behind time?” For some, they’re a day to get through as quietly as possible, while others see them as a life-affirming moment to gather all their people around them. There seems to be a gender divide: according toa YouGov poll, women are twice as likely as men to see a big birthday as a chance to celebrate. Michael (of MikeFest fame) wonders if this is linked to “the outdated sense that organising a party or openly asking for what you need” – namely, some company on your special day – “is inherently unmasculine”. But the clearest distinction runs along generational lines, with people in their 20s, 30s and 40s being much more likely to treat their birthday as a major event.For this generation, the traditional milestones that once clustered around this time of life have become less attainable – and in some cases, desirable. The latestONS datashows that the number of people getting married in England and Wales continues to fall year on year, and among those who do get married, the median age is at historic highs of 34.8 for men and 33 for women. Last year, the birthrate was at its lowest since 1977 and the average age of a first-time homeowner climbed to 34. There are many reasons, from political failings to the tectonic plates of our culture shifting beneath our feet, but the common denominator is financial squeeze.Oyinda sent save-the-dates almost a year in advance for her 30th: four days in Mykonos that she wanted to treat “like a wedding”. Her guests arrived at a villa decorated with her childhood photos and were given personalised gift bags and a printed itinerary including a meal made by a private chef, a boat trip and several beach clubs, all of which she saved up to subsidise. “Growing up, I thought I’d have reached lots of milestones by 30, but for people my age things like getting married and buying a house requirea lotof money,” she says. “We still want to lean into life experiences and be celebrated even when we may not achieve those things. I wanted to go all out for my 30thand be as extra as I could be, to celebrate how much I’ve grown as a person and the friends I’ve made over three decades.”View image in fullscreenKrisha and friends in the Dominican Republic for a week-long birthday celebration.Photograph: Manish AroraKrisha, who flew to the Dominican Republic for a week of hiking, safaris, horse riding and massages to mark a new friend’s birthday, feels similarly – why not “spend on a bucket-list experience” in a time when saving for a house deposit feels futile? She also flags the double standards when you’re rallying around one person versus a couple. “I find it interesting that when I tell people I flew across the world for a birthday party they say it’s insane, but when it’s for a wedding they don’t question it.”Where people put their money is changing, but what about when you can’t afford it full stop? Polly from the Midlands felt backed into a corner by her friend’s many invitations, which came to feel like a referendum on their relationship. “She had several events planned for her 40th, ranging from a trip to Portugal to smaller pub gatherings. She wanted to stretch things out across the year, but it came with a lot of friend guilt for me,” Polly says. “I really struggled to tell her that I couldn’t afford that much. I had a lot of anxiety trying to think of my wording and excuse. I feel as if I’ve now been put in a different tier to her other friends who earn high salaries – I can always tell now that the ‘no pressure’ comments are targeted at me and I feel like the poor friend holding back the group.”She and the birthday girl have known each other for a long time, but the different value they each place on birthdays has given Polly pause. “I love to see my friend having fun, celebrating herself and living her best life, but it’s quite excessive just for a birthday,” she says. “To me, age and numbers are arbitrary and I prefer to celebrate achievements or special occasions: engagements, weddings, promotions, babies. Personally, I’d always choose to keep things small. An evening laughing over wine, a perfectly picked card – those are more than enough.”Although there’s evidence of pharaohs putting on feasts in ancient Egypt, the adult birthday party is a relatively recent phenomenon, picking up steam in the west around the 1900s as a way for wealthy people to show off their social standing. Anna Goldfarb, friendship expert and author of Modern Friendship: How to Nurture Our Most Valued Connections,says commercial venues have played a role in making showy celebrations mainstream. “Most of our grandparents would have spent their birthday with family at home, but in the 70s and 80s suburban businesses like cinemas and fast-food chains started offering kids’ parties as a way to drum up profit,” she says. “Those kids grew up with the idea that a birthday equals a big gathering where you get all this attention. Huge parts of pop culture, like MTV’s My Super Sweet 16, have only added to the feeling that you should get to be a prince or princess for a day.” Many cultures’ coming-of-age traditions have come to be associated with big parties, from bar- and batmitzvahs to quinceañeras.Of course, adding social media to the mix has been like dousing a fire with petrol. We see how thousands of other people – including the ultra-rich and terminally attention-hungry – are celebrating themselves and our visions of a low-key picnic in the park start to wilt. The baseline of normal gets skewed by Dua Lipa dancing on a chartered yacht for her 30th, or Kris Jenner being serenaded by Bruno Mars at 70. Even for those of us who aren’t millionaires, the visibility of being online ups the ante on a day that can already feel like a litmus test for how loved we are.“I have seen adults have full meltdowns, and they’re not bad people, they’ve just got these very set ideas of how the day should go,” says Tom, a photographer based in Brighton. “Recently I was hired to work a party and the person redid their entrance three times, because the crowd wasn’t screaming loudly enough. She actually grabbed a microphone to shout at her friends and family: ‘That will look shit on TikTok, do it again.’”The behaviour of some birthday divas can cause lasting reputational damage. Oliver’s cousin wanted her garden party to look perfect, but her preoccupation with perception rubbed him up the wrong way. “She had quite a specific dress code: she wanted everyone to dress in an outfit inspired by her, because she’s had many wild fashion eras. But the week before the party she became this monster on WhatsApp, demanding to see pictures of everyone’s outfits and giving us notes,” he says.double quotation markPeople are having more elaborate events to recreate that feeling of interconnected community. To have the friend from school meet the colleague, or the cousin meet the partnerView image in fullscreenBirthday hiking in the Dominican Republic.Photograph: Manish Arora“Things got worse the day before, when she sent this long message saying that the expense of hiring a marquee and decorations and huge floral arrangements was higher than she’d realised, and could we all bring £50 in cash to chip in. It was the tackiest thing, and it put people in a bad mood. But you wouldn’t know it from all the staged photos of us laughing and nursing the one watery cocktail we were handed. The whole thing just left a bad taste because it was like she cared more about pulling off this Pinterest board vision than actually spending time with us.”Even when you’re not modelling your event on the Met Gala, a mismatch between expectation and reality still stings. Amina, who was raised in a family “that didn’t really do Christmas but always made a big deal of birthdays”, invited 100 people to a London park to play games and ring in her 30th. When the forecast said rain, she moved it indoors to a bar – and only 10 people showed up. “I didn’t want the people who were there to think I was ungrateful or a brat, but they could tell I was hurt. I don’t want to need other people’s validation to feel good on my birthday, but it made me spiral about why my friends jumped at the chance to flake out.”On reflection, Amina realised that “some people just don’t register birthdays the way I do. I was really upset with one of my close friends who turned up hours late and couldn’t even remember my age. Then I recalled the time when I’d just got home from backpacking, had zero money in my account, and was sitting doing some work in a cafe. The waiter brought over chai and a samosa and said that same friendhad called up and had it sent over. They’ve shown me care in other ways, so maybe it doesn’t make sense to judge our whole friendship on one day.”Goldfarb believes that the weight we’re putting on birthdays now tracks with a wider sociological trend around how we relate to one another. “Friendships used to be based on favours and context – something that researchers call ‘social identity support’. Your friends were all people who lived nearby, knew your family and would come through for you in a pinch,” she says. “But now we tend to outsource favours: we call an Uber to pick us up from the airport or hire someone to look after our cat. Our friendships are based more around entertainment and pleasure, so the group trip or party becomes the focal point. Plus, we move around a lot more. We can have friends who know nothing about where we grew up or what we’re like at home, and we crave the context that deepens those bonds.”double quotation markIt’s my chance to celebrate the achievements of the last 40 years, to have the people who’ve championed me in the room, and to say thank youThis is why, even if you’re not usually the type to covet the limelight or love socialising in large groups, you may still feel the pull to have a birthday that brings all the threads of your life together. “I think people are having more elaborate events to recreate that feeling of interconnected community. To have the friend from school meet the colleague, or the cousin meet the partner, means being recognised for all the roles you play in your life. It makes you feel whole,” says Goldfarb.This rings true for Kejal, who is treating her next birthday as a way to honour the circle she’s gathered around her. “Turning 40 feels different to other birthdays. At this age, I’m crystal clear about who gives me energy, and my friendships are a reflection of who I am,” she says. “What I want most is for the weekend to be about connection, not just a boozy dinner and a hangover. I want us to leave with core memories.”We live in an age where we have less to call our own. Fewer of us have homes we can freely decorate in a style that represents us, and even smaller identity markers such as music and films are streamed, not physically held. Against this backdrop, it makes sense that people are treating their birthdays as an opportunity to express who they are. For Kejal, it’s “my chance to celebrate the achievements of the last 40 years, to have the people who’ve championed me in the room, and to say thank you, properly, in a way that is uniquely me”.For all the tales of smiling extortion and tantrums over RSVPs, the majority of people going big on their birthdays are seeking the same thing: meaningful togetherness. Perhaps the only way to get all the people you love in one place these days is to promise them the time of their lives. Or, at the very least, second place in the talent show.Some names have been changedExplore more on these topicsLife and styleFriendshipSocial etiquetteFamilySocial trendsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Readers reply: What is the true Breakfast of Champions? | Breakfast | The Guardian
description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions chews on how best to start the day – from porridge to champagne, beer and cheesecake …
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions chews on how best to start the day – from porridge to champagne, beer and cheesecake …
Content: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner ….Photograph: Chris Ryan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBreakfast, lunch, and dinner ….Photograph: Chris Ryan/Getty ImagesNotes and queriesBreakfastReaders reply: What is the true Breakfast of Champions?The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions chews on how best to start the day – from porridge to champagne, beer and cheesecake …Read this week’s new question:What do you wish you could buy in vending machines?Sun 2 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheCommonwealth Gamesopened in Glasgow earlier this week. As the athletes limber up and engage in protein-maxxing (or is it carb-maxxing?), getting ready to compete, it made me wonder: what is the best breakfast food, or combination of foods, to set you up in the morning? Not necessarily as a top-tier athlete, but simply as someone who is ready to go out there andwin the day.Tom, Tunbridge WellsSend new questions tonq@theguardian.com.Readers replyOne that stops you feeling hungry until five minutes before lunch.yogainspainSauteed mushrooms with a hint of garlic in fromage frais served on a slice of lightly toasted, freshly baked authentic French baton spread with the very best Normandy butter. Delicious, and truly the breakfast ofchampignons.ThereisnoOwlLast night’s leftover curry, with the sauce fully mixed into the rice so all remains moist, placed within arm’s reach of the bed. For real champions, washed down with brown ale.Jason90Last night’s leftover takeaway curry and abloody caesar. Kill or cure.unclestinkyEgg salad sandwich.Patti Powell, Little Rock, ArkansasSteel-cut oatmeal. Everybody knows that.Jay Robinson, by emailA leader on a residential course for the national professional qualification for headship opened day one with the question: “What is the breakfast of champions?” The answer, apparently, is “feedback”. Twenty years on, it has stuck in my memory.Ben Greene, by emailView image in fullscreenCrumbs! Cheesecake to start the day …Photograph: nomadnes/Getty ImagesChampagne.RBEtutaCheesecake.dfic1999Breakfast isn’t really breakfast unless it’s turkey with all the trimmings.EddieChorepostWasn’t that the favourite saying of Suleiman the Magnificent?bricklayersoptionOnly when he got Hungary.EddieChorepostMicrowaved poached egg (one glass, one teaspoon of water, 35 seconds) on bread, coffee. Puncture the yolk.AlkahestNo breakfast through the morning, then, around lunchtime, a high-fibre, high-protein first meal plus a couple of portions of fruit and some coffee. Leaves a clear head through the morning, then carries you through the afternoon and sets you up for an evening meal.DorkaliciousSame as the lunch and dinner of champions … a bar of chocolate.adogsatonmypizzaFor me, it will always bebircher-style muesli. I like to mix together a bag of frozen berries, a kilo of yoghurt and a few cups of oats in a big Tupperware and keep it in the fridge for breakfast all week.MsUnderstandingA flatmate used to buy two kebabs on the way back from the pub, eat one straight away and keep the other for his breakfast. Salt, fat, carbs, spices – perfect hangover cure.Randomusername222Lester Piggott, the 11-time champion jockey whose struggle with his weight was a feature of his career, breakfasted – so went the mythology – on a cigar and a cough. Not many calories there.NationOfSimianView image in fullscreenBreakfast for sports heroes … cold pizza, warm beer.Photograph: Posed by model; Dmytro Betsenko/Getty ImagesA rollie and a large mug of black coffee.manicstteacherA five-egg omelette cooked with finely diced peppers and onion, accompanied by sauerkraut, kimchi and kombucha. A glass of water and a cup of tea or coffee as preferred. Delicious, and keeps your gut happy.GrasmereGardensCold pizza and warm beer. (For sports hero wannabes the morning after.)DavidGervaisBlack coffee, toast and salty butter. All the major food groups there (starch, fat, salt, caffeine). Might add a smear of honey or jam if I feel like pushing the boat out.SharonHowardView image in fullscreenForget cornflakes … doner kebab, Berlin-style.Photograph: Arnulf Hettrich/imageBroker/ShutterstockPasta or rice with chicken or fish, or scrambled eggs on toast, according to the nutritionist of Spain’s football team. A little soy sauce is permitted.alexitoA mashed sardine mixed with finely chopped onion and balsamic vinegar on a buttered rice cake. Absolutely delicious, though one’s breath leaves a bit to be desired.PatDavisonA poached egg on toasted wholemeal with Marmite, seeds, sourdough with some roasted tomatoes drizzled with olive oil, followed by a large portion of mixed berries with Greek yoghurt, all washed down with sparkling water with half a lemon squeezed into it.ZenthewonderdogView image in fullscreenSumo wrestlers sharing achankomeal after morning training at the Kise sumo stable in Tokyo.Photograph: Mathias Cena/AFP/Getty ImagesBroth (miso and chipotle paste) and noodles, perhaps with frozen peas. Followed by pinot grigio.mathurinA couple of six-minute boiled eggs, a bagel with salmon, cream cheese and capers, a bowl of Weetabix, OJ and coffee. Covers a lot of food groups and fills you up. Twenty-five years or so ago, when I used to drink, my answer was a pint of ice-cold Diet Coke: it used to work wonders in the morning and early afternoon.catchytitledSalad, according to the recent articlein the Guardian.TobermoryNightlifeCoffee, cigarette, spanakopita.Nepthsolem“Sex, breakfast of champions!” is an old chestnut no one seems to have mentioned so far.exlangrandeflaneuseView image in fullscreenNot forgetting the traditional breakfast of champions …Photograph: Posed by models; Westend61/Getty ImagesSurely it depends on the champion. A champion sumo wrestler probably needs a different breakfast from a chess champion.GoldgreenChorizo, the cooked salami-style one, sliced lengthways into fairly thin rashers, cooked slowly so the spiced fat runs, eaten dunked into the yolk of an egg fried in the fat. Some buttered toast would be good here, too.The waitress inKurt Vonnegut’s novel Breakfast of Champions says “breakfast of champions” to every customer she serves a martini to. There must be something in that.adamcgfPorridge made with water, plus a dollop of full-fat Greek yoghurt, sprinkled with a nutty granola or mixed seeds. Or both. Not enough to weigh you down, but keeps you going till lunch and great for the gut.SpockleView image in fullscreenPopular choice … can you top porridge?Photograph: NataBene/Getty ImagesScrambled egg, served with diced tomatoes on the side, lasts me till lunchtime without any initial over-full sensation. Some chives are a nice addition, if I have them.nigeljonesLonger term, the best strategy to win at life may be to skip conventional breakfasts completely. Athletes have all sorts of reasons for specialised diets, but there is increasing evidence that staying healthy into later life might mean restricting the hours we eat.Restricted eating hours may reduce cognitive decline in older age, researchers findRead moreThe scale of trials is small so far, but it appears that eating meals over eight to nine hours has advantages in reducing the incidence of dementia compared with the same food intake over 12 hours. The basic regime started with healthy foods and reducing intake by500 calories a day, but adding a shorter eating period came out ahead.The studies effectively meanteating meals between 10am and 6pm. The findings may well be linked to the fact that our metabolism responds more effectively to food around the middle of our waking day than it does at the extremes.For example: “The body releases the most insulin – the hormone that helps move sugar from blood into cells – from 12-6pm, and the lowest during sleep.” There’s a whole body of evidence that the more recent trends of extended snacking over 14 hours or more is one of the worst possible ways toorganise your food intake– with a whole heap of factors that are probably contributing to that.leadballoonBut does it have to be in the morning? I felt best when my schedule supported intermittent fasting, but for me something like 7am to 4.30pm. I can’t sleep on a full stomach and love waking up ravenous.bitthebeatMy platonic ideal of breakfast consists of plain, high-protein Greek yoghurt, berries or other fruit and a sprinkle of muesli. The protein keeps me full, the muesli gives good mouthfeel and the berries are high in flavour and antioxidants. This breakfast never bores me (ooh, pomegranate pips today!). I have been eating this every workday for over 10 years. Perhaps thanks to all of the antioxidants, I’m not dead yet.Rebekah Zinn, Olympia, WashingtonView image in fullscreenMartini … as served in Kurt Vonnegut’s 1973 satirical novel Breakfast of Champions.Photograph: Posed by model; Lighthouse Films/Getty ImagesThe true Breakfast of Champions is by Kurt Vonnegut Jr. Alternatively, good black Mexican coffee. Huevos rancheros with fried bananas and frijoles de olla.Buen díato you all!Gerardo Martinez Casas, Mérida, MéxicoI’ve radically changed my eating patterns over the last six months and breakfast has changed more than anything else. First, I eat it much later, about 11. I’m usually up by six and just have coffee and then a walk. Somehow, this routine seems to suppress my appetite. I have 5% fat Greek yoghurt with chopped peanuts, cashews, walnuts, flax seeds, sunflower seeds and pumpkin seeds along with half a chopped banana, apple, satsuma, raspberries or strawberries and a few blackcurrants. It’s totally delicious and usually keeps me going till dinner at about 7.Mark Fletcher, by emailI had lurched from one unhappy breakfast to another through much of my life. My gut is not my strongest organ. So when one of my older mentors suggested steel-cut oats [coarse oatmeal], as a recent retiree, I decided to give it a try. The results are very successful. No indigestion an hour after breakfast. My gut issomuch happier and so is my cardiovascular system. All kinds of odd cravings are now gone. It’s very affordable and local (there is an oat processing mill in our neighbourhood). I make my oats a week at a time in a rice cooker, with a handful of raisins, and heat up each day’s breakfast in the microwave.Fred Tepfer, Eugene, OregonView image in fullscreenKeep it simple …Photograph: Alberto Grosescu/AlamyMaybe nothing other than a cup of coffee if I was playing an important match or a big run.PeteTheBeatBlack. 50% vodka.Jason90Every fibre of my being desires fibre for breakfast.Sagarmatha1953I’m afraid the Breakfast of Champions is in a glass case in the department of ancient history. There was a place in Brighton, the Market Diner, which shovelled out a creation called the Gutbuster. This was long, long before the Ministry of Marketing, Advertising, Publicity and Foul Lies invented the “full English” and similar terms of nonexistent japery. It consisted of nearly everything on a decent caff menu, apart from perhaps Spam, on one plate.View image in fullscreenCould you find room for a ‘Gutbuster’?Photograph: Radharc Images/AlamyIt was so effective as a breakfast of champions that after successfully tucking one inside, if there was the slightest squeak from a notorious family of troublemaking Herberts, all that was required was to breathe Gutbuster halitosis on one of ’em to have the whole clan fleeing over the South Downs, shrieking in terror.It wasn’t bad value, either: lovely caff, good people and not greedy. There’s probably a poncey version called The Nonpareil or some other nonsense lurking between Shoreham Harbour and Roedean, but nothing will ever equal the “Gutbuster”.bricklayersoptionThe hill I will die on: Breakfast cereal is for babies – I eat salad in the mornings, like a grownup | Jacq KellyRead moreLittle Chef used to provide Olympic breakfasts (though possibly not at the behest of the IOC).EddieChorepostPredictable, but porridge and toast will keep you going till lunch. Nothing fancy. Oats, 50/50 milk/water, salt, sugar or sweetener and dried or tinned fruit with local bakery-made wholegrain toast with butter and jam. Nothing overprocessed. You need fuel to keep you going.OlddogandgrumpPure OJ, dish of mixed fruits, three Weetabix with whole milk and two poached eggs with a large, crispy rasher of bacon. Good coffee.DeborahGellerExplore more on these topicsBreakfastNotes and queriesFoodDiets and dietingHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Decades on from the US’s disastrous campaign in Afghanistan, Trump is making all the same mistakes | Simon Tisdall | The Guardian
description: The president has blundered into a ‘forever war’ with Iran he can’t win, but refuses to end. Such hubris has a long history, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Author: Simon Tisdall
Headline: The president has blundered into a ‘forever war’ with Iran he can’t win, but refuses to end. Such hubris has a long history, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Content: A woman walks past rubble in southern Tehran after Israeli/US airstrikes in April 2026.Photograph: Majid Saeedi/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA woman walks past rubble in southern Tehran after Israeli/US airstrikes in April 2026.Photograph: Majid Saeedi/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpDecades on from the US’s disastrous campaign in Afghanistan, Trump is making all the same mistakesSimon TisdallThe president has blundered into a ‘forever war’ with Iran he can’t win, but refuses to end. Such hubris has a long historySun 2 Aug 2026 07.31 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIt’s five years this month since the chaotic retreat of US forces from Kabul. The Nato-backed invasion and occupation of Afghanistan, launched after the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks on New York City and Washington DC, is now widely regarded as a failure. It cost the lives of more than 2,400 US and 450 British troops, and tens of thousands of civilians (the exact number is unknown). Although al-Qaida terrorists were routed, their Taliban hostsreimposed repressive, misogynistic Islamist ruleafter regaining power in 2021. Afghanistan became a byword forill-considered western interventionismand nation-building. It was the archetypal “forever war”, a phrase firstcoined during Vietnam.If this cautionary tale had any lasting value, it was as a deterrent to politicians and generals tempted to rashly embark on open-ended conflicts without just cause, defined, achievable aims, and an exit strategy. Dismayingly, the forever war lesson had to be learned all over again in Iraq, which the US and UK invaded in 2003 and departed, having caused huge harm for scant benefit, in 2011. “Never again!” was the passionate cry at the time and since. And yet, it seems, the same disastrous pattern is now repeating after Donald Trump’s incomprehensibly foolish decision to attack Iran. A war he termed a “little excursion” is entering its sixth month andhas been escalating rapidly. It, too, has a forever feel.That this nightmare is happening again defies all reason. How can it be? Immediate causes of the war aside, answers may be found in persistent US exaggerations and misconceptions about the level and extent of external threats, mixed up with political dishonesty, national hubris, naivety and misplaced idealism. Recalling the harrowing US experience in Afghanistan, Carter Malkasian, a National War College professor who served as a civilian adviser to US forces in Helmand and Kabul,suggeststhe basic premise for keeping troops in Afghanistan for 20 years – a belief the country would otherwise revert to being a safe haven for international terrorism – was fatally flawed.“Nothing of the sort occurred. Over the past five years, not a single act of terrorism against the US was carried out by a group based inAfghanistan,” Malkasian wrote. “Washington spent roughly $1tn on the war. More than 775,000 American service members were deployed … all to defend against a threat that turned out to have been exaggerated.“Five years on, the greatest danger is not that a terrorist safe haven might once again emerge in Afghanistan. A graver threat comes from the risk of collective forgetting.” In short, “fears of the moment” should not cloud memories of the dreadful long-term costs – human, financial, geopolitical – of endless forever war.View image in fullscreenA US military Chinook helicopter lands on a field in Afghanistan in 2019.Photograph: Thomas Watkins/AFP/Getty ImagesIf the Afghan war was prosecuted on the basis of a false assumption, so much more so was the invasion of oil-rich Iraq. George W Bush’s claim in 2002 that Saddam Hussein’s regime possessed stockpiles of readily usable chemical and biological weapons and was seeking a nuclear bombproved untrue. Untrue, too, was the claim from the then vice-president, Dick Cheney, that Iraq “aids and protects” al-Qaida. The subsequent occupation and insurgency became part of an even larger forever war – Bush’s “global war on terror”.According to Brown University’s Costs of War project, an estimated 940,000 people were killed in direct post-9/11 violence in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, Yemen and Pakistan between 2001 and 2023. Up to 3.8 million died indirectly in post-9/11 war zones.It’s easy to second-guess decisions about war and peace taken under the pressure of horrific events. The disingenuous pursuit of political, military and commercial agendas, and the manipulation of intelligence and public opinion, is harder to excuse. Yet was any war ever launched without ulterior motives? The much-discussed new film of Homer’s epic poem, the Odyssey, concerns the aftermath of the 10-year-long Trojan war, which was ostensibly triggered by the abduction of the beautiful Helen of Sparta. Yet, prosaically, the warmay have been more about fair tradethan a fair maiden. The US maintained it fought the Vietnam war to support democracy and halt the spread of communism – the discredited “domino theory”. But it was also very much about US exceptionalism and global hegemony. In that sense, little has changed.What else makes American politicians risk costly entanglements in foreign wars they can’t control and usually lose? Insecurity – meaning fear – is a common denominator. Like Bush before him, Trump and Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, have greatly and knowingly exaggerated the immediacy and existential nature of the Iranian threat. Like Iraq in 2003,Iran possesses no nuclear weaponsand there is zero firm evidence it is trying, or has recently tried, to acquire them. There is a recurring paradox here: it’s the spectacle of the world’s most powerful country once again fearfully tilting at shadows.Trump’s overbearing hostility to weaker neighbours such as Venezuela, Cuba, Colombia, Panama and Greenland has a forever aspect, too. It is rooted in the foundational myth that the US has a unique mission – and right – to oversee the western hemisphere, a view it later extended to the rest of the world. Likewise, greed is forever.Abandoning altruistic ideas of democracy promotion, Trump seeks to exercise economic as well as geopolitical dominance. He has tried to monetise the wars inUkraineandGaza. His focus on the strait of Hormuz shows how security policy and financial and commercial interests invariably intersect.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion33:00Is Iran a ‘forever war’? – Stateside with Kai and CarterLack of effective UN mediation and peacekeeping, the hollowing out of US diplomacy, which has accelerated under Trump’s lickspittle secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and astubborn refusal to accept the militarily inevitableall play a role in turning US-led conflicts into intractable quagmires. In Trump’s case, ego is also a factor. It seems he would rather kill thousands more civilians, risk committing war crimes, set the Middle East ablaze and destroy Republicans’ electoral chances than admit he was wrong over Iran. Such extreme behaviour illuminates another pernicious aspect of the forever war phenomenon. Its utter pointlessness is fundamentally immoral. In its sheer un-reason, itoffends against the laws of God and man. War without end is the death of hope.As he frantically twists and turns over Iran, it’s plain that Trump perceives the bottomless pit on the edge of which, thanks to him, the US totters – and has no idea how to avoid it. One day, he talks about talks. The next, he hits out with massive, murderous violence. Careless of their people’s suffering, implacable Iranianhardliners relish his dilemmaand turn the screw, mounting widening regional militia attacks and global economy-spooking drone and missile strikes. Lost in a maze of denial, Trump tries in vain to bomb his way out of trouble while desperate for a deal that can somehow be sold as a victory.Neither option is going to work. This abysmal Iranian catastrophe is already defining Trump’s presidency. The bloody stain, the blame and the shame, if not the war, will last forever.Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentatorExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionIranUS foreign policyAfghanistanIraqMiddle East and north AfricaSouth and central AsiacommentShareReuse this content

title: Why Andy Burnham’s devolution pledge will be tricky to deliver | Richard Partington | The Guardian
description: Sharing income tax with England’s regional mayors could tackle inequality but many councils are ill-equipped for an enlarged role
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Sharing income tax with England’s regional mayors could tackle inequality but many councils are ill-equipped for an enlarged role
Content: Westminster has largely clung on to its role as political ringmaster.Photograph: ullstein bild Dtl./ullstein bild/GettyView image in fullscreenWestminster has largely clung on to its role as political ringmaster.Photograph: ullstein bild Dtl./ullstein bild/GettyEconomics viewpointDevolutionWhy Andy Burnham’s devolution pledge will be tricky to deliverRichard PartingtonSharing income tax with England’s regional mayors could tackle inequality but many councils are ill-equipped for an enlarged roleSun 2 Aug 2026 07.19 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 16.41 EDTShareOn the road to Downing Street,Andy Burnhampromised to transfer power from Westminster to every postcode in the country. After his first two weeks in office, the size and complexity of this project are becoming clearer.With a date set for theautumn budget, the work of filling in the detail that will underpin his devolution plans begins – starting with his proposal tohand England’s regional mayors a share of income taxto support local economic development.Despite its history as a patchwork of nations, the UK is among the most fiscally centralised countries in the developed world. The Centre for Cities estimates as little as 5% of tax revenue currently stays with mayors and local authorities. The rest goes straight to Whitehall and is allocated by central government. By contrast, 14% of tax stays local in France, and 22% in Japan.For years British devolution has been a messy patchwork in which Westminster has largely clung on to its position as ringmaster; just ask the parties pushing for independence in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. But the system inEnglandis the messiest of the lot.Successive governments have followed a piecemeal approach. Under the Conservatives, the creation of dozens of ringfenced funding pots fostered a begging-bowl culture. They were also no match for the billions of pounds in central government grant funding cut under austerity.Burnham allowing mayors to retain a share of locally generated tax revenues is, therefore, a good idea in principle. Many economists say the idea – firstannounced by Rachel Reevesearlier this year – would help to tackle Britain’s deep regional inequalities.In practice, the Institute for Fiscal Studies estimates that between 6% and 9% of local income tax revenues would be sufficient to fully replace the so-called integrated settlements, or central government grants, the mayoral authorities currently receive.But it will take time to introduce the plan and there are wrinkles to iron-out – not least how to avoid weaker local economies falling behind.The danger is the current fastest-growing mayoral authorities are typically the country’s wealthiest.The Guardian view on England’s centralised state: Andy Burnham must unbundle it | EditorialRead moreLondon, and the runaway success story that is GreaterManchester, are in pole position. The West Midlands and South Yorkshire are in a slower lane. If the winners get to keep a rising share of income tax, the laggards would risk a self-fulfilling cycle of weak growth; limited scope for investment, and yet weaker growth.The reforms will also take a long time to bear fruit for a prime minister in a hurry.It will be 2028 before the income tax plan comes into full effect. Dozens of new mayoralties are also still in the process of being created – with a deadline of the end of that year to give people in places including Essex, Stoke-on-Trent and Warrington similar powers to the trailblazing mayoralties ofLondonand Manchester.Last month theOrganisation for Economic Co-operation and Developmentgave devolution a ringing endorsement. But it also warned that the starting point in Britain makes it challenging. Several vital building blocks need to be put in place to make Burnham’s agenda a success.First and foremost will be the challenge of repairing the damage caused by the Tory austerity years. English local government is ashadow of its pre-2010 self. Most places lack the staff and expertise to use their new money and powers well, at a time when many are struggling to do the basics such as collecting bins or filling potholes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAcross England’s town halls, the workforce has plunged since 2009 from 2.2 million to about 1.1 million. While Greater Manchester and the West Midlands have established sophisticated analytical, policy and delivery teams – enabling them to make better use of the devolved powers – the OECD says many authorities have a shortage of resources and have limited technical expertise.The risk of making bad spending decisions is high. The shenanigans inTees Valley,Birmingham, and the multibillion-pound debts amassed inWoking,WarringtonandThurrockare a serious red flag. Labour inherited abroken local audit system, evidenced by the fact that just 1% of places published audited accounts for 2022-23 by the original deadline.The loss of theAudit Commission(abolished by the Tories) and thedeath of local journalismhas removed important checks and balances. Labour knows this, and has plans to strengthen the role of the new Local Audit Office, which has picked up some of the commission’s functions, and could lean on the National Audit Office.While the public has greater trust in local government than in its Westminster representatives, surveys show that only about 35% of people report that their trust is high or moderately high, well below the OECD average of about 45%.However, devolution could be transformative for the economy. Local leaders are best placed to understand how to support growth in their area.According to the Centre for Cities, measures to integrate bus, tram and train networks in the six largest English cities outside London would better connect 1.2 million people to their nearest city centre, generating productivity gains worth an estimated £17bn. The OECD finds that countries with higher levels of tax and spending devolution tend to have higher wages.At present, the UK’s second-tier cities significantly underperform their peers elsewhere in the G7. Among the bottom 20 big cities in the G7 for productivity, seven are British. Powering-up the UK’s regions would make a big difference.There is no doubt that on the road to transfer power from Westminster to local leaders Burnham will encounter more than a few potholes. But the path is well worth pursuing.Explore more on these topicsDevolutionEconomics viewpointEconomic policyAndy BurnhamInequalityEnglandLondonManchestercommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m all for the nanny state – but we should abolish fines for holidays in term time | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett | The Guardian
description: Some parents are sticklers for the rules, yet mass civil disobedience by parents in England and Wales suggests many agree with me, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: Some parents are sticklers for the rules, yet mass civil disobedience by parents in England and Wales suggests many agree with me, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Content: ‘Value to taxpayers is often mentioned in these discussions, but the wellbeing and mental health benefits for children can be economic as well as holistic.’Photograph: MBI/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Value to taxpayers is often mentioned in these discussions, but the wellbeing and mental health benefits for children can be economic as well as holistic.’Photograph: MBI/AlamyOpinionSchool holidaysI’m all for the nanny state – but we should abolish fines for holidays in term timeRhiannon Lucy CosslettSome parents are sticklers for the rules, yet mass civil disobedience by parents in England and Wales suggests many agree with meSun 2 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePerhaps it’s my stage of parenthood, or the fact that I’ve been lying awake at night, but I think I have an idea that could secure the electoral future of the Labour party. All Andy Burnham needs to do to win a landslide at the next general election is abolish fines for parents who take their children on term-time holidays.More than 2 million– around a fifth–have taken their children out of school because they could not afford to travelduring holidays, according to a national survey released this month. A record459,288 fines were issuedto parents last year.This issue has recently become relevant to me because my son starts school in September, so this year will be the last in which we will be allowed to take term-time trips. Obviously, as I contemplate the preposterous costs for summer holidays, I have developed a new and vested interest in being able to get away with my family. It’s deeper than that, though: I didn’t get many childhood holidays, for financial and circumstantial reasons. As a result I feel very passionately that all small people need leisure time away. Without wanting to turn this into a big sob story, I was so desperate to go on holiday like my friends that I used to collect brochures from high street travel agents andspend hours poring over the different hotels, with kids’ clubs, beaches, swimming pools and waterslides that I could only dream of.Living in a wealthy middle-class area has further radicalised me. I have heard enough parents casually admit that they simply incorporate the fine into their budget to understand that a two-tier system exists. Fines for term-time holidays discriminate unfairly against low-income and Send families, who for the aforementioned financial and circumstantial reasons (too expensive, too crowded for children with sensory or mobility issues) will struggle to take their children away at peak times or cover the fines for doing so in term time. Handing out fines also discriminates against people who work in certain professions, such as farmers, members of the military or people who work in the leisure and tourism industry, and those who have family living a great distance away.Also, fines don’t even work. Taking your child out of school for a holiday is an ongoing act of mass civil disobedience on the part of the public inEnglandand Wales (Scotland and Northern Ireland do not have automatic fines). Considering how law-abiding we generally are, I find this quite extraordinary. It implies there is a passionate and significant proportion of the public who believe in the importance and the value of a family holiday to the extent that they are willing to break the law to give their kids one. I also suspect many find the rules off-puttingly paternalistic (even as a socialist who loves the “nanny state”, I consider it a huge overreach).Of course, there are inevitably people who get very exercised about everyone following the rules. These objectors think you should simply plan your holidays around the school calendar, and if you can’t afford to go anywhere, tough. I have met people in real life who have said this in conversation, and they are always the sorts who take their children on gastronomic cycling tours of the Dordogne every summer. In other words, they have a certain level of privilege and don’t seem able to make the imaginative leap to barely being able to scrape together enough cash for a few rainy days in a caravan near Prestatyn.Don’t get me wrong: there are reasonable objections to my proposition. School attendance and its impact on education is an important issue – I fundamentally believe that. What I don’t believe is that schools should be such a high-pressure environmentthat one term-time holiday a year – which would still need to be authorised at the headteacher’s discretion – will always have a disastrous impact on learning. With school refusals at record highs and a crumbling Send system, term-time holidays are clearly not the most urgent cause of poor educational outcomes. The coalition government did much to damage the state education system. It also, incidentally, made the system for unauthorised absences at state schools muchmore punitive. Many of the politicians responsible were privately educated and went on to send their children to fee-paying schools where parents are free to take their kids on term-time holidays.If I’ve managed to convince you, perhaps I will risk losing you when I say that I don’t believe these trips even necessarily need to be “educational”. On the few holidays I was taken on, we went to museums and old workhouses and castles and ruins, and yes, it’s beneficial to do that. It’s also good for children to see the worried frowns on their parents’ faces melt away – to socialise, to practise their swimming and eat new foods. Memories of fun and togetherness can last a lifetime, sustaining us through tough times. Value to taxpayers is often mentioned in these discussions, but the wellbeing and mental health benefits for children can be economic as well as holistic.By all means, also look at other measures, such as penalising travel companies that engage in unreasonable profiteering, and staggering or shortening the summer holidays – and providing proper childcare during them. But this should be an open goal forBurnham. He says he cares about alleviating the cost of living pressures on families, allowing them to enjoy life. Abolishing fines would be one effective way of doing that, while correcting a source of social inequality. And it’s a vote winner.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsSchool holidaysOpinionSchoolsChildrenEnglandWalescommentShareReuse this content

title: Struggling to get through summer? Treat yourself like a beloved dog – and six other survival tips  | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: August usually sends me into an anxious funk, but I think I’ve worked out how to handle 2026’s terrifying heat and apocalyptic images, writes Emma Beddington
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: August usually sends me into an anxious funk, but I think I’ve worked out how to handle 2026’s terrifying heat and apocalyptic images, writes Emma Beddington
Content: Dog day afternoon … frozen treats are just the thing.Photograph: Anna Okhotska/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDog day afternoon … frozen treats are just the thing.Photograph: Anna Okhotska/Getty ImagesOpinionHealth & wellbeingStruggling to get through summer? Treat yourself like a beloved dog – and six other survival tipsEmma BeddingtonAugust usually sends me into an anxious funk, but I think I’ve worked out how to handle 2026’s terrifying heat and apocalyptic imagesSun 2 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 12.47 EDTShareUnfortunately for hairdressers, “How’s your summer going?” is a loaded question this year. Even basking lizards and barbecue obsessives are wavering in their sun worship as cataclysmic wildfires engulf our nearest neighbours (andthreaten the UK), Wales andparts of England experience drought, andfarmers issue dire warnings about our food supplyin the near future. Rescue centres are filling up withdehydrated hedgehogsand the Environment Agency is having torescue fish. Lazy, joyful, sunscreen-scented days are giving way to stifling, existentially terrifying ones spent skulking in the dark (assuming you don’t need to be out in the extreme heat, asmany workers do), sweatily scrolling throughapocalyptic images.Vanity Fairhas decreed it’s a “sad-girl summer”, highlighting the female singer-songwriters soundtracking the myriad anxieties of an “undeniably cruel” 2026 season, but it’s not just the girlies who are sad – many of us are struggling and we still have August to survive. How?I’m a veteran of sad-girl summers (possiblySad summers– some people get seasonal affective disorder when it’s hot and bright). For years, July and August have sent me into an anxious, distressed funk, afflicted by brain shutdowns that leave me useless for days at a time. That means I’m ahead of the curve in finding little survival tactics, so here are some, if you find yourself struggling with what used to be the carefree, fun season.Treat yourself like a beloved dogLook at canine heatwave advice and apply it to yourself. Little walks in the coolest parts of the day, frozen treats, wet towels and top-ups of chilled water will all help maintain your mental equilibrium. Naps won’t hurt either.Start your day with a bookDefer your engagement with the horrors – they’ll still be there in half an hour; they don’t need to be the first thing to hit your eyeballs. Immerse yourself in something – anything – engaging offline for a while. If your concentration is shot and you fear you will struggle not to scroll, the novelist Naomi Alderman is running a brilliant reading version of Couch to 5K onher Substack.Take up a temporary hobbyDistract yourself with something ultra-low stakes. Last year, I tried growing melons. My misshapen babies were inedibly disgusting, but tending them helped during my twitchiest hours. This summer’s project is “making elaborate salads that would cost £17 in London”. Every day, I craft a photogenic heap of fancy, fibremaxxing fodder, take a picture, save it on my phone in a folder called “lunch” (that I will delete in September), then feast. It’s daft, but it is the high point of many distressing, scratchy-brained days.Delete your weather appI am not saying weather apps are gaslighting us, but it can feel like that when you are in the grip of summer derangement. Watching a tantalising chance of rain in five days’ time fall from 90% to 40% to 20%, then disappear altogether, or temperatures hover stubbornly around the mid-30s is at best a waste of time, at worst, actively maddening. For a few weeks, switch off and experience weather in the way your ancestors did: as an awe-inspiring, often awful but occasionally wonderful thing that happens (possibly because you have displeased the gods).Become a bit nocturnalIt is often too hot to sleep at your normal bedtime and there’s a special quality to summer nights that never quite get dark or cold. Last night, I saw bats, a hedgehog and many foxes in my suburb, but I enjoy late wanders around big cities too. There is almost always something unhinged going down that affirms how the inside of my head feels.Enjoy what summer still does wellNamely fruit. The blackberries are already ripe (yes, worrying), there are peaches so juicy you have to eat them over the sink, fat and fragrant green figs and chunks of crisp, sweet watermelon to be bought. Also, not every apricot I’ve tried has been a sour marble of disappointment and I’ve even eaten melons my French in-laws wouldn’t have drop-kicked off their dinner table in righteous fury. This glut of good fruit is one puny (and doubtless temporary) upside.Remind yourself you’re rightIt’s sane and rational to feel angry, grief-stricken and frightened. Wouldn’t it be weirder if you didn’t?Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
