title: Why we’re all obsessed with Jimothy the raccoon, the internet’s animal of the moment | Elle Hunt | The Guardian
description: From Grumpy Cat to Moo Deng, viral animals have long united people online. Are they becoming our only source of collective enjoyment, asks freelance journalist Elle Hunt
Author: Elle Hunt
Headline: From Grumpy Cat to Moo Deng, viral animals have long united people online. Are they becoming our only source of collective enjoyment, asks freelance journalist Elle Hunt
Content: Jimothy the raccoon scuttling around his Seattle neighbourhood in July 2026.Photograph: Instagram/c1vrgr1View image in fullscreenJimothy the raccoon scuttling around his Seattle neighbourhood in July 2026.Photograph: Instagram/c1vrgr1OpinionAnimalsWhy we’re all obsessed with Jimothy the raccoon, the internet’s animal of the momentElle HuntFrom Grumpy Cat to Moo Deng, viral animals have long united people online. Are they becoming our only source of collective enjoyment?Sun 2 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 10.23 EDTShareAnyone who enjoys memes (who doesn’t?) has surely by now accumulated a mental menagerie of internet-famous animals. Mine include: Grumpy Cat, the Ikea monkey,Moo Dengthe pygmy hippo,Paul the oracle octopusand – my personal favourite –Roger the hot kangaroo(go on, look him up).Now we have Jimothy, a raccoon with short spine syndrome. A familiar sight in his neighbourhood in Seattle for his unusually rounded appearance and scuttling movement,Jimothy went viralon Instagram two weeks ago and has since taken over the world. Within weeks of his debut, there has been fan art, merchandise,multiple tattoos, astadium “theme night”and evena civic ceremony.Even going by the internet’s longstanding enthusiasm for weird little guys, the scale and suddenness of his ascent has been striking. It’s easy to see why people, brands and even baseball teams have jumped on Jimothy: he’s cute, unproblematic and not at all political. Unlike with Taylor Swift’s wedding, say, or the Coldplaykiss cam couple– to name two recent shared, seismic cultural moments – Jimothy poses no ethical quandary. He’s just a funny- looking racoon. This places him in that rare, dwindling and highly prized category of “stuff that everyone can agree is good”.Animals have served this purpose online for as long as there’s been social media, and indeed influenced its modern form and function.It’s been 14 years since Ikea monkeywas spotted; you can probably instantly picture him, pensive in his stylish shearling coat. Some of these viral animals’ meanings are still evolving (Doge the side-eyed shiba inu is now some kind ofMusk-related currency? I admit I lost the thread there) while others effectively became celebrities: I dropped everything to cover Grumpy Cat’s passingin 2019.View image in fullscreenSeattle Mariners baseball fans show their support for Jimothy at T-Mobile Park in Seattle, 21 July 2026.Photograph: Lindsey Wasson/APYou can tell the story of the internet, and with it the 21st century, through the animals it has rallied around. As a petfluencer pioneer, Grumpy Cat’s merchandising and brand deals were mind-boggling back in 2013; now everything can be monetised. Three years later, in May 2016, the online outpouring that greetedthe fatal shootingof Harambe the gorilla at Cincinnati zoo in hindsight signalled a shift to a darker experience of the internet and society.Now, animal content is not just a pillar of the internet but load-bearing infrastructure, with cute pictures and funny videos providing respite from an angry, anxiety inducing internet.This is perhaps one reason why recent years have seen non-human main characters emerge at an astonishing pace, with social media monitoring not just the Jimothy situation but alsoNeil the sealin TasmaniaandPunch the infant macaque in Japan. Having gone viral in February, Punch receiveda reported 2,500 cardsfor his first birthday this week. When Moo Deng recently turned three, she hada three-day celebration, mass sing-along and “hippo-friendly” cake.Internet history shows we’ve always come together over animals, but increasingly they feel like our only common ground,becausethey’re depoliticised, uncomplicated and benign. It’s not just brands: people are hailing Jimothy as “the hero we need right now” (including in song).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe most heartening, human takeaway from Jimothy’s viral moment is that it suggests we really do desire more unity and connection; we just don’t feel comfortable doing so in public, or at scale, on anything other than the most innocuous topic. But as with so many of thenice thingsperiodically enabled by the internet, we’re not even allowed that for long: late on Wednesday,the White House shared a memeshowing Jimothy wearing a Maga cap. This is why we can’t have nice things.This exposes the sad truth of Jimothy, our furry folk hero: he won’t break us out of our online silos. With algorithms distorting our shared reality, he may not even have travelled that far across them. Just now a friend, who spends as much time online as I do, sat down next to me and asked what I was writing about. He met my one-word answer with confusion and an immediate Google search: “Who’s ‘Jimothy’ – and how is he ‘bridging political divides’?”Elle Hunt is a freelance journalistExplore more on these topicsAnimalsOpinionInternetSocial mediaDigital mediaSeattlecommentShareReuse this content

title: Apparently, I’ve got ‘comfort creep’. I prefer to think of it as finally knowing what I like | Polly Hudson | The Guardian
description: Routine isn’t a failure of imagination – it’s the reward for having done enough experimenting. So, yes, I’m going to my favourite restaurant again – and ordering my favourite dish, writes Polly Hudson
Author: Polly Hudson
Headline: Routine isn’t a failure of imagination – it’s the reward for having done enough experimenting. So, yes, I’m going to my favourite restaurant again – and ordering my favourite dish, writes Polly Hudson
Content: What a lovely non-surprise!Photograph: frantic00/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWhat a lovely non-surprise!Photograph: frantic00/Getty ImagesOpinionLife and styleApparently, I’ve got ‘comfort creep’. I prefer to think of it as finally knowing what I likePolly HudsonRoutine isn’t a failure of imagination – it’s the reward for having done enough experimenting. So, yes, I’m going to my favourite restaurant again – and ordering my favourite dishSun 2 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 03.11 EDTShareFeeling seen isn’t always a positive thing. “Comfort creep: do YOU have it?” Good Housekeeping asked, accusingly. I was certain that I did, even before knowing what it was. And that this was not good.“Same holidays, same TV shows, same restaurants, same wine … If your life lacks excitement, it’s time for an anti-comfort crusade!” OK, guilty as charged, but hang on a second. When did the comfort zone become a horrific dystopia from which you must escape at all costs? Comfort? Ugh, the worst! Run, screaming, as fast as you can.What about those of us who have comfort creep and don’t want to crusade against it, thanks? In today’s non-figurativelyburning world, what’s wrong with battening down the hatches and refusing to budge from your comfort zone? After years of being ashamed, carrying it as a guilty secret, while trying to avoid the fuddy-duddy-sounding (but accurate) phrase “I know what I like”, I’m ready to admit I’m a routine queen. I’m in good company, too: the female cast members of Friends had the same meal, daily, for a decade.In 2010, Courteney Coxtold the Los Angeles Times: “Jennifer [Aniston], Lisa [Kudrow] and I ate lunch together every single day for 10 years. And we always had the same thing – a cobb salad. But it wasn’t really a cobb salad. It was a cobb salad that Jennifer doctored up with turkey bacon and garbanzo beans and I don’t know what. She just has a way with food, which really helps. Because if you’re going to eat the same salad every day for 10 years, it better be a good salad, right?”Cox put her finger right on it there. It’s no coincidence that comfort creep is a mostly middle-aged occurrence and so can be billed as a miserable, joyless rut in which you’re stuck; proof you’ve given up, surrendered to the blah. It could, alternatively, be viewed as reaching a point where you have sampled much of what life has to offer and curated the choices down to a bespoke selection that suits you perfectly. Welcome to your good-salad days.When I catch up with my closest friend, we invariably go to the same restaurant. That’s our place. After trying a few, we found one that was great. Even better (or worse, depending on your point of view), after sampling various menu options, we discovered something particularly delicious, so that’s what we both have. It’s not that we’re too set in our ways to take risks – it’s that we’ve already taken them. They were fine, but not as nice as the sea bass.So now we’re regulars with a regular. The staff recognise us and vice versa; we’re at the exhilarating stage of being able to say – albeit slightly self-consciously – “the usual, please” when they come to take our order. It’s not quite “where everybody knows your name” territory, but it’s not far off. A reassuring, convivial little corner of the planet where we’re sure what’s what and that we will enjoy all of it. On a practical level, it also means we’re spared the boring bits of meeting up – deciding where to go and what to have when we get there. Tedious logistics are moot for ever more; let’s get on with the good stuff.Similarly, there are a few TV shows I restart whenever I’m overwhelmed by events in real life.Comfort-watching, it’s called– and there it is, the C-word again, soothing billed sneeringly as unfavourable. I also have a favourite knife – my comfort knife, I suppose. If I’m chopping anything, that’s the knife I’m using, guaranteed. Maybe this sounds desperately sad to the kind of thrill-seeker who would grab randomly at the cutlery drawer, but why would I settle for the rest when I could have the best? I know what I like and what isn’t going to cut it.It seems as though one person’s dull is another’s discerning – it just depends where you’re standing. More than enough about the times we’re living through is uncertain – I’m not sure about you, but I’ll take all the cosy, familiar comfort I can get.Polly Hudson is a freelance writerDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on drought: hot, dry conditions make inequality starker  | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Water is a vital shared resource, and privatisation has made a just transition harder
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Water is a vital shared resource, and privatisation has made a just transition harder
Content: A stone bridge believed to date back to 1800, which has been exposed due to low water levels in the Taf Fawr valley in Merthyr Tydfil, Wales.Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA stone bridge believed to date back to 1800, which has been exposed due to low water levels in the Taf Fawr valley in Merthyr Tydfil, Wales.Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty ImagesOpinionDroughtThe Guardian view on drought: hot, dry conditions make inequality starkerEditorialWater is a vital shared resource, and privatisation has made a just transition harderSun 2 Aug 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareCompared with rising heat-related deaths, and devastating wildfires in the Cairngorms and Suffolk, the announcement that the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) is consideringmoving its hydrangea collectionfrom Surrey to Greater Manchester and North Yorkshire might seem unimportant. But it points to geographical differences in exposure to global heating that have arguably never been more evident than this summer, with last monththe driest on record. Seven areas of south and east England areofficially in drought, along with the whole of Wales.A drought is less easily measured than a heatwave, which isdeclared by the Met Officewhen the maximum temperature exceeds a set threshold on three consecutive days. But the fact that drought is harder to quantify does not make it less damaging. Water shortages are exposing specific vulnerabilities and inequalities, as well as the UK’slack of preparednessfor climate change overall.Some of the unfairnesses revealed in recent weeks are shocking in their predictability. Exemptions that allow golf courses and schools with large sports grounds to water lawns, when councils and householders are banned from doing so, have led tojustifiable anger. But while the insulation of elites from hardship is nothing new, the heightened impact of such patterns in extreme weather requires attention. Privileges such as guaranteed water for golf courses cannot survive a drought. People whose housing, jobs or health make them vulnerable must be shielded.Andy Burnham has yet to set out his plans for greater public control of water companies. Nationalisation ofThames Waterremains a welcome possibility. But it is vital that this industry’s role in exacerbating scarcity and injustice is addressed. Its bosses and shareholders are not solely to blame. The decision to privatise the water industry was taken by a Conservative government, while regulators bear responsibility for chronically weak oversight, particularly of Thames Water, which has been staving off collapse for years. But the extraction of billions of pounds of profits by businesses set up as regional monopolies, while infrastructure including wastewater treatment and storage was neglected, and debts piled up, has been a disgraceful failure. Drought conditions reveal how dangerous this is, since when people are asked to make sacrifices, it is vital that they have a sense of shared responsibility towards a common good.At least new reservoirs, which store water gathered in winter for use in the summer, are on the way. After three decades during which no major ones were added, the industry has pledgedto build 10, with two in the dry east of England given priority status. But questions remain over the viability of plans to build thousands of new homes in drought-prone areas, and thedifficulties faced by farmers, who want it to be made easier to build reservoirs specifically for use on their crops. Water recycling and conservation efforts are also far behind where they should be, with household water use in England and Wales among the highest in Europe.With the climate in the south ofEnglandincreasingly resembling that of the Mediterranean, those able to move may increasingly look north – following the RHS’s hydrangeas. Global heating will reinforce old patterns of inequality, but it will also create new ones. Societies and governments must prepare for both. This summer’s drought makes it clear how urgent this is.Explore more on these topicsDroughtOpinionWater industryExtreme heatEnglandWalesInequalityeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on global corporate tax: a $500bn prize that states must seize | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Donald Trump may reject the negotiations, but he cannot veto a global effort to make multinational companies answer to governments
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Donald Trump may reject the negotiations, but he cannot veto a global effort to make multinational companies answer to governments
Content: ‘Donald Trump’s US walked out last year and urged others to follow. None did.’Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Donald Trump’s US walked out last year and urged others to follow. None did.’Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesOpinionUnited NationsThe Guardian view on global corporate tax: a $500bn prize that states must seizeEditorialDonald Trump may reject the negotiations, but he cannot veto a global effort to make multinational companies answer to governmentsSun 2 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareGovernments are told that public services must shrink because money is tight. Yet a new Tax Justice Networkreportsays that countries could capture an extra $500bn a year without raising corporate tax rates. The answer is to tax multinational profits where real economic activity happens – known asunitary taxation. No new profit is created. Revenue simply shifts from tax havens where profits are “booked” to the countries where workers produce and customers spend.Making that principle a global tax standard depends on UN talks opening inNew Yorkon Monday. Modelled on the UN climate regime, a fiscal framework convention would create the governing body and procedures, with protocols providing detailed rules. The UN wants agreement by late 2027. Donald Trump’sUSwalked out last year and urged others to follow. None did.Rich countries gain most when firms pay tax where people work, not where profits vanish in havens, because their economies are the largest. Britain would collect about £13bn extra a year in tax receipts – two‑thirds of thecost of an NHS-style social care system. EU governments could raise enough to quadrupleclimate-adaptation spending. Poorer countries also benefit. The report calculates that the global south would receive $156bn in one year – more than the International Monetary Fund has outstanding in loans to those nations.For the first time in decades, multinationals could be taxed where they actually do business. Rules built for the corporate world of the 1920s – when national industrial giants dominated – would finally confront today’s companies organised around intangible assets and global supply chains, as well as profits of an altogether different scale. In 1929, General Motors made the equivalent of $4.7bn. Apple’s profit last year was $112bn. What the report calls “diversified” tax havens such asSwitzerlandand theNetherlandscould offset losses by raising rates. Pure booking centres such as the Cayman Islands could not.The talks suggest states are beginning to reclaim powers surrendered under globalisation to corporate lawyers and private tribunals. One protocol would let countries tax digital and other cross-border services without waiting for firms to establish domestic offices, blunting Mr Trump’strade threats. A second could go further, shifting tax disputes fromsecretive investor-state arbitrationinto a more open, publicly accountable UN-led system.The direction is unmistakable. Ireland, which is facing an estimated $11bn annual tax loss, has already begun putting aside part of its “windfall corporate tax receipts” in a new fund – an admission that the revenue won’t last.IndiaandNigeriahave legislated so that companies profiting from their economies should not escape the tax net just because they operate across borders.Britain has belatedly backed a UN-led shift towards taxing real activity. Defending rules entwined with its offshore network was politically indefensible and economically perverse. The US can sit out the negotiations, but it cannotshieldAmerican companies from others’ rules. The success of these talks has largely been down toAfrican nationsinsisting on consensus where possible and majority rule where necessary. That denies the US and any rich-country bloc an effective veto. Backed by India, Brazil and other developing powers, an African-led coalition can now press a simple claim: countries should be free to tax value created within their economies. Britain should help them prevail.Explore more on these topicsUnited NationsOpinionTax and spendingCorporate governanceTax avoidanceDonald TrumpAfricaGlobal economyeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: India’s gen Z have discovered the power of collective action | India | The Guardian
description: Letters: The recent Cockroach Janta party protests had widespread support, says Bhaskar Mani. Plus a letter from Nand Lal Rathore
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: The recent Cockroach Janta party protests had widespread support, says Bhaskar Mani. Plus a letter from Nand Lal Rathore
Content: Supporters of the Cockroach Janta party in Delhi celebrate on 25 July after India's education minister resigns.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersView image in fullscreenSupporters of the Cockroach Janta party in Delhi celebrate on 25 July after India's education minister resigns.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersIndiaLettersIndia’s gen Z have discovered the power of collective actionThe recent Cockroach Janta party protests had widespread support, saysBhaskar Mani.Plus a letter fromNand Lal RathoreSun 2 Aug 2026 12.12 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 12.47 EDTShareA crucial point that your editorial on India’s gen Z protests (28 July) missed out was that the protests the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) launched in Delhi, hunger strikes and all, were not just supported by young, restless or unemployed people. It was wholeheartedly supported by their parents and grandparents, the old and the middle-aged, even well-off young adults with good jobs and little children. And this was not just in Delhi, but across the country in the huge metropolises of Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Bengaluru, as well as smaller towns. And it was all peaceful, for which credit goes to the ethos of the protests and the CJP.All of this was suppressed in the mainstream media, print and TV, and even distorted to suggest that it was violent in parts. This reflects not just the overwhelming angst and fear of young graduates facing poor prospects, but the significant grievances of a people who are seeing and experiencing their democracy fading away.Bhaskar ManiBengaluru, IndiaYour editorial captures an important truth: movements that begin with a single grievance often evolve into broader demands for justice, accountability and democratic reform. India’s gen Z protests are not simply about leaked exam papers; they reflect a generation’s frustration with institutions that have failed to protect merit and opportunity.I could not help thinking aboutPakistan. Here, too, students, jobseekers and marginalised communities have long expressed concerns about governance and access to justice. Yet these struggles rarely transform into sustained, nationwide civic movements. Local protests often remain isolated and receive limited attention or fail to generate the solidarity required for lasting institutional reform.Whether in India or Pakistan, young people deserve institutions they can trust, exams they can believe in and public systems that reward merit rather than connections. The significance of India’s movement lies not only in political consequences but in the emergence of a generation that has discovered the power of peaceful collective action. Its long-term impact will depend on whether that energy strengthens democratic institutions rather than deepening divisions.Nand Lal RathoreChachro,Sindh province, PakistanHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Traffic, mobiles, music … let’s turn the volume down | Pollution | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an editorial on the health impact of noise pollution
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an editorial on the health impact of noise pollution
Content: A council officer measuring noise levels in Haringey, north London.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenA council officer measuring noise levels in Haringey, north London.Photograph: AlamyPollutionLettersTraffic, mobiles, music … let’s turn the volume downReaders respond to an editorial on the health impact of noise pollutionSun 2 Aug 2026 12.12 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 12.47 EDTShareYour editorial is right that noise pollution deserves to be treated as a public-health issue rather than a mere irritation (The Guardian view on noise pollution: keep it down, 28 July). Yet one obvious source of urban noise receives little attention: modified cars and motorbikes whose exhausts and engines have been made far louder than manufacturers intended.Anyone living in a city or town knows the difference between the background hum of traffic and the explosive revving, popping and roaring produced by a small minority of drivers and riders. These vehicles can wake entire terraces, disrupt outdoor spaces and make life less pleasant for everyone else.What is most baffling is the lack of enforcement. Excessively noisy exhausts are already unlawful, yet action by the police appears rare. Why are police not being held more accountable for enforcing existing noise laws? The MOT regime also seems inadequate. A vehicle can be failed for being “excessively noisy”, but there is no routine objective decibel measurement comparable to the precise testing applied to emissions, brakes or lights.The UK hastrialled roadside noise camerasthat combine microphones with number-plate recognition, and similar systems operate in other countries. Rolling out such technology more widely would be a straightforward, visible and popular way to improve quality of life in towns and cities.Mark EbdenFrome, SomersetAs someone who is autistic and suffers from misophonia, or extreme sensitivity to noise, I feel noise pollution has increased exponentially since the Covid pandemic.To the problem of leaf blowers and automatic hand dryers (which are so loud I can’t use public toilets that have them), I would add things like public phone use and announcements in public places.For me the problem is so severe that I now struggle to navigate public spaces, but as you point out, such noise pollution affects all of us, even if we aren’t aware of it, with considerable knock-on effects for wildlife.Deana HeathLiverpoolYour editorial struck a chord, although it’s not traffic or nightlife that upsets me, but unasked-for music. I’m a musician and composer, and the way my brain is wired does not allow for what other people call “background music”. For me, it’s all in the foreground.I used to like going to one-day international cricket matches, but they have introduced musical “stingers” to accompany highlights such as hitting a six or taking a wicket. This has resulted in my deciding to no longer attend. It’s the same in restaurants – often waiters cannot turn down the piped racket because it’s controlled elsewhere.Edward CollierCheltenham, GloucestershireLoud music in shops causes me considerable annoyance. After a recent move to Wales, I have been disappointed to find in this “land of song” that a visit even to an upmarket food store involves an aural assault by what can best be described as nasal wailing.Sue ZlosnikHolt, WrexhamShrubs, trees and hedges are some of the best sound barriers, as well as good wind breakers and air filters. They are also temperature moderators and good for our mental health. They should be considered essential in urban environments.Chloë ThompsonEynsham, OxfordshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Humanist weddings are deeply personal and meaningful | Weddings | The Guardian
description: Letter: Mair Garland responds to an article by Rachel Connolly on what makes a good ceremony these days
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Mair Garland responds to an article by Rachel Connolly on what makes a good ceremony these days
Content: ‘Humanist celebrants are knowledgeable, passionate and unashamedly geeky about creating meaningful non-religious ceremonies.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Humanist celebrants are knowledgeable, passionate and unashamedly geeky about creating meaningful non-religious ceremonies.’Photograph: AlamyWeddingsLettersHumanist weddings are deeply personal and meaningfulMair Garlandresponds to an article by Rachel Connolly on what makes a good ceremony these daysSun 2 Aug 2026 12.12 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 12.47 EDTShareAs a humanist celebrant, I was saddened by Rachel Connolly’s conclusion about humanist weddings (What makes a good wedding these days? I say flirting and chaos, but not three days in a French castle, 29 July). She writes: “The idea of being married in a humanist service by someone wearing, say, skinny jeans and a black T-shirt gives me willies.” I must disclose my ownership of several pairs of skinny jeans, but I have not worn these in my role as a celebrant (though never say never – I’m always guided by couples’ dress codes).Ms Connolly seems to have the impression that a humanist ceremony represents a compromise to the formal and ceremonial rituals we’d traditionally associate with a religious wedding. On the contrary, humanist celebrants are knowledgable, passionate and unashamedly geeky about creating meaningful non-religious ceremonies that are deeply personal to couples and their families.A non-religious ceremony needn’t be unceremonious or casual. I’d love for Ms Connolly to come to one of our weddings to see what the fuss is about, especially with theforthcoming legalisationof humanist marriage ceremonies.Mair GarlandLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? description: Brief letters: Wicked wickets | Regatta antics | Rock salt of ages | Spuds for dinner | Making a meal of it | Chef’s kiss
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Brief letters: Wicked wickets | Regatta antics | Rock salt of ages | Spuds for dinner | Making a meal of it | Chef’s kiss
Content: An editorial said ‘cricket’s moral code conceals a rich history of cheating and convenient national myth’.Photograph: Marvin woodyatt/AlamyView image in fullscreenAn editorial said ‘cricket’s moral code conceals a rich history of cheating and convenient national myth’.Photograph: Marvin woodyatt/AlamyBrief lettersCricketLettersCricket has always had its dark artsWicked wickets | Regatta antics | Rock salt of ages | Spuds for dinner | Making a meal of it | Chef’s kissSun 2 Aug 2026 12.12 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 12.47 EDTShareRegarding your editorial on cricket fair play (30 July), as an elderly cricket fan, I can remember being told as a small boy to watch a Yorkshire wicketkeeper who was known, when standing up to the bowler, to nudge the stumps with his toe when the ball was close enough to make it look like “bowled out”. But in those days, league cricket was serious business and not played for fun.Tony BrownKingston, Ontario, CanadaMay I present the Seagull outboard race scandal of 1963? At a regatta in Coverack, I was hanging over the bow to keep it down when we were overtaken by a faster boat. With a boathook, I carefully pushed his fuel tap shut; he mysteriously stopped several yards short of the finish line. Did we carry away the prize: 2/6d? My lips are sealed.Jonathan FletcherHelston, CornwallRe dating fossils precisely (Letters, 30 July), I once bought a carton of rock salt whose label said the salt was 10m years old. It then advised that it should be used before the following August.Richard BarnardWivenhoe, EssexWhen I started out as a social worker in 1969, a client told me that dinner was the meal that had potatoes (Letters, 28 July).Ron GouldBrighton, East SussexBreakfast, brunch, elevenses, lunch, afternoon tea, dinner … I’ve given up and just graze all day.Dr Bob AronIlkley, West YorkshireSurely dinner is whenever the person who’s cooking it says it is.Pete BibbySheffieldHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: ‘Ready for next 100 years’: Glasgow 2026 chief hails revamped Commonwealth Games | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Phil Batty said the event can carry on for another 100 years, saying: ‘The Commonwealth Games are relevant, matter and are here to last’
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Phil Batty said the event can carry on for another 100 years, saying: ‘The Commonwealth Games are relevant, matter and are here to last’
Content: The chief executive of Glasgow 2026, Phil Batty, said the Games had ‘absolutely exceeded my expectations’.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe chief executive of Glasgow 2026, Phil Batty, said the Games had ‘absolutely exceeded my expectations’.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersCommonwealth Games 2026‘Ready for next 100 years’: Glasgow 2026 chief hails revamped Commonwealth GamesPhil Batty hails ‘phenomenal’ success of event‘The Games are relevant, matter and are here to last’Sean Inglein GlasgowSun 2 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis year’sCommonwealth Gameshave been “phenomenal” and have shown the events have the potential to carry on for another 100 years, the chief executive of Glasgow 2026 has told the Guardian. Phil Batty also said that the revamped Games, which included only 10 sports rather than the 19 in Birmingham four years ago, showcased a formula that made them financially sustainable as they head to Amdavad in 2030.“What a phenomenal 11 days,” Batty said. “I have had absolute pride in the way that the city and the Commonwealth has come together. These Games have not only exceeded expectations. They have demonstrated that major events can flex and evolve to be fit for purpose in the future.Australia’s Louise Hoskins, 76, wins historic Commonwealth Games gold medalRead more“What we’ve seen here in Glasgow is that you can put on an incredible Games, which is different but still feels as brilliant as it ever has been, and is ready for the next 100 years. And these Games have proved once and for all that the Commonwealth Games are relevant, the Commonwealth Games matter, and the Commonwealth Games are here to last.”There have been several criticisms about the Games, ranging from the long list of absentee stars – includingBritain’s 800m Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson, the Canadian swimmer ­Summer McIntosh and the Olympic100m champion Julien Alfred, along with limited visibility on TV and the lack of sell-out crowds. However Katie Sadleir, the chief executive of Commonwealth Sport, said she shared Batty’s positive assessment. “These Games have absolutely exceeded my expectations,” she said. “People are talking about it on the streets. I’ve met with athletes. I’ve met with Commonwealth Games Associations and everyone is going away buzzed about what happened.”Organisers said that the projected spend for the event was £162.6m – a fraction of the £543m spent at Glasgow 2014 and the £680m on Birmingham in 2022. They pointed out that Glasgow had also benefited from £4.7m that had been spent on upgrades, including a new track and replacement pitch at Scotstoun ­Stadium and the upgrading of Tollcross International Swimming Centre. Organisers also released TV ­figures showing that 11.4 million people had watched in Australia on Channel 7 and close to four million in Canada on CBC. However, they did not say how many people had watched in Britain, either live on TNT/HBO Max, or through Five’s highlights show.View image in fullscreenPhil Batty said: ‘I have had absolute pride in the way that the city and the Commonwealth has come together.’Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPTV audiences for the opening ­ceremony were reported to have peaked at about 800,000 on Channel 5, with a further 50,000 on TNT, well down on the five million that watched on the BBC in 2022. However Sadleir defended the decision to choose Warner Brothers Discovery after the BBC made an offer that was said to be a “fraction” of the WBD bid.“The BBC has been a fantastic partner for a very long period in terms of the Commonwealth Games, and we are doing BBC Radio, so they are involved,” she said. “But I look after the Commonwealth movement of 74 countries, and it is my ­responsibility to look globally in terms of viewership.”Some British athletes are concerned their medal-winning performances over the past week have not attracted the interest of previous Games because of the lack of BBC ­coverage. However Sadleir insisted many people were now streaming and not watching on linear TV. “We are so pleased with the WBD deal,” she said. “The world is moving in terms of how people are consuming sport. I’ve been sitting in the stands with people watching the live sport and seeing them watching HBO Max with their four screens and they’re streaming it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Linear is still very important, but where we’re moving to is a much wider look and feel about how people are consuming the Games. And for £4.99 for 600 hours compared to 200 hours in Birmingham, we are very pleased with that relationship.“We have a very young demographic that we are trying to attract. Those people aren’t watching linear TV; they are streaming and watching it on their phones and devices.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Emma Finucane lands keirin to claim historic fourth Commonwealth gold | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Emma Finucane picked up a fourth gold medal in Glasgow on the final day of a Commonwealth Games dominated by Australia
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Emma Finucane picked up a fourth gold medal in Glasgow on the final day of a Commonwealth Games dominated by Australia
Content: Emma Finucane on the velodrome podium. ‘To stand here and have four golds, I have no words,’ she said.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEmma Finucane on the velodrome podium. ‘To stand here and have four golds, I have no words,’ she said.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026Emma Finucane lands keirin to claim historic fourth Commonwealth goldWelsh cyclist had won in two sprints and time trialAustralia dominate Games with 171 medals, 70 goldSean Inglein GlasgowSun 2 Aug 2026 15.06 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Welsh cyclist Emma Finucane wrote her name into the history books on the final day of theCommonwealth Games, but Glasgow 2026 will be remembered most for Australia’s dominance.Before the Games, the Australia swimmer Sam Short had told reporters: “I’m so pumped – I can’t wait to go over there and smash those Pommies up.” And the whole Australia team seemed to get the memo as they finished with 171 medals, of them 70 gold. That put them a staggering 61 clear of England, who won 110 medals, with Canada third after winning 62.‘Ready for next 100 years’: Glasgow 2026 chief hails revamped Commonwealth GamesRead moreDespite the medal gap to Australia, Team England chef de mission, Jonathon Riall, issued a bullish assessment of the performance. “To finish the Games with 110 medals and second place on the medal table is an incredible achievement, one that every athlete, coach, support staff member and national governing body should be immensely proud of,” he said.“For Team England, success is about more than medals. It can mean achieving a lifetime best, overcoming adversity simply to reach the start line, or standing on the podium with a medal around your neck. We have seen all those different ways of winning throughout these Games.“We won medals across nine sports, saw established champions deliver once again on the biggest stage and watched a new generation announce themselves on the Commonwealth stage. This team has embodied everything Team England stands for, and it has been an immense privilege to lead them.”Finucane will certainly go down as one of the athletes of the Games after becoming the first sprint cyclist to win four track gold medals at the same Commonwealth Games.The Welsh cyclist added to the golds she had already won in the team and individual sprints and 1,000m time trial, with a bravuro victory in the keirin.Finucane, who won Olympic gold as part of the Great Britain sprint team at Paris 2024, moved to the front with two laps to go, daring others to get past her. None of them could as she won by half a bike length ahead of the Olympic champion, Ellesse Andrews of New Zealand.“I was convinced they would come round me,” admitted Finucane. “Honestly it is hard to put into words. I could have easily gone out in the semis.“After Paris, everything was a huge learning curve for me emotionally,” she added. “That week was really tough, and what I came away with was hard to process. But going into these Games I’ve learned to handle pressure better and regulate my emotions more.”Finucane now plans to take a holiday with her sister before shifting her focus towards the track world championships in Shanghai in October.View image in fullscreenEmma Finucane of Wales sprints down the home straight to win the women’s keirin final.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian“I definitely did feel the pressure but throughout the week I just rode my own race,” she added. “The team sprint was a big aim. The last time we rode it was four years ago and we got a bronze medal.“To come back as the same team and win gold was iconic. Singing on the podium with the team was insane. I just rode each race as it came. I went out there and left everything on the track. To stand here and have four golds, I have no words.She added: “I don’t think I’ll ever believe that I’ve made history here. I can’t believe little me has done this. Ten-year-old Emma is screaming inside, like, ‘What is going on?’ I hope I’ve inspired the nation to get on to a bike and get into a velodrome. I can’t believe I found this sport and this sport found me.”Earlier on the last day, Leigh Hoffman became the first Australian cyclist to win four medals at one Games by winning the 1km men’s time trial, ensuring he took home three gold and one silver.And there was more success for Australia in the para bowls as 76-year-old Louise Hoskins became theoldest athlete to win goldin Glasgow.Hoskins and her partner, Serena Bonnell, secured a 6-3, 4-4 win, leaving Hoskins delighted. “It is incredible. I’m still pinching myself,” she said. “I never thought I’d ever get gold at my age. Get out there and have a go, and never give up.”Elsewhere Jamaica fell short of pulling off another epic Commonwealth Games upset as they went down 56-48 to New Zealand in the women’s netball final. However England missed out on bronze after being thrashed 68-50 by Australia, who recovered from ashock one-point defeat to Jamaicaon Saturday.“Fourth place is agonising,” admitted the England captain, Fran Williams. “It’s the position nobody really wants to finish in when you’re just outside the medals. We just weren’t clinical enough today, and credit has to go to the Diamonds.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“Australia managed to show up stronger than us on the day it mattered most. It hurts at the moment, but there are so many lessons to take from this experience.”At least England were able to win three more gold medals on the final day. Emma Reid successfully defended her women’s 78kg judo title, Katherine Rednall triumphed in the women’s bowls singles final and Matthew Robertson defeated the home favourite Fin Graham in the velodrome to win the C1-C3 3,000m individual pursuit.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Gianni Infantino could face leadership challenge as Fifa council members rebel | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: Gianni Infantino is facing a rebellion from members of the Fifa council who are attempting to force an extraordinary general meeting that could develop into a leadership challenge
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Gianni Infantino is facing a rebellion from members of the Fifa council who are attempting to force an extraordinary general meeting that could develop into a leadership challenge
Content: Gianni Infantino is facing growing pressure from Fifa Council members.Photograph: Sergio Pérez/EPAView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino is facing growing pressure from Fifa Council members.Photograph: Sergio Pérez/EPAGianni InfantinoGianni Infantino could face leadership challenge as Fifa council members rebelCouncil wants to trigger emergency general meetingMembers demand review of Balogun decisionExclusive byMatt HughesSun 2 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 11.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGianni Infantino is facing a rebellion from members of the Fifa council who are attempting to force an extraordinary general meeting (EGM) that could develop into a full-blown leadership challenge.The Guardian has learned that moves to call an EGM were already under way before the emergence of Infantino’s abortive plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup, with council members demanding an independent review into the unprecedented decision tolift Folarin Balogun’s suspensionduring the World Cup, which involved multiple phone calls from Donald Trump.Gianni Infantino ‘has lost Uefa’s confidence’ after Fifa chief scraps World Cup sell-off planRead moreTheFifacouncil is the world governing body’s main decision-making forum composed of 28 representatives of the six confederations, eight vice-presidents and Infantino. Under Fifa rules a motion from 50% or 19 of the 37 council members can trigger an EGM.It is understood that the rebels had already reached double figures before it emerged that Infantino had secretly proposed to sell 20% of a new World Cup operating company to Thrive Capital, an investment company founded by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.The unhappy council members had been planning on calling for Infantino to resign if he refused to sanction an independent review of the Balogun affair, which led to the Norwegian FA filing an official complaint to the International Olympic Committee alleging Fifa had breached rules on political neutrality by bowing to pressure from Trump.Fifa has insisted all along that it followed due process, with the decision taken independently by its ethics committee, but has yet to publish a written report on the hearing.The rebels are likely to have been emboldened by Infantino’s U-turn over the World Cup sell-off debacle, with the plan abandoned in a statement from Fifa in the early hours of Saturday morning afterUefa, Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – and the Asian Football Confederation denounced it.Uefa and Concacaf both issued further statementscondemning Infantino and calling for a thorough review of Fifa’s governance on Saturday, but it is unclear if they have sufficient support from the rest of the world to oust him.The Confederation of African Football and the South American Conmebol remain fully behind Infantino, while the Qatar Football Association issued a statement yesterday backing him to stay as president.Of the 37 council members 14 are from Europe and North America so support from Asia will be required to put real pressure on Infantino.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere can be no letup. Humiliated Infantino must stand down at Fifa or be removed | Nick AmesRead moreThe Fifa council is not due to meet until November with the rebels attempting to move quickly to force an EGM, where Infantino would be asked to explain himself. A refusal to commission an external review into Balogun would lead to more active attempts to oust Infantino, with alternative presidential candidates already being sounded out.Qatar’s stance has definitely ruled out a presidential bid from Paris Saint-Germain’s president, Nasser Al-Khelaifi, and much will depend on whether Victor Montagliani, the Canadian who is president of Concacaf, has the appetite to take on Infantino. A campaign from the AFC president, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, who lost narrowly to Infantino in the 2016 Fifa election, would be difficult without his own confederation’s support.Infantino has already secured more than 200 letters of support endorsing his re-election campaign, but they can be withdrawn and the deadline for other candidates to announce an intention to stand is not until 18 November.Another potential vehicle for removing Infantino would be an emergency Fifa congress to trigger a vote of no confidence in the president, which can be called if letters are submitted by 43 associations.View image in fullscreenThe rebels are likely to have been emboldened by Infantino’s U-turn over the World Cup sell-off debacle.Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPAExplore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoFifaFootball politicsUefanewsShareReuse this content

title: UCI president backs night-time drug testing after Tour de France controversy | Tour de France | The Guardian
description: The UCI president, David Lappartient, has given his support to night-time testing, as happened at the Tour de France, in ‘exceptional cases’
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: The UCI president, David Lappartient, has given his support to night-time testing, as happened at the Tour de France, in ‘exceptional cases’
Content: David Lappartient said transparency is paramount in the UCI.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenDavid Lappartient said transparency is paramount in the UCI.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersTour de FranceUCI president backs night-time drug testing after Tour de France controversyDavid Lappartient says selective night testing is justified‘We always have suspicion in cycling, due to our past’Jeremy Whittlein GenevaSun 2 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UCI president, David Lappartient, has said there will “always be suspicion in cycling” and insisted this year’s men’sTour de Francewas clean. Lappartient, speaking at the start of stage two of the Tour de France Femmes in Aigle, also said he supported night-time testing during races in “exceptional cases”.Lappartient added that the absence of any positive test announcements by the International Testing Agency (ITA) indicated that last month’s men’s Tour was drug free. “The ITA never make a press release about negative results, only about positive results,” said Lappartient. “We didn’t see any press release in the Tour de France, so it seems there was nothing in the Tour.”It’s double Dutch as Lorena Wiebes wins second stage of Tour de France FemmesRead moreTadej Pogacar, the five-time champion, and his rival Jonas Vingegaard were subjected to night-time tests,at 5am and 2am respectively, by the ITA midway through this year’s race. “We will not support something they do every night on the riders. The normal hours [of testing] are not in the night,” said the head of cycling’s governing body.“However, we support the ITA if they have to do some specific test, because we know that, with micro-dosing EPO, that’s something you can’t detect six or seven hours after. So, for the riders to know that the ITA may come, that’s always a fear.“We always have suspicion in cycling, due to our past. I know what has been done to fight against doping. Night testing is a tool in this fight, but it is not a tool to use every day. You must use it very exceptionally. It’s not suspicion about any rider, but it’s a global message to the bunch.”View image in fullscreenNight-time testing is a deterrent that sends ‘a global message to the bunch’, said David Lappartient.Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPALappartient is an International Olympic Committee member alongsidethe besieged Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, and was re-elected UCI president unopposed for a third term in September last year. He believes involving stakeholders is key to successful reform of sports governance. “I will not interfere in Fifa’s matters, but I can tell you that in the UCI transparency is important,” Lappartient said.“When we want to make a reform of professional cycling, we will first make a presentation to the teams, the riders and the organisers. We have consultation with the stakeholders.“I will not give advice to Fifa, but I think it’s important to work with this kind of transparency.”Explore more on these topicsTour de FranceCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kuwaki wins Women’s Open after Henseleit’s unlucky break off marshal’s leg in playoff | Women's Open | The Guardian
description: The 23-year-old wins her first major championship as Japan now has back-to-back Women’s Open victories
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: The 23-year-old wins her first major championship as Japan now has back-to-back Women’s Open victories
Content: Shiho Kuwaki of Japan won the AIG Women's Open 2026 at Royal Lytham & St Annes.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenShiho Kuwaki of Japan won the AIG Women's Open 2026 at Royal Lytham & St Annes.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAWomen's OpenKuwaki wins Women’s Open after Henseleit’s unlucky break off marshal’s leg in playoffJapanese 23-year-old wins her first major championshipEngland’s Charley Hull and Lottie Woad finish tied sixthEwan Murrayat Royal Lytham & St AnnesSun 2 Aug 2026 16.41 EDTFirst published on Sun 2 Aug 2026 15.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was no surprise that an extraordinary Sunday at the Women’s Open ended in such circumstances. Has the ankle of a marshal ever before played a crucial role in the outcome of a major championship? A competition that looked for so long as if no one wanted to win rumbled on at Royal Lytham & St Annes until fate played its hand.Glory for Shiho Kuwaki, pain for Esther Henseleit. That barely explains the half of it. Henseleit had forced a playoff with a stunning birdie from 45ft on the final hole of regulation play. On the first visit back to the 18th, Kuwaki played a glorious approach to secure her four and the extension of the tournament.Clicky Ponting and ‘known cheats’ on the golf course: the crisis in UK sportsmanshipRead moreWhat happened next was beyond anyone’s comprehension. Kuwaki found the fairway with a perfect drive. Henseleit cut her tee shot to the right, where it looked in enough bother before hitting the lower leg of a volunteer. The ball ricocheted to the bottom of a gorse bush. Henseleit did exceptionally well to advance the ball up the fairway but the clear advantage was with Kuwaki. Her four secured the trophy. Henseleit has legitimate cause to bemoan horrible fortune.Earlier, this was a tournament where the nerves associated with the pursuit of a major championship were writ large across the faces of those looking to win the Women’s Open’s 50th edition.View image in fullscreenShiho Kuwaki celebrates victory on the 18th green at Royal Lytham & St Annes.Photograph: Luke Walker/Getty ImagesKuwaki’s is the most unlikely of triumphs. Perhaps her lack of experience in this domain actually helped the 23-year-old as those around her wilted. Kuwaki had played in only one Women’s Open before, missing the cut at Royal Porthcawl last year. Lytham provided such a contrasting storyline and Japan now has back-to-back Women’s Open victories.Henseleit needed a birdie three at the last to halt Kuwaki. She sat 45ft from the hole in two, with the odds firmly stacked against her. The ball was 5ft from the hole when Henseleit knew its destination. Kuwaki surely feared the worst but she need not have worried.Henseleit earlier offered a snapshot of what played out on this major Sunday. The German tied Kuwaki’s minus five with a tap-in birdie at the 15th. From the very next tee, Henseleit hooked a three wood into long grass. A bogey ensued. It was as if anyone who earned a proper view of the Women’s Open trophy was immediately blinded by the light.View image in fullscreenEsther Henseleit misses her crucial putt in the playoff.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAYealimi Noh held a three-shot lead after 54 holes. She even increased that advantage by one before wobbles started at the 4th. Noh posted a 74 before admitting it “stung” to fall short in this manner. She was one shy of the playoff mark of five under.On the final hole, in the final group, Henseleit and Noh had the opportunity to force Kuwaki into extra time. Both missed the fairway, with approaches leaving only the remote chances of birdies. Noh left her attempt short, moments after her playing partner had stunned the crowd.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRyu Hae-ran, seeking a third major win in as many starts, carded a three over par 74. Jeeno Thitikul? 73. Nelly Korda closed in the manner of a world No 1 with a 68 – the lowest round among the top 13 names on the leaderboard – catapulting her into a share of fourth.Charley Hull and Lottie Woad never seriously looked like delivering a British winner for the third time in a row at Lytham. Hull’s 72 left her at minus one. Woad’s putter was colder than a winter’s morning in Siberia during her 73, which meant the same aggregate. Neither undertook media duties, which given their standing here was less than impressive. Tied sixth is hardly the stuff of disaster.Anna Nordqvist signed off with a 68 before admitting the stresses and strains associated with her European Solheim Cup captaincy. Nordqvist will name her four captain’s selections on Monday for the clash against the United States, which takes place in the Netherlands in September. Intrigue surrounds whether Ireland’s Leona Maguire will keep her place in team Europe despite indifferent form. Nordqvist made some calls to players during Women’s Open week, which she conceded affected her own performance at Lytham.“I think it’s hard to put it in words how hard it has been,” Nordqvist said. “I felt like as soon as I came off the course, it was just so much stuff about Solheim Cup, which has been hard because I really wanted to go and enjoy this week.“I felt really off the first day but managed to battle through. I played really well the second day and then yesterday, I didn’t really play that badly, but mentally I was just exhausted. I think it [the size of the job] has been a lot more than I expected. There has been a lot more practical stuff to deal with. Maybe looking back, it was going to be a tough task to do both [play and be a captain], but I’m very proud of myself for how I’ve done it.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's OpenGolfnewsShareReuse this content

title: Leeds stage thrilling comeback to sink Liverpool in Chicago friendly | Friendlies | The Guardian
description: Leeds came from two goals down to beat Liverpool 4-2 in a pre-season friendly at Soldier Field, Chicago
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Leeds came from two goals down to beat Liverpool 4-2 in a pre-season friendly at Soldier Field, Chicago
Content: Liverpool’s Ifeanyi Ndukwe and Lukas Nmecha of Leeds tussle for possession.Photograph: Daniel Bartel/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLiverpool’s Ifeanyi Ndukwe and Lukas Nmecha of Leeds tussle for possession.Photograph: Daniel Bartel/Getty ImagesFriendliesLeeds stage thrilling comeback to sink Liverpool in Chicago friendlyLiverpool 2-4 LeedsCalvert-Lewin scores twice as Leeds come back from 2-0 downAndy Hunterat Soldier FieldSun 2 Aug 2026 18.40 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter 45 minutes at Soldier Field the tale of Liverpool’s pre-season tour of the US was of three straight wins and Andoni Iraola’s ideas taking shape thanks in no small part to Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak. After 90, with Liverpool’s expensive duo off the scene, it centred on a stirring Leeds fightback and the recurrence of a fragility that Iraola could well do without.Daniel Farke’s team staged a convincing comeback to inflict a first defeat of pre-season on the new ­Liverpool head coach. Dominic ­Calvert-Lewin, twice, Brenden Aaronson and Sean Longstaff all scored in the space 25 minutes as Liverpool failed to deal with Leeds’ strength at set-pieces and the disruption caused by a series of half-times changes. The drop-off from Liverpool, who led 2-0 at half-time, following the departures of Wirtz, Isak, Trey Nyoni and Rio Ngumoha was drastic.“Why are there so many fans?” an incredulous Chicago police officer asked his colleague as the crowds descended on Soldier Field, a stadium as impressive in design and location as the skyline that towers behind it. More than 32,000 had been present the previous night to see Robert Lewandowski mark his home debut for Chicago Fire with both goals in a 2-1 win over Dean Smith’s Charlotte FC. The lure of Liverpool and Leeds, even for a friendly, attracted an eye-catching 49,128 to the edge of Lake Michigan.Wirtz and Isak had missed the midweek win over Wrexham in New York having started pre-season training only on Monday. Ring-rusty or not, they both brought an immediate improvement to Liverpool’s performance level and displayed a rapport that will be crucial to realising Iraola’s vision next season.Isak looked sharper, more aware of his teammates and more involved in a Liverpool performance than he did during a first season hindered by fitness and injury problems. The Sweden international played all four of his country’s games at the World Cup and, Liverpool will hope, may not need too much time to get back up to speed as a result. That appeared the case here.It was Isak who instigated the counterattack that led to Liverpool winning a corner having weathered early set-piece pressure. Dominik Szoboszlai took it, Milos Kerkez deftly flicked it across the six-yard box and Luke Chambers lashed in the finishing touch. Isak also led Liverpool’s pressing game with an aggression and relentlessness that augurs well.Wirtz was involved in much of Liverpool’s best work during his 45 minutes on the pitch. His instinctive link-up play with Isak and Ngumoha, who gave James Justin a torrid time at right back, caused Leeds frequent problems. Liverpool’s second goal five minutes before the break was a delight. Nyoni, who has enjoyed a fine tour at the heart of Iraola’s midfield, floated an inch-perfect cross into Jeremie Frimpong’s run down the right. Frimpong hooked the ball back across goal first time and Wirtz stole in between three Leeds players to slide home. On the touchline Farke berated the officials over an offside call that went ignored in the buildup.Nyoni, Ngumoha, Wirtz and Isak were replaced as planned at the interval by Ryan Gravenberch, making his first appearance under Iraola, Lewis Koumas, Federico Chiesa and Curtis Jones respectively. Farke also made four half-time changes and the introduction of Calvert-Lewin, the new signing Harry Wilson, Longstaff and Aaronson brought the necessary improvement. The contest was completely transformed.The Leeds comeback commenced with a mistake by Kerkez. His over-elaborate back-heel was seized on by Ethan Ampadu, who released Aaronson in space on the left of the Liverpool penalty area. The USA international beat Giorgi Mamardashvili with a confident low finish. Calvert-Lewin levelled from close range after Joe Rodon flicked on a long throw from Ampadu and, just two minutes later, a third of Farke’s half-time substitutes put Leeds ahead in slapstick fashion. Jones attempted to sweep away Aaronson’s low cross into the Liverpool area and succeeded only in turning the ball against Longstaff. The Leeds midfielder looked sheepish after the rebound trickled beyond a stunned Mamardashvili.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLeeds were not done there. Worryingly for Iraola, his team were undone by an identical routine to Calvert-Lewin’s first goal. Another Ampadu long throw, another flick on, this time by the commanding new recruit Tarik Muharemovic, and the former Everton striker inflicted more punishment on Liverpool by converting a towering header off the underside of the crossbar.Explore more on these topicsFriendliesLiverpoolLeeds UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: The five big beasts are gone: who will be the Premier League’s next alpha manager? | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Arsenal’s Mikel Arteta is perhaps best placed to fill the void but the coaching contenders are legion as another season looms
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: Arsenal’s Mikel Arteta is perhaps best placed to fill the void but the coaching contenders are legion as another season looms
Content: The big beasts of the Premier League and the possible contenders to join their realm this season.Composite: Getty Images, ReutersView image in fullscreenThe big beasts of the Premier League and the possible contenders to join their realm this season.Composite: Getty Images, ReutersInside footballArsenalThe five big beasts are gone: who will be the Premier League’s next alpha manager?Jonathan WilsonArsenal’s Mikel Arteta is perhaps best placed to fill the void but the coaching contenders are legion as another season loomsSun 2 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareThis used to be a land of giants. This used to be a land where big men fought. This used to be a land where Sir Alex Ferguson and Arsène Wenger tussled, then José Mourinho joined the fray. This used to be a land where Jürgen Klopp made Pep Guardiola reconsider, and he changed his style and won anyway.Not any more. Next season will be the first since the inauguralPremier Leaguein 1992 not to feature any of the five big managerial beasts – not Ferguson, not Wenger, not Mourinho, not Klopp and not Guardiola.Who should win the men’s Ballon d’Or?Read moreWhat’s come over our great land? The Premier League is still our home, but where have all the heroes gone? Where’s the man who ruled by fury? Or the man who made virtues of broccoli and sobriety? Where’s the man who made the conference room the pitch? Where’s the gegenpressingmeister, or the cold philosopher of the positional game? Now they take a man who instigated some interesting pressing patterns and they call him a regular hero. Where are the men who are willing to play the game?You don’t have to be a nostalgist in the vein ofBill Andersonto think that the Premier League looks a little diminished. Régis Le Bris took over at Sunderland two summers ago and already he is the fourth longest-serving manager currently at a Premier League club. While his quiet authority impressed last season, the understated Breton is no one’s idea of a main character. And it’ll take a while before the meeting of the two longest-servers, Mikel Arteta and Unai Emery, looks like a clash of the titans, even with the twist that Emery was Arteta’s predecessor at Arsenal.Tottenhamappointed Roberto De Zerbiin March and, the promoted sides excepted, he has already been a Premier League manager longer than 11 of his rivals. All long-running dramas go through this process. Major characters move on, new ones arise. At least they are easier to tell apart than in House of the Dragon: they don’t all have the same hair, and they are not all bafflingly interrelated. Still, it will take time for the new breed to become familiar. Quirks have to be learned, strengths and weaknesses understood.View image in fullscreenRoberto De Zerbi has the charisma of a leading figure.Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/PAThe result is that this season looks as hard to call as any in living memory. Perhaps the Premier League has entered its Arsenal era and Arteta will soon squat like a giant toad across English football. But retaining the league is difficult, particularly given the emotional outpouring that inevitably comes with ending a lengthy drought. Neither Declan Rice nor Bukayo Saka looked especially fresh at the World Cup, whileWilliam Saliba damaged his back. It would be no great surprise if Arsenal started the season slowly.But who is equipped to take advantage? The previous two league title winners are under new management.Enzo Maresca– Guardiola’s replacement at Manchester City – is a curious manager in that his record is rather better than the experience of watching his teams play. Although his reputation was enhanced by Chelsea’s decline after his departure, it shouldn’t be forgotten just how frustrated Leicester and Chelsea fans became at times with the cautious nature of his football. Arne Slot showed at Liverpool that it is, at least in the short term, possible to thrive when following one of the big beasts but it remains an enormous challenge to succeed somebody who has defined the personality of a club.Andoni Iraola impressed at Rayo Vallecano and Bournemouth, but the truth is that it’s impossible to know how anybody will adapt to the greater scrutiny of a club such as Liverpool, no matter how composed they may previously have appeared.There’s a lingering doubt about his Bournemouth’s propensity to concede late goals. It may be thata deeper bench offersan immediate solution but equally that could indicate a problem with load management – and that is not going to be made any easier by involvement in the Champions League. Iraola has always relied on extremely physical training sessions, but they will have to be tempered, at least to an extent, by the demands of European football, in which Iraola has little experience.Similar questions can be asked of Michael Carrick at Manchester United. He did enough last season that United effectivelyhad to appoint him, without doing enough to offer overwhelming proof of his abilities. Signings so far seem to have addressed the right areas in the squad, but the big issue is whether he can handle the demands of playing in multiple competitions. United finished third last season without ever playing a team who had played fewer matches than them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhere all 20 Premier League clubs should strengthen before the seasonRead moreSo demanding is the modern calendar that fatigue may end up being a bigger factor than any manager. If you are a superclub, the key to having a bad season, as United have demonstrated, is to have one so bad that you don’t qualify for any form of European competition.View image in fullscreenXabi Alonso endured an awkward few months at Real Madrid but has the time to impose his ideas at Chelsea.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersWhich is extremely good news for Chelsea. Not only do they have, in Xabi Alonso, one of Europe’s most promising young managers but he has timeto impose his ideasand his side will be fresher than their opponents in almost every game this season.Emery’s domination of the Europa League has paradoxically given him a reputation of not quite being of the highest tier, but if Aston Villa can find a way ofwinning games beyond Morgan Rogersthrashing long-range efforts into the top corner, he has a great opportunity to impose himself. De Zerbi, who has the charisma of a leading figure, should also find himself in the Champions League qualification shake-up given Tottenham’s summer signings and their lack of European football.The big beasts may have gone but that simply means the Premier League is entering a new phase. What matters now is the battle to be the next alpha. Arteta is perhaps best placed, but the contenders are legion. The land awaits its next giant.Explore more on these topicsArsenalInside footballMikel ArtetaMichael CarrickRoberto De ZerbiUnai EmeryAndoni IraolaEnzo MarescacommentShareReuse this content

title: Man arrested after Scottish woman found dead inside suitcase in Athens | Greece | The Guardian
description: Greek police say 26-year-old Afghan national is believed to have left Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s body in derelict building
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Greek police say 26-year-old Afghan national is believed to have left Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s body in derelict building
Content: Elisabeth-Jane Ross is believed to have died between five and seven days before her body was found on 18 July.View image in fullscreenElisabeth-Jane Ross is believed to have died between five and seven days before her body was found on 18 July.GreeceMan arrested after Scottish woman found dead inside suitcase in AthensGreek police say 26-year-old Afghan national is believed to have left Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s body in derelict buildingHelena Smithin AthensSun 2 Aug 2026 14.29 EDTFirst published on Sun 2 Aug 2026 10.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreek authorities have arrested an Afghan national in connection with the death of a Scottish woman whose body was found in a suitcase in an abandoned building in central Athens.Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, a charity worker described as an “angel full of innocence and goodness” by friends, had been in Greece for almost three weeks when she is believed to have died.Police sources said the suspect was a 26-year-old Afghan citizen who had allegedly confessed to the crime. He had been brought in for questioning by Greece’s homicide division last Thursday, two days after Ross’s body was publicly identified.A statement released by police on Sunday said: “A criminal file has been opened against a 26-year-old foreign national for intentional homicide, robbery and violation of the law [regarding] weapons.”Explaining the accusation of ownership of illegal weapons, security officials said “various arms – some real, some fake” had been discovered in the suspect’s home, also thought to be in the downtown area of Kypseli where the body was discovered.He is expected to be charged on Monday.Throughout the investigation, Greek authorities had worked closely with the UK’s National Crime Agency (NCA) and Police Scotland, according to the statement.Ross, who had strong links with the charity sector in Greece, is the daughter of a prominent lawyer in Edinburgh, where she also lived.She was reported to have friends in Kypseli, where her body was discovered on 18 July by a homeless man in what had once been a car park. Wrapped in cloth, it had been placed in a suitcase left in a decrepit, rubbish-strewn building at the site.Sources told the Guardian that the suspect’s alleged use of credit cards that belonged to Ross had contributed to police identifying him.“He was caught on camera withdrawing money with the cards from various ATMs,” one said. “The credit cards belonged to Ms Ross. That played a big role in leading us to him.”For days, investigators were unable to make headway, citing the lack of fingerprints or DNA on the suitcase. Adding to the mystery was the discovery that her mobile phone had been used until the time when the body was publicly identified last week.Police had described text messages sent to her father and other members of her family as deliberately misleading. The messages had spoken of her “need to be alone”.The Briton’s “dispersed movements” in the days leading up to her death had made the quest to track her killer even harder.After leaving the home of close friends in Keratsini, a suburb close to the port of Piraeus, where she had stayed for two weeks after flying to Greece, she had gone her own way, renting an apartment in the district of Exarchia in downtown Athens.Greek media outlets reported the suspect had been found in possession of the keys to the rental apartment and that he was “the partner” of one of the Briton’s friends.“As confirmed, the victim arrived in the country on June 26 and stayed at the home of friends until July 10, from where she departed to an unknown [address],” the police statement said.The homicide division said it had made the announcement after amassing evidence that proved the Afghan had “placed the body in the case and carried it to the abandoned car park” in Kypseli.Analysis of CCTV footage had played a role.“The subsequent preliminary investigation … using investigative material and digital analysis of video footage, proved the involvement of the 26-year-old foreign national in the incident. [He] was brought in [for questioning] on 30 July and confessed to his actions,” the statement said.It remains unknown how Ross died. Media reports quoted the suspect as telling police that when he visited the flat in Exarchia he had discovered her lifeless body in the bathroom.An initial on-site postmortem showed there were no evident signs of injury or struggle on the Briton’s body but proved inconclusive because of advanced decomposition. Authorities have fast-tracked toxicological tests and analysis of vital organ tissues to determine the cause of death.Grigoris Leon, who heads the Hellenic Society of Forensic Medicine, told the Guardian that examination of the lungs and eyes would help provide answers and determine “whether she had died a natural death”.As tributes have poured in, flowers have been left beside the abandoned lot in Kypseli. One note read: “Here lies an angel.”One friend in Edinburgh agreed with that, saying: “We have lost an angel, an angel full of innocence and goodness who only wanted to help people wherever she went.”The UK Foreign Office previously said: “Our thoughts are with Elisabeth’s family during this difficult time. We are providing consular support and are in contact with the local authorities.”A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We are aware of the death of a Scottish woman in Athens and are liaising with authorities in Greece. Officers are providing support to her family in Scotland.”Explore more on these topicsGreeceScotlandEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: RFK Jr tells US families to vaccinate children against measles amid outbreak | Robert F Kennedy Jr | The Guardian
description: Health secretary, longtime vaccination skeptic, spent years boosting misinformation about vaccines including MMR
Author: Ed Pilkington
Headline: Health secretary, longtime vaccination skeptic, spent years boosting misinformation about vaccines including MMR
