Content: Robert F Kennedy Jr participates in a cabinet meeting at Camp David in Thurmont, Maryland, on 31 July.Photograph: Daniel Heuer/ReutersView image in fullscreenRobert F Kennedy Jr participates in a cabinet meeting at Camp David in Thurmont, Maryland, on 31 July.Photograph: Daniel Heuer/ReutersRobert F Kennedy JrRFK Jr tells US families to vaccinate children against measles amid outbreakHealth secretary, longtime vaccination skeptic, spent years boosting misinformation about vaccines including MMREd Pilkingtonin New YorkSun 2 Aug 2026 16.37 EDTFirst published on Sun 2 Aug 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRobert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, on Sunday told American parents that they should get their children vaccinated againstmeasles, as the surge in infections hasreached numbersnot seen in the past 35 years.Kennedy, a leading vaccination skeptic who has spent years amplifying misinformation about vaccines, including the shot that protects against measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), made his call in the course of a contentious interview with CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday morning.His remark came as the incidence of measlescrossed a milestone– the US has now officially recorded 2,371 confirmed infections so far this year, surpassing the total tally in 2025 of 2,289.Taken together, the past two years have seen more measles infections in the US than the rest of the 21st century combined. The last time agreater numberof measles cases were recorded in a single year was in 1991.Kennedy’s statement was extracted from him by Dana Bash, CNN’s host, who invited him to use his “bully pulpit” to talk directly to parents as the new school year approached. She urged him to tell families that they should vaccinate for measles “because it is safe and it will help them save their children’s lives”.US surpasses 2025’s record number of measles infections as cases climbRead moreThe health secretary replied: “Parents should get their children vaccinated for measles. A measles vaccine is effective, it stops measles in about 97% of the cases. People should get vaccinated.”Later in the interview he added that people should also get the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, the main protection against the disease that has been a particular target of the anti-vaccination movement.The health secretary’s call for parents to vaccinate their children for measles contrasts starkly with the many years in which Kennedy has been a leading proponent of misinformation questioning the efficacy and safety of vaccinations. Even since he became the country’s top health official, he has depicted a measles vaccination as a personal choice and claimed inaccurately that the power of the inoculationis waning.The call also comes late in the day, given the rate at which measles is spreading in the US. The 37 new measles outbreaks that have already been recorded this year are putting the US in danger of losing the measles elimination status that it has held since 2000.Kennedy continues to shrug off criticism that his work as a prominent vaccine skeptic, both before and after he entered theTrump administration, has exacerbated the problem. Asked whether he took any responsibility for the measles surge, he said: “Absolutely not.”He went on to blame the outbreaks on religious communities who eschew vaccines and on global health conditions.Any hope that Kennedy’s measles statement might indicate a change of heart were dashed in the rest of the CNN interview in which he turned combative. Batting off questions from Bash, the health secretary responded with personal attacks.He accused the CNN host of “saying nonsense”, “repeating like a parrot” and “making assertions you can’t support”. In one especially demeaning remark he said Bash had become “flustered”.“I’m not flustered at all,” she asserted in a calm voice. “I am frustrated because you are the HHS secretary and you are talking about things that lead to vaccine hesitancy in this country.”In a further comment dripping with condescension, Kennedy told Bash “you probably don’t understand this because you’re not a scientist”.The journalist riposted: “But you’re not, either.”The health secretary’s belligerent approach, in which he at times appeared red faced while frequently poking his finger towards Bash, attracted the attention of commentators. The journalist Aaron Rupar described the performance as “RFK Jr’s epic CNN crashout” and said in apost on Xthat Kennedy’s “yelling” sounded like “a rabid dog barking”.‘It’s a peptide wild west’: how RFK Jr is clearing way for a market of untested drugsRead moreAndy Kim, the Democratic US senator from New Jersey, took from Kennedy’s comments that he and Donald Trump had no plans to prepare for a possible next pandemic. “The only thing they have a plan for is trying to distract you from the fact that they’ve taken away healthcare from millions,”Kim said.Kennedy used the CNN exchange to spread further misinformation about other aspects of public health. He claimed that both respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) that is a major cause of infant mortality and Lyme disease were caused by manipulation of germs in laboratories.The suggestion has been contradicted bydecadesof scientific evidence that suggest they both have natural roots. RSV was initially identified in the 1950s, two decades before such experimentation, known as “gain-of-function” research, started.During the interview, Kennedy repeatedunfounded claimsthat there was a link between Tylenol use during pregnancy and autism, and poured doubt on the efficacy of vaccines to protect children against Covid-19.Speaking to CNN’s State of the Union later in the show, Ashish Jha, who advised Joe Biden’s White House on its Covid response, said he was heartened to hear Kennedy say that “every kid in America should be getting the MMR vaccine”. But he added that much else of what the health secretary had said “just isn’t true”.Jha said that the dramatic rise in measles cases on Kennedy’s watch was not coincidental. “The administration has not done enough to promote vaccines. It has not done enough to highlight the harms that come from measles.”Explore more on these topicsRobert F Kennedy JrUS healthcareMMRVaccines and immunisationHealthUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: National Gallery security staff segregated like ‘second-class citizens’, curator claims | National Gallery | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Outsourced guards, largely from minority ethnic backgrounds, barred from staff hub for mainly white employees
Author: Dalya Alberge
Headline: Exclusive: Outsourced guards, largely from minority ethnic backgrounds, barred from staff hub for mainly white employees
Content: Security staff are consigned to a ‘stifling’ basement space with no facilities.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenSecurity staff are consigned to a ‘stifling’ basement space with no facilities.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyNational GalleryNational Gallery security staff segregated like ‘second-class citizens’, curator claimsExclusive: Outsourced guards, largely from minority ethnic backgrounds, barred from staff hub for mainly white employeesDalya AlbergeSun 2 Aug 2026 11.10 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe National Gallery’s security staff, of whom the vast majority are from minority ethnic backgrounds, are facing shocking segregation, a senior curator has claimed.Its outsourced guards are barred from the building’s high-quality “hub” – bright and airy recreation rooms that are available to the institution’s mainly white employees. They are not allowed to take their breaks there, or even sit in that area.Instead, they are relegated to a “stifling” basement space with broken furniture, continuing problems with rodents and no natural light or air-conditioning.Staff liken it to Upstairs, Downstairs, the television drama series that explored class relations in Edwardian England.The curator, who wished to remain anonymous, told the Guardian: “It’s almost become a running joke within the National Gallery. Security staff are being treated like second-class citizens.”View image in fullscreenThe National Gallery basement room used by outsourced security staffThe insider said gallery employees – everyone from curators to marketing staff – used thehub, which was created in previously underused spaces between and beneath the gallery’s exhibition halls, while outsourced security staff were prevented from doing so.They said: “There’s this beautiful hub area. You’ve got all the in-house, largely white staff in there. This has got potentially divisive for the gallery in the sense that the poor facilities in a basement area are used by black and Asian security staff.”While the hub has a heavily subsidised canteen and its own chef, the basement space is described as “dingy, dirty and dark”, with a kiosk offering little more than a KitKat and no cooked food.“It wasn’t meant for people,” the curator said. “It was meant for storage.”The National Gallery has reportedly told them that restricting the hub access is about avoiding overcrowding, but the security staff are still barred during weekends and holidays, when there are virtually no National Gallery employees using it.The curator added that on any one day there were perhaps 60 guards on site, but barely a handful took their break at the same time. “So the argument that the hub’s overcrowded is probably pushing it a bit,” the curator said.Security staff are represented by the PCS union, which believes they are being treated with “absolute contempt”, warning of the basement space: “Most dangerously, it is unventilated and accessible only by ducking under pipes.”Security staff are also said to feel the gallery is putting the collection at risk in expecting an individual guard to cover as many as four rooms at once.One observer said guards could only be in one room at a time and it was easy to distract them. Incidents in recent years have included activists from Just Stop Oil hurling tomato soup over Van Gogh’sSunflowersand attacking Velázquez’sRokeby Venuswith hammers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe basement is said to be stifling and inadequately ventilatedOn 1 July, PCS wrote to the gallery’s director, arguing that forcing a largely black and Asian workforce into the basement while the largely white staff “enjoy fresh air, sunlight and decent break and food facilities” was “potentially discriminatory under the Equality Act 2010”. PCS is still awaiting a reply.Nick Marro, the PCS culture group secretary, told the Guardian: “There is no excuse for the two-tier workforce … Our members deserve equal treatment.”Outsourced security staff are employed by CIS Security, which declined to comment.The National Gallery said: “Security staff do not have access to the hub offices. This has been the position since those offices were established due to wider space constraints, with dedicated facilities provided elsewhere in the gallery for security staff and other contractors.”The gallery said CIS had recently conducted a staff survey on workplace facilities and was implementing improvements in response to the feedback received.It said it had consulted security staff on what catering they wanted and they said they preferred to have a subsidised vending machine, which had since been installed.“The gallery closely monitors its estate and works with specialist contractors to manage and address any pest-control issues as part of its routine facilities management programme,” it said.“We do not comment on security operations, staffing levels or deployment arrangements, as these are kept under constant review and discussing them publicly could compromise security.”Explore more on these topicsNational GalleryLondonTrade unionsMuseumsnewsShareReuse this content

title: EU citizens in UK get letters telling them post-Brexit residency rights were given ‘in error’ | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: After years of building lives in UK, potentially thousands of EU citizens could be told they have no right to remain
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: After years of building lives in UK, potentially thousands of EU citizens could be told they have no right to remain
Content: A van driving around central London in June 2021 to remind EU citizens living in the UK to register for settled status.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA van driving around central London in June 2021 to remind EU citizens living in the UK to register for settled status.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockImmigration and asylumEU citizens in UK get letters telling them post-Brexit residency rights were given ‘in error’After years of building lives in UK, potentially thousands of EU citizens could be told they have no right to remainLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentSun 2 Aug 2026 08.42 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UKHome Officehas started stripping some EU citizens of their post-Brexit residency rights, in a move that has raised concerns about Britain’s compliance with its withdrawal agreement with Europe.The UK internal affairs authority has told at least 100 people that they were given residency rights “in error”, disrupting their lives just as they come to the end of their five-year “pre-settled status” and prepare to upgrade to the permanent “settled status”.A Portuguese woman working in the NHS and researching a PhD in Britain says her life has been turned upside down after being told by the Home Office she was granted post-Brexit rights to live in the country “in error”.She was granted pre-settled status under the EU settlement scheme, similar to 1.3 million others who had been in the country for fewer than five years before the UK left the EU.She had expected that this would be upgraded to settled status without issue and was dismayed when the Home Office told her her status was a mistake.“I feel so overwhelmed, because this is going to influence so many spheres of my life,” said Gabriela, whose name has been changed to protect her identity. She said she was fearful of the hostile environment that may kick in if her legal right to stay in the UK expired.“I can lose my job, I maybe don’t have the right even to rent the property that I’m living in now, because of course I have to prove my right to live here to the landlord to rent a place.“My bank account might also be affected. I work in the NHS as well, I work with other surgeries as well, so I have three different contracts in different places and I don’t know how it’s going to be if this happens, It’s just very stressful.”Gabriela is one of more than 1 million EU citizens who were granted “pre-settled status” to remain legally in the UK because they had been in the country for fewer than five years before Brexit.The Home Office is now reviewing the cases of those who are required to apply to have their status upgraded to full “settled status”, including children, non-European Economic Area (EEA) citizens and anyone who arrived after 31 December 2020.It declined to say how many people it had written to, but through a freedom of information request the3million campaign group has been told that 95 people were contacted in March alone.Gabriela is Brazilian-Portuguese, however she did not have a Portuguese passport at the time of her application, something that is now being questioned by the Home Office.In a five-page letter, the Home Office said: “It has come to our attention that you were granted pre-settled status without the evidence required to confirm that you meet the definition of ‘relevant EEA citizen’ before midnight 31 December 2020, when the UK legally cut ties with the EU.“On the basis of the information and evidence that is currently available, it is therefore considered that your pre-settled status was granted in error,” it added.Gabriela said she had been totally open with the Home Office and had “not excluded anything” including the fact that her father is Portuguese, making her an EU citizen by birth.“Citizenship is by blood so it is not something I have changed since I was born,” she said.Monique Hawkins, the acting chief executive of the3million, said the impact of the Home Office’s retrospective review was devastating for many.The group has knowledge of dozens of cases but fears there may be hundreds or thousands like Gabriela who will be hit by similar letters threatening removal from the country.“People applied to the EU settlement scheme in good faith and were granted status by the Home Office years ago. They acted on those decisions in good faith by building their lives in the UK and putting down roots.“We hear from people who are progressing in their jobs, from those whose children are in schools and have known no other country, and now, five years on, when they apply for settled status, they are being told that it was all a mistake. Imagine building a life somewhere and having it ripped out from under you like this.”Gabriela is appealing against the Home Office decision but the issue of “in error” cases has raised alarm bells at the Independent Monitoring Authority (IMA), the statutory body set up to monitor the implementation of the EU citizens chapter of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement (WA).In a statement, it said it “has raised concerns with the Home Office that the policy may be incompatible with the EU withdrawal agreement”.Hawkins said that under the WA, status “should only be removed if it is genuinely proportionate to do so”, but said “the Home Office is simply side-stepping that … entirely”.She said the approach was “completely unacceptable” and called on the Home Office to reconsider its policy.The Home Office said it had a longstanding policy not to routinely comment on individual cases.It said people who it judged had been granted status in error could apply to remain through other inmigration routes such as visa stays.It added that it would allow people to stay until their pre-settled status had expired, during which time they could seek alternative arrangements. They could also apply for full settled status, and if that was refused, legally they could appeal.The subheading and main text of this article were amended on 2 August 2026. A reference to “hundreds of thousands” of people potentially receiving letters threatening removal should have been to “hundredsorthousands”.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeBrexitForeign policyEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Climate change kills’: Pedro Sánchez speaks plain truth to Spain’s deniers | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: PM has long history of speaking out on realities of global heating but political opponents remain unnmoved
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: PM has long history of speaking out on realities of global heating but political opponents remain unnmoved
Content: Pedro Sánchez: ‘It’s not enough to address the consequences of the climate emergency … we have to reduce its causes.’Photograph: Mariscal/EPAView image in fullscreenPedro Sánchez: ‘It’s not enough to address the consequences of the climate emergency … we have to reduce its causes.’Photograph: Mariscal/EPAClimate crisis‘Climate change kills’: Pedro Sánchez speaks plain truth to Spain’s deniersPM has long history of speaking out on realities of global heating but political opponents remain unnmovedSam Jonesin MadridSun 2 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJust over four years ago, Spain’s prime minister,Pedro Sánchez, visited a small town in the south-western region of Extremadura that had been affected by one of the wildfires devouring tens of thousands of hectares of land across the country.That summer’s blazes had lefttwo people deadin the northern region of Castilla y León and another man therefatally burned after the excavator he was using to try to dig a firebreakto protect his town was swallowed up by the flames. Astreet-sweeper in Madrid had collapsed and died from heatstrokewhile on shift in soaring temperatures that summer. The paramedics who tried to save him noted that his body temperature was 41.6C (107F).“I want to make something very clear,”the prime minister told reporters in Extremadura that dayin 2022. “Climate change kills: it kills people, as we’ve seen; it also kills our ecosystem, our biodiversity, and it also destroys the things we as a society hold dear – our houses, our businesses, our livestock.”View image in fullscreenPedro Sánchez (centre) visits fire-affected areas of Extremadura in 2022.Photograph: Ballesteros/EPAEarlier this week – amid wildfires that have consumed more than 180,000 hectares (428,915 acres) of land in the first seven months of 2026 – he repeated the same blunt warning.“The climate emergency kills,”he said on Monday. “And that’s why it’s not enough to address the consequences, which we do; what we have to do is reduce its causes, anticipate its effects, and, consequently, better prepare our country to protect people’s lives.”Just as he has been one of the most vociferous European leaders when it comes to criticisingIsrael’s conduct in GazaandDonald Trump’s war in Iran- anddefending the benefits of immigration– so Sánchez has long deployed unvarnished language to raise awareness of the climate emergency.On the face of it, that may come as little surprise: as a country on the southern frontier of the world’s fastest-heating continent,Spainis becoming increasingly vulnerable to the effects of the climate emergency, be they droughts, desertification, erratic weather patterns, heavy rains or wildfires.11:13Race against time to contain wildfires in France and Spain - The LatestAwareness, and perhaps personal experience, of the growing scale of the crisis is increasingly common. According toa survey published in December 2024by Spain’s state research institute, the Centre for Research Studies, 84% of Spaniards see the climate emergency as “a real threat to human wellbeing and to the health of the planet”.Despite the floods and the fires, however, there is little political common ground, and opposition parties have rejected Sánchez’s plans fora “state pact” to prepare Spain for the climate emergency.On Monday, Spain’s conservative People’s party (PP) accused the government of using the “mantra” of climate crisis to mask its “poor management” of natural disasters.As well as claiming the Sánchez administration had seized on the climate emergency as a wedge issue, the PP’s spokesperson, Ester Muñoz, appeared to question the notion of a human-driven climate crisis.“That the climate changes is something that has occurred throughout the history of humanity and the Earth – that’s obvious,” she said. “Now how do we humans act in the face of things that change?”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA forest engineer surveys the wildfire damage in Ávila, Spain.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersThe PP’s record on the climate crisis and emergency response is, to put it mildly, mixed. When floods hit Valencia at the end of October 2024, its PP regional president –who eventually resigned– was having a three-hour lunch with a journalist and did not arrive at the response centre until the early evening, by which time many people had drowned in their homes, garages and cars.Europe burns: a visual guide to the wildfiresRead moreUnlike her erstwhile Valencian counterpart, the PP president of the Madrid region, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, has been quick to ask the central government to step in and assume overall control of the wildfire response. But Ayuso, a rightwing populist, has questioned thescientific basis of the climate emergency and claimed it is an “agenda”pushed by “lobbies” and “communists”.Her views are reminiscent of those held by the far-right Vox party, which is adamant that the current wildfires have nothing to do with the climate emergency and everything to do with a failure to clear rural areas of excess vegetation and to invest in firefighting services. The PP has forged a series of regional alliances with Vox,heralding a possible national coalition if it wins next year’s general election.Experts and climate scientists say the blazes are down toa combination of factors: the abandonment of rural areas; an abundance of highly flammable, dry vegetation, and an increase in heatwaves driven by climate breakdown.On Wednesday, a Vox MEP, Jorge Buxadé, attempted to push the party’s denial agenda by posting whatpurported to be an official air ministry documentshowing that temperatures of more than 44C had been recorded at observation stations around Spain as far back as the 1950s.Spain’s state meteorological office, Aemet, responded on social media by pointing out that the document was a fake.“We’ve reviewed the data, and all but one station’s data are false,”said Aemet. “If they were true, they wouldn’t deny climate change: there were heatwaves before, but now they’re more frequent and intense.”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisSpainPedro SánchezEuropeExtreme heatWildfiresfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We cannot magic up more water’: the supply problems putting housing targets in England at risk | Water | The Guardian
description: Council leaders say crumbling infrastructure and lack of water are jeopardising government’s plans for new homes
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: Council leaders say crumbling infrastructure and lack of water are jeopardising government’s plans for new homes
Content: Low water levels on a reservoir in Walthamstow, north-east London. Half the country is in serious drought, raising questions over whether there will be enough water for new homes.Photograph: Matthew Chattle/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLow water levels on a reservoir in Walthamstow, north-east London. Half the country is in serious drought, raising questions over whether there will be enough water for new homes.Photograph: Matthew Chattle/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesWater‘We cannot magic up more water’: the supply problems putting housing targets in England at riskCouncil leaders say crumbling infrastructure and lack of water are jeopardising government’s plans for new homesSandra LavilleEnvironment correspondentSun 2 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe government’s housebuilding agenda is hitting the stark reality of a lack of water and crumbling infrastructure across the east and south-east ofEngland.Half the country was declared to be inserious droughtthis week, for the second consecutive year, with the Environment Agency warning of dire consequences for the economy, environment and wildlife.The parts of England in extreme water stress with residents underhosepipe bansare also where the government’s “build, baby, build” agenda is being targeted. Labour has promised to build1.5m homesby the end of this parliament – a strategy retained by Andy Burnham.Environmental pressures are already extreme in the south and east of England. In one area where increased housing numbers are being demanded, fenlands are close to collapse from over-extraction of water; in another, chalkstreams are having to be artificially maintained.Some water companies are clear there is “insufficient” water for new homes, a situation exacerbated by crumbling infrastructure.“We cannot magic up more water,” said Paul Harvey, the Independent leader of Basingstoke and Deane council, which is being told to build more than 1,000 houses a year inHampshire. “They say ‘build, baby, build’ but it is something we cannot just wave a wand and do.“The evidence of our water cycle study, which looked at whether we have enough water supply and sewage treatment capacity to meet the needs of future residents, showed demands for water from new housing may outstrip the limits of sustainable supply.”View image in fullscreenThe dried-mud basin of Grafham Water, in Cambridgeshire. The local MP Pippa Heylings says a lack of water is a ‘deal-breaker’ for the government’s growth plans for the county.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyAcross Hampshire, Kent, Hertfordshire, Essex andCambridgeshire, drought linked to the climate crisis and the failure of the water industry to build critical infrastructure means growth plans are hitting environmental barriers.Ali Morse, the water policy manager at the Wildlife Trusts, said: “This week we’ve seen drought declared across half of England, but even under normal conditions,water scarcityis emerging as an urgent issue.“If we don’t secure new water supplies and become more efficient with our use, it’s clear that, under a changing climate, we won’t have enough water to meet the needs of both society and the environment in future … but what most don’t realise is that across large parts of the country, we’re already reaching this limit.“Mapping by theEnvironment Agencyshows that even under normal flow conditions, there isn’t any additional river water available to serve new homes or industry across roughly a third of the country.”Around Basingstoke, the struggle to find water for the existing population is causing huge environmental damage to one of the largest remaining alkaline fens in southern England, pushing it toward irreversible ecological collapse, according toNatural England, which advises the government.The situation is so critical that the Environment Agency hasbanned South East Waterfrom taking more water from the Greywell chalk aquifer. The water company is appealing against the decision.South East Water has also failed to build a pipeline to channel water from the Surrey Hills to Basingstoke that it promised would be completed by 2030. Water regulators initially disallowed funding and there is no sign of the vital piece of infrastructure being built in the near future.View image in fullscreenDry grass at Parker’s Piece in Cambridge. The government wants to build 150,000 homes in Greater Cambridgeshire but measures to improve the supply of water have not been delivered.Photograph: Martin Pope/Sopa Images/ShutterstockThe housing target for Basingstoke has been increased from 830 to 1,150 new homes a year. In neighbouring East Hampshire, the number of homes required a year has risen by 98% to 1,142.Basingstoke and Deane council, Natural England and the Environment Agency have been unable to approve a local plan because there is not enough water to meet the government’s growth demands.Harvey said: “The Labour government’s unrealistic imposed housing targets don’t take account of the fact that the Environment Agency, Natural England and the water companies are all waving red flags about whether the water exists to supply them.”Damian Hinds, the Conservative MP for East Hampshire, said there were serious questions about the long-term resilience of water supplies for existing customers, especially in times of drought, and about whether the planned housebuilding was sustainable.“The existing water infrastructure is not capable of supporting development on that scale without infrastructure investment, which has yet to materialise,” he said.In Cambridgeshire, chalk streams are already being artificially filled by the Environment Agency because of over-extraction of water. Yet ministers are suggesting Greater Cambridgeshire can host another 150,000 homes as part of the creation of adevelopment corporation to spur growthand take decision-making away from elected councils.Lack of water is already a critical issue aroundCambridge. The 5,726 residents of the fenland village of Waterbeach – where another 4,500 homes are planned – are under a hosepipe ban.The Environment Agency initially refused plans for the new homes because of water scarcity, the significant risk to the environment and the inadequacy of the strategy from CambridgeWaterto meet future demand. But it lifted the objections in November 2024 as long as measures to increase water efficiency were adopted in Cambridgeshire.View image in fullscreenThe green square amid the brown outfield during a match at Maidenhead and Bray cricket club in Berkshire.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesThese include a credit scheme where developers pay to offset the water increases their housing developments will cause; conservation measures including a limit of 89 litres per person per day; promised investment in infrastructure from Cambridge Water, including a new reservoir; and a scheme where farmers can use land to store water.But two years on, the credit scheme is not up and running and no developer has paid in any money.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCritics say the water efficiency measures and promised new supplies will not be enough to meet the needs of the 150,000 homes and commercial developments the government is demanding.Sam Davies, a former independent councillor on Cambridge city council, said: “Residents are being told: ‘Don’t fill up your paddling pool, the splash pool is closed because there is no water.’ But commercially that growth is just ripping away at speed and no one wants to talk about the lack of water.”None of the water efficiency and supply promises take into account datacentre growth in Cambridgeshire,including one of the largest being planned in Englandat the innovation campus in Sutton.Pippa Heylings, the Liberal Democrat MP for South Cambridgeshire, said: “If you want growth then water is a deal breaker, that is the crux of the issue. Locally it was agreed that growth needed to be staggered, and that the water transfer scheme and the new Fens reservoir had to be built in order to support it.“But the government are now attempting to ‘unlock’ growth on the promise of water credit sales that have no evidence-base nor monitoring, and which are not up and running yet two years in.”View image in fullscreenBottled water is delivered to Royal Tunbridge Wells on 18 July after a failure at a South East Water treatment works.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAIn the Tonbridge and Malling area of Kent, as in Hampshire, South East Water says there is insufficient supply to build the 19,000 homes demanded by the government by 2042.Matt Boughton, the Conservative leader of the council, said: “There is not one specific water infrastructure improvement that would solve this. It is the culmination of a water sector that has simply not kept up with modern demand, and which is already facing significant increases in demand in terms of housebuilding over the last 20 years.“But ultimately it boils down to this: you can drill as many boreholes into acquifers as you want, but if the water isn’t there, you are still trying to extract the same natural resource from the ground which isn’t available.”Back in Basingstoke, council leaders are due to meet the new chief executive of South East Water this week to demand answers about when theSurreyHills pipeline will be built, and what level of housing the likely supply of water can support. They are also seeking a meeting with the housing minister Matthew Pennycook.Harvey said the council wanted to support a sustainable level of housing, but argued it was impossible to build homes while the infrastructure that made those properties livable was starved of funding.View image in fullscreenAll Saints church surrounded by the scorched grass of Blackheath Common in south-east London.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesHe said: “Roads, schools, GP surgeries and now, most fundamentally of all, water. The investment that should have built the Surrey Hills pipeline, upgraded the treatment works, and ended reliance on the crumbling Greywell source was instead siphoned off to shareholders and executives. Now the bill has come due.“This is what decades of water privatisation and successive governments’ failure delivers: a water company caught between a regulator that won’t fund the infrastructure and an environment that can no longer sustain the abstraction.”Nick Price, the head of water resources for South East Water, said: “We understand and appreciate the level of urgency surrounding the issues of water security and infrastructure delivery in the district.“We are reviewing and progressing options to reduce the risk to customers and the environment as quickly as possible.”A government spokesperson said: “We will build the homes this country needs and our water delivery taskforce will make sure that this is not constrained by water capacity, alongside our action to improve water efficiency and invest in new infrastructure like reservoirs.“Water companies have a duty to plan and deliver the infrastructure needed for new homes, and we’re working with areas like Cambridge and Basingstoke and Deane to address water supply challenges.”The government defended the creation of the Greater Cambridge Development Corporation and said it remained committed to the water credit scheme. It said officials were in regular contact with Basingstoke and Deane council and were listening to their concerns.Explore more on these topicsWaterHousingWater industryHousing marketExtreme heatCambridgeshireCambridgefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cleveland police failed to arrest man who later killed two-year-old girl | Police | The Guardian
description: Harrison Simpson was subject of arrest warrant for breaching court order 18 months before killing girlfriend’s daughter
Author: Neha Gohil
Headline: Harrison Simpson was subject of arrest warrant for breaching court order 18 months before killing girlfriend’s daughter
Content: Isabelle Rose Welsh was the victim of a ‘sadistic’ campaign of abuse, the judge said.Photograph: Cleveland police/PAView image in fullscreenIsabelle Rose Welsh was the victim of a ‘sadistic’ campaign of abuse, the judge said.Photograph: Cleveland police/PAPoliceCleveland police failed to arrest man who later killed two-year-old girlHarrison Simpson was subject of arrest warrant for breach of court order 18 months before killing girlfriend’s daughterNeha Gohiland PA MediaSun 2 Aug 2026 12.47 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCleveland police failed to arrest a paedophile for breaching a non-molestation order, 18 months before he sexually assaulted and murdered and his girlfriend’s two-year-old daughter, a court heard.Isabelle Welsh died on 14 September 2025 after what police described as a “campaign of violence” against her. The two-year-old collapsed at her home in Teesside after weeks of abuse that left her covered in bruises and with 21 broken bones.The toddler’s mother, Alexandra Walker, 26, and Walker’s boyfriend, Harrison Simpson, 22, were convicted of murder and child cruelty on Thursday after a trial at Teesside crown court.View image in fullscreenAlexandra Walker and Harrison Simpson.Photograph: Cleveland police/PASimpson was also convicted of sexually assaulting Isabelle before her death. Walker was cleared of that charge.The pair were jailed for life, with minimum terms of 28 years and six months for Simpson and 22 years for Walker, both minus time spent on remand.Cleveland police admitted that officers failed to execute a warrant issued by Teesside magistrates court for Simpson’s arrest in March 2024, according to the Sunday Times.Simpson had failed to attend court for breaching a non-molestation order, which is an injunction designed to protect victims of domestic abuse, when the warrant was issued in March 2024.It is understood the non-molestation order was in place after reports Simpson had harassed and threatened a woman.Cleveland police said in a statement: “Multiple inquiries and arrest attempts were carried out to try to locate and arrest him, but these proved unsuccessful.”It added: “We recognise the time Simpson had an outstanding arrest warrant is far from adequate. A review of this was immediately conducted upon his arrest for murder.“This review, along with a determination to continually improve our processes around suspect management, has led to a number of recent changes, such as ongoing improved visibility across the force around outstanding warrants, a comprehensive data system which tracks all outstanding warrants, and stringent oversight including a governance group led by a superintendent.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAt the sentencing, Justice Norton said Isabelle’s murder was “distressing” and said the two-year-old had endured a “sadistic” campaign of abuse.“Any death is a tragedy. The death of a very young child at the hands of those who should have cared for, protected, and loved her – as she no doubt loved them – is particularly distressing for all involved,” the judge said.A statement by the family of Isabelle Welsh previously said: “Isabelle should have had her whole life ahead of her, but she was taken from us in the most heartbreaking way. She was so loved and our lives will never be the same without her.”The senior investigating officer Det Ch Insp Steve Chatterton said the case was one of the worst he had dealt with. “The pain and suffering she experienced at the hands of Walker and Simpson was sickening,” he said.Explore more on these topicsPoliceCrimeNorth of EnglandEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kremlin connections: the Russia links to a £600m UK theme park | Business | The Guardian
description: French company Puy du Fou worked with a sanctioned oligarch on plans for a Crimea resort longer than disclosed, and later courted Iran and China
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: French company Puy du Fou worked with a sanctioned oligarch on plans for a Crimea resort longer than disclosed, and later courted Iran and China
Content: The Roman Colosseum spectacle at the Puy du Fou theme park in France. The company hopes to win planning approval for a £600m site in Oxfordshire. Photograph: Nathaniel Noir/AlamyExclusive: French company Puy du Fou worked with a sanctioned oligarch on plans for a Crimea resort longer than disclosed, and later courted Iran and ChinaByRob DaviesSun 2 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 08.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn February 2014, thousands of “little green men” – Russian soldiers in unmarked uniforms – flooded intoCrimea, seizing control of military bases and infrastructure.Their arrival marked the opening salvo of Vladimir Putin’s annexation of the peninsula, an operation that ultimately escalated into the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.In the months that followed the Crimean incursion, Washington and Brussels imposed sanctions on a host of Putin allies for allegedly providing backing for the assault. Among them was Konstantin Malofeyev, a bushy-bearded media mogul, whose far-right ultranationalist ideology has led him to be known as the “Orthodox oligarch”.Amid a western backlash, one powerful French family took a contrarian approach, extending the hand of friendship to Moscow and to Malofeyev.View image in fullscreenKonstantin Malofeyev is the founder of pro-Kremlin television channel Tsargrad.Photograph: Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP/Getty ImagesA month after EU sanctions against Malofeyev took effect, Philippe and Nicolas de Villiers, the father-and-son team behind a globally renowned theme park company called Puy du Fou, travelled to Yalta, Crimea’s historic Black Sea resort.In the splendour of the Livadia Palace, where Joseph Stalin, Franklin D Roosevelt and Winston Churchill had once thrashed out the post-second world war order, De Villiers Sr and Putin discussed the French company’s plans for two new parks.The venues, one of them in newly occupied Ukrainian territory, were to be a partnership with Malofeyev, and would “highlight Russia’s history and the significance of Russia’s soul”.In the end, those grand plans never bore fruit. Puy du Fou now has its sights set on different horizons.Within days, it is expected to win planning approval for a £600m park in ruralOxfordshire, complete with re-enactments, mock medieval castles, themed villages, hotels and restaurants.Map showing the planned Puy du Fou UK theme parkBut even as the company prepares to dramatise more than 1,000 years of British history, new evidence raises questions about the firm’s depiction of its own past.Puy du Fou has previously played down its past flirtation with Russia and Malofeyev, claiming it began winding down the partnership once EU sanctions were imposed in July 2014.But new documents seen by the Guardian indicate that the relations continued for many months and may, according to experts, have tested the very limits of EU sanctions. They also raise questions about the family’s willingness to work with other autocratic regimes.The documents reveal:Puy du Fou worked with Malofeyev’s company until August 2015.The French company made payments to a key Malofeyev aide.Executives discussed the risk of breaching sanctions.When the plan collapsed, Puy du Fou turned to new horizons, including Iran.The Chinese Communist party had script approval for a Shanghai park.To Russia with Love“When I see the spiral of sanctions and counter-sanctions, I think European leaders are irresponsible,” Philippe de Villiers, then 65, told the French radio station RTL in August 2014. “I would gladly swap [French leaders François] Hollande and [Nicolas] Sarkozy for Putin,” he added.A 34-year-old Nicolas put it more romantically.“He [Putin] is different from how we expected. He has sweet words and sweet eyes.”View image in fullscreenEmmanuel Macron with Nicolas and Philippe de Villiers at Puy du Fou in 2016.Photograph: Loïc Venance/AFP/GettyFresh from being charmed in Yalta, both men said their dream of expanding the business into Russia need not be derailed by the increasingly fraught relations between Moscow and the west.New evidence seen by the Guardian offers some insight into the partnership they had been building.At least one of the parks was to be named Tsargrad (translation: Imperial City), the same name Malofeyev uses for his own media company.View image in fullscreenA ‘term sheet’ document governing a 50:50 venture called Puy du Fou Tsargrad.Nicolas de Villiers and Malofeyev had already signed a “term sheet” document governing a 50:50 venture called Puy du Fou Tsargrad, according to a document seen by the Guardian.The timing of the agreement, signed on 12 July 2014, could not have been worse.On 30 July 2014, the Orthodox oligarch was placed under sanctions by the EU, over his alleged financial backing for the annexation of Crimea. The sanctions were designed to leverage western economic power to punish alleged participants in the Crimean incursion and deter further aggression.The sanctions, Puy du Fou told the Guardian, spelled the end of the partnership.“As the sanctions regime began to be implemented, in waves, we stopped working with a … now sanctioned individual we had been introduced to as a local partner.“When the wider international effort was clearly stalled and not improving, we quite appropriately took the decision we did not want to be involved in Russia, and thus withdrew from all our potential projects and partners there, which took a little over a year to unwind in an orderly fashion.”Material seen by the Guardian appears to indicate an ongoing relationship with associates of Malofeyev, geared towards keeping the project alive.In bed with an oligarchIn September 2014, two months after Malofeyev was placed under sanctions, Puy du Fou staff circulated a document internally, outlining how the Tsargrad project might be restructured to reflect the geopolitical situation.Organisational charts envisaged Malofeyev providing startup funding and short-term loans to a Russian entity, Tsargrad Puy du Fou LLC, which would pay the proceeds of operations to a bank account held by Puy du Fou International.Notes attached to the document refer to the account using Russian roubles to “avoid probable effect of sanctions”.View image in fullscreenChart showing plans for an offshore company jointly owned by Konstantin Malofeyev and Puy du Fou.Phase two of the scheme, according to the document, would involve the Russian entity being housed within an offshore company, jointly owned by Malofeyev and Puy du Fou.The offshore company would hold the intellectual property to the park’s carefully scripted shows and collect dividends flowing from Tsargrad’s takings, distributing them to Puy du Fou and Malofeyev.Another chart in the same document indicated that Malofeyev could remain a “minority shareholder” in a fund owning 50% of the offshore entity.Internal correspondence seems to suggest that Puy du Fou was aware of the risks of the reorganisation, telling its Russian partners in 2014 that it approved of the scheme but was wary of “the international context and the issue of sanctions”, which could expose the company to penalties.There is no evidence that this structure was ever put into place.But documents suggest that financial transactions with Malofeyev associates continued into 2015, funding activity that appeared to envisage the project going ahead as planned.View image in fullscreenA budget for an early phase of the Tsargrad projectA January 2015 budget document, seen by the Guardian, indicates that Puy du Fou continued casting actors for the project, even hiring a sports hall in Russia to stage the auditions.The 23.5m roubles (almost £500,000) budget included itemised sums for office rental, payment of staff and 75 wristwatches engraved with the Tsargrad Puy du Fou logo, described as “gifts”.Most of the payments were marked 31 January 2015, while at least one appears to cover a period up until April 2015.Puy du Fou said: “There have inevitably been some low-level supplier/consultancy fees on either side as one cannot explore an international project for free; these has never been with any sanctioned entity, in compliance with French and EU law.”Internal records raise questions about how Puy du Fou complied with sanctions law.They suggest that some of the transactions took place in partnership not with Malofeyev directly but with a business called Marshall Capital (MarCap).View image in fullscreenThe Viking show in the Puy du Fou theme park in Les Epesses, France.Photograph: Dimitri Carol/AlamyWhen the US followed the EU by placing Malofeyev under sanctions in December 2014, it also imposed restrictions on MarCapbecause of the Orthodox oligarch’s role as its managing partner.Records indicate that payments to MarCap employees during 2015 were funded, at least in part, by Puy du Fou.The French company’s main point of contact for ongoing discussions about the project and its budget, documents suggest, was Yury Leonov, an employee of MarCap and a key subordinate of Malofeyev.Correspondence with Leonov continued during July 2015, when he wrote directly to Nicolas de Villiers to discuss “payment of January’s invoice”.View image in fullscreenAn email header showing correspondence in July 2015, with Oleg Ochinsky copied in.Email exchanges between Puy du Fou staff in July and August were also copied to Oleg Ochinsky, a known business associate of Malofeyev, who was described in one internal document as Malofeyev’s “DG”, understood to mean “general director”.One such email sent in July 2015, a year after Puy du Fou claims to have begun winding down its project, bore the subject line “meteorological studies”.Puy du Fou does not appear to have taken a final decision to end its association with Leonov, Ochinsky and the Tsargrad project until at least August 2015.Michael Ruck, a partner and sanctions expert at the law firm K&L Gates, said: “The circumstances in this matter appear to raise questions in relation to sanctions compliance and whether the relevant restrictions would prohibit any of the ongoing activities.“When sanctions are imposed and a person or organisation is designated, the relevant restrictions apply immediately. There is no automatic wind-down period and any transactions undertaken which breach the sanctions restrictions are prohibited unless a specific licence or derogation is issued providing for such a wind-down period.”Puy du Fou declined to answer whether it obtained such a licence.It did not address the apparent transactions with MarCap employees or why it discussed “meteorological studies” with Leonov on a project that was winding down. The company said it had been “caught off guard by the rapid deterioration of the geopolitical situation in Russia and Crimea”.“Quite properly we cancelled this initiative once attempts to de-escalate the conflict had clearly failed and the international sanctions regime was being properly established,” it added.View image in fullscreenPhilippe de Villiers at an anti-abortion rally in Paris in January 2025.Photograph: Bastien Ohier/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty ImagesIf Philippe de Villiers found it hard to break from Malofeyev, the reasons were as much cultural as financial.There was a natural kinship between the French politician and the Orthodox oligarch, underpinned by faith and a brand of far-right politics deeply suspicious of groups such as Muslims and LGBT people.Philippe de Villiers is a career politician, a former minister in the government of Jacques Chirac who once harboured presidential ambitions and is feted as a hero by many in the Vendée region of westernFrance, where Puy du Fou is based.He founded his own party, Mouvement pour la France, in 1994. MPF’s manifesto included a ban on the construction of new mosques and a prohibition on gay marriage and same-sex adoption.As a leading figure in the far right in France, he has declared Islam incompatible with the French Republic and railed against LGBTQ+ rights. He is no longer involved in running the Puy du Fou business but remains a director.Critics, including left-leaning historians in France, have claimed that the family’s deeply traditionalist Catholic worldview has skewed the version of history depicted at Puy du Fou.Disneyland for dictatorsIn promotional material on its website, Puy du Fou sets out its ambition to “conquer the world”, a mission that has seen the company explore projects in countries ranging from Singapore to Spain and from India to Italy.In 2024, it opened the temporary City of Light show in Shanghai, bringing its brand of immersive drama to China.Guests donned red cloaks and entered an interactive choose-your-own-adventure show set in the 1930s, getting up close and personal with actors as they engaged in carefully choreographed fights or stage musical numbers.Puy du Fou’s success has always been underpinned its scripts, the first of which were written by De Villiers Sr.Capable of transforming mere re-enactment into gripping theatre, the scripts are perhaps the company’s most valuable asset.View image in fullscreenA gladiatorial fight at the Puy du Fou theme park in Les Epesses.Photograph: Abaca Press/AlamyIn China, the Guardian understands, the company appears to have been content to let Beijing apparatchiks, rather than its own staff, have the final say over the scripts.Internal messages, seen by the Guardian, show how senior executives bemoaned the “control of scripts by the government” yet appeared to accept this as an inevitability.Puy du Fou said: “As with any project in any country, there is a statutory approval process which in China also includes any scripts being shown to the relevant authorities for prior approval.“For absolute clarity, at no time did any individual nor any authority in China ever write or have control of any Puy du Fou scripts.”China was just one of Puy du Fou’s international ventures.Another proposed partnership might be particularly surprising, given the views of Philippe de Villiers about Islam.A letter seen by the Guardian – first published by the French satirical magazine Le Canard enchaîné – shows how the company courted the Iranian theocracy.Sent in 2016 by Philippe de Villiers to Iran’s ambassador to France, the letter expresses interest in a project that would showcase the “cultural refinement and historical depth of this great civilisation”.View image in fullscreenA mockup of Puy du Fou’s plan for its theme park in OxfordshirePhotograph: Puy du Fou/PAPuy du Fou said: “In 2016, at a time when sanctions were being lifted from Iran and many international companies were thus looking to invest again in the country, its French ambassador approached Puy du Fou to see if we were interested in pursuing a project there.After what Puy du Fou described as a “very preliminary initial engagement”, the Iran plan went the way of Tsargrad.Today, irrespective of the De Villiers’ sometimes controversial past, Puy du Fou’s international ambitions are flourishing. A Spanish park, which opened in 2021, is thriving and Puy du Fou now looks primed for its greatest international adventure yet, the conquest of Britain.Visit Britain, the tourist authority, has swung behind the project, as has the UK government itself. Planning approval is expected within weeks, with the opening scheduled for 2029.But as the first visitors flock through its doors to soak up British history, as told by Puy du Fou, questions remain about the story this French institution tells about itself.This article was amended on 2 August 2026. An earlier version stated that it was in September 2022 that Puy du Fou said it was wary of a proposed company reorganisation; in fact, this was in 2014.Explore more on these topicsCrimeaFranceTheme parksOxfordshirefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Undercover police unit closed down over unjustified surveillance, spycops inquiry told | Undercover police and policing | The Guardian
description: Senior officer behind closure says SDS caused ‘incalculable harm’ by infiltrating groups that posed no threat
Author: Rob Evans
Headline: Senior officer behind closure says SDS caused ‘incalculable harm’ by infiltrating groups that posed no threat
Content: PSNI chief constable Jon Boutcher, who closed the SDS when he was at Scotland Yard’s counter-terrorist division.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAView image in fullscreenPSNI chief constable Jon Boutcher, who closed the SDS when he was at Scotland Yard’s counter-terrorist division.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PASpycops scandalUndercover police and policingUndercover police unit closed down over unjustified surveillance, spycops inquiry toldSenior officer behind closure says SDS caused ‘incalculable harm’ by infiltrating groups that posed no threatRob EvansSun 2 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 01.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn undercover police unit that spied on tens of thousands of political activists had to be shut down amid severe criticisms and recriminations, the spycops public inquiry has heard.Jon Boutcher, a senior police officer who took over responsibility for the Special Demonstration Squad (SDS) unit, concluded within months that it had to be wound up because it was conducting unjustified surveillance and was badly run.He said most of the political groups being infiltrated “posed no threat to public order, let alone democracy”. They included pro-Palestinian supporters and leftwing groups.In contrast, very few undercover officers were being directed to infiltrate terrorist groups, he said. “At that time, society faced an increasing and enduring threat from international terrorism from which people were losing their lives, while almost no undercover capability existed to infiltrate those dangerous terrorist groups.”Boutcher, who was a detective chief superintendent in Scotland Yard’s counter-terrorist division at the time and is now the chief constable of thePoliceService of Northern Ireland, said the unit had to be closed down “pretty quickly”.Undercover police officer exposed by his own blunder, spycops inquiry hearsRead moreThe SDS had once been lauded as a “jewel in the crown” of Scotland Yard by its supporters within senior ranks.In searing criticism from an officer who has been involved in leading covert policing for years, Boutcher said the “abusive and inappropriate behaviour” of the SDS undercover officers had damaged members of the public.The officers routinelyformed intimate relationships with womenthey were spying on without telling them their real identities. Boutcher said the “sexual abuse of many vulnerable women by some SDS operatives” caused “incalculable and intolerable harm”.He said the SDS should never have spied on grieving families, such as the relatives of Jean Charles de Menezes,the innocent man shot dead by police on the London Undergroundin 2005. Nor should they have collected highly intrusive information about protesters, such as their friendships and living arrangements.View image in fullscreenA memorial to Jean Charles de Menezes outside Stockwell tube station in London. Boutcher said the SDS should never have spied on the dead man’s family.Photograph: Stephen Kelly/PAThe inquiry is examining the conduct of139 undercover officers in the SDSand another covert unit who infiltrated mainly leftwing organisations between 1968 and at least 2010. They assumed fake identities and pretended to be political activists in deployments that usually lasted four years.This week the inquiry heard how, in its final days, there was a “toxic” atmosphere between the unit and the more senior Scotland Yard ranks.Boutcher, with the agreement of his superiors, disbanded the SDS in what he called “quite a groundbreaking” decision as it had been running covert operations for 40 years.He said the SDS mounted “almost like a rearguard action” to justify its existence in what he characterised as a “very much siege mentality in many ways”.He said he suspected the SDS was gathering an “extremely limited” amount of useful information, and asked the unit to draw up a list of its successes in the previous five years. During that time, theundercover officers had spied onenvironment groups, the Socialist Workers party and campaigns against racism and the arms trade.The purported triumphs that were put forward by the SDS were “embellished and exaggerated”, almost “akin to fairytales”, Boutcher said.He also said he was concerned that public money allocated to the unit was not properly accounted for.The officers were claiming “vast amounts of overtime”, he said. When drastic cuts to these payments were proposed, many of them threatened to resign, the inquiry heard.Boutcher said the unit was poorly trained, and all but one of the undercover officers refused to undergo further training.Initially, Boutcher believed the SDS could be reformed and in particular re-oriented to infiltrate terrorist groups. But he concluded this was not possible because the SDS had become “insular and very parochial” and was resistant to change.Explore more on these topicsUndercover police and policingSpycops scandalPoliceMetropolitan policeLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Two helicopters collide outside Athens as Greece battles to control wildfires | Greece | The Guardian
description: Fire department says two-person crew of one aircraft killed in incident during gale-force winds to west of capital
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Fire department says two-person crew of one aircraft killed in incident during gale-force winds to west of capital
Content: Wreckage of a firefighting helicopter lies on a road after two helicopters collided while battling a major wildfire near Psatha, Greece.Photograph: Hellenic Red Cross/ReutersView image in fullscreenWreckage of a firefighting helicopter lies on a road after two helicopters collided while battling a major wildfire near Psatha, Greece.Photograph: Hellenic Red Cross/ReutersGreeceTwo helicopters collide outside Athens as Greece battles to control wildfiresFire department says two-person crew of one aircraft killed in incident during gale-force winds to west of capitalHelena Smithin Athens and agenciesSun 2 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTFirst published on Sun 2 Aug 2026 09.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo firefighting helicopters have collided west of Athens, killing the two-person crew of one of the aircraft, as efforts to control a massive wildfire barrelling towards the outskirts of the Greek capital intensified.Footage showed one of the helicopters losing control in the face of gale-force winds that have pushed flames towards settlements on Athens’ western fringes.“The pilots … were taken unconscious to hospital, where their death was confirmed,” said the fire department’s director of communications, Vassilis Vathrakogiannis.The Greek prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis said the two dead were a Dane and a Greek. The two crew members of the second helicopter were rescued.The helicopters had been leased from Australia’s McDermott Aviation, part of a fleet of 15. The company has said it has supported operations inGreecefor the past seven years.As Europe’s wildfire crisis fractured along different routes, and in further proof of the destructive force of climate-driven wildfires across the continent, the blazes ripped through Greece’s tinder-dry landscape, up mountain slopes and down to the sea, before encroaching on the capital.Warning of “extremely difficult” days ahead, Mitsotakis underlined the threat posed by gusts that in recent days have exceeded 78mph (125km/h).“When the winds blow with such force, even the dozens of aircraft we have at our disposal cannot operate safely,” he wrote on social media.More than 100 homes were destroyed overnight in fires that broke out around the popular coastal village of Porto Germeno, about 45 miles (70km) north-west of Athens. By Sunday, more than 500 firefighters and forest commandos had been dispatched to keep the flames at bay.View image in fullscreenA firefighting helicopter drops water over a forest near Porto Germeno, north-west of Athens, on Sunday.Photograph: Michael Varaklas/APThe eastern Mediterranean, no stranger to wildfires, has had a relatively calm summer to date, leaving Greeks to watch in horror as the blazes have hit farther west.As the advance of wildfires in Spain was finally curbed and officials inFranceannounced that a mega-fire – four times the size of Paris – had begun to be contained, the blazes in Greece have prompted mass evacuations and devastated huge swathes of land from Crete to the southern Peloponnese, the Ionian isle of Cephalonia and islands across the Aegean.Last week three Greek firefighters died from injuries sustained while they fought blazes.Extreme winds have been a blessing – in bringing down summer temperatures – but also a curse, with their-gale force strength obstructing firefighting efforts.Greece’s civil protection minister, Evangelos Tournas, a retired air force general, said at the weekend that the fire department had been “pushed to its limits”. He said high winds had created “extremely difficult conditions resulting in many cases where aircraft either cannot draw water or cannot carry out drops due to extreme turbulence”.View image in fullscreenPeople using olive branches to beat back the flames in the Megara valley, in western Attica, Greece, on Sunday.Photograph: Louisa Gouliamaki/ReutersFrance’s largest wildfireremained contained after 224,000 people wereforced to fleein what may have been the largest peacetime evacuation in French history. But active pockets still burned across 160 sq miles (420 sq km) of devastated forest.Thousands remained unable to return home, and nearly 3,000 firefighters were deployed against the Gironde mega-fire and a second blaze in Provence that had stopped advancing but remained uncontained.“The fire is now fixed, which does not mean that the fire is extinguished,” the Gironde prefecture said on Sunday, using the French firefighting term for a blaze whose advance has been stopped and whose perimeter has been contained.The region remained under France’s highest red forest fire alert. Dry conditions and soaring temperatures around Bordeaux, combined with afternoon winds, created a continued risk of renewed flames.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA deer in the forest in Le Temple, Gironde.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersAdditional firefighters from Ukraine, Lithuania and French Polynesia were expected on Sunday and Monday to reinforce the operation.Weather tracker: Why Europe’s wildfires are proving so fierce and difficult to stopRead moreHundreds of miles away, nearly 1,500 firefighters were battling a separate fire in the south-eastern Var department that tore through roughly 7 sq miles in little more than a day.Authorities said the fire in the Gros Bessillon hills was stabilised on Sunday morning, meaning its perimeter had not expanded overnight. But unlike the Gironde fire, it had not yet been declared contained.Firefighting aircraft supported crews working to keep the flames away from villages among the vineyards, olive groves and wooded hills of the region known as Green Provence. About 2,500 people were evacuated as the fire threatened communities.The blaze was the fourth major fire to strike the central Var since 19 July. A separate, smaller fire near Brignoles earlier in the week forced the Hollywood actor George Clooney and his family,along with about 700 other residents, to evacuate before it was brought under control.View image in fullscreenSmoke above Montfort-sur-Argens, near Correns, in Var, on Saturday.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersThe prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said France’s wildfires were generally under control but cautioned that conditions remained highly changeable.He announced that a national coordinator attached to the prime minister’s office would oversee reconstruction in fire-ravaged areas. More than 450 sq miles have burned across France since the beginning of the year.Fires in France andSpainalone have driven roughly a third of a million people from homes and holiday sites, emptied communities at the height of the summer and stretched firefighters, aircraft and emergency services across simultaneous disasters.The crisis is unfolding on the world’s fastest-warming continent.Europehas heated at more than twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service.Higher temperatures and prolonged drought leave forests and scrubland drier and more combustible, allowing fires to spread faster and burn more intensely. Human-caused climate breakdown doubled the likelihood of the extreme fire conditions that fuelled the French blazes, scientists at World Weather Attribution calculated in a rapid analysis on Thursday while the fires were still burning.The Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsGreeceWildfiresSpainFranceExtreme heatExtreme weatherEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘She showed love for everyone’: how did Daphy Michel end up frozen to death in a Pittsburgh bus shelter? | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: Haitian immigrant with mental illness found dead after ICE released her in 20F weather wearing summer clothes
Author: Alba Asenjo Domínguez
Headline: Haitian immigrant with mental illness found dead after ICE released her in 20F weather wearing summer clothes
Content: ‘Based on all available information during the investigation, the pathologist ruled Ms Michel’s death a homicide.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images/Michel familyView image in fullscreen‘Based on all available information during the investigation, the pathologist ruled Ms Michel’s death a homicide.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images/Michel familyICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)‘She showed love for everyone’: how did Daphy Michel end up frozen to death in a Pittsburgh bus shelter?Haitian immigrant with mental illness found dead after ICE released her in 20F weather wearing summer clothesFamily to sue after woman released from ICE custody froze to deathAlba Asenjo DomínguezSun 2 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the night of 26 February this year, the Michel family inPennsylvaniaexpected to see their loved one, Daphy, again very soon.After she had spent six months in jail, a judge had dismissed criminal charges against her and one of her brothers was told she would be released soon, probably the next day.He was worried about her severe mental illness, but was assured that someone would call him so he could pick her up. That was on a Thursday, and that call never came. The next one he received was on Monday, from a Pittsburgh hospital informing him that Daphy Michel, 31, had died.“At the court, I saw my sister. I saw Daphy. She wasn’t having any problem,” he said through an interpreter in an interview with Pittsburgh’s Action News 4, in which he asked to remain anonymous. He said that Michel came fromHaitito the United States in 2022 hoping to build “a safer life”.Maintenance workers had raised the alarm when they found her at a bus shelter on Pittsburgh’s South Side, more than 20 miles (32km) away from home and dressed in summer clothes. It was 20F (-6.6C) that morning. She was not breathing and had no discernible pulse, according to the local Port Authority police.In June, the medical examiner’s officeruled her deatha homicide. On Saturday, a lawyer for the familyannounced their decisionto file a lawsuit “very soon” because they want to see justice done.Michel was a resident of Charleroi and had been living in the US since 2022, having moved to the Pennsylvania community that has a significant Haitian immigrant population.Many questions remain about her life and death, but advocates say that the combination of lack of attention to mental health issues in detention, negligence in releasing vulnerable detainees and the sometimes informal cooperation among police forces triggered a cocktail of circumstances that ended in tragedy in early March this year.View image in fullscreenA screengrab from camera footage shows Daphy Michel sitting at a bus stop at 9.40am on 1 March in Pittsburgh.Photograph: Pittsburgh Regional TransitMuch detail from the three days spanning the moment Michel had the criminal charges against her dismissed in court, was arrested by ICE officers and released and then died a lonely death are still unclear. But footage from bus stop cameras released by Pittsburgh Regional Transit andobtained by Pittsburgh’s Public Sourceshow she didn’t move from the bus stop where she was found dead for more than 24 hours.The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) acknowledged that ICE processed Michel and placed her in removal proceedings before expected deportation – despite the fact she had a hearing in her asylum case coming up – right after she was released from Washington county jail to the south-west of Pittsburgh.The DHS then said in astatement on Xin June that ICE had “NOTHING to do with this woman’s death” because “she passed away THREE days after ICE encountered her”.The DHS also said Michel was “an illegal alien from Haiti” and that she was released “with all of her belongings, including a fully charged phone, in sunny weather in the middle of Pittsburgh, where public transport is readily available”. The DHS has not responded to questions from the Guardian regarding this story.Joseph Murphy, an immigration and civil rights attorney representing members of the Michel family in Pennsylvania, disputes many of those federal claims.He asserted that “neither her entry nor her presence in the United States were illegal” and that her phone, even if charged, wasn’t of any help because her plan had lapsed while she was in jail.He emphasized that it was freezing cold that day in Pittsburgh, that the south side of the city can be a “dangerous neighborhood” and, above all, that Michel’s mental illness was “obvious” and, for that reason, she shouldn’t have been left alone in the middle of a city she was unfamiliar with.“It was a very bad judgment call” by ICE, Murphy said. The attorney also said Michel didn’t speak English, and was illiterate and undereducated.She had been in jail for six months after suffering a mental health crisis on the street in Charleroi. People familiar with her noted that it had appeared she had refused to bathe during her time behind bars, highlighting the depleted state she must have been in when she was handed from local to federal enforcement and was soon spat out on to the streets of Pittsburgh with a ankle monitor.“At no point have I seen ICE show concern about people reaching their final destinations [after release from detention]. That hasn’t been the practice under either past or current US administrations,” said Adrianna Torres-García, deputy director of Free Migration Project, a Philadelphia-based organization that provides legal services for immigrants facing deportation.“Once people leave the detention center or jail where they were held, it’s as if it’s no longer ICE’s responsibility – they don’t worry about anything else, nor do they help them get to their destination, make plans or anything of the sort. Sometimes they just hand them a bus ticket, and that’s it,” they said.Torres-García added: “When Berks [the Berks County Residential Center in Pennsylvania, a detention center that closed in 2023] was still open, they would do things like hand someone a bus ticket and say: ‘Well, good luck,’ regardless of whether it was summer or winter, or whether the person had family. We were the ones who stepped in, community and grassroots organizations, to pick that person up, find out where they wanted to go and get them to their destination.”View image in fullscreenMichel on the ground at a bus stop in Pittsburgh at 7.55am on 2 March.Photograph: Pittsburgh Regional TransitIn June, the Allegheny county medical examiner’s office ruled Michel’s death a homicide, saying she was a “vulnerable adult” suffering from “untreated severe mental health issues and a significant language barrier”.“Based on all available information during the investigation, the pathologist ruled Ms Michel’s death a homicide. A homicide ruling is a standard manner of death determination indicating the death was caused by the actions of another individual. A homicide determination is not to be interpreted as a declaration of criminal guilt,” Jim Madalinsky, senior public information officer for public safety at the Allegheny county police department, said.
