Detectives began investigating last month.Haddy Gassama, senior policy counsel at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), said that ICE releasing people far away from their homes and sometimes without their belongings or medication is something that “happens enough that people have started to flag it”.“There’s no sort of legal requirement or categorical legal requirement that ICE returns someone exactly to the point of arrest, but the agency is supposed to have discretion on where they’re supposed to drop people, and part of that discretion is that you know they’re supposed to take into account the vulnerability of the person,” Gassama said. “This includes looking at, for example, the weather that day, if this person has any physical or mental issues, where dropping them far away from where they were picked up would cause them any kind of danger. I think this really raises a question around ICE’s own internal practices and the need for stricter guidelines and standards on their practices of release.”Some members of the Charleroi and Pittsburgh communities wonder to what extent an ugly narrative against Haitians from Donald Trump, close allies and the Make America Great Again (Maga) right wing might have influenced what happened to Michel.In 2024, in Springfield, Ohio, bomb threats and neo-Nazi marches followed Trump’s false claims of Haitians eating people’s pets, andCharleroi attracted rightwing YouTubers and KKK groups posting recruitment pamphlets on local Facebook groups. Pennsylvania is among the states with the largest population of Haitians, numbering roughly 27,000.In September 2025, Michel was arrested on misdemeanor charges. According toPittsburgh’s Public Source,a neighbor witnessed what she believed to be Michel having a mental health crisis, holding a knife and yelling.Murphy, the attorney, wondered why this incident wasn’t reported until more than 24 hours later. In any case, Michel spent six months in jail before a district judge dismissed criminal misdemeanor charges against her in late February, a period of time behind bars that some advocates consider excessive given the charges.Also, how she was treated in jail might have been crucial, Gassama said.View image in fullscreenMichel lying on the ground at the bus stop at 8.57am on 2 March.Photograph: Pittsburgh Regional TransitAnother fact some members of the community can’t get out of their heads is that Michel was alone at the bus stop for many hours without receiving any discernible help.Jaime Martinez, executive director and founder of Frontline Dignity, an immigrant rights and rapid response organization in Pittsburgh, received a call to the organization’s hotline from somebody near a bus shelter on the night of 1 March. The caller said she had talked to a Haitian woman who seemed to need help. Through Google Translate, she understood that the young woman didn’t speak English and believed that she was going to be picked up to go home. Martinez was out of town at that time and referred the caller to other rapid response numbers. The anonymous caller may have contacted the police, but it’s unclear whether that happened or whether there was a response.Since then, Martinez has felt devastated that he might have been able to save Michel, although there’s no way to know whether the call was about her.“I believe that we need to observe all our brothers and sisters as neighbors,” Martinez said. “Because there could have been other people who saw her at that bus stop and who just didn’t think of her like somebody they should help. There were plenty of buses, plenty of people that drove those buses, that saw her for many hours and they did absolutely nothing. We have a responsibility as neighbors, as humans, we need to have a radar to detect what’s going on in our community and in the spaces that we occupy.”In her obituary, Michel’s family described her as a “person with a kind heart”.It read: “Since she was a child, she showed great respect, courage and love for everyone. She was always ready to help those who needed her help and her presence brought joy and happiness and light into the lives of all who knew her.”Her parents, three sisters and two brothers believe they need to find justice for Michel, who was born in 1994 in Aquin, a city in the south of Haiti, who didn’t live to turn 32, attend her immigration hearing or even sleep in her own bed again. The family is grieving and staying private, while many friends aren’t speaking in public out of respect for the family.Surrounding the Michel family is a broad community of locals and immigrants who recognized Daphy Michel as a neighbor and do not want the case to be forgotten. They have also asked for support for Haitian communities in the US since the supreme courtruled in Junethat the Trump administration has theright to terminatethe temporary protected status (TPS) of hundreds of thousands of Haitians and several thousand Syrians in the US.Some people are organizing vigils and fundraisers over Michel’s death.“It is an absolute tragedy that Daphy died,” said Jasmine Rivera, executive director at the Pennsylvania Immigration Coalition.Murphy, the family’s attorney, worked with the community to arrange Michel’s funeral back in March andspoke tothe western Pennsylvania outlet TribLive about all the unanswered questions.He also concluded of Michel: “This person was loved.”Explore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)US immigrationPennsylvaniaHaitiSocial historyUS politicsMental healthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Callas, Beethoven, bee-eaters or storks: competition seeks to redesign euro notes | Europe | The Guardian
description: The EU is using a currency revamp as an opportunity to be less neutral and try some finely balanced identity-building
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: The EU is using a currency revamp as an opportunity to be less neutral and try some finely balanced identity-building
Content: Some of the designs shortlisted by the ECB for the first full redesign since the single currency’s paper money entered circulation in 2002.Composite: ECBView image in fullscreenSome of the designs shortlisted by the ECB for the first full redesign since the single currency’s paper money entered circulation in 2002.Composite: ECBEuropeCallas, Beethoven, bee-eaters or storks: competition seeks to redesign euro notesThe EU is using a currency revamp as an opportunity to be less neutral and try some finely balanced identity-buildingPhilip OltermannEuropean culture editorSun 2 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsEuropebest represented by the bold intellect of Marie Curie, the sprawling imagination of Miguel de Cervantes and the intense musical genius of Ludwig van Beethoven? Or by a migrating stork and a bee-eater, swooping across borderless plains and enjoying freedom of movement across European countries?The quest to settle this issue has engaged a surprising number of people across the continent, after more than 6 million people voted in a survey within just a week of its launch to determine whether the newly redesigned euro bank notes should depict either cultural figures or birds and waterways.The 10 proposals for a full redesign – the first since the single currency’s paper money entered circulation in 2002 – were unveiled by the chair of theEuropean Central Bank, Christine Lagarde, last week. They include five proposals on the culture theme and five on the wildlife theme.Each offers a different graphic interpretation on colours and motifs for the €5, €10, €20, €50, €100 and €200 notes that were determined by the ECB in advance.View image in fullscreenA €20 note design by studios Rubio & del Amo and Cruz más Cruz featuring Marie Curie.Photograph: ECBEurope’s cultural life is represented on the front of the notes by the American-Greek soprano Maria Callas; the German composer Beethoven; the Polish-French scientist Curie; Cervantes, the author of Don Quixote; the Renaissance polymath Leonardo da Vinci; and the Austrian pacifist and women’s liberation leader Bertha von Suttner, with public scenes of artistic and intellectual activity on the reverse.The birds selected for the wildlife-themed notes are the wallcreeper, the kingfisher, the bee-eater, the white stork, the avocet and the northern gannet, over different landscapes typical of the continent.View image in fullscreenA design by Isabelle Daëron featuring a wallcreeper.Photograph: ECBFeedback from thesurvey on the ECB’s website, which closes on 21 September, will feed into but not solely determine which design the central bank chooses as a winner at the end of 2026. A spokesperson said the outcome of a second, quantitative survey and the verdict of a jury of designers would also have a bearing on its choice. A combination of the two themes is not expected.The new notes, which will continue to be printed on paper rather than polymer as in some countries such as the UK, will not come into circulation until 2030 or 2031.The 10 shortlisted designs, picked from 1,241 applications to an open call in 2025, are all by creatives who don’t usually design bank notes, and some look radically different from paper money anywhere else around the globe.A Dutch book designer, Joost Grootens, hascropped the images of cultural figures tightly around their eyes, accentuating their vision rather than their iconic status, while Jan Robert Dünnwelle, a German illustrator, has rendered the same personalities in thefree-flowing, sketchy style of a graphic novel.View image in fullscreenOne of Jan Robert Dünnweller’s proposed designs, with Leonardo da Vinci.Photograph: ECBIn the French artistIsabelle Daëron’s proposals, the birds are flying across a vertical layout rather than the more conventional horizontal one, as are those of Ville Tietäväinen, a Finnish graphic designer who hasdepicted the bird’s journeys in sequence, progressively moving from the mountains to the sea.View image in fullscreenOne of Ville Tietäväinen’s designs, featuring an illustration of an avocet.Photograph: ECBPhilippe Geoffroy, the head of section for new banknotes at the ECB, said: “The feedback from the public has been very clear. They want money that feels European.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn Britain, the Bank of England drew some ire earlier this year when it announced that redesigned notes would depict wildlife instead of historical figures such as Winston Churchill or William Shakespeare. To some commentators, the “apolitical” animal motifs epitomised the struggle to identify shared cultural rallying points in politically polarising times.The new euro notes seem to take a step in the opposite direction. Until now, euro banknotes have deliberately depicted “neutral” motifs in order to avoid offending individual member nations: imaginary bridges, doorways and windows that exemplify historic architectural styles without depicting specific real-life European buildings or places.New notes including the face of the mythological princess Europa in the watermark and the hologram stripe were introduced in 2013 without changing the overall design.Yet while the current redesign is similarly motivated by the need for new security features, the EU is also not letting an opportunity for identity-building go to waste.“The main reason behind the re-design is to stay well ahead of counterfeiting,” Geoffroy said. “But along the way we want to increase identification with the single currency and make it more graphically meaningful. We want to move away from neutrality.”The lineup of cultural icons is not only finely balanced to represent different corners of the eurozone (albeit with a glaring hole in the Baltics). It also showcases artists and thinkers who cannot be claimed by just one country, either because their work transcended borders or because of their migratory biography.Callas was born in New York but her career flourished in Greece and Italy. The career of Curie, who discovered radium and polonium with her husband, Pierre, spanned Warsaw and Paris. Von Suttner spent time in Prague, Tbilisi and Vienna.While none of the birds that would be depicted on the wildlife notes are exclusively found in Europe, they would be paired on their flipside with pictures of buildings that house the EU’s political, legal and financial institutions in Brussels, Strasbourg, Luxembourg and Frankfurt.Explore more on these topicsEuropeEuropean Central BankEuropean monetary unionEuropean UnionnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Free up the ganja’: Rastafarians in Kenya fight to decriminalise marijuana | Kenya | The Guardian
description: Marijuana plays a sacred role among Rastafari followers and they say criminalising it violates their rights
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: Marijuana plays a sacred role among Rastafari followers and they say criminalising it violates their rights
Content: Ras Dimo (left), Ras Masinde (right) and others pray at a gathering venue for Rastafarians in Kibera, Nairobi on 18 July, 2026. In 2021, the Rastafari Society of Kenya filed a court petition seeking the exemption of the religion’s followers from arrest and prosecution for using marijuana for religious purposes. Photograph: Edwin Ndeke/The GuardianMarijuana plays a sacred role among Rastafari followers and they say criminalising it violates their rightsByCarlos Mureithiin NairobiSun 2 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbout a dozen people sang along to the pulsing vibrations of drums and a tambourine in a dimly lit room in Nairobi’s sprawling Kibera neighbourhood. For more than an hour they belted out song after song, the lyrics suffused with references to Ethiopia, Jah, Zion, Rastafari and Haile Selassie I.One songwent: “No night in a Zion, there is no night there / Hallelujah there is no night there / Rastafari is our light, and we need no other light / Hallelujah there is no night there.”The singers and musicians were members of the House of Nyabinghi, one of the main denominations, or “mansions” of Rastafari, a religion and socialmovement that recently came under the spotlight inKenyaafter a court ruling on 15 July dismissed a petition to decriminalise the use of marijuana for spiritual purposes.Three days later, the House of Nyabinghi – named after and inspired by a legendary east African woman whose name means “mother of abundance” or “she who possesses many things” – met for their weekly communal gatherings, which Rastafarians call a “groundation”.View image in fullscreenRastafarians gather in Kibera, Nairobi.Photograph: Carlos Mureithi/The GuardianA red, yellow, and green flag and images of Rastafari’s influences such asHaile Selassie I, Bob Marley and the Jamaican political activist Marcus Garvey embellished the walls. Sizzles and crackles were often heard as some of those gathered lit marijuana, its scent filling the air.Among those attending was Ras Orudi, who came to Rastafari after being inspired by Jamaican reggae artists such as Peter Tosh while at secondary school in the mid 2000s. “Rastafarians are not rejecting the system,” said the 38-year-old, who serves as a herbalist. “They are trying to integrate into the system while defending their rights.”View image in fullscreenRas Orudi, 38, began following Rastafari while at secondary school.Photograph: Carlos Mureithi/The GuardianAlso in the room was Ras Ndeto, who was inspired by an encounter in the early 1990s in Nairobi with a Rastafarian from Guyana who taught him “livity”, the Rastafari spiritual practice of righteous and natural living centred on a plant-based “ital” diet and the growing of dreadlocks.The 56-year-old said the court’s decision marginalised followers of the religion and added that they would appeal to a higher court. “We still feel that we are a minority group in this country, because even our culture is still looked down upon,” said Ndeto, who holds the title of prophet and is the spokesperson for the Rastafari Society of Kenya. “We are living like terrorists in our own country.”View image in fullscreenRas Ndeto, 56, said the court’s decision marginalised followers of Rastafari.Photograph: Edwin Ndeke/The GuardianAn Afrocentric religion, Rastafari is centred on the beliefs that the former Ethiopian emperor Haile Selassie I is the messiah and God incarnate, and that Black people are oppressed by Babylon – a metaphor for western capitalism and imperialism.The movement emerged in the 1930s within marginalised Afro-Jamaican communities after Protestant leaders declared that the crowning of Haile Selassie I as emperor was the fulfilment of a biblical prophecy. The movement is named after his pre-coronation name, Ras Tafari Makonnen.The religion was embraced around the world partly due to the influence of Rastafari-inspired reggae music from artistes such as Bob Marley and the Wailers, Burning Spear and Culture.View image in fullscreenArtwork and a banner on a wall at the meeting venue for the House of Nyabhingi in Kibera, Nairobi.Photograph: Carlos Mureithi/The GuardianRas Dimo, who holds the title of priest and often leads prayers in Kibera, became enlightened about Rastafari just before finishing secondary school, partly through reading books examining the connection between Black people and the Bible. “I was inspired to know that Black people are not cursed as imperialists tried to make us think,” the 43-year-old said. “We are living in a time when many people are blinded.”Like many other Rastafarians in Kenya, Dimo was born into a Christian family and later became Rastafari. They adopt the title Ras, which means“head” or “chief”inAmharic, the most widely spoken language in Ethiopia.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRastafarians chant during a ‘groundation’ - loopThe population of Rastafarians in Kenya is unknown. In 2019, a court recognised Rastafari as a legally protected religion in a landmark ruling after a pupil alleged discrimination when her school expelled her due to her dreadlocks.‘Many Rastas were chased away, but we’re determined to remain’: Ethiopia’s religious community under threatRead moreMarijuana, a product of theCannabissativa plant,is a sacrament in the faith, and Rastafarians believe consuming it puts them in a meditative state that helps them connect more deeply with the divine. Followers in different parts of the world are pushing for its decriminalisation. In 2023, the islands of Antigua and Barbuda approved allowing Rastafarians to grow cannabis and smoke marijuana.In 2021 the Rastafari Society of Kenya filed a court petition seeking the exemption of Rastafarians from arrest and prosecution for cultivating, possessing and using the plant as a sacrament, or a requirement that the government create a legal framework for the practice.The society said the law violated their rights to freedoms including of religion and equality. The court dismissed the petition on 15 July, saying the society had failed to prove that the law unconstitutionally violated Rastafarians’ rights, among other reasons.View image in fullscreenRas Masinde, 50, began growing dreadlocks and reading about Rastafari in the 1990s.Photograph: Carlos Mureithi/The GuardianRas Masinde, another follower in Kibera, became curious about Rastafari as a child after encountering a man with dreadlocks. He became rebellious, refusing to cut his hair, and after finishing secondary school in the 1990s, started growing dreadlocks and reading about the Rastafari religion, before eventually finding a community.“We as Rastafarians are urging Black people to go back to their roots and culture,” said the 50-year-old. “Wefyah bun(denounce or condemn) colonialism and imperialism, and we say that every man and woman and child … is equal before the eyes of the almighty the creator.”He issued a rallying call: “Free up the herb. Free up the ganja seed.”Explore more on these topicsKenyaCannabisAfricaDrugsReligionFreedom of religionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Stock market turmoil sheds stark light on the opaque AI economy | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Investors scramble to make sense of a shock Chinese challenge to the dominance of western chipmakers
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Investors scramble to make sense of a shock Chinese challenge to the dominance of western chipmakers
Content: A lithography machine at ASML in Veldhoven, the Netherlands. The Chinese have broken the Dutch company’s hold over deep-ultraviolet lithography, a technique essential to the computer chip supply chain.Photograph: Bart van Overbeeke Fotografie/AS/ReutersView image in fullscreenA lithography machine at ASML in Veldhoven, the Netherlands. The Chinese have broken the Dutch company’s hold over deep-ultraviolet lithography, a technique essential to the computer chip supply chain.Photograph: Bart van Overbeeke Fotografie/AS/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)AnalysisStock market turmoil sheds stark light on the opaque AI economyAisha Down,Dan MilmoandGraeme WeardenInvestors scramble to make sense of a shock Chinese challenge to the dominance of western chipmakersSun 2 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTShareEven for the rollercoaster world of AI, last week was particularly volatile as investors scrambled to keep up with developments that threatened the dominance of the largest western chipmakers.It began with a double whammy. On Monday, the Chinese memory chipmaker CXMT floated on the Shanghai stock market, soaring by 466% in value to 3.3tn yuan (£365bn).That same day, it was reported thatChinahad developed its own tools to carry out deep-ultraviolet lithography, a technique essential to the computer chip supply chain over which the Dutch company ASML had held a monopoly.AI-linked shares, particularly chipmakers, dropped around the world, sending many indices sliding. South Korea’s main share index, the Kospi,fell 11.5% on Tuesdayand a further6% on Wednesday, dragged down by its two biggest companies – the semiconductor maker SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics.On Thursday, the main US tech index, the Nasdaq, fell into correction territory at one point after dropping more than 10% from its recent high, before easing back. Nvidia lost more than 5% by Thursday evening, by which time it had beenovertaken by Apple as the world’s largest listed company.The next day there was a big rebound, when strong financial results from Amazon and Microsoft calmed traders’ nerves. The Kospi jumped nearly 20% – although the week’s slump still means it recorded its worst month since the height of the global financial crisis in October 2008.So, what exactly do these advances mean, and why have they got western investors so jittery?CXMT’s debut is impressive. But the company is arguably more of a boon to the global AI economy than a threat. It makes dynamic random-access memory (Dram) chips, which store the data that other AI chips draw on for their calculations.There is a global shortage of Dram chips, which is why phones and computers are expected to getfar more expensive. Crucially, they are not graphics processing units (GPUs) – which are the key chips and the “brains” in an AI system.This means, put simply, that CXMT is not a threat to GPU maker Nvidia, the biggest company in the AI economy and the only onemaking a profiton AI. They produce complementary, not competing goods.View image in fullscreenChina’s president, Xi Jinping, speaks at the opening of the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Beijing. China is making rapid advances in the semiconductors used to drive AI.Photograph: Greg Baker/AFP/Getty ImagesThe Chinese company could be a threat to SK Hynix and Micron, which do make memory chips. However, Alvin Nguyen, an analyst at the research firm Forrester, said the sell-off in these shares was an “overreaction” given that the global memory chip shortage is likely to continue until 2030.“SK Hynix, Micron, others, they can’t produce enough memory chips to begin with … the demand keeps growing even higher,” Nguyen said.A more serious concern could be the news that China can make the lithography tools. These are essentially extremely precise lasers that allow chipmakers to etch the thinnest lines in the world into wafers of silicon.Until now, only ASML could manufacture such machines. If this week’s reports are correct, Beijing could – in theory – produce GPUs that rival Nvidia’s. This would spell trouble for the world’s biggest company, and therefore Wall Street. But a serious competitor is still years away.“Fabs [semiconductor fabrication plants], as I know them, still take years to develop,” said Nguyen.Mark Boost, the chief executive of the UK cloud company Civo, agreed. “Investors are overreacting to the short-term threat,” he said. “Manufacturing a handful of [deep-ultraviolet] machines is a massive symbolic victory, but not a commercial replacement for ASML overnight.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Fabs run on efficiency and yield, and until these Chinese tools can match western reliability, ASML’s global dominance remains structurally safe outside mainland China.”Long term, this week’s advances are gamechanging for the AI economy, although in many ways they should have been predictable. Given US export controls,China has had little choice but to develop domestic capabilities.Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at IG, an online share trading company, said: “These Chinese chip companies appear poised to do to the big chipmakers what they have done to steel, automobiles and a host of other industries, namely undercut them and outcompete them on price.”It may be that last week’s correction is an overreaction – but also a reasonable response to a circular and extremely opaque AI economy that rests heavily on the fate of a single company, Nvidia.Its shares are gradually creeping up again, although they are still below what they were last week. A contributing factor to the investor skittishness appears to be yet another circular, opaque deal.Last Sunday, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia was considering providing a $250bn (£186bn)backstopto OpenAI for a large datacentre project. This comes roughly half a year after a $100bn deal between the two companiesfell apart.It was a significant factor in Nvidia’s decline over the week, according toMorningstar. The anxiety that underlies this is that the company has become the “central bank of AI” – holding up vast parts of the economy, and the global stock market, in ways that most people, investors included, do not understand.Many believe that it cannot last. What is on the other side is less clear.“Nvidia knows the gravy train’s going to run out,” Nguyen said. “Everybody’s waiting for them to fall apart. I don’t know that they will because what they do still has value … at some point in the future, they’ll no longer be one of the most valuable companies in the world. Maybe … they’ll be worth only $2tn. It’s still pretty good.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ChinaNvidiaStock marketsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Ariana Grande to take ‘a step back’ from public life due to ‘endless, ongoing scrutiny’ | Ariana Grande | The Guardian
description: Singer was due to reunite with Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey in London production of Sunday in the Park With George
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Singer was due to reunite with Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey in London production of Sunday in the Park With George
Content: Ariana Grande at the Critics Choice awards in January. The singer and actor has announced she will take a break ‘from public-facing work and appearances which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny’.Photograph: Richard Shotwell/APView image in fullscreenAriana Grande at the Critics Choice awards in January. The singer and actor has announced she will take a break ‘from public-facing work and appearances which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny’.Photograph: Richard Shotwell/APAriana GrandeAriana Grande to take ‘a step back’ from public life due to ‘endless, ongoing scrutiny’Singer was due to reunite with Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey in London production of Sunday in the Park With GeorgeSian Cainand agenciesSun 2 Aug 2026 19.23 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 19.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAriana Grande has announced plans to take a break from public-facing work after her tour ends due to “endless, ongoing public scrutiny”. She is pulling out of the upcoming London revival of Sunday in the Park With George.The pop singer was due to appear opposite her Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey in a new production of Stephen Sondheim’s critically acclaimed musical at the Barbican in 2027.A representative for Grande told People: “Ariana will be taking a step back from visibility after she completes the Eternal Sunshine Tour.“She looks forward to finishing the tour and ending it on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny.“This tour has been a beautiful experience for her. She loves her fans and has loved every minute of this tour so much.”Ariana Grande: Petal review – calm, controlled anger at exes, fans and the mediaRead moreSunday in the Park With George will go ahead as planned and Grande’s part will be recast, the production company Empire Street Productions said.A statement to the Press Association said: “Empire Street Productions have said following this evening’s announcement from Ariana Grande’s team, we can confirm that she has decided to step back from Sunday in the Park with George.“We know this cannot have been an easy decision, and she makes it with our complete understanding and support.“We wish her nothing but the best. The production will open at the Barbican in summer 2027 as planned, and casting will be announced in due course.”The musical, created by Sondheim and James Lapine, debuted on Broadway in 1984 starring Mandy Patinkin and Bernadette Peters.The show is inspired by the Georges Seurat painting A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, and follows Seurat as he tries to complete the portrait, exploring his relationship with his lover and muse, Dot.Grande’s announcement came days after she released the music video forPetal, the title singlefrom her newly released eighth studio album, which sparked speculation about her weight loss and her health.One of her new songs, Like I Do, includes a possible dig at years of headlines about her weight: “I’ve got shit to talk, keeps me well fed.”Grandebecame emotional during a 2024 interviewwhen asked by a journalist how she handled the pressure “to always look perfect”.She described herself as being “a specimen in a petri dish since I was 16 or 17. I have heard it all. I have heard every form of what is wrong with me. And then you fix it and then it is wrong for different reasons.”She added: “It is hard to protect yourself from that noise. I think that it’s something that is uncomfortable no matter what scale you’re experiencing it on.” Comments about weight could be “uncomfortable” and “horrible”, she said.“From what you are wearing, to your body, to your face, to your everything – there is a comfortability that people have commenting on that that I think is really dangerous. I think it is dangerous for all parties involved.”Grande shared the interview again on her social media in November, “as a loving reminder to all”.The Eternal Sunshine tour will arrive in the UK in August, with a 10-night residency at the O2. Her final London show on 1 September will mark the end of the tour.Grande has won three Grammy awards in a music career that took off in 2013 after the release of her debut album, Yours Truly.She found fame playing Cat Valentine on the Nickelodeon television shows Victorious and Sam + Cat.She was nominated for an Oscar for her role as Glinda in the big-screen adaptation of Wicked.Press Association contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsAriana GrandePop and rockMusicalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Could a couch-to-5k for books get you back into reading?  | Books | The Guardian
description: With smartphones stealing our attention, we’re picking up fewer books than ever. A novelist shares her eight-week scheme to get you back into the habit
Author: Naomi Alderman
Headline: With smartphones stealing our attention, we’re picking up fewer books than ever. A novelist shares her eight-week scheme to get you back into the habit
Content: Get with the programme … is the books couch-to-5k for you?Photograph: Alina Rudya/Bell Collective/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGet with the programme … is the books couch-to-5k for you?Photograph: Alina Rudya/Bell Collective/Getty ImagesBooksCould a couch-to-5k for books get you back into reading?With smartphones stealing our attention, we’re picking up fewer books than ever. A novelist shares her eight-week scheme to get you back into the habitNaomi AldermanSun 2 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDo you feel that it’s harder to read than it used to be? Not harder to read emails, texts and social media posts, of course. We’re reading those all day long. Harder to sit down and lose yourself in a book? How long is it since you even sat down with a weekend newspaper and read it cover to cover? Do you feel that you used to have a life-sustaining reading habit, everything from fun popcorn novels to serious nonfiction, classic and contemporary, many genres and writers, but somehow it’s gone away? It doesn’t feel like a decision that you made. It just happened.I feel like that. At least more like that than I’m comfortable with. I’m a novelist and I present programs about thinking on the BBC, and yet even I am finding that I’m reading less than I used to. It seems more of an effort and less of a consistent, persistent habit than it was. I hate this feeling. I still have the habit of acquiring books, buying them, getting them from libraries, being sent them. And I do still read. Compared with many people, I probably read an enormous amount, but I know it’s not as much as I used to read. And I know where the time has gone.It is, of course, the damn phones.The other day I was sitting with a friend who is a doctor and an expert in public health – that is, large-scale interventions that might improve the health of millions of people by a tiny bit. I found myself saying: “I don’t think it’s a coincidence that smartphones are about the same size and shape as a packet of cigarettes.” We talked about how the really massive public health crisis from tobacco was caused by the arrival of cheap mass-market cigarettes, which you could smoke endlessly without having to do the ritual of emptying, cleaning and refilling your pipe, and which were not as expensive as cigars. We talked about how people didn’t know, when they started smoking those cheap mass-market cigarettes during the first world war, how deadly they would be. We talked about how it’s not our fault.My friend said that he too misses his regular reading habit. I think of him as an avid reader, but we’re remembering each other from a few years ago. In the trenches in the first world war, men smoked cigarettes to steady their nerves. During the pandemic, when we couldn’t speak to each other in person or give each other a hug, we all got glued to our smartphones. It’s not our fault, but we are going to have to fix it now. My friend said that he wished someone would do a couch to 5k-style training program for reading. And then I couldn’t stop thinking about it.double quotation markDo you feel that you used to have a life-sustaining reading habit but somehow it’s gone away?The problems of people not reading are well documented. Students are apparently arriving at university unable to read a whole book. A2024 reportby the OECD has found that literacy has declined or stagnated in most developed countries. In his forthcoming book, The New Dark Ages, James Marriott traces the problems for society that are increasingly coming out of a lack of literacy. Marriott argues that when we’re not reading, we’re increasingly unable to follow complex arguments and find the problems with them. We tend to be more swayed by cartoonish figures with simple slogans we can repeat. We will believe gossip and treat it seriously rather than thinking through the intellectual ideas behind politics or business.It’s a public health crisis of intellectual health, and most governments don’t seem minded to do anything about it. It’s the damn phones, but dealing with the phones means tussling with the massively wealthy American technology companies that are protected by Donald Trump. It would be straightforward to force technology companies to give us ways to use the useful services on the phones with all the pernicious features turned off. But it would take political will to do it.While we’re waiting, if nobody is going to do it for us, for now, we’re going to need to do what we can for ourselves.View image in fullscreenNaomi Alderman.Photograph: Pål Hansen/The ObserverSo I thought about the couch to 5k for reading, how you could do it. I worked on designing the couch to 5k for my running app Zombies, Run several years ago, so I know the theory. When I mentioned the idea on mySubstack newsletter, Whatever Works, readers bit my hand off with excitement (much like a zombie). It suddenly seemed very urgent. There is no more time to wait.We used to live in a world where the only way to get information, or to be entertained, or to simply pass the time when you were waiting, or queueing, or on a bus, was reading. Well, we also used to live in a world where the only way to get places was to walk. Then we invented technologies that are very useful in some ways, but we had to take on exercise programs to help us get enough movement in our lives. That’s where we are with reading now.We just need to accept that and get on with it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSo I’ve designed a program. Eight weeks, with three separate tracks. It’s mostly for people like me, who remember that they had a life-sustaining reading habit once but feel that it has somehow fallen away. Over eight weeks, we are working ourselves back to reading half an hour every day, with two or three longer sessions during the week. There are also tracks for people who are really time-limited and just want to be reading 20 minutes a day, and people who feel that they’re basically still reading, but know that they are shying away from the more challenging stuff they want to be tackling.The response has been extraordinary. After the first week of the program, people are already saying that they’re finding their morning routine goes more quickly now they’re not brain-fogged from scrolling first thing, that reading in stressful times is making them feel calmer and not more anxious as scrolling did, that they can watch a long film without being tempted to look at their phone. They are rediscovering the simple joy of being gripped by a great book after as few as two or three days of working on this together. Fans have put together homemade digital and printable trackers to keep themselves motivated. Teachers are already asking me how to introduce this idea into schools.Try these habits to reinvigorate your reading | LettersRead moreIt’s really exciting to find out how easy it is to put this right. The program is running right now, and if you’re reading this, you’re not too late to join. Just start from the beginning. All you have to do is put down your phone, pick up a book, and read for 10 minutes. That’s day one.There is so much joy in books, and it’s all still there waiting for us. All we have to do is take it back from the technology billionaires, one day of reading at a time.Seenaomialderman.substack.comfor further detailsExplore more on these topicsBooksLiteracyHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From The Wizard of Oz to Trainspotting: 25 films to watch before you turn 25 | Movies | The Guardian
description: As AI slop takes over our screens, what better antidote for enquiring minds than a magical film? We ask directors, producers and critics to pick one must-see movie for each year – from infancy to young adulthood
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As AI slop takes over our screens, what better antidote for enquiring minds than a magical film? We ask directors, producers and critics to pick one must-see movie for each year – from infancy to young adulthood
Content: Illustration: Yuewei Nino Li/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Yuewei Nino Li/The GuardianMoviesFrom The Wizard of Oz to Trainspotting: 25 films to watch before you turn 25As AI slop takes over our screens, what better antidote for enquiring minds than a magical film? We ask directors, producers and critics to pick one must-see movie for each year from infancy to early adulthoodSun 2 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 16.40 EDTShareScreentime has a bad rep these days: it’s allegedly at the root of everything from the collapse of media literacy to the rise of the far right. For parents, and indeed anyone who cares about the future of the planet, the relationship children have to their screens is a particular hot potato.Orson Welles’ advice to young people to be selective about your viewing – “Don’t be marinated, don’t soak yourself in films” – has never been more relevant in the era of AI slop and doom-scrolling. So we asked film-makers, critics and industry names for the joyful, imaginative and thought-provoking films that every child and young adult should see. Here is their curated list of just 25 screen experiences worth having.Catherine BrayAt the age of …1Fantasia(1940)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Disney/Cinetext/AllstarMy first child is due in autumn and it’s made me think about what I’d like to share with them in their journey into the magical world of movies (I know they will be asleep or crying, but allow a man to dream). Disney’s Fantasia holds some of my own earliest film memories: the music; the dancing ostriches; Mickey Mouse just trying to have a rest. If cinema is the fusion of sound and image into something greater than the sum of its parts, then Fantasia is truly visceral and joyous cinema. I hope my wee one will feel the same.Tom Nicoll, director2The Snowman(1982)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Channel 4/AllstarWith its winsome, crayon textures, The Snowman is a dream. Young James delights in showing his miraculous visitor around his domestic domain, but it’s the Snowman who expands the kid’s horizons, as they soar above the Sussex countryside. In the morning, the snow has melted, but the magic remains.Michael Leader, author of The Animation Atlas3My Neighbour Totoro(1988)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Studio Ghibli/Tokuma-Shoten/Nibariki/Kobal/ShutterstockHayao Miyazaki’s animation is a beautiful, meditative film about illness, grief and the power of nature. My daughter was three when she first watched it and was totally mesmerised. It is a real shift in tone from the usual American fare and offers something different for kids to connect with.Imran Perretta, director4Muppets Take Manhattan(1984)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Tri Star/Kobal/Rex/ShutterstockComing at the tail end of “peak Muppets”, and directed by Frank Oz (also at his creative apex, having just done The Dark Crystal), this film sees Kermit and friends take their ensemble play to the Big Apple with the dream of opening on Broadway. Things are not as easy as they seem and they encounter hardships and learn life lessons. The film is full of laughs and inspired cameos (including Joan Rivers inflicting her version of an extravagant makeover on a permed Miss Piggy). It’s a deserving entry in the canon of great 1980s New York City films.Michelle Carey, founder of Red Balloonalliance5Chicken Run(2000)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Cinetext/Dreamworks Skg/AllstarA masterclass in stop-motion, I’d choose this for every five-year-old, mainly having seen the effect it had on mine. Drawing heavily from classic second world war adventure films, this tale of plucky chickens who dream of a life outside their electric-fenced egg farm is filled with slapstick, action and gags that hit kids and grownups alike, all wrapped around a message about the fundamental right to freedom. It’s The Great Escape – with chickens.Briony Hanson,director offilm, British Council6The Wizard of Oz(1939)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Allstar/AlamyThe Wizard of Oz changed my life when I was six years old. It is a visual delight that expands imaginations and every six-year-old should see it.Prano Bailey-Bond, director7Scooby-Doo(2002)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Warner Bros/AllstarMy younger self thought Scooby-Doo was a masterpiece. My current self agrees. It has everything you need from a film: a compelling story, an incredible cast of characters, mystery, thrills and laughs. It’s pure pop spectacle. Rewatching it as an adult, I could see that this was also a film with big ideas: it’s an autopsy of the American project post-9/11, an examination of gender relations and performance at the beginning of a new century, and a deeply felt exploration of the value of friendship under late capitalism. The exact kind of film a seven-year-old should be watching.Naqqash Khalid, director8Labyrinth(1986)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Tristar Pictures/AllstarDavid Bowie may have been the Thin White Duke but he was also Jareth the Goblin King in Jim Henson’s charming family fantasy adventure. A ludicrously bewigged Bowie taunts and tantalises Jennifer Connelly’s Sarah as she undergoes a perilous journey to find her kidnapped baby brother.Alex Larman, author of Lazarus: The Second Coming of David Bowie9The Amazing Mr Blunden(1972; remade in 2021)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Hemdale Film Corporation/AllstarI can’t remember exactly how old I was when I saw this ghost story, directed by Lionel Jeffries, but it affected the smaller me deeply, mainly by introducing me to a kind of exhilarating dread. I saw two kids in 1918 find themselves in a lonely country house haunted by two other kids who died in a fire 100 years earlier (instigated by, of all people, Diana Dors in a Regency bonnet); they head to 1818, save the kids, do in the baddies and inherit the lovely house. The estimable Mark Gatiss’s remake should really be the gateway drug to the source – your nine-year-olds may never be the same again.Andrew Pulver, associate editor, film, the Guardian10The Princess Bride(1987)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Landmark Media/AlamyIt’s whimsical fun for a kid, but also has a bunch of jokes for the grownups that go over your head until you revisit it in a fit of nostalgia as, say, a hungover 24-year-old looking for a comfort watch. Rob Reiner, what a talent you were.Julia Jackman, director11Mulan(1998)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Everett Collection/AlamyBrilliant songs, sweeping romance and a great way to introduce younger audiences to the comic brilliance of Eddie Murphy as Mushu the dragon. Based on the Chinese legend of Hua Mulan, this fun adventure about identity follows a girl who disguises herself as a boy, because people won’t let her do what she wants when she’s a girl. They’re furious when they find out!Rhianna Dhillon, critic12The Witches(1990)View image in fullscreenPhotograph:  Alamy/Once you hit your preteens, it’s time to cue up this dark and delightful adaptation of Roald Dahl’s book. Anjelica Huston goes from glam to gruesome when she transforms into the bald, child-hating Grand High Witch, determined to wipe out the kiddos of the world with a new magic potion. Young viewers will root for Luke (who is turned into a mouse) and his grandmother, who use cleverness, bravery and trust in each other to triumph over the witless witches.Rebecca Fons, Barbicanhead ofcinema13Princess Mononoke(1997)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Everett Collection/AlamySpeaking as a fully grown adult, The Wind Rises sits high atop my list of favourite Miyazaki films, but I’m not sure I’d feel that way had I not grown up alongside the reverence for nature instilled in me by this earlier classic. It is a film so beautiful, frightening, hardcore, playful and prescient about the pained relationship between nature and technology – and a child can grasp its profundity as easily as an adult. In Miyazaki’s films, children are often more capable of achieving wisdom than the rigid adults trying to make the old ways endure. That seems about right.David Osit, director14Ferris Bueller’s Day Off(1986)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Paramount/AllstarYou would not have caught me watching a John Hughes film for love nor money in my youth. It was my assistant who got me into the film about 10 years ago – she declared one day on a set that she was a big Hughes fan and this was one she held close. I watched it and thought it waspretty damn funny– with all its un-PC flaws ignored.Elizabeth Karlsen, producer15Run Lola Run(1998)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Warner Home/AllstarSince I was young, plenty of films have made me yearn to be a director, but I left a matinee of this in the summer of 1999 both completely envious and fizzing with excitement, desperate to make a movie that very day. It’s a brisk but profound film about how your whole life can change in the next 20 minutes, and how true destiny and blind chance may not be as far apart as we imagine. It’s also propelled by a pulse-quickening techno score, so I defy you not to be moved – both literally and figuratively.Edgar Wright, director16The Umbrellas of Cherbourg(1964)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: AlamyWhen I was a teenager, most of my favourite films involved guns and swearing. So a film shot in bright pastels about young lovers in a French port where everyone singsall the way through the moviewas a hard sell. But there was nothing else on and iPhones didn’t exist yet, so I went and it changed me. It’s a musical about how disappointing life is – a lesson best learned early – and one of the most beautiful films ever made.Gareth Tunley, director17Get Out(2017)View image in fullscreenPhotograph:  Blumhouse/AllstarJordan Peele’s film, in which a young photographer realises something isn’t quite right while meeting his girlfriend’s family, is the perfect gateway for a young cinephile – so much fun you barely notice it’s teaching you how to watch.Farhana Bhula,director of Film418Gaza: Doctors Under Attack (2025); Louis Theroux: The Settlers(2025)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: BBCThese films depict Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and the ethnic cleansing of the West Bank. The images are heartbreaking and unforgettable: there are horribly mutilated children facing death; medics in wrecked hospitals knowing they themselves are targets. Theroux’s documentary shows the chilling smile of a settler woman who knows she has the power to drive Palestinians from their homes. Pictures seen when young stay in the mind for a lifetime. Never was the need for such films so urgent. Remember Martin Luther King: “The ultimate tragedy is not the oppression and cruelty by the bad people but the silence over that by the good people.”Ken Loach, director19Trainspotting(1996)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Channel Four Films/AllstarIt has been 30 years since we made Trainspotting, and the film Danny Boyle put together fromIrvine Welsh’s brilliant bookhas taken on a life of its own. Its iconography still seems to be everywhere, which is gratifying if a little overwhelming. We are immensely proud of the film we made and what it has to say about being young and pushing back on what’s expected. The good people at the BBFC insist that you have to be 18 to see the film and we must abide by the law. But if you are old enough, I highly recommend the film. It is even screening at the Edinburgh International film festival this year.Andrew Macdonald, producer of Trainspotting20Blue(1993)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: RGR Collection/AlamyWe were art students in 1993 when Derek Jarman’s final film was released. Blue landed like a manifesto: an invitation to question everything and to believe that art could change the way you see the world. Derek Jarman described Blue as “an infinite possibility, becoming tangible”. In this devastating yet profoundly hopeful farewell to film-making, he created a work that has continued to shape us and redefined the possibilities of cinema for ever.Iain Forsyth and Jane Pollard, co-directors21Cléo from 5 to 7(1962)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Moviestore Collection/AlamyTwenty-one feels like a beginning and so something from the French New Wave seems appropriate; all that energy, excitement and idealism. I thought about the cool of À Bout de Souffle or the coming-of-age anxieties of Truffaut’s Antoine Doinel films, but for its spirit of playfulness, its style and beauty, I’d chooseAgnès Varda’s Cléo from 5 to 7, in which a tarot reading causes Corinne Marchand’s pop star to evaluate her life in real time. Optimism, transformation, connection - it’s all the stuff of early adult life.David Nicholls, novelist and screenwriter22Do the Right Thing(1989)View image in fullscreenPhotograph:  Universal/AllstarSo stylish, so dynamic, so urgent: I love Spike Lee’s film for inviting young minds to interrogate the past and the present and determine their own ideas of community, power, justice and personal morality – questions more relevant than ever to those inheriting our fragile Earth.Eva Yates,director of BBC Film23The Girl Chewing Gum(1976)I first saw this in the 1990s when I was studying film at Central Saint Martins, where John Smith – who directed it – was a tutor. It was made when he was a post-grad student and mostly filmed on a busy London street corner in a single, unscripted documentary shot. John later added his voice directing, controlling and commenting on the action. This retrospective narration (which becomes deliberately unreliable) wittily interrogates how a film manipulates and constructs meaning. Nowadays it’s widely regarded as an avant garde masterpiece.Carol Morley, director24Morvern Callar(2002)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: RGR Collection/AlamyA film byLynne Ramsaythat captures the feeling of being young, adrift and still free to take one giant swing before you calcify into a responsible adult! Many people I know find viewing this movie a rite of passage – it rearranged their entire being. It’s a movie you can come back to in 20 years to see where you stand in relation to its freewheeling spirit. Would its spell have worn off? And what does that say about you?Sandi Tan, director and writer25The Graduate(1967)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Cinetext Bildarchiv/Lawrence Turman/Embassy/AllstarAt 25, it’s time for your quarterlife crisis. So sit down to this dark, existential masterpiece, an age-gap sex romp which is actually about the terrible twentysomething burden of making irreversible life choices. Dustin Hoffman is Benjamin, a college graduate embarking on a long hot summer of torpid indecision (a friend of his father advises going into “plastics”), who is seduced by the sensual older woman, Mrs Robinson, gloriously played by Anne Bancroft. Her own cynicism is a counterpoint to Benjamin’s callow ennui. The subversive sexual politics are funny, alarming and desperately sad.Peter Bradshaw, Guardian film critic

title: ‘I loved the Police from the get-go’: Elaine Paige’s honest playlist | Music | The Guardian
description: The singer and actor is partial to Mozart and once did Édith Piaf at karaoke, but to which musical showstopper does she owe everything?
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The singer and actor is partial to Mozart and once did Édith Piaf at karaoke, but to which musical showstopper does she owe everything?
Content: Diva patrol … Elaine Paige, who loves her crooners, too.View image in fullscreenDiva patrol … Elaine Paige, who loves her crooners, too.Honest playlistMusic‘I loved the Police from the get-go’: Elaine Paige’s honest playlistThe singer and actor is partial to Mozart and once did Édith Piaf at karaoke, but to which musical showstopper does she owe everything?As told toRich PelleySun 2 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withI used to sing All I Have to Do Is Dream by the Everly Brothers with my schoolfriend who lived over the road, when I was 11 or 12. I sang the harmony and she sang the melody.The song I do at karaokeThe only time was on holiday in Nice with a friend. We’d been out for a lovely supper and had far too much rosé, and I was about to play Édith Piaf in the West End. I ended up singing Hymne à l’amour, and he did Fools Rush In.The first single I boughtMagic Moments by Perry Como from the record shop in Barnet High Street, for my mother’s birthday. She loved Perry Como, Andy Williams, Matt Monro – all those crooners.The song I know every lyric toWhen I was in Hair in 1968, we were in the pub having a snifter before the show when the company manager came in and said: “Jeanie’s off – and so are her understudies. Paige, you’re up.” I was terrified. Jeanie comes up through a trapdoor, covered in beads, singing Air. Somehow I knew every word.The best song to play at a partyRoxanne. I’ve loved the Police from the get-go.The song I can no longer listen toShall We Dance? from The King and I. My co-star Jason Scott Lee pulled out after three months. After that I had to dance with a catalogue of different kings in a huge crinoline dress, wearing thick stockings, suspenders, corsets and layers of underwear.The best song to have sex toI do have a bit of a penchant for Wicked Game by Chris Isaak. But I’m not saying I’ve tried it!The song that gets me up in the morningI wake up to Radio 4, then switch to Radio 3. I’m a big Mozart fan – one of the first things I ever sang in public was a Mozart aria: Deh vieni, non tardar from The Marriage of Figaro.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPaige, Perón … Elaine sings Evita in 1980.The song that changed my lifeDon’t Cry for Me Argentina, because without it, I probably wouldn’t be talking to you today.The song that makes me cryEv’ry Time We Say Goodbye by Cole Porter, because it reminds me of my mum. My dad was an estate agent, but he also had a band, the Arcadians, and would go out gigging. Mum and I would wave him off, then listen to records on the radiogram.The song I’d like played at my funeralOh God, I don’t want to think about it. Maybe George Michael’s cover of The Long and Winding Road – I was a huge fan, he had the most beautiful voice, and it’s a lovely song.Elaine Paige’s new album Miscellaneous Paige is out now.Explore more on these topicsMusicHonest playlistfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Aurora Orchestra/ Collon review – Freud analyses Mahler to decipher music from the heart | Classical music | The Guardian
description: An acted prelude by Jane Mitchell teased out the composer’s motivations for his engrossing First Symphony before the orchestra assayed the work from memory
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: An acted prelude by Jane Mitchell teased out the composer’s motivations for his engrossing First Symphony before the orchestra assayed the work from memory
Content: Music lesson … Sarah Twomey plays Sigmund Freud and Jack Bardoe Mahler as members of the orchestra look on.Photograph: Mark Allan/BBCView image in fullscreenMusic lesson … Sarah Twomey plays Sigmund Freud and Jack Bardoe Mahler as members of the orchestra look on.Photograph: Mark Allan/BBCClassical musicReviewAurora Orchestra/ Collon review – Freud analyses Mahler to decipher music from the heartRoyal Albert Hall, LondonAn acted prelude by Jane Mitchell teased out the composer’s motivations for his engrossing First Symphony before the orchestra assayed the work from memoryClive PagetSun 2 Aug 2026 12.18 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Ridiculous,” “offensively trivial”, “a complete disaster,” just some of the critical barbs hurled at Gustav Mahler’s First Symphony following its Budapest premiere in 1889. A babel of such invective echoed around the Albert Hall launching the ingenious theatrical presentation – in effect, a staged programme note – that preceded Aurora Orchestra’s performance of the work in all its maverick majesty. Over an hour, actors and musicians took us on a light touch, deep dive into the circumstances surrounding the genesis of a symphony that frankly baffled its first audience.“For those that listen closely, everything about me is explained in this music,” declared a beguiling Jack Bardoe, perfectly encapsulating Mahler’s combination of frenetic energy and artistic neuroses (“A bomb encased in razorblades,” is how one-time friend Ferdinand Pfohl put it). The setting was a psychiatrist’s office, with Sarah Twomey a forthright Sigmund Freud (“Tell me about your mother”) linking the composer’s compulsion to write music with a need to re-enact childhood trauma. Paternal cruelty, eight siblings lost in infancy and a disastrous love affair fostered a deeper understanding of what made Mahler tick.View image in fullscreenSource material … mezzo-soprano Natalie Lewis sings Songs of a Wayfarer.Photograph: Mark Allan/BBCFreudian trip: how psychoanalysis and skydiving are helping Aurora orchestra open up Mahler’s FirstRead moreJane Mitchell’s meticulously crafted script was interwoven with Nicholas Collon and the orchestra’s illuminating musical examples, including, I kid you not, crucial information on the breeding cycle of the cuckoo. Natalie Lewis, meanwhile, gave velvet voice to the earlier Songs of a Wayfarer, vital source material for Mahler’s symphonic odyssey.Did it ultimately enhance the performance – by heart – of the symphony itself? Well, yes and no. On the one hand, much of the music arrived like a familiar friend. If the opening felt a touch brisk and the offstage brass sounded overly present, at its best – in the duelling ländlers of the second movement or the eerie tread of the third – Collon caught the music’s pioneering spirit. On the other hand, all those examples robbed us of a certain element of surprise, like the finale’s breathtaking modulation from C major to D (in the event, strangely rushed). The last five minutes, however, worked their usual magic, Mahler’s repurposed cuckoo calls ringing out on the horns to remind us of the engrossing music lesson that had come before.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicProms 2026Aurora OrchestraGustav MahlerPromslive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The simplest, coolest item in your wardrobe’: 14 of the best white T-shirts for men | Men's fashion | The Guardian
description: Fabric, fit, weight and drape – there’s more to picking the perfect tee than meets the eye. Our menswear expert rounds up his favourites
Author: Peter Bevan
Headline: Fabric, fit, weight and drape – there’s more to picking the perfect tee than meets the eye. Our menswear expert rounds up his favourites
Content: Not so plain white tee. Jacob Elordi in the TV show Euphoria showing his white T-shirt cred.Composite: HBOView image in fullscreenNot so plain white tee. Jacob Elordi in the TV show Euphoria showing his white T-shirt cred.Composite: HBOThe FilterMen's fashionReview‘The simplest, coolest item in your wardrobe’: 14 of the best white T-shirts for menFabric, fit, weight and drape – there’s more to picking the perfect tee than meets the eye. Our menswear expert rounds up his favouritesHow to buy secondhand clothes online that you’ll actually wearPeter BevanSun 2 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Ididn’t think about Marlon Brando when I got dressed this morning. Or James Dean or Steve McQueen, for that matter. But every time you pull a white T-shirt over your head, they’re the ones you should have in the back of your mind.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Before they came along, a white T-shirt was just underwear. They made the silhouette cultural shorthand for effortless style and, ever since, it’s been the simplest – and coolest – thing in every wardrobe. These days, Jacob Elordi’s off-duty wardrobe usually consists of a white T-shirt – whether that’s under a cardigan, tucked into tailored trousers, or just visible at the hem of a zipped-up work jacket.View image in fullscreenDone to a tee: Ayo Edebiri, right, and Jeremy Allen White, wearing his character’s trademark white T-shirt, in a scene from TV drama The Bear.Photograph: Chuck Hodes/APFinding the perfect white T-shirt can be harder than it looks – weight, drape, neckline, fabric, fit and the shade of white itself all matter when something’s so minimal in design. As a stylist, I bring a few iterations to every fitting because it’s the basic that gets along so easily with everything else: denim, tailoring, casual shirts, smart trousers and sports shorts. Here’s how to choose the right one, plus the best white T-shirts you can buy now.The best white T-shirts for menBest cult pick:Merz b Schwanen 215 classic fit T-shirtMerz b Schwanen215 loopwheeled classic fit T-shirtfrom£85£85 at Stuarts£95 at Merz b SchwanenView image in fullscreen£85 at Stuarts£95 at Merz b SchwanenFew white T-shirts have made a cultural impact like Merz b Schwanen’s 215. It’s the top Jeremy Allen White wears throughoutThe Bear– and itturned a 115-year-old, niche German heritage label into a cult menswear label overnight. If you’ve seen the show, you’ll understand why: a classic crew neck; a snug, considered fit through the torso; and considered details often missed by other brands – triangle inserts under the arms to relieve stress on the seam, and baseball stitching (a crisscross, zigzag pattern). It’s worth noting that it runs small, though, so size up.Merz b Schwanen215 loopwheeled classic fit T-shirtfrom£85£85 at Stuarts£95 at Merz b SchwanenBest high-street white T-shirt:M&S Autograph Supima cotton crew neck T-shirtM&SAutograph supima cotton performance crew neck T-shirt£20£20 at M&SView image in fullscreen£20 at M&SI’ve tried a number of high-street white T-shirts this year, and this one – by Marks & Spencer’s premium line Autograph – is my favourite. It’s relaxed, but not oversized. It’s lightweight, but still substantial. And it’s made from Supima cotton, which has longer fibres, so it’s softer, stronger and more resistant to pilling. At £20, it’s the best argument you’ll find for skipping the designer brands.M&SAutograph supima cotton performance crew neck T-shirt£20£20 at M&SThe insider’s favourite:CDLP lyocell-blend T-shirtCDLPMidweight T-shirt£95£95 at CDLPView image in fullscreen£95 at CDLPFrom Stockholm, CDLP is the basics brand every man in fashion swears by – it’s a strong choice for a plain, minimal tee for the kind of person who doesn’t even like logos on their gym kit. Its cult lyocell-blend T-shirt is the one every fashion insider has in their wardrobe – it’s well-cut, nicely constructed, soft, and breathable enough to hold up in a heatwave. OK, £95 isn’t cheap, but it’s worth it.CDLPMidweight T-shirt£95£95 at CDLPThe sustainable choice:Asket the T-shirtAsketThe T-shirt£45£45 at AsketView image in fullscreen£45 at AsketAsket wears its sustainable fashion credentials on its sleeve – you cansee the full supply chainof every garment, from the factory where it’s stitched, to the carbon, water and energy breakdown. This tee is milled, cut and sewn in facilities in northern Portugal and uses 5.7kg CO2 in the production process. According toCarbonfact, a sustainability platform that helps brands such as APC, Ganni and Finisterre understand their carbon footprint, that’s well below the typical 10.6kg per T-shirt. Green credentials aside, it’s a weighty organic cotton design with hems built specifically to minimise shrinking and twisting. Even better, if it starts to look a little worse for wear,Asket will take it backin any condition and you’ll get money off your next one.AsketThe T-shirt£45£45 at AsketBest oversized white T-shirt:Arket 270gsm oversized T-shirtArket270gsm oversized T-shirtfrom£35£35 at Arket£35 at AsosView image in fullscreen£35 at Arket£35 at AsosArket promises affordable basics that look as if they cost way more than their RRP. This oversized T-shirt hits the mark. It’s the kind you’d expect to see on an off-duty creative director in east London: considered and relaxed, and best worn with work trousers and trainers. The jersey has a weight that looks expensive – and the sleeves hit just above the elbow, exactly the right length for this cut.Arket270gsm oversized T-shirtfrom£35£35 at Arket£35 at AsosBest value for money:Rise & Fall classic cotton crew neck T-shirtRise & FallClassic cotton crew neck T-shirt£40£40 at Rise & FallView image in fullscreen£40 at Rise & FallRise & Fall has a commitment to skipping the markup you see with many of its competitors – which, according to the brand, can be as much as 80% more. It does this by partnering directly with factories andmaking small, just-in-time runs of each garment, which are then sold direct-to-consumer to forgo wholesale margins and expensive overheads. This T-shirt has credentials usually reserved for ones closer to the £70 mark, with weighty organic cotton, a proper collar, and a versatile shape that disappears under a shirt or jacket but still looks great worn solo.Rise & FallClassic cotton crew neck T-shirt£40£40 at Rise & FallBest for layering:Uniqlo Airism crew neck T-shirtUniqloAirism crew neck T-shirt£14.90£14.90 at UniqloView image in fullscreen£14.90 at UniqloThis is the T-shirt that does the important (albeit thankless) job of layering nicely underneath everything else. Uniqlo’s Airism fabric looks like cotton but is blended with other materials to work more like sportswear – controlling moisture and odour, and feeling smooth on the skin – so you can layer up a shirt, jumper and jacket without profusely sweating by the time your commute’s over. At less than £15, it’s a T-shirt you can buy multiples of.UniqloAirism crew neck T-shirt£14.90£14.90 at UniqloThe gold standard:Sunspel Classic T‑shirtSunspelClassic T‑shirt£95£95 at SunspelView image in fullscreen£95 at SunspelIf you ask most menswear obsessives to name the definitive white T-shirt, Sunspel’s Classic is the one they’ll say. Part of that’s down to the fit – close and body-skimming for a smart finish that also looks good under layers. The brand has more than a century’s experience making T-shirts, and heritage goes a long way in the menswear world. This one’s handmade in the brand’s UK factory using lightweight Supima cotton that’s traceable to the California farm it’s from.SunspelClassic T‑shirt£95£95 at SunspelBest for channelling James Dean:Reiss Count air-water cotton tailored-fit T-shirtReissCount air-water cotton tailored-fit T-shirtfrom£48£48 at Reiss£48 at NextView image in fullscreen£48 at Reiss£48 at NextSome men want a T-shirt with a little breathing space, while others want the kind James Dean would wear – one that leaves nothing to the imagination. Reiss caters to the latter with the Count: it’s tailored for a close fit and made from the brand’s signature “air-water cotton” – cotton that’s finished using a specific air and water treatment that softens the fibres for an ultra-smooth finish. It’s tapered at the waist, too, so it’s the closest to tailoring you’ll get with a T-shirt.ReissCount air-water cotton tailored-fit T-shirtfrom£48£48 at Reiss£48 at NextBest white T-shirt for travel:David Gandy Wellwear cotton crewDavid GandyPure cotton crewfrom£15£15 at David Gandy£25 at M&SView image in fullscreen£15 at David Gandy£25 at M&SYou only want to pack one or two T-shirts when you’re travelling – especially if you’ve got a budget airlineacting like your carry-on owes them money. You want a T-shirt that stays clean for longer and looks good with anything. David Gandy Wellwear’s cotton crew has an anti-odour and antibacterial treatment so it can cope with an eight-hour flight, a few hours’ sightseeing and a dinner reservation.David GandyPure cotton crewfrom£15£15 at David Gandy£25 at M&SBest designer white T-shirt:Margaret Howell short-sleeve T-shirtMargaret HowellShort sleeve T-shirt£125£125 at Margaret HowellView image in fullscreen£125 at Margaret HowellMargaret Howell is one of the most respected names in British design, loved by the type of person who can spot a Robin Day chair from across the room. This T-shirt encapsulates why: it’s a relaxed, lightweight take that does the highbrow nonchalant thing well. Theslightlyoff-white colour will fit in perfectly if you have a lot of stone, sand and faded khaki in the rest of your wardrobe.Margaret HowellShort sleeve T-shirt£125£125 at Margaret HowellBest multipack white T-shirts:H&M three-pack regular fit T-shirtsH&MThree-pack regular fit T-shirts£19.99£19.99 at H&MView image in fullscreen£19.99 at H&MBuying a multipack makes sense if you wear a T-shirt every day, but only if the quality is actually there. H&M’s set of three regular-fit white T-shirts offers a straight-up silhouette that works in almost every scenario, and the fabric and weight punch well above the price.H&MThree-pack regular fit T-shirts£19.99£19.99 at H&MBest white T-shirt for the lived-in look:Cos brushed-cotton T-shirtCosBrushed-cotton T-shirt£25£25 at CosView image in fullscreen£25 at CosCos has been making this brushed cotton T-shirt since the brand launched (in 2007), which tells you everything you need to know. The soft fabric means it feels closer to your old, slubby sweatshirt than a standard tee – the type of T-shirt Jeff Bridges’ the Dude would wear in The Big Lebowski (though he’d probably go for a V-neck).CosBrushed-cotton T-shirt£25£25 at CosBest American import:Todd Snyder premium jersey teeTodd SnyderPremium jersey tee£59£59 at Todd SnyderView image in fullscreen£59 at Todd SnyderIf you’ve been watchingLove Storyon Disney+ – the Ryan Murphy series about JFK Jr and Carolyn Bessette that’s had everyone obsessing over 90s New York – you’ll already know Todd Snyder’s vibe. He even wrote the foreword toAmerican Style, a forthcoming book celebrating JFK Jr’s legacy.This tee is very much on the same moodboard. It’s slim enough to wear under a jacket for your meeting in Midtown but nice enough to wear on its own while you cycle around the city. The Portuguese cotton is also soft enough to satisfy even the most discerning American scion.Todd SnyderPremium jersey tee£59£59 at Todd SnyderWhat you need to knowHow to choose the perfect white T-shirtThere’s no such thing as one perfect white T-shirt. Some might see it as a one-and-done situation, but having a favourite tee doesn’t mean it’s right for every occasion.It’s best to think “rotation” rather than “one-hit wonder”. I have 14 that I wear regularly: a lightweight one for layering; something more designed for dressing up; a slinky style à la Brando for a night out; one that sits nicely under a blazer for work; the comfiest one for travel; an oversized option for the beach (just watch the sun cream marks); and the rest for everything in between.There are a few universal rules. Number one:the fabric needs to look and feel premium– that usually means leaning towards natural fibres such as cotton rather than anything that feels too synthetic. Heavier textiles tend to look more expensive, but thin T-shirts have a place too for layering and when it’s above 30C.Number two:it needs to fit correctly. If there’s a T-shirt you like on the upper body but the hemline is somewhere around your crotch, get it tailored. Your local dry cleaner is usually a safe and convenient bet; just check the Google reviews beforehand. If you’re choosing something oversized, it needs to look intentional. Personally, I love a boxy T-shirt – one that’s a little cropped (I’m 5ft 8in) and roomy through the body without drowning my frame.Number three:pay attention to the small stuff. Since it’s so simple in design, the finer details really matter, such as the collar, shoulder seam, sleeve length and overall construction. Take note when you’re in the changing room – not just how it looks in the mirror straight-on but also how it moves with your body. If it’s significantly pulling anywhere on your body while you walk, that usually means it’s too tight – unless, of course, you’re aiming for a slim-fitting T-shirt to show off the work you’ve been putting in at the gym.How should my white T-shirt fit?The fit of your white T-shirt matters more than anything else – but it’s not a one-size-fits-all situation because it depends entirely on how you’re wearing it.Wearing it on its own, untucked, the hemline should sit around the middle of your fly – or, if you’re feeling bold, the top, which means a flash of midriff every time you raise your arms (the tried-and-testedPaul Mescal fit). Sleeves should hit somewhere between mid and lower biceps, and a thick collar tends to look most expensive. A straight or boxy tee cut from a heavy cotton works best here because it will hold its shape throughout the day.If you’re layering, you want something closer-fitting that sits neatly under a shirt, jacket or jumper without bunching – in this case, go for a less prominent collar, since you don’t want it competing with whatever’s on top. The same logic applies when tucking into tailored trousers: excess fabric will ruin the line of your outfit. If any of your current collection feel too big, you could try an army tuck – gathering the excess fabric at the sides and folding it back before tucking it in.How to keep a white T-shirt whiteYou might think keeping a white T-shirt white means hot washes and aggressive detergents, but you’d be wrong. The golden rule is simple: cold wash, inside out. Excessive heat breaks down cotton fibres over time and causes white fabric to turn yellow or grey, while washing inside out protects the surface of the fabric from fading.For tougher stains – the inevitable mark of sun cream, the rogue splash of bolognese or red wine – a stain remover such asVanishapplied directly before washing should do the job without the need to crank up the temperature. Just don’t be tempted to bleach: it might seem like the obvious fix, but over time it’ll yellow your whites faster than almost anything else. Instead, you could trysodium percarbonate.
