When mixed with warm water, it separates into oxygen to lift organic matter; soda ash to neutralise minerals; and water, which leaves no residue – unlike harsher chemicals, so it’s a safe, eco-friendly alternative.The worst culprit of all is the armpit stain – that yellowy-grey area that appears after a few months of wear. The best defence is to act fast: if you’ve been sweating, rinse the underarm area with cold water while it’s still wet (the stains set in once the sweat dries). For anything that’s already past it, a paste of baking soda and water left on the stain for 30 minutes before washing is an easy fix, and it won’t damage the fabric like bleach.For more, readhow to wear a quarter-zip jumper without looking like a finance broPeter Bevan is a stylist and fashion journalist covering menswear, womenswear and beautyExplore more on these topicsMen's fashionThe FilterMen's topsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Chez Rose, London W1: ‘One of the dining highlights of 2026’ – restaurant review | Food | The Guardian
description: Chez Rose offers a sort of hospitality that feels centuries old, but when done well, will never be old hat
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: Chez Rose offers a sort of hospitality that feels centuries old, but when done well, will never be old hat
Content: Chez Rose, London W1: 'showstopping cuisine'.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenChez Rose, London W1: 'showstopping cuisine'.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodReviewChez Rose, London W1: ‘One of the dining highlights of 2026’ – restaurant reviewChez Rose offers a sort of hospitality that feels centuries old, but when done well, will never be old hatGrace DentSun 2 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 14.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChez Rose has just appeared on Pollen Street, Mayfair, but to the casual passerby, it looks as if it could have been established in 1974. This is, of course,poudre aux yeux; until recently, this was Jason Atherton’s Little Social. Yet, with some strategically placed tablesen terrasse, vintage mirrors, thoughtfully scattered doilies and, later, bread baskets, and what you have is France in the eye of the British beholder. Not the full ’Allo ’Allo-ification, but that elegant, sexy pastiche of everyday French dining that adult Brits gobble up like school kids devouring Milka chocolate.CrepesSuzette,pouletrôtiwithvin jauneand morels, dover sole meuniere with Menton lemon…Ooh là là. If you can’t get intoBouchon Racinein Farringdon, go here instead.Chez Rose is by Spencer Metzger, whose CV is an embarrassment of edible riches: The Ritz andRow on 5were his culinary sandpit, until Chez Rose allowed him to model a whole place in tribute to his late grandmother, Rosemary. There are framed photos of the Metzger family around the room, and some items from her house, if diners would stop stealing them. Rosemary wasn’t French, and neither is Metzger, but within one mouthful of the first snack of red prawn and tomato on a crisp crostini, zinging with a mouthy lemon, which arrived on a pretty doily, it feels churlish to quibble. In fact, if Metzger’s non-Frenchness upsets you, it just leaves more 70% chocolate souffle with vanilla ice-cream for the rest of us.View image in fullscreenThe ‘utterly marvellous’ courgette flower with ricotta and sauce vierge, Chez Rose, London W1.The day-to-day cooking is in the hands of head chefMark Catchpole, whose CV takes in Roganic, Attica and The Fat Duck. The menu is a single sheet with a pretty logo, then a list of temptations: wild mushroompersilladewith preserved truffle; Orkney scallop with Café de Paris butter; Cornish cod with mussel sauce and samphire; Aylesbury duck breast with black figs; and a T-bone steak for two at £145.Of a Friday lunchtime, and just weeks after opening, Chez Rose is lively. We arrive at midday and begin with a round of snacks: Cantabrian anchovies on a bed of young curd. There are anchovies, and then there are these Cantabrian anchovies: fat, glossy, smooth, salty; totally addictive. The Brits have been scared off anchovies by whiskery, bitter, tinnedmonstrositieshurled over badsalade niçoise. Fishy purgatory. Served like this at Chez Rose, though, they feel as sweet and naughty as chocolate profiteroles.The longsuffering Charles pops a plate of Vesuvius tomatoes on the order, recklessly suggesting we need vitamin C. It’s a good move. This is a plate of the sweetest, ripest tomatoes we’ve tasted this summer – vivid red, yellow, purple-black – then chunks of ripe, sweet peach over a cool layer ofstracciatella. Like all good French cooking, it is ruthless simplicity that blows your mind and has you pointing at the plate saying: “Aren’t tomatoes amazing?”, as if they’re a brand new invention.Next up, a stuffed courgette flower; a dish almost every eatery in the south of France serves all summer long, with varying success. Suspend your tiny violins; I’ve eaten so many poor versions. Here at Chez Rose, it’s a whole new dish entirely, and utterly marvellous. How is this courgette flower so crisp and delicious, I marvel, prodding at the rich ricotta innards, and licking up puddles ofsauce vierge. “A courgette flower is always delicious,” argues Charles, who, being French, is wounded I’d say otherwise. He forgets the various backstreet cafes from Nice to Juan-les-Pins where I’ve eaten the equivalent of old daffodil heads in Castrol GTX.View image in fullscreenThe ‘unmissable’ 70% chocolate souffle vanilla ice-cream, at Chez Rose, London W1.Glasses of Domaine de la Bégude Bandol rosé 2024 arrive in those tiny, cute single-glass jugs. The wine list is weighty, and the sommelier brimming with facts on each listing. Chez Rose offers a sort of hospitality that feels centuries old, but when done well, will never be old hat.An entire john dory arrives on the bone, alongside a serving of pommes puree. The potato is, I will attest, half butter, half spud. No longer seriously categorised as a vegetable, it’s more like love/future coronary problems in a bowl. But with the future of Planet Earth being uncertain, I devour it in its entirety. There are simple podded peas with yet more butter, and one of those zingily dressed mounds of fresh lettuce that, I’ll admit, only French cuisine truly nails.The dessert menu offersmousse au chocolatwith olive oil and creme caramel, but the 70% chocolate souffle felt unmissable. You have to pre-order it, and it arrives as a showstopper: bold as brass, high and glossy. The souffle is one of the dining highlights of 2026. Ask the kitchen to bake an engagement ring into one – there’s no way any sane person could refuse you after that.Allez,allez, allez.Chez Rose5 Pollen St, London. W1S 1NE, 020 7870 3730,chezroselondon.com.Open all week, lunch: noon–2.30pm (3.30pm Sun), dinner: 5.30pm (6.30pm Sun)–9.15pm (last seating). About £90 a head a la carte (Sunday lunch £49 for two courses, £59 for three), all plus drinks and service.Explore more on these topicsFoodGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make gambas al ajillo – recipe | Seafood | The Guardian
description: Conjuring memories of sun-drenched holidays and cool tapas bars, this dish is deliciously messy
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: Conjuring memories of sun-drenched holidays and cool tapas bars, this dish is deliciously messy
Content: Felicity Cloake's Gambas Al Ajillo.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake's Gambas Al Ajillo.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.Felicity Cloake's masterclassSeafoodHow to make gambas al ajillo – recipeConjuring memories of sun-drenched holidays and cool tapas bars, this dish is deliciously messyFelicity CloakeSun 2 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a devotee of the small, sweet and winningly cheap cold-water prawn, I don’t often find myself at the court of the king variety, but as a way to conjure happy memories of holidays past, sunny terraces and cool tapas bars, this particular dish is hard to beat. Served sizzling hot and drenched in red, garlicky oil, it’s deliciously messy stuff, and best paired with bread and an icy drink.Prep5 minCook15 minServes4 as a tapa, 2 as a starter8 sustainablysourced raw shell-on king prawnsSalt and black pepper4 garlic cloves120ml olive oilA few flat-leaf parsley stems4 small dried chillies, or 1 tsp cayenne pepper or paprika, or ½ tsp chilli flakes2 tsp sherry vinegar, or wine vinegar or lemon juiceBread slices, to serve1 Raw shell-on prawns are best …For the best-flavoured results, you need the prawn shells, but don’t worry if you or your guests prefer not to faff about peeling them at the table, because you use the shells separately here. Raw shell-on prawns are easiest sourced frozen – supermarkets, especially east Asian ones, have them, or find them, often with greater traceability, online.View image in fullscreen2 … but if you can’t get themThat said, if you can only find cooked shell-on prawns, use those instead – you’ll just need to warm them through in step 8 instead. And if you can get your hands only on peeled prawns, you can also use them, but consider adding a teaspoon of Malaysian shrimp paste in step 7 or a dash of fish sauce in step 8, should you have either to hand.3 Peel the prawnsPeel the shell-on prawns by twisting off their heads, then, laying one prawn flat on your other hand, use a fingernail to get under the shell and peel down the back, then twist off the tail. Put all the shells in a bowl. Run a small, sharp knife down the back of each prawn and, if it’s obvious and visible, hook out and discard the dark line of digestive tract (if you can’t see it, it’s probably clear, so don’t worry about this).View image in fullscreen4 Salt the prawnsSprinkle the prawn meat lightly with salt and set aside (you can prep this dish ahead of time up to the end of step 6; if doing so, store the salted prawns in the fridge for up to two days). Squeeze the contents of the prawn heads into a small bowl, then put the spent heads in the bowl with the rest of the shells.5 Prep the garlicPeel all the garlic, and squash two of the cloves with the flat side of a knife; leave the other two cloves intact for now. Put the oil in a frying pan on a medium-low heat (this makes a fair bit of oil for dipping, so cut down the quantity a little, if you prefer), then add the squashed garlic (keep back the remaining whole cloves for now), the prawn shells and the squeezed-out heads.View image in fullscreen6 Fry the garlic and shellsFry, stirring frequently, for five to seven minutes, until the prawn shells turn a deep pink; make sure the garlic doesn’t catch and burn. Meanwhile, finely slice the remaining garlic and roughly chop the parsley (this is the traditional herb of choice here, though if truth be told I prefer coriander). Pass the shell oil through a sieve into a bowl, then discard the solids.View image in fullscreen7 Fry the chilliReturn the oil to the pan on a medium-high heat and add the chilli in whatever form you’re using it; small dried chillies look pretty, but cayenne pepper or paprika taste just as good. If you use chilli flakes, though, do so with caution, because the prawns should still be the dominant flavour. Fry for 30 seconds or so.View image in fullscreen8 Add the prawnsAdd the prawns to the pan, cook, stirring, for a minute more, then add the sliced garlic and cook, still stirring, for a further minute – the prawns should by this stage be just cooked through. Mix the vinegar or lemon juice into the small bowl of prawn head juices, then stir this mixture and the parsley into the prawn pan. Season and serve at once with bread.9 Alternative seafoodA similar approach works with most seafood. Gently heat the oil with the squashed garlic in step 5 until it begins to colour, then scoop out and discard. Turn up the heat, add the sliced garlic, chillies and cleaned, dried and sliced squid, scallops, clams, whelks, chunks of fish, etc, and stir-fry until just cooked through.Explore more on these topicsSeafoodFelicity Cloake's masterclassFoodShellfishSpanish food and drinkSnacksStarterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘£5,800 on a watch?!’ What happened when five couples kept separate money diaries – then revealed all to their partners? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Rachel forked out £700 for beauty treatments, Kojo confessed to a £25 cigarette habit, and Jake indulged his love of fancy timepieces. Were their other halves forgiving or furious?
Author: Georgina Lawton
Headline: Rachel forked out £700 for beauty treatments, Kojo confessed to a £25 cigarette habit, and Jake indulged his love of fancy timepieces. Were their other halves forgiving or furious?
Content: Illustrations: Sandra Navarro/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustrations: Sandra Navarro/The GuardianLife and style‘£5,800 on a watch?!’ What happened when five couples kept separate money diaries – then revealed all to their partners?Rachel forked out £700 for beauty treatments, Kojo confessed to a £25 cigarette habit, and Jake indulged his love of fancy timepieces. Were their other halves forgiving or furious?Georgina LawtonSun 2 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 11.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘What’s the point buying a £189 health tracker if you’re a smoker?’Rachel and Kojo, NorthamptonRachel, 38, met Kojo, 41, in 2020, a year after divorcing the father of her two children, Amanda and Miles. Rachel works for the NHS, earning £27,000 a year. Kojo earns £32,000 as a school caretaker. They live in a three-bedroom home they bought in 2024 for £325,000. Their son, Marcus, and Rachel’s 13-year-old daughter, Amanda, live with them, while Miles, 17, splits his time between them and Rachel’s ex. The couple divide their £1,750 monthly mortgage and household bills. They each contribute £500 to a joint account for shared expenses, while keeping the rest of their finances separate. Rachel receives £150 a week in child maintenance from her ex-husband.View image in fullscreenRachelMondayI work three days a week at a local hospital and have to pay to park – a complete joke (£8.50). No lunch cost as I’m microdosing [weight-loss drug] Mounjaro. On my break, I ordered another Mounjaro pen (£220). I also paid the weekly carpool fee for Miles and Amanda as they need transport after school (£60). Total: £288.50TuesdayI bought a gym set online before my shift (£50), drove to work (£8.50) and bought some fruit and a wrap from the canteen (£7.20). Total: £65.70WednesdayI went to work (£8.50) and afterwards headed to a bar to meet a school friend for a wine and some chicken wings (£11.50). My appetite is coming back. Stopped at Asda for crisps, salad and chicken nuggets for the kids’ snacks (£11.23), and bought an eyelash-perming set online (£12.50). Total: £43.73ThursdayA self-care morning. I had some skin treatments: a polynucleotide injection (£350), Botox, which I get every three months (£150), and 1ml filler in my cheeks and chin (£175). I feel great. Total: £675FridayI picked up Marcus, Amanda and Miles from school and took them to Nando’s as a treat (£65.32). It used to be cheap! Later, tidied the house and went shopping with Marcus and Kojo. Total £65.32SaturdayKojo, Marcus, Amanda and I went to a safari park. It was £130 for four, which is a lot, but Marcus loves the lions. I paid half from our joint account (£65). Kojo paid the other half plus lunch. Total: £65SundayOrdered some face serums online (£45) and a phone case for Amanda after hers broke (£12). Did a family shop at Tesco, which Kojo paid for. Total: £57Weekly total: £1,260.25KojoMondayI walk to work and I get my food covered, so I generally don’t spend much in the week. I bought a packet of 20 Benson & Hedges (£18.50), which I smoke on the way to and from work. Total: £18.50TuesdayOrdered new headphones (£75.50) and a Hume health watch (£189) as my birthday is coming up. I like tracking my sleep and hormone stats. Total: £264.50WednesdayThey served shepherd’s pie in the school canteen, which I hate, so I bought a cheese and ham baguette at a nearby cafe (£4.89). Total: £4.89ThursdayI bought some cigarillos, which I don’t tend to smoke as fast as cigarettes, as I’ve been smoking a bit more lately. Only a 10-pack this time. (£6.89). Total: £6.89FridayI went to a department store with Rachel and bought Marcus a new pencil-case for school (£5.55), trainers (£32.50) and socks (£3.20), as well as a top Rachel wanted (£22.50). Total: £63.75SaturdayWe went to the safari park and I paid half (£65) plus parking (£9). I also covered lunch for the four of us. We got burgers, chips and colas (£54.88). It was a fun, but expensive, day. Total: £128.88SundayThe Tesco shop cost £135.30, which is about normal. I usually split it with Rachel, but I got it this week. Total: £135.30Weekly total: £622.71The big reveal …Rachel describes herself as “highly strung” when it comes to talking about money after separating from her former partner: “I ended up with nothing in my divorce.” When she and Kojo got together, she expected he might be more cautious about spending money on her children. Instead, she says: “He treats them as his own.”She is nervous about revealing her diary to him. She has increased her spending on beauty in recent years, trying to tackle low body confidence after three kids. Last month she flew to Turkey for a breast augmentation, at a cost of £5,000. Kojo was taken aback, but told Rachel to do what felt right. “I helped her research the clinic, but it was all her savings,” he said. Rachel puts larger purchases, such as her monthly Mounjaro injections and her Botox treatments, on her personal Amex, for which she pays off the minimum each month. “I’ve got a debt of around £2,500,” she says, during the diary reveal. “I didn’t know it was that high,” Kojo responds.Kojo is shocked at the cost of the treatments Rachel had during the week: “I had no idea how expensive all this was,” he says. “We could put some of that money towards a kitchen extension.” He reflects on how quickly these treatments have been normalised: “When we met, Rachel wasn’t doing any of this.” Rachel says a kitchen extension is out of their budget anyway and defends her purchases as paramount for her mental health. “I’m a mum. My treats make me look and feel better, unlike Kojo’s smoking.” His £25-a-week cigarette habit, which he keeps hidden from the family, is more expensive than she thought. She also finds his health tech splurges contradictory. “What’s the point in buying a £189 health watch if you’re a smoker?” she asks.Kojo found the diary-sharing fine, except for the smoking reveal. “I’d like to give up. I’m a bit ashamed of how much I spent. Rachel has been on at me for years to quit.” He says the task demystified their finances and showed them where they could work together more effectively. “I see where we can plug a few holes,” he says. “A £1,260 spend per week from Rachel is a lot.”The task also illuminated Rachel’s body insecurities to Kojo. “Maybe it’s my fault: I need to tell her how beautiful she is more regularly,” he says. “She doesn’t need to spend all that on beauty treatments, but I won’t try to control her choices.”‘I like buying food in bulk, but Jasper buys stuff as and when, which annoys me as it’s less economical’Caitlin and Jasper, BristolCaitlin, an accountant on £94,000, and Jasper, a tax adviser on £103,000, both 34, met on Tinder 10 years ago. They got married in 2024 and Caitlin is six months pregnant with their first child, conceived by IVF. They live with their six-year-old chihuahua, Beanie (“a diva”), in a five-bed Victorian house, which they are renovating. The cost of that, at £20,000, is split between them, with Jasper also putting in his bonus from work. The pair pay £3,500 into a joint pot each month to cover bills, holidays, house expenses and their two cars, but also have separate bank accounts.View image in fullscreenCaitlinMondayI ordered a cute baby outfit online from a sustainable brand (£19.20) while I worked from home. I also bought some new cushion covers for our spare room sofa (£28). Total: £47.20TuesdayOur food shop from Tesco arrived. It was £83.45; we split it (£41.72). I like buying food in bulk, but Jasper buys stuff as and when, which annoys me as it’s less economical. I got some milk before the shop arrived (75p) and a dog treat for Beanie (£2.20). Total: £44.67WednesdayI paid for the wood (£295) for new skirting boards at B&Q and a sander from Argos (£25), as Jasper said he didn’t want to shell out from the joint account. The measuring and calculating was easy, but the sanding is much more laborious. Jasper says he will help, as my mobility isn’t great. Total: £320ThursdayWe are going to London next weekend to see friends and booked a bougie hotel on the Elizabeth line at £200 per night for three nights. I paid half (£300). Total: £300.FridayI went to the office in Bristol city centre. I got just under half a tank of petrol on the way (£32). For lunch, I bought an egg sandwich, a Diet Coke and Quavers (£5.99). On the way home, I stopped to get ginger and Thai curry paste for dinner (£4.34). Total £42.33SaturdayWe went to the pub after walking Beanie. Jasper paid, as he is drinking beers and I’m only on the Diet Cokes. Total: £0SundayNo spending today. The baby is really active at the moment. I stayed in and relaxed.Weekly total: £754.20JasperMondayI drove to my office in the city. Parking is £10 a day. Petrol is about £7 there and back. I spent £10 for lunch – a chicken and bacon baguette and crisps – from a little independent place near me. Total: £27TuesdayHeaded to work again, but I got a duck wrap instead of the chicken and bacon (£27 total). In the evening, I bought a garden strimmer and tools (£43). I’m not good with plants, but I like pottering in summer. Total: £70WednesdayRinse and repeat at work (£27), but I went back to the chicken for lunch. Very exciting. I also ordered some picture frames for things we need to hang up (£44). Total: £71ThursdayCommuting and lunch costs were the same (£27). Later, I paid for my half of the hotel in London (£300). I also bought some football tickets for a match next week in London with a mate (£75). Caitlin isn’t coming. She hates football. Total: £402FridayI got the train to London for a last-minute meeting, but can expense that. I got a bento box, edamame and Diet Coke at lunch (£13.99) and stopped at Boots for razors (£1.27). Total: £15.26SaturdayWe had a nice walk and went to the pub. I got a few beers and Caitlin’s Diet Cokes (£32.54). I also ordered calamari for us (£7). Total: £39.54SundayI did a little late-night clothes splurge that I didn’t tell Caitlin about: shirts and shorts from Zara and Asos (£354.32). Justified, though, as we have a holiday coming up. Total: £354.32Weekly total: £979.12The big reveal …The task diary wasn’t too revealing for Caitlin and Jasper. “I’m an accountant, so love all this,” Caitlin says. “We spend on the big things in life: house, IVF treatment. It’s good to see how far we’ve come. I’ve wanted kids for so long and I’ve dreamed of a house like the one we have now.” By Caitlin’s admission, Jasper grew up “more middle class” than her, with parents who own a property business, so is more casual with money. She sees herself as more frugal – something she puts down to her heritage. “My family is from Yorkshire. My grandmother lived on a farm while her father worked in the mines.”After the diary reveal, Caitlin was surprised at Jasper’s clothing splurge. “£300 in one online shop is insane to me. He could go on Vinted.” Jasper is unrepentant. “I work hard for my money, so I don’t care,” he says.They’ve found they bicker over money sometimes, such as during the IVF. “We spent £8,000 on fertility treatments in Portugal, which worked. But Jasper didn’t like me spending an extra £400 a month on supplements during that time. That caused a divide. But I was so desperate for a baby, I wanted to maximise our chances. It wasn’t a waste of money as I got pregnant. Who’s to say they didn’t work?” Now it’s the renovation that causes friction, as costs rise.Recently, Caitlin wanted to splurge £500 on a vintage coffee table, but Jasper said no. “It was too much – we didn’t need it.” When Caitlin suggested redoing all the skirting boards with a professional, he also put his foot down, deeming it “an unnecessary hole in the budget”. Caitlin took it upon herself to buy the wood and a sander. He says Caitlin was a bit annoyed that the cost came from her own personal expense. “She wanted to do it,” he says, “but I was surprised at the cost of the wood (£295). I admit that it’s a spend that I will also benefit from, and it looks really nice.” Jasper has since helped with the sanding.‘I should have sorted my £250 speeding ticket earlier. It’s really increased’Martha and Gary, BrightonMartha, 64 and Gary, 70, have been together for five years and have an 11-year-old whippet called Peggy, who used to belong to Gary’s adult son. Gary is a semi-retired electrician with an annual income of about £45,000 from part-time work and his pension, while Martha is retired and lives off her pension and the pension of her late husband Dave, who died in 2016, which is £2,200 per month. They top up a shared account with £350 a week to cover household costs, groceries and alcohol, while keeping the rest of their spending separate. Martha set up all the bills and expenses, which come out of the joint account. Their house was bought by Martha in 2024 for £425,000.View image in fullscreenGaryMondayI drive to work three days a week for a big electric company. They cover parking, but I get lunch. I brought a sandwich from home and later bought a coffee (£3.48) and sausage roll (£2.72). Total: £6.20TuesdayI had three coffees at work (£10.45), which was a lot for me (I usually have one or two). I later made a 20% contribution (£1,200) to vet fees for Peggy, with insurance covering the rest. I was happy to do it, because she needed her stomach pumped and I would never let her suffer, but it is a lot. Total: £1,210.45WednesdayI bought a Bluetooth speaker from a shop after work as ours broke (£12.50). I had two coffees, but got one free with my loyalty card (£3.48). Total: £15.98ThursdayI had the day off and Martha made me sort out my speeding ticket (£250). I should have done it earlier, as it’s really increased. Total: £250FridayI paid for fish and chips for us on the pier (£24.50) and we walked Peggy (she’s recovering slowly). Later, we went to the pub (£43.84). Total: £68.34SaturdayI got a small top-up shop from our local Co-op (£38.99), but we usually go to Asda. Later, we went to our regular social club and had a few drinks (£45.21). Total: £84.20SundayI paid £350 into our joint account to cover next week’s expenses, but didn’t spend anything else. Total: £0Weekly total: £1,635.17MarthaMondayI usually walk Peggy while Gary is at work. We didn’t go far as she’s recovering from her operation. I bought some chocolate, poo bags and wine from the newsagents on the way home (£11.40). Later, I bought a Dorothy Perkins dress on Vinted (£12.40). Total: £23.80TuesdayI walked Peggy a little further today and had breakfast at a cafe on the pier (£17.50). I ordered two more items on Vinted (£39.34), but also sold a top for £11, so was happy with that. Total: £56.84WednesdayI walked Peggy then went to a pilates class that is prepaid at my local gym. On the way back, I walked to our florist to get some peonies as they are in season at the moment (£16). Total: £16ThursdayI bought some trousers on Vinted (£6.34) and a new lamp for our bedroom from La Redoute (£40) and some more flowers from the garage (£8) when I got petrol (£23.96). I helped Gary do his speeding ticket, which I was cross about. Total: £78.30skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFridayI bought a designer bag from Gucci I’ve had my eye on for ages on Vinted and was very pleased (£250). On the way back from the fish and chip shop with Gary, I stopped at my local vape shop to get some liquid as well as a new vape. Didn’t tell him the cost (£33). Total: £283SaturdayI bought us a round at the social club (£21.41), Gary got the rest. Total: £21.41SundayWe stayed in and I cooked a roast. I won an auction on eBay for a pair of heels (£19.50) and also paid £350 for the next week to our joint account. Total: £19.50Weekly total: £498.85The big reveal …Martha admits that she doesn’t keep track of her money and that she has a weakness for browsing on Vinted, typically spending about £100 a week on secondhand clothes while only making back about £50 a week from sales. “It doesn’t really balance out,” she sighs. During the week’s diary, this difference was significantly higher after she spotted a bag she couldn’t resist for £250, something Gary thought was “crazy”. She also spends about £30 a week on flowers, which Gary was unaware of: “They just die in a few days – it’s pointless.” His worst spending habit is keeping driving tickets to himself. “I make plans to deal with my fines immediately, but then I panic and I forget and they build up.”During the reveal, Martha chastised him for ignoring the speeding ticket. “It was about to go to court,” she says. “It’s already £250. I don’t know why he does this, it always gets worse.” Meanwhile, Gary was intrigued by the amount Martha spent on vaping: “It’s a lot for flavoured air.” Martha says Gary should start taking coffee in a flask to work to cut back on his £15-a-week habit, but he refuses as he likes the ritual.Keeping a money diary was hard for Gary as he “has never been good with maths or admin”. His biggest expense is generally his beloved whippet. After the dog became seriously ill last month, insurance covered 80% of the £6,000 veterinary bill, leaving Gary to pay the remaining 20%, plus a £250 excess, some of which fell in the diary week. During the reveal, Martha expresses disappointment that he doesn’t have better insurance but Gary corrects her: “She’s an old dog and I only insured her last year. All of the insurance options were expensive.”The two would repeat the task if needed. “Looking at what I spend has helped me feel more on track with things,” Gary says. “I’m going to be better with the parking tickets and fines.” His attitude to money is by his own account “anxious”. He says it’s because when he got divorced from the mother of his two children, she ended up with half of his pension. “I was very cautious when I met Martha, but now I’m more open,” he says.‘I don’t feel bad buying nice things. I’m someone who spends all the time’Jake and Ryan, LondonJake, 45, met Ryan, 36, on a dating app in 2024. Jake works as a creative director earning £75,000 a year, while Ryan earns £52,000 as a graphic designer. The couple bought a three-bedroom home in 2024 for £625,000 with a deposit largely from Jake’s family. They split their £2,250 monthly mortgage and bills equally and pay £800 each into a joint account for shared expenses, including a cat called Mariah. Ryan is cautious with money and likes to build up savings; Jake, on the other hand, loves luxury watches and has spent more than £15,000 on his collection over the last three years. They’re looking to adopt soon.View image in fullscreenJakeMondayUp at 5.30am for the gym in our building before work. I commute to east London but we live in the west, so it’s a nightmare time-wise, even if it only costs £4.60 a day on Transport for London. Grabbed a coffee at the station (£3.90) and my weekly protein meal prep delivery arrived at home while I was at work (£58). It’s expensive, but stops us buying takeaway or eating out, which Ryan, especially, loves. Total: £66.50TuesdayAnother early start and another commute (£4.60). Picked up a protein shake after the gym (£4.20) and paid my annual Headspace [mental health app] membership (£49.99). I was tempted to grab lunch from a local bistro, but ate one of my meal prep boxes instead. Total: £58.79WednesdayWorked another long day and commuted by train (£4.60). After work, I met Ryan for drinks and nibbles at our local pub. We split the bill (£28.50). On the way home, I bought some toiletries from Boots (£14.20) for an upcoming work trip to Milan. Total: £47.30ThursdayDid the commute (£4.60). During my break I ordered some new gym clothes and supplements online (£57). I know I already have enough, but I like feeling good when I train. I used another protein meal prep for lunch. Total: £61.60FridayBack to work. Another commute (£4.60) and I picked up coffees for my team because we’d had a big client win (£19.40). Used another meal prep for lunch, then stopped at Sainsbury’s for cat food, nuts and protein bagels (£8.30). Met Ryan for a drink in Soho (he paid). Total: £32.30SaturdayRyan went to meet his brother and I had a lie-in browsing watches in bed. I ended up buying the Omega I’d been looking at for months. It cost £5,800 on a 0% finance deal. Ryan went mad. Total: £5,800SundayTreated us both to pastries on a walk to a park near our house (£9.20) and ordered next week’s protein meal prep boxes (£58). In the evening, Ryan and I ordered Vietnamese because neither of us wanted to cook (£35). Total: £102.20Weekly total: £6,168.69RyanMondayOffice day in central London. The commute from west London isn’t cheap – my tube fare was £7.20. I bought a croissant at the station (£3.50) and spent the evening working from home on some personal design projects. I also bought a couple of house plants online (£32) because I’m slowly turning the flat into a jungle. Total: £42.70TuesdayWorking from home today, so no commuting costs. I made lunch from leftover salad bits in the fridge and spent most of the day designing. I bought a new ceramic plant pot (£18) and some bits for the house (£12.50). I’m never done decorating and adding. Total: £30.50WednesdayBack into the office. Tube fare was £7.20. I forgot my lunch, so bought a soup, baguette and coffee near work (£12.45). On the way home, I picked up some soil and fertiliser for my plants (£14.99). I met Jake for drinks (£28.50) then cooked Thai for us at home. Total: £63.14ThursdayWorking from home again. I spent most of the day designing and had a quiet evening. I ordered some new sketchbooks and art supplies for my personal projects (£22.50). I like making art for friends. Total: £22.50FridayOffice day again. Tube fare was £7.20. After work, I met a friend for drinks in Soho (£48) and Jake came for one. I ordered some socks on Amazon before bed (£9.80). Total: £65SaturdayI met my brother for lunch. We went to a small Italian restaurant and my share came to £32. Afterwards, I bought a big snake plant (£25) from a market, which I definitely didn’t need. Total: £57SundayQuiet day at home. I did the Lidl food shop (£65) and went to the gym. Later, we discussed the watch thing over a takeaway and I calmed down a bit. Total: £65Weekly total: £345.84The big reveal …When Jake revealed his watch buy, Ryan was upset. “I can’t understand spending £5,800 on a piece of jewellery, especially without talking to me first,” he says. Ryan describes the purchase as “disappointing”, because the couple had agreed to prioritise saving for a future adoption. “I really want kids, but sometimes I feel like Jake isn’t as serious about it as I am,” Ryan says. “He bought a £2,000 secondhand Rolex in February. It’s not really about the watch itself. It’s what it represents. We’re supposed to be putting money towards a kids’ fund.” Jake disagrees. “I don’t think that buying myself something I’ve worked hard for means I’m not interested in parenthood. I’m still contributing to the house, the bills and our savings. I don’t feel every spare penny has to go towards a future plan.”The couple have very different relationships with money. Ryan grew up in a rural Irish household where money was tighter and treats were rare. “If I ever bought something for myself, my friends back home would say: ‘You’re very good to yourself.’ It’s a sarcastic Irish thing. You’re not supposed to be seen treating yourself. Jake is the opposite. He’s also vainer than I am and spends a lot on clothes and protein supplements, whereas I don’t care.”Jake says the watches are partly about celebrating his success after years of working hard. “I don’t feel bad buying nice things. I’m someone who spends all the time. I save, I work long hours and I wanted something that felt like mine.” He was raised in London by finance-savvy parents who taught him the importance of investing. They helped him with £50,000 towards his share of their house deposit. He admits this may influence his spending. “My parents talked about money openly,” Jake says. “They taught me to only buy expensive things if everything else – bills, mortgage – was under control. We are in the prime of our lives, so why not? I’ve had support that Ryan hasn’t had, but I also think it’s made me more conscious of long-term goals.”Ryan feels this overlooks the fact that Jake has had a leg up. “Jake’s parents gave him a huge advantage, which I’m grateful for because it helped us buy our home. But these big splurges seem so indulgent.” The task was tricky as it highlighted what Ryan perceives as a different attitude towards future plans. “Maybe we aren’t as aligned as I thought. Maybe kids need to go on hold, because we can’t afford to have them and spend like this,” he says.‘I just hate being showy with cash’Lara and Max, BarcelonaLara and Max, both 30, began dating last year. Max moved into Lara’s city centre apartment after just two months. Max earns £62,000 as a freelance advertising copywriter. Lara earns £89,000 working in tech, taking a pay cut from £149,000 when she moved to Barcelona from the US. She receives an extra £149,000 a year in stock compensation from her job, which she will cash out when she leaves. They pay €1,950/£1,664.15 in rent and bills, which they split. Lara covered the majority of a recent £20,000 car cost, while Max contributed £5,000.View image in fullscreenLaraMondayFirst of the month, so the rent was due: €900 plus bills at €75, each (€975/£827). The landlord put the cost up last year; Barcelona is in high demand. I bought some coffee, sheep’s cheese and lentil chips from our local deli after work as I worked from home (€8.50/£7.22) Total: €983.50/£834.22TuesdayI visited my office in the city centre, which I do around twice a week. Petrol is probably €5 (£4.24) there and back. I went to my favourite little cafeteria and ate swordfish and croquettes (€15/£12.73). On the way home, I had a massage and acupuncture appointment (€70/£59.42). Total: €90/£76.39WednesdayI worked from home so asked Max to go to his co-working space – our apartment isn’t huge. Jeans I had ordered for him arrived (€120/£101.86). He tried them on when he got back and liked them. He’s got better at accepting my gifts. Total: €120/£101.86ThursdayI commuted on the train today (€2.60/£2.21) because I had a meeting in a co-working space and couldn’t park there. I ordered some tapas and a fizzy water (€22/£18.67). In the evening, I went for a mani-pedi (€55/£46.49) and bought a dress for a friend’s wedding and a new bikini from a Spanish designer I like (€250/£212.21). Total: €329.60/£279.58FridayStarted an organic meal subscription so we don’t have to cook as much (€45/£38.20). Went to a pilates class at lunch (€15/£12.73). Bought a new painting for our apartment and relaxed at home as Max went out (€150/£127.33). Total: €210/£178.26SaturdayMax and I walked to a market and grabbed brunch with friends. He paid.SundayI booked a second acupuncture appointment as the first was so useful (€70/£59.42).Weekly total: €1,803.10/£1,538MaxMondayI transferred my half of the rent to Lara (€975/£827.63). It still feels like her apartment at times, because everything is in her name, but I’m keen to put my stamp on things. Today, I bought a mid-century chair she preapproved (€250/£212.21). Total: €1,225/£1,039.84TuesdayI worked from home alone. I popped out to get some avocados and yoghurt for lunch (€4.40/£3.73). Total: €4.40/£3.73WednesdayI walked to the co-working space Lara made me join, which is €75/£64 a month, so we can have some space as we both work from home a lot. I go about three times a week, so it works out good value, about €6.25/£5.31 a visit. I brought my own lunch. I liked the jeans Lara bought me but I’d never spend that on myself. Ordered some Thai food for us both (€26.22/£22.26). Total: €32.47/£27.57ThursdayI headed to my co-working space and then met some mates at a bar (€29.73/£25.24). We watched a World Cup game. Total: €29.73/£25.24FridayA friend was playing in a band. I went there to support them while Lara stayed in. Of course, I got a few rounds in. Total: €38.41/£32.26SaturdayLara and I went to a food market. I got pancakes, coffee and eggs for us. Total: €38.50/£32.65.SundayI went to the gym. My membership is paid monthly (€50/£42.44), but I visit once a week, so each trip costs about €12.50/£10.61. Splurged on new trainers online (€75/£63.66). Total: €87.50/£74.27Weekly total: €1,456.01/£1,235.56The big reveal …The task feels odd to Max and Lara, neither of whom usually track their spending. “There was a time as a student, or right after university, when I had to watch what I spent,” Max says, “but I haven’t kept track for a long time. The task was laborious, but also reminded me how lucky I am not to have to worry about money usually.” Post-task, Max is shocked at how much Lara spent on beauty treatments: two massage and acupuncture sessions, plus a manicure and pedicure, seems excessive to him. Then there’s the organic meal delivery subscription Lara started without running it past him: “We don’t need it.” But Lara is unrepentant and points out that, actually, Max was the week’s big spender after splurging on furniture and designer shoes. “I don’t deserve that title if the furniture is for both of us,” he says.Money has always been a loaded topic of conversation for the couple because of the disparity between their incomes. “Max wasn’t used to being with someone on my salary. Maybe he found it emasculating.” This is vehemently denied by Max: “I just hate being showy with cash.”Lara says she likes to buy Max gifts such as the jeans she gave him during the task – it’s something he used to struggle with. She recalls a toe-curling reaction from him after purchasing him a designer shirt, for £100, early on in their relationship. “Now I think he loves being a kept man,” she smiles. In general, Lara splurges more – last month, she bought their flights for a weekend trip to Athens – but she admits feeling anxious that her personal spending would appear outrageous to her partner. “It’s taken me a while to adjust to her earnings,” Max says, “but not because of some outdated gender norms. I appreciate her gifts.” Max says his bashful attitude toward money is linked to his upbringing. He describes growing up “fairly well off” in Scotland. His father is titled and inherited land from his father. However, Max feels uncomfortable about extravagant displays of wealth. “My parents tried to keep up with the Joneses by making out they had more than they did sometimes.”In Barcelona, he feels self-conscious that his salary eclipses the national average. He hates the term “digital nomad”; it’s a sentiment shared by Lara, who learned Spanish on moving to the city and participates in local housing protests in an attempt to mitigate her impact on gentrification. Living here has helped her to save, for which she’s grateful. She says her $200,000 (£149,000) salary didn’t go as far in the US. She’s barely noticed the pay cut in Spain and, as her stock has gone up so much, she’s now better off. “The States is hyper-capitalist – I felt pressured to buy more, get a bigger apartment. It was nonstop.”Names have been changedThis article was amended on 2 August 2026 to remove wording which indicated that Barcelona is the capital of Spain.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘You owe parking fees’: experts warn of fake RingGo text scam | Scams | The Guardian
description: Criminals hope by using threats of enforcement action, people will panic and click link to bogus parking app site
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: Criminals hope by using threats of enforcement action, people will panic and click link to bogus parking app site
Content: Apps such as RingGo allow the user to pay for their car parking using a smartphone.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenApps such as RingGo allow the user to pay for their car parking using a smartphone.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianScam watchScams‘You owe parking fees’: experts warn of fake RingGo text scamCriminals hope by using threats of enforcement action, people will panic and click link to bogus parking app siteShane HickeySun 2 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou use parking apps a lot – you have several on your phone – but it is not always straightforward. Sometimes there is a lack of reliable mobile signal, or the app crashes or behaves oddly, or it does not seem to want to accept your bank card.Also, it is sometimes hard to keep track of which apps you have used when. So when you receive a text from RingGo saying you owe it money, you are not totally surprised.“A routine review of open parking charges has identified an amount that is still due,” it says. “To reduce the risk of further financial charges and any administrative action within our parking services, please arrange settlement promptly.”A link is provided for you to pay the outstanding charge.However, the message is a scam – one of a number that are circulating at the moment, and not only targeting RingGo customers.Criminals hope that by using threats of enforcement or legal action, people will panic and click the link, resulting in them losing money and their financial details to fraudsters.Graham Conway, the managing director of the leasing company Select Car Leasing, says clicking on the link takes you to a site that is a close copy of the real RingGo website. Advances in AI have allowed scammers to create convincing clones of existing sites.“The link is key because it sends you to a counterfeit page that almost mirrors the real RingGo site. If you then put in your username, password or card details, it goes directly to the criminal gangs, who can drain accounts or sell on your personal information,” Conway says.What it looks likeAt least two text messages are circulating and have almost identical language.One warns that a “billing review” has found a parking charge is owed. Another says that a “routine review” has identified an amount that is outstanding.The recipient is then asked to visit the site, put in their vehicle registration number and view the specifics of the charge. The link starts with the word “ringgo” but then has a series of unassociated words.In order to activate the link, the user is asked to respond “Y” to the text. If the link does not work, they are asked to copy and paste it into a browser.What to doThere are a number of red flags that mark this out as a scam. In some of the examples seen by the Guardian, the text is signed off as “RingGo Customer Servicess”. Poor spelling is a frequent sign of a fake. As is the web address, which bears no relation to the real RingGo site.And the fact that the link may not work is another flag.The real RingGo logo. Advances in AI have allowed scammers to create convincing clones of existing sites.Photograph: sourceSerpil Hall, a security expert from Datos Insights, says this is specifically for iPhone users, as Apple’s iMessage service disables links in messages from unknown senders.“The moment someone replies, even with a single letter, iMessage reclassifies the sender as known, and the link becomes active. The scammers are not guessing at this – they know the mechanics and are engineering around it deliberately,” she says.“The choice of RingGo as the brand to impersonate is not random either. Parking payment services are a well-worn target because the notification is plausible to almost any driver, the amounts involved are small enough not to trigger immediate scepticism, and there is a genuine sense of consequence attached to ignoring it.”The country code on the texts seen by the Guardian is Morocco, although Hall says the criminals are almost certainly not based there: they will typically try to find low-cost ways to route messages and make them harder to trace.Also, both messages had a “report spam” button at the bottom, meaning Apple has already flagged them for possible fraud.A spokesperson for RingGo says anyone who receives one of the messages should not – under any circumstance – click on the link, and should delete them.Customers can verify their parking history on the RingGo app or by logging on to the website.If you receive one of the texts, you can report it to the National Cyber Security Centre by sending it to 7726.If you have clicked on a link of this sort and inputted some of your financial details online, immediately contact your bank and report it. Also change your passwords, starting with your banking ones.Explore more on these topicsScamsScam watchMotoringConsumer affairsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Poirot’s hotel was the place to stay in Istanbul’: the book that inspired my travels | Literary trips | The Guardian
description: Falling in love with a novel motivated these five travel writers to immerse themselves in locations from the Yukon and Kyrgyzstan to the Côte d’Azur
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Falling in love with a novel motivated these five travel writers to immerse themselves in locations from the Yukon and Kyrgyzstan to the Côte d’Azur
Content: The Library Room at Pera Palace Hotel in Istanbul.Photograph: Tuncsel UlkuView image in fullscreenThe Library Room at Pera Palace Hotel in Istanbul.Photograph: Tuncsel UlkuLiterary trips‘Poirot’s hotel was the place to stay in Istanbul’: the book that inspired my travelsFalling in love with a novel motivated these five travel writers to immerse themselves in locations from the Yukon and Kyrgyzstan to the Côte d’AzurSun 2 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIstanbulInspired by Agatha Christie’s Murder on the Orient ExpressView image in fullscreenI visited Istanbul because ofMurder on the Orient Express,even though the city only makes a fleeting appearance in the novel.In fact, one of the things I love about Agatha Christie is that she doesn’t fart about with long descriptions of place. Part of the charm of her detective novels is that they are welterweights, all knotty muscle and six-packs, feinting one way then smacking you in the chops with an unexpected revelation. An extra stone of description would kill that energy.And it’s possible to read Murder on the Orient Expressand miss how important the city is, both to the novel and its author. Christie is a master of misdirection and buried clues. Even her autobiography is notably guarded about her personal life. She doesn’t hide the fact, however, that her first trip to Istanbul was a landmark. She went as a solo traveller after her first marriage broke down and the city became the starting point for her life’s second chapter.She often stayed at thePera Palace Hoteland allegedly wrote a draft of Murder on the Orient Expressin one of its rooms. Pera Palace is still going; its suite 411 is named in Christie’s honour and kitted out with an antique typewriter and copies of her novels. From Istanbul, Christie undertook intrepid overland adventures to the Middle East. Amazingly, in those days you could travel from Haydarpaşa station on the city’s Anatolian side all the way to Baghdad, Mosul and Tehran.View image in fullscreenMarcel Theroux in Pera Palace Hotel, Istanbul.One Easter egg buried in the pages of Murder on the Orient Expressis the name of the hotel that Poirot visits in its second chapter: the Tokatlian. Christie is so sparing with details that this really stands out. The handsome facade of the Tokatlian is still intact. You can read the name carved on the masonry of its upper storeys, but today it houses shops and offices. It couldn’t be more central: it stands on a corner of İstiklal Avenue, the long, pedestrianised thoroughfare that runs through the heart of the Beyoğlu district. At one end is Taksim Square; at the other, theTünel, the amazing Victorian funicular that is the second-oldest underground railway in the world, after the London Underground.I sneaked into the Tokatlian and had an underwhelming wander: the hotel shut down many years ago. But once upon a time, this wastheplace to stay in Istanbul. It’s where Christie herself spent her first nights in the city. In her autobiography, she describes going to a restaurant on a nearby backstreet run by White Russians. That is almost certainly Rejans, renamedIstanbul 1924, and still doing good business serving Russian-inspired food and flavoured vodka.Poirot doesn’t stay the night in Istanbul. He barely has time for a bath and a bowl of soup before he has to get across the Golden Horn to Sirkeci station and catch the 9pm train to Paris, which he finds mysteriously crowded. That train doesn’t run any longer, sadly, but the echoing interior of Sirkeci and its fetching pink facade give you a tantalising flavour of what it must have been like to travel by train in that era.One thing that’s clear is that Christie knows far more about Istanbul than she makes explicit in Murder on the Orient Express. She doesn’t show off any local knowledge; there’s not a glimpse of a hammam or a mosque, no one smoking a shisha, no sense of Turkish food – or any food for that matter. But the book is still rooted in Istanbul and an intriguingly understated introduction to it.Istanbul’s unique geography and blended cultures shape the opening chapters. Christie perfectly understands the logistics involved in moving Poirot around the city. And just as she leaves clues that enable an alert reader to solve the mysteries in her novels, she drops hints at what it is that makes Istanbul special. This is a gift: her reticence leaves anyone travelling in her footsteps free to make their own discoveries.Marcel TherouxYukon and AlaskaInspired by Jack London’s The Call of the WildView image in fullscreenA grizzly bear in Yukon, Canada.Photograph: Robert Postma/Getty Images/Design Pics RFI came toJack Londonthrough Mr Hill, the best English teacher I ever had, and so from early on a love of the North – breathlessly capitalised – and a love of words went hand in hand. It’s the story of Buck, a Californian house dog, abducted to work pulling sledges in the Yukon gold rush who, chapter by chapter, frees himself from the shackles of civilisation.View image in fullscreenI liked Buck but it was the Yukon that held me. “The stars leaping in the frost dance, and the land numb and frozen under its pall of snow.” Here was the midnight sun and endless spruce forest, the noble wolf and 50 degrees below, and solitary men grinding a living from the land. It was a place that seemed impossibly distant, not only in space but in time.I made it there two decades later. I spent five months paddling the length of the Yukon River, from its source in the Pelly Mountains. It was a place of superlatives. The river is 2,000 miles long and, where it meets the Bering Sea, some of its channels can be seven miles from bank to bank.Rereading the book this past week, placenames that once sounded like invocations have become familiar to me: Five Fingers, Little Salmon, Sixtymile. Outside Circle City, where Buck attacked the troublemaker Black Burton in a bar, I saw my first grizzly. In Dawson, where in a wager Buck pulled a sled that weighed 1,000lbs, I visited London’s cabin, or the half that remained (the other is on display in California).View image in fullscreenAdam Weymouth at the rear of a canoe on the Tatchun River, Yukon.Photograph: Peter MatherLondon spent fewer than nine months in Dawson, and most of those in bed with scurvy. His experience of this “Northland”, as he calls it, is not the one of the characters he beatifies. What he wrote was an idea, a backdrop for forging a new version of oneself. These lands were “new and naked”, operating under the “law of club and fang”, an ongoing tussle between the outsiders who had come into the country and the wild nature that they found there. Apart from their role in the tragic denouement, Indigenous people scarcely get a mention. If anything, they are one more facet of this wild nature to be contested, rather than people who built a communal, grounded life here for millennia before the rest of the world showed up.As I travelled in the Yukon, and met the Tr’ondëk Hwëch’in and the Tlingit tribes, and heard about the terrible legacies of the gold rush, I came to better see through London’s fantasy. Yet I could not deny its lure. I could have moved to the Yukon in a heartbeat. “I may never in my life get to Alaska,” wrote the US essayist Edward Abbey, “but I am grateful that it’s there.” London’s writing acknowledges that need for such escape in all of us. For conjuring the seed that first led me to that place, it’s a book that I’ll always hold dear.Adam WeymouthSouth of FranceInspired by Françoise Sagan’s Bonjour TristesseView image in fullscreenMenton on the Côte d’Azur.Photograph: Kirk FisherIt was 1964 and I was a bored 15-year-old in Basingstoke. I’d already discovered that literature could be scandalous. A couple of years earlier, my girlfriends and I hid behind the rattan sofa in the living room of one of the more “alternative” family homes after school and read out the rude bits in Lady Chatterley’s Lover. When I got my hands on a copy of Françoise Sagan’s 1954 novellaBonjour Tristesse, labelled asuccès de scandaleby the French press and literary establishment, I was away. Away from my dull, small country town existence and my equally boring family.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenI wanted to be French, like the protagonist, 17-year-old Cécile; I wanted to sit in a Paris cafe. I wanted to discuss philosophy with elegant adults while drinking an aperitif and smoking a Gauloises (untipped). My list of wants was endless. I dreamed of staying in a white-walled villa on the Côte d’Azur, the sun burning through the bedroom window on my bare body, gauzy curtains blowing in the warm wind. Not icy patterns on the inside of the glass in a semi on a new-build estate in Hampshire. I wanted warm caressing sea and hot sand, not the freezing English Channel and painful pebbles. I wanted to ride in an open-topped car along the corniche dressed in a Givenchy cocktail dress and Cartier jewellery to casinos, not a Westward Ho! holiday camp in the same hand-knit, turquoise sweater as my brothers. I wanted to be treated as an equal by grownups and live my life in dangerous colour. I wanted to write a hedonistic novel of shocking immorality – as Françoise did at 18. And I wanted to not be a virgin.By 1969, I had an artist boyfriend and was staying in the apartment of a schoolfriend’s film-star uncle in Paris. So many boxes ticked! I marvelled at the sophistication of Parisienne women, swooned at the lemony chewing-gum smell of the Métro and the soft whoosh of the trains with different classes of carriage, the beauty of the regimented Tuileries. We bought baguettes and croissants and learned how to tear them apart to eatà la française, the proper way. Because in Paris it seemed there was a proper way for everything.View image in fullscreenElaine Kingett in Cap d’Antibes in 1979.It was in 1971 that I finally got to the Côte d’Azur, to Port Grimaud and Saint-Tropez, and found the France I’d been searching for: heat, blinding sunlight, blue sky and sea. Sunbathing topless, covered in baby oil, reading Valley of the Dolls and smoking Gitanes. Thepan bagnat,moules farciesandfrites. The celebration of indulgence and liberation, such a contrast to the rules and regs of Paris.In 1979, my husband and I were back there, on holiday with a load of friends, staying in a white-walled villa with two grand pianos in Cap d’Antibes, driving an open-topped, gold Beetle. And that’s where I conceived my longed-for first child, after dinner one night at theHotel du Cap-Eden-Roc. Seems dreams can come true. Now I just need to write that novel …Elaine KingettElaine runswriting holidays in SpainKyrgyzstanInspired by Chinghiz Aitmatov’sThe White ShipView image in fullscreenRukh Ordo cultural complex.Photograph: Marina Pissarova/AlamyThe smoky smell of grilled meat drifted out of cafes and over sunbathers, swimmers and a group of elderly ladies dressed in sun hats selling dacha-grown berries by the bucket-load. After a long, hard winter in Kyrgyzstan, life looked sweet on Central Asia’s “beach”, sand-fringed Issyk-Kul, the world’s second largest mountain lake after the Andes’ Titicaca.View image in fullscreenThis visit in 2011 wasn’t my first to Kyrgyzstan but it was the first time I’d dipped my toes into the lake’s frigid water. I’d wanted to do so ever since reading The White Ship(first published in 1970 and translated by Mirra Ginsburg) by Chinghiz Aitmatov, who was born in a village in the north-west of Kyrgyzstan in 1928.In the story, a lonely seven-year-old boy – abandoned by his divorced parents – dreams of morphing into a fish. That way he can better look out for his father who, he believes, captains the white ship that sails on Issyk-Kul. This moving novel, in which the lake features heavily, reads like a fable, mixing in Kyrgyz legends, clans and myths. There are many references, for example, to the “horned Mother Deer”; the Bugu clan – Kyrgyzstan has 40 historical tribes, each represented by a sun ray on the national flag – consider their earliest ancestor to be a deer.One of the first people I met at Cholpon-Ata, the busiest stretch of the shoreline, was a Russian woman, a factory manager from an industrial city in Siberia, who was visiting Kyrgyzstan with her family. She told me that she’d just tried a fresh peach, rather than a canned one, for the first time. I have never forgotten the pleasure that spread across her face as she described it to me. She also believed that the environment – fresh mountain air and the lake’s slightly saline properties – to be health-giving, good for her asthmatic son. Just as in Aitmatov’s book, the lake was expected to offer hope and perhaps answers. Above us, paragliders hovered in the cloudless sky.View image in fullscreenCaroline Eden with a statue of Chinghiz Aitmatov.Photograph: Caroline EdenIssyk-Kul in summer remained a place of simple pleasures, of buckets and spades, sandcastles and blow-up beach balls. Only the backdrop of the chocolate-brown mountains of the Tian Shan range hinted at our altitude of 1,600 metres (5,270ft). Once I’d had enough sun, and enjoyed the cooling effects of fresh cherries and a Baltika beer, I set off to nearby Rukh Ordo, an open-air museum also on the lake.The museum, pitched as a spiritual centre promoting world peace and respect for different religions, was a place to wander, with chapels and yurts scattered along the shore. Pleasingly, I learned that after Aitmatov’s death in 2008, Rukh Ordo was dedicated to his memory. Before getting a bus back to the town of Karakol, where I’d based myself, I found a statue of him and had my photograph taken alongside it. A final personal tribute to Kyrgyzstan’s beloved literary son.Caroline EdenCornwallInspired by Daphne du Maurier’sFrenchman’s CreekView image in fullscreenLandmark Trust have a holiday cottage at the head of Frenchman’s Creek.Photograph: John MillerI first readFrenchman’s Creekaged 12 or 13. I can’t recall how it came into my orbit; maybe it was on the bookshelves at home, or one of my worldly aunts pressed it into my hands. The effect was instant. From the dreamy, almost hallucinogenic opening chapter, I was swept up in this girls’ own adventure, gasping aloud at the daring feats of our sassy heroine, Lady Dona St Columb, as she escapes her stodgy husband and their feckless court life in Restoration-era London.View image in fullscreenRetreating to their Cornish estate with her two children, she discovers their long-neglected country house is being used as a base for a wanted man – a French pirate (of the passionate, artistic variety, natch). They embark on a wild and dangerous romance in and around the Helford River, as she joins him on board his ship, even dressing as a cabin boy to launch raids on the oafish locals. But when her husband and his friends show up, determined to hunt down her swashbuckling lover, she must make a choice – sacrifice him to certain death, or risk her own life to save him.As an adventure-hungry teen, it wasn’t just the bold Dona and her below-decks antics that lured me in, but the almost physical immersion in the setting. Like all Du Maurier’s novels, Frenchman’s Creek employs all the senses to transport the reader, conjuring a mysterious, untamed Cornwall that bore no resemblance to the muddy campsites and ice-cream vans of my childhood holidays. Here was a lawless land of secret tributaries, hidden pools and wooded riverbanks where anything could happen.Reading the novel again recently (and still gasping at every turn), I was inspired to finally make my pilgrimage, summoning the spirit of Dona as I headed west from London.Frenchman’s Creek is a real place. It’s about 15 miles south of Falmouth, part of aria– a flooded river valley open to the sea – described in the book as “a narrow inlet, branching from the parent river, its short, twisting course running westward into a valley”. Nowadays it’s owned by the National Trust and apart from a few tastefully placed signs and footpath markers, it remains its enchanted self, unchanged from how it would have appeared to the novel’s 17th-century characters. It’s more accessible now, with a 3.8-mile circular walk from the village of Helford following the creek itself. Through the trees you can glimpse the sailing boats anchored in the main channel and it’s easy to imagine Dona wandering among the oaks, spying the white sails of the pirate ship hidden up the creek, her heart pounding as she descends to the water’s edge.View image in fullscreenLois Pryce reading Frenchman’s Creek in a creek.Du Maurier excels not only at setting and plot but also at subversive female characters. Written in 1941 as an escape from the grim realities of war, and reflecting her own resistance to domesticity, the novel’s themes of female lust, infidelity and disregard for maternal duties would have been controversial, even shocking. Refreshingly, Du Maurier never attempts to justify or apologise for her protagonist’s actions.This is a book that deserves to be read breathlessly in one sitting, far from the distractions of the modern world. Fortunately for today’s reader, there’s aremote holiday cottageowned by the Landmark Trust, tucked away in the woods at the head of the creek, with no wifi or phone signal. Ask yourself, what would Dona do?Lois PryceExplore more on these topicsLiterary tripsTravel writingEurope holidaysDaphne du MaurierAgatha ChristieJack LondonUnited Kingdom holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The pro-Israel lobby has swayed US presidents since Truman. It must end with Trump | US political lobbying | The Guardian
description: Our new book tracks the growth over nearly eight decades, of the most powerful foreign policy lobby in US history
Author: Eli Clifton
Headline: Our new book tracks the growth over nearly eight decades, of the most powerful foreign policy lobby in US history
Content: Illustration: Jordan Bohannon/The Guardian/Getty Images/White HouseView image in fullscreenIllustration: Jordan Bohannon/The Guardian/Getty Images/White HouseThe featured essayUS political lobbyingThe pro-Israel lobby has swayed US presidents since Truman. It must end with TrumpOur new book tracks the growth over nearly eight decades, of the most powerful foreign policy lobby in US historyIan LustickandEli CliftonSun 2 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 15.43 EDTShareIn 1948, with war raging inPalestine, Harry Truman found himself trapped.On one side were Zionist lobbyists and the president’s domestic political advisers, who were urging him to support the establishment of a Jewish state in as much of Palestine as possible. On the other were his top foreign policy and national security officials, led by the secretary of state, George C Marshall. Their unanimous recommendation was to prevent the establishment of a Jewish state, which they believed would trigger war in the Middle East and endanger the future of US relations with the Arab and Muslim world.With the exception perhaps of George Washington, no diplomatic or military leader in American history had a reputation for patriotic virtue and skilled devotion to duty comparable to that of Marshall. Truman was in awe of the secretary of state, who, as chief of staff of the US armed forces, had been hailed by Winston Churchill as “the true organizer of victory” in the second world war. After the war, it had been Marshall who launched the plan named after him to rebuild Europe.In the mid-1940s, Marshall pushed quietly but steadily against the Zionist movement’s proposals to establish a Jewish state in Palestine. He was concerned that American support would open opportunities for the Soviet Union to exploit Arab anger, put Middle Eastern oil supplies at risk in the event of a war between the Soviet Union and the United States, and require the deployment of unavailable American troops to prevent bloodshed and instability in Palestine. These were, indeed, the strongly held views of virtually all of Truman’s most important military and foreign policy advisers.double quotation markExploiting the fact that most voters were ignorant or uncaring on the issue, the [Israel] lobby used enormous resources ... to punish or reward politiciansTruman was personally and deeply moved by the suffering of Jewish survivors of the Nazi “Final Solution”, but also irritated by and at times furious with the constant hectoring to which he was subjected by campaigners for recognition of a Jewish state in Palestine, including the World Zionist Organization and a host of other Jewish delegations, friends and politicians. Despite his personal exasperation, he could not ignore them. Coming in an election year that would pit him against Governor Thomas Dewey of New York, pressures from the Zionist lobby forced him into an excruciating and embarrassing position.With Palestine engulfed by civil war, Arab states threatening to invade and the last British soldiers about to leave the country, Truman called a meeting of his top advisers on 12 May 1948. According toMarshall’s own accountof the meeting, he warned Truman against adopting the policy strongly advanced by Clark Clifford, his main political adviser, to recognize the state of Israel before it was established.View image in fullscreenPresident Harry Truman shakes hands with secretary of state George Marshall in Washington DC on 29 May 1947.Photograph: Hulton Archive/Getty ImagesSuch a move, according to Marshall, would be a “transparent dodge to win a few votes”, he said, leaving the “great dignity of the office of the President … seriously diminished”. Marshall declared he would not personally be able to vote for Truman should he bow to political pressure on the issue. A shaken Truman closed the meeting by saying he agreed with Marshall.However, within two days, exquisitely sensitive to the tenuousness of his hold on the presidency and the power of Zionist sympathizers to throw New York’s electoral votes to the Republicans, he ordered that the US recognizeIsrael.Today, the influence of the groups loosely known as the Israel lobby has only become more powerful. Truman’s bind – caught between his sense of the national interest and the domestic political price of defying a powerful lobby – was something that, in the decades to come, president after president would experience.How to burst the Israeli bubble | Noam SheizafRead moreTo fast forward: Donald Trump’s decision to go to war on Iran earlier this year came after a sustained campaign by Israel to convince the US to join the disastrous operation. It also came in defiance of several of his top advisers, as well as the45%of Republicans who hold an unfavorable view of Israel. That decision may be most quickly explained as yet another example of the erratic policymaking that define Trump’s two terms as president. But a closer examination of the experience of several of his predecessors reveals that this presidential decision is more the rule than the exception.The fact is that from Truman to Trump, most American presidents have caved to the demands of Israel and its advocates. Driven by the fear of domestic political defeats, presidents have regularly rejected or abandoned foreign policies that both they and their most senior advisers believed were in the best interests of the US and at the expense of making meaningful progress in bringing a peaceful resolution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.Our new book, Israel’s Lobby, tracks the growth over decades of the most powerful foreign policy lobby in American history. Comprised of a panoply of organizations, groups and individuals who advocate American policies that explicitly favor the interests of Israel, the lobby was nurtured – and has been encouraged and guided – by Israeli governments. Exploiting the fact that most voters were ignorant or uncaring on the issue, the lobby used enormous resources and concentrated attention to punish or reward politicians at every level depending on their willingness to follow lobby instructions.Over 20 years after the Truman episode, for example, President Gerald Ford launched what he referred to as a “reassessment” of US policy in the Middle East. The initiative had been advanced by Ford and his secretary of state, Henry Kissinger, as a way to escape from two years of embarrassing failures to move toward a comprehensive Arab-Israeli peace agreement. Both Ford and Kissinger had become intensely dissatisfied with Israeli stonewalling.View image in fullscreenPresident Gerald Ford talks with secretary of state Henry Kissinger, in Vladivostok, Soviet Union, on 23 November 1974.Photograph: Consolidated News Pictures/Getty ImagesThe reassessment was conducted by the committee of “Wise Men” convened by Kissinger: former government officials who had served as pillars of the postwar US foreign policy establishment. The unanimous recommendation of the committee was pressure on Israel to withdraw from the West Bank and Gaza Strip in order to achieve a comprehensive peace, in cooperation with the Soviet Union.Clear indications that Ford intended to accept this recommendation triggered a powerful mobilization by leading Israel lobby organizations, such as the Conference of Presidents of Major Jewish Organizations and the American-Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac). The lobby’s decisive achievement was aletterdrafted by Aipac and delivered to Ford demanding that the president “make it clear … that the United States, acting in its own national interests, stands firmly with Israel in the search for peace in future negotiations”, signed by 76 senators.Ford was “mad as hell” at what he believed to be an Israeli campaign to use the lobby to obstruct diplomacy. But he was cowed. To protect his chances for election the following year, Ford rejected the unanimous recommendation from the “Wise Men”, returning instead to the step-by-step process that had so infuriated him, a process of essentially buying slices of the Sinai Peninsula – seized from Egypt in 1967 – from Israel with increasing amounts of aid and then returning them to Egypt. Ford and Kissinger also vastly increased the scale and scope of US support for Israel.That included a sweeping new collection of US political, economic, military and diplomatic commitments made in a US-IsraeliMemorandum of Agreementthat, along with secret annexes, was signed on 1 September 1975. Aides to Kissinger described the guarantees and concessions made to Israel in these negotiations as “mind-boggling” and “simply incredible”. In his memoir, Ford wrote bitterly about the Aipac letter signed by three-quarters of the Senate that had ruined his diplomatic plans and cast a pall on his election campaign.A ‘magic pill’ made Israeli violence invisible. We need to stop swallowing it | Diana ButtuRead moreIndeed, Ford lost the election to Jimmy Carter. The lobby hoped Carter, who won 71% of the Jewish vote, would abandon aspirations for a comprehensive Middle East peace, but he was quick to disappoint. The president set his sights on a peace treaty resolving the core issues of the Arab-Israeli conflict. With high poll numbers and an American public that seemed ready for a commonsense, problem-solving president, Carter voiced his belief in March 1977 in the need for a “Palestinian homeland” as a key feature of the Middle East peace he wished to achieve.The pro-Israel lobby immediately mobilized against Carter’s peace initiative. In a closely held50-page memorandumfor the president in early June, Carter’s senior adviser on domestic political affairs warned him that he would suffer serious consequences, including risks of failing to receive the renomination of his party, as a result of lobby opposition to his public consideration of a Palestinian homeland. Undeterred, Carter offered direct criticism of what he describedin an Oval Office meetingas the prime minister Yitzhak Rabin’s increasingly inflexible positions. His differences with Menachem Begin, who became Israel’s prime minister in May 1977, were even sharper. Meanwhile Carter began intensive communications with Egyptian, Syrian and Palestinian leaders.In October 1977, the US secretary of state Cyrus Vance issued a joint communique with Soviet foreign minister Andrei Gromyko committing the superpowers to achieving “as soon as possible a just and lasting settlement of the Arab-Israeli conflict”. Though fully expecting opposition to the president’s Middle East policy, the administration was stunned by the nearly apoplectic reaction to the US-Soviet statement by both the Israeli government and the lobby. Profoundly concerned with the political damage, Carter requested a meeting with the Israeli foreign minister Moshe Dayan in New York. According to Zbigniew Brzezinski, Carter’s national security adviser, who was present at the meeting, “Dayan in effect blackmailed the President by saying that unless he had assurances that we would oppose an independent West Bank and that we would give them economic and military aid, he would have to indicate our unwillingness in his public statements here in the United States … ‘I can go,’ said Dayan, ‘to the American Jews.’” Faced with this threat, Carter surrendered.The next day, Vance and Dayan issued a joint statement summarizing a US-Israeli “working paper” prepared in the early hours of the morning.
