The statement affirmed negotiations would be dramatically scaled back and would not frame a Palestinian homeland as a central issue. The end result was a celebrated “separate peace” between Israel and Egypt that earned Carter, Begin and Sadat Nobel peace prizes, but also led to the isolation of Egypt in the Arab world and the assassination of Sadat. It also set the stage for Israel’s invasion of Lebanon in 1982 and settlement projects that resulted in Israel’s de facto annexation of the West Bank and Gaza Strip.View image in fullscreenEgyptian president Anwar Sadat, left; US president Jimmy Carter, center; and Israeli prime minister Menachem Begin clasp hands on the north lawn of the White House after signing the peace treaty between Egypt and Israel, on 26 March 1979.Photograph: Bob Daugherty/APIt is likely, 13 years later, that President George HW Bush felt just as Carter must have felt when, faced with the Israel lobby’s ferocious opposition to his Arab-Israeli peace initiatives, he made public his frustration with its influence. In a failed effort to boost the prospects for the upcoming Madrid peace conference, Bush suspended US loan guarantees amounting to what Israel was spending on housing in occupied territories and faced ferocious opposition from the Israel lobby for doing so. In a press conference he described his exasperation.“We’re up against very strong and effective, sometimes, groups that go up to [Capitol Hill]” Bush said. “I heard today there was something like a thousand lobbyists on the hill working the other side of the question. We’ve got one lonely little guy down here doing it.”The lobby’s ability to thwart presidential peace initiatives was on particularly powerful display again during the Obama administration. No president before him had entered the White House with such detailed knowledge of the Israeli-Palestinian dispute, such a record of personal engagement with both Jews and Palestinians, and such a sustained commitment to closer American relations with Arabs and Muslims. Fully embracing a “two-state solution” to the problem, he launched a high-profile peace initiative to be jumpstarted by a full-scale Israeli freeze on West Bank settlements.But a storm of outrage in Israel and among leaders of Israel’s lobby in the United States, and the public feud that erupted between Barack Obama and Benjamin Netanyahu, proved more costly to the former than the latter. Obama quickly reversed course, in effect replacing peace process envoy George Mitchell, who was closely identified as friendly to the Palestinians, with Dennis Ross, a lobby insider,whose advice to ditch the effortaltogether the president quickly implemented. Instead of pressing Israel to stop settlements, Obama made a personal call to Mahmoud Abbas, president of the Palestinian Authority, threatening to pull $450m in American aid to the Palestinians if Abbas did not withdraw an anti-settlement resolution put forward at the UN security council. In Obama’s address to the United Nations General Assembly in the first year of his second term, he shifted dramatically from language used in his previous UN speeches. Instead of criticizing Israeli settlements and pressing for a two-state solution, he identified himself with Israeli victims of Palestinian terrorism, opposed any UN action contrary to Israel’s insistence on direct negotiations between the parties, and condemned challenges to the legitimacy of Israel as a Jewish state.View image in fullscreenPresident Barack Obama, center, arrives with Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, left, and Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas, right, to make a statement on Middle East peace talks in the east room of the White House on 1 September 2010.Photograph: Jason Reed/ReutersThe reason for Obama’s dramatic retreat is easily inferable from his memoir, A Promised Land, in which he complains about Aipac’s ability to cow American politicians into obeisance by invoking fears of being labelled antisemitic, and emphasized his own particular vulnerability to such threats as “a Black man with a Muslim name who lived in the same neighborhood as Louis Farrakhan”.double quotation markIn the wake of the genocide, the politics of the issue in America have changed as numerous Americans react with passion to Israeli onslaughtsMore recently, in Joe Biden, the Israel lobby found a president who genuinely believed the Jewish state deserved the “special relationship” with the US. The firmness of that commitment was put to the test by Israel’s response to the 7 October 2023 attacks by Hamas and Islamic Jihad.Socialized into accepting the lobby’s mantra that any “daylight” between Washington and Jerusalem would encourage Arab intransigence, and remembering the political punishment Obama received for showing “tough love” to the Israelis, Biden, quashed all recommendations from his top advisers to do something meaningful to stop the Israeli onslaught on Gazan Palestinians. When he did make limited complaints about excessive civilian casualties and implemented minor delays in American resupply of Israeli armaments, the Republican Jewish Coalition responded by slamming the administration for inserting daylight into the US-Israel relationship, while Aipac sent a detailedmemorandum to members of Congressdefending Israeli actions as limited, necessary and designed to reduce civilian casualties.The experience of these administrations demonstrates the wisdom and extraordinary insight of America’s first president, George Washington. In his Farewell Address, Washington warned that the American system of government could all too easily be exploited by a group with a “passionate attachment” to a foreign country. In a system designed to rely on the mobilization of countervailing power to limit the effects of factions driven by self-interest or very particular points of view, Washington argued that since any faction committed to the interests of another country would not naturally find its influence checked by effective domestic opposition, it would therefore drive the United States into exaggerated and dangerous commitments abroad and implicate it in quarrels and wars contrary to the country’s interests.In the wake of the genocide, the politics of the issue in America have changed as numerous Americans react with passion to Israeli onslaughts in Gaza, Lebanon and the West Bank. Biden and Kamala Harris paid heavy costs for knuckling to Israel and its lobby.Nearly a thirdof voters who voted for Biden in 2020 and did not vote for Harris in 2024 said that ending Israel’s violence in Gaza was the top issue influencing their voting decisions. Across both parties, support for Israel has plummeted; sixty percent of Americans hold an unfavorable view of Israel, and a record number of Israel critics are winning congressional primaries.But these losses have not deterred Israel or its lobby from working to reverse Trump’s 2024 campaign promises to avoid wars in the Middle East, to pursueeven closer relationsbetween the US and Israeli militaries, and to spend millions to thwart the rise of critics of the country.The destruction of Palestine is breaking the world | Moustafa BayoumiRead moreTo be sure, American supporters of Israel and its governments have every right to express their opinions and work to shape public policy, and the lobby is by no means the only vehicle for moneyed interests that warp American democracy. Moreover, American presidents have free will: the George W Bush administration was run by many who were in perfect ideological alignment with the Israeli right. An incompetent and gullible Trump is plainly responsible for yielding to Israeli pressure and dragging the US into the latest war.But unless other groups are able to act freely with other interests in mind – and without the threat of antisemitism accusations – US policy in the Middle East will remain dangerously distorted. Both to secure and advance American interests abroad and to protect American freedoms at home, Americans must unite to prevent any foreign power from enjoying the influence over policy and public debate that Israel has exercised, both directly and through the faction operating on its behalf.Eli Clifton is a co-founder and senior adviser at the Quincy Institute for Responsible StatecraftIan Lustick is professor emeritus of political science at the University of Pennsylvania specializing in Arab-Israeli relations and US foreign policyThis essay was adapted from the bookIsrael’s Lobby: America in the Grip of a Foreign Power, out11 August by Atria/One Signal Publishers

title: ‘We were able to live their experiences with them’: the ripple effects of our series about life in coastal towns | Young people | The Guardian
description: A year-long project exploring the lives of young people in coastal areas required a great deal of groundwork to give them a genuine voice and ensure they were properly heard. Their stories captured the imagination of audiences and policymakers alike
Author: Gautam Malkani
Headline: A year-long project exploring the lives of young people in coastal areas required a great deal of groundwork to give them a genuine voice and ensure they were properly heard. Their stories captured the imagination of audiences and policymakers alike
Content: Orson, a dancer, on Blackpool beach.Photograph: Polly Braden/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOrson, a dancer, on Blackpool beach.Photograph: Polly Braden/The GuardianInside the GuardianYoung people‘We were able to live their experiences with them’: the ripple effects of our series about life in coastal townsA year-long project exploring the lives of young people in coastal areas required a great deal of groundwork to give them a genuine voice and ensure they were properly heard. Their stories captured the imagination of audiences and policymakers alikeGautam MalkaniSun 2 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOur journalists always try to spend as long as they can in places to more fully understand things and explain what’s going on. But they don’t often get the chance to keep returning and reporting over a period of 12 months.“You very rarely have the resources and time to be able to have that back and forth over a year and form ongoing relationships with people,” says Guardian journalist Lisa Bachelor, who was able to do just that as part of a long-term project exploring the lives of young people in coastal towns across England and Wales. The year-long series,Against the tide, wrapped up last week.One year, 17 towns, dozens of voices: what we heard along the coast of England and WalesRead moreThe series was initially sparked by research showing that young people living in England’s coastal areas have disproportionately higher rates of undiagnosed mental health conditions. Working alongside the documentary photographer Polly Braden, Lisa sought to put the voices of 16- to 25-year-olds front and centre to explain what was going on and what can be done.Given those aims, and the duty of care to the young people featured, the project required a lot more groundwork than usual. “As a reporter or photographer, you weren’t just thinking: I need to go there, find that person, get that angle, do it by this time,” says Lisa. “So it took that pressure off.”“That meant we were able to live their experiences with them rather than just come in and tell their stories,” adds Polly. “We could be there in those moments when things were actually happening. That was a really big privilege.”Their approach didn’t just make for deeper insights, it also resulted in more wide-ranging impacts. These included taking some of the young people to give evidence to parliament, spurring local councils to take concrete actions, hosting an exhibition of the photography and even collaborating with a railway organisation that wants to use the material in local train stations. The project’s ripple effects also included less tangible impacts – and proved transformative for everyone involved.View image in fullscreenMillicent, a 22-year-old fine art graduate from Jaywick.Photograph: Polly Braden/The GuardianFrom the outset, Lisa and Polly wantedAgainst the tideto be guided by the concerns expressed by young people, rather than the preconceptions about their lives. Coastal towns and communities consistently dominate UK deprivation statistics, and young people who live in them face some of the country’s worst educational attainment levels and grapple with local challenges such as the seasonal nature of many jobs.“Before we started, we went to Blackpool, to Harwich, lots of the places featured in the series, and we sat with young people and listened,” says Polly. “We spoke about what it’s like to be represented by someone coming from outside your town, to be photographed in your town, and they would tell us how it was really annoying to be told that they were from the most deprived place again and again, and how did we expect them to feel good about where they lived? Having discussed this with them, Lisa and I could then try to address those concerns. We asked them to show us all the amazing creativity in their town and we’d go with them and see all the things they were doing.”‘When I leave, part of me stays’: why Scarborough’s youth won’t turn their backs on the seaside town they loveRead moreIndeed, some of the mostmemorable momentsfrom the series capture the young people’s hopefulness, resilience, talent, creativity and humour. The articles, photography and videos stand as a direct challenge to the negative stereotypes perpetuated by some parts of the British media that seem to revel in blaming young people and making everything seem hopeless and bleak. The reporting teams on Against the tide also worked with local organisations to make sure the young people were properly supported throughout the experience.“Many of them have told us how great it is to feel like they’ve finally been listened to, which is one of the big things we wanted to achieve,” says Lisa, who is editor of the Guardian’sSeascape series.“And they didn’t just feel proud to be part of a story about their own town, but also part of a bigger national story about what it’s like to be young today,” adds Polly.View image in fullscreenCohen, 19,  set up his business, Co Co Mascots, in one of his many attempts to find work.Photograph: Polly Braden/The GuardianBy helping to give people a genuine voice, the series captured the imagination of audiences and policymakers alike.Lisa and Polly had always wanted to involve politicians in some way, but they never imagined they would end up being invited to take 16 young people from coastal places to parliament to give evidence about their lives to MPs. That memorable day in May also allowed people from the different coastal towns to meet each other. “It was quite a big thing for them to come together – some of them hadn’t travelled that far before,” explains Lisa. “And one of the things we kept hearing was that young people and communities on the coast have much more in common with each other than they probably do with those in equivalent inland towns. The things that knit them together are so often the same.”‘If you hear your town is scum all the time that sinks in’: the young people in Blackpool refusing to be written offRead moreSome young people featured in the series have subsequently been approached by local councils, broadcasters and film-makers. The sense of recognition and empowerment has been profound. “One young woman told us she actually feels like she’s part of what’s going on where she lives now. And she talked about just how much of a difference that makes,” says Lisa.Others have had their voices more literally amplified in the form of voice recordings that feature in anexhibition of Polly’s photographs, which opened at the Arnolfini gallery in Bristol last month. The exhibition will move toColchester’s Firstsite galleryin October.Meanwhile, a rail organisation in Lancashire has approached the team about displaying some of the material from the series on posters along a coastal railway line. Other work created by local young people is being put up at Blackpool North train station in an arrangement that will run for the next 10 years.View image in fullscreenFrom left, Charlie, 17, and Keane, 19, from Eastfield, and Jack, 17, from Scarborough, on Oliver’s MountPhotograph: Polly Braden/The GuardianThe series has also proved transformative for Lisa and Polly, the wider team of reporters and audio and video producers, and the various organisations and academics they collaborated with. “I can’t express just how much collaboration there has been every step of the way on this project, how that’s unlocked things,” says Polly. “So it’s changed me because I want to work like that much more going forward.”“Yes, this has been absolutely transformative,” Lisa adds. “I’ve been reporting and editing for over 20 years at the Guardian and this series has really made me want to work more deeply with other groups of people.”And of course, the series has also altered their own perceptions of the coastal towns – and sometimes even of themselves. Lisa grew up in Hull, a port city. “When I was young it had the dubious accolade oftopping the ‘crap town of England’ list,” she explains. “But my experience growing up there was of a strong community, a real feeling of togetherness and a fantastic music and arts scene. So I hadn’t realised when I started this series how much I would recognise my past self in a lot of the things the young people were talking about in terms of how their towns are depicted and how it is contrary to what they want to say about the place they come from.”Against the tide was produced by the Guardian’sSeascapeteam in collaboration with Polly and also included contributions from journalists across the Guardian.Explore more on these topicsYoung peopleInside the GuardianNewspapers & magazinesMental healthEnglandWalesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I have an understanding housemate’: the student who makes videos of fungus on faeces | Fungi | The Guardian
description: Alfred Drummond-Herdman’s extraordinary timelapses have been viewed by millions – and led him to identify new species
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: Alfred Drummond-Herdman’s extraordinary timelapses have been viewed by millions – and led him to identify new species
Content: Alfred Drummond-Herdman examines the gill of an inkcap mushroom under a microscope.Photograph: Emily Whitney/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAlfred Drummond-Herdman examines the gill of an inkcap mushroom under a microscope.Photograph: Emily Whitney/The GuardianNature heroesFungi‘I have an understanding housemate’: the student who makes videos of fungus on faecesAlfred Drummond-Herdman’s extraordinary timelapses have been viewed by millions – and led him to identify new speciesThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentPatrick GreenfieldSun 2 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlfred Drummond-Herdman is possibly the only person in the UK who is sent animal faeces in the post out of goodwill. His bedroom in Edinburgh is full of the stuff: clothes have been removed from his wardrobe and cupboards, replaced with terrariums and plastic containers housing sections of cowpats, grouse droppings and rabbit pellets.“I have a very understanding housemate,” he says.But what emerges from the containers has made the 27-year-old trainee lawyer a natural history sensation on social media: brightly coloured contortions of fungi, photographed every 30 seconds as they develop, to create timelapses that are viewed by millions of people around the world.Inkcaps, fieldcaps and ascobolus, which look a bit like barnacles, all emerge from the dung he collects, including two new species that he has formally identified – with more on the way. The extraordinary images are a rare insight into the world that surrounds us all, but few ever get to see.Timelapse of fungiDrummond-Herdman is a self-taught amateur taxonomist who became fascinated with fungi that grows on dung, known as coprophilous fungi, when walking in the Ochil Hills on the edge of Stirling during the pandemic.Cowpats from highland cattle, like many other herbivores, are home to thousands of fungi spores, which race to fruit and produce mushrooms from the moment they have been deposited.“In Scotland one summer, I came across cowpats that had all sorts of mushrooms growing from them. It was like a forest. It was so bizarre, you could not miss it. I went online to identify them, and that was really the beginning of the rabbit hole that I have been going down ever since,” he says.View image in fullscreenAlfred Drummond-Herdman sets up a time-lapse to record fungi growing inside a terrarium in his Edinburgh bedroom.Photograph: Emily Whitney/The GuardianAccording toestimates by Kew, at least 2 million fungi species are waiting to be discovered around the world. From his bedroom in Edinburgh, Drummond-Herdman is doing his bit, working with other enthusiasts and experts on forums to study and identify British specimens.He has attractedmore than 60,000 followers on Instagram, and some of his posts get millions of views. Among the most recent is a video of aslime mould, known as dog’s vomit slime mould, appearing to consume a living ant. Another is aconecap mushroomgrowing on deer droppings.Slime mould appears to consume a living ant“I am enthralled by the bizarreness and the contrast between something like a cowpat – the last things anyone wants to spend time around – and the incredible beauty and complexity of the fungi. Usually when you see these things in the wild, you’re just getting a snapshot of their lifecycle. The timelapses show it all,” he says.The bat that weighs the same as a teaspoon of salt – and the biologist who rediscovered itRead moreVia webcam, Drummond-Herdman shows me his microscope station and the containers positioned around his bedroom, explaining that the boxes of dung do not smell because they were produced by herbivores and are mostly undigested plants. He says he hopes that his videos inspire a greater appreciation of nature conservation in the UK, particularly fungi.“I am trying to shout about them in the right way. The whole point of this is not to name a random species that 10 people read about in a journal. I want to show that taxonomy is the frontline of biodiversity research. Researching habitat loss and native species is nothing without it,” he says.Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.Explore more on these topicsFungiNature heroesTaxonomyBiologyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Chaos of border crossing gives way to limbo for Moroccans on Ceuta’s streets | Spain | The Guardian
description: People among the more than 50,000 who entered Spanish enclave this week describe the journey and their prospects
Author: Okba Mohammad
Headline: People among the more than 50,000 who entered Spanish enclave this week describe the journey and their prospects
Content: People rest on a beach under the supervision of Guardia Civil officers in Ceuta on Saturday.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople rest on a beach under the supervision of Guardia Civil officers in Ceuta on Saturday.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesSpainChaos of border crossing gives way to limbo for Moroccans on Ceuta’s streetsPeople among the more than 50,000 who entered Spanish enclave this week describe the journey and their prospectsOkba Mohammadand Javier Jennings Mozo in CeutaSun 2 Aug 2026 09.11 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour days ago, Youssef El Abbas saw an opportunity to reclaim the life he had lost seven years earlier. News was circulating that about 400 people had swum fromMoroccoto the neighbouring Spanish enclave of Ceuta on the north African coast, approximately 12 miles (19km) across the strait of Gibraltar from mainland Spain.Here was a chance for the 44-year-old Moroccan father of four to return toSpain, from which he had been deported when his residency expired after the loss of his job in Bilbao in 2019.El Abbas took a taxi and headed to the city of Tétouan, south of the enclave. While en route, he saw Facebook posts and news reports claiming that the Moroccan authorities were allowing people to pass through their side of the border. That meant that unlike those who had crossed the previous night, he could simply travel overland before swimming for just five minutes across the border from Moroccan to Spanish territory to avoid the Spanish border controls.View image in fullscreenPeople returning to Morocco on Sunday after crossing into Ceuta.Photograph: Reduan Dris/EPAHe reached Tétouan to find the city completely overwhelmed. “Young men were running through the streets, flooding every corner,” he said. By the time a second taxi took El Abbas to Fnideq, the town bordering Ceuta, he realised that the usual blockades and checkpoints preventing people without European documents from even approaching the frontier had been removed.View image in fullscreenYoussef El Abbas in Ceuta.Photograph: Okba Mohammad“The Moroccan police were shouting at us: ‘Go, go, go! Run now, run into Spain,’” he said. “The night before, they were beating people. But that morning they were letting us through. Nothing made sense.”Despite the crowds, El Abbas noticed the police were only letting Moroccans cross over. “All the sub-Saharan migrants were being pushed back by force.”He reached the border at 2.45pm on Wednesday. By 3pm, after a short swim, he was standing on Spanish soil. Not everyone was so lucky.“In just 10 minutes in the water, I saw four people floating dead in Moroccan waters,” he said. “People were pulling their bodies out.” They were among at least 72 people who drowned or were crushed trying to reach the Spanish territory.El Abbas is just one of the50,000 or so people to have crossed into Ceuta this week, in what Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, described as “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”.Map showing location of Ceuta between Morocco and Spain, and another map showing line of Morocco-Ceuta border and Tarajal breakwaterMadrid has attributed the latest influx to “human-trafficking mafias” that have taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta or Melilla – the other Spanish enclave on the north African coast – could not be summarily returned under special rules.double quotation markThe same hand that helped me out of the water was the one that later hit meYoussef El AbbasBut there has also been speculation that the Moroccan authorities may have opened the border to signal their displeasure at Sánchez’s recent visit to Algeria, which supports efforts to free the disputed territory of Western Sahara from Moroccan occupation.Morocco’s ambassador to Spain, Karima Benyaich Millán, said Rabat was not happy about the mass crossing, adding that it hoped those in Ceuta would return.Moroccan government sourcestold the Europa Press news agencythat the surge of people entering Ceuta was down to “criminal organisations” and insisted that Rabat’s cooperation with Spain remained “exemplary”.In May 2021, Rabat loosened border controls –allowing 10,000 people to cross into Ceuta over the course of two days– during a diplomatic standoff triggered after Madrid allowed a Western Sahara independence leader to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain.View image in fullscreenA man bends down to pick up a pair of shoes from debris washed up on Ceuta’s shore.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersEl Abbas said he had never stopped dreaming of returning to Spain, where he had worked mainly in the hospitality sector for 14 years. Since being deported to Morocco in 2019, he has lived apart from his wife and four daughters, who remain in the northern Spanish city of Bilbao, while scraping by with occasional work repairing mobile phones alongside his father.“I never stopped thinking about coming back,” he said. “In Morocco, I was alive, but I wasn’t really living.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhy is Ceuta a migration flashpoint and how were so many people able to cross from Morocco?Read moreThe return has been bittersweet. When he swam ashore in Ceuta, a Spanish Guardia Civil officer extended a hand to pull him from the sea. But that gesture of aid eventually gave way to one of violence. Three days after arriving, the group of people he was with were surrounded by a military patrol and beaten.“The same hand that helped me out of the water was the one that later hit me,” he said.El Abbas’s story is hardly unique. Although more than 48,000 people had crossed back into Morocco by Friday night, hundreds are still sleeping in parks, public squares and on pavements, waiting for a chance to move on or simply to find somewhere to rest. It appears to be virtually impossible for migrants to leave Ceuta for mainland Spain.Said, 17, from Casablanca, was sitting on a kerb a few hundred metres away. He, too, had joined the Ceuta-bound crowds when he heard that the border was open. But the jubilation had given way to reality and all he had was a bottle of water and the carton of yoghurt a local resident had given him.3:37Tens of thousands of migrants cross into Spanish enclave Ceuta from Morocco - videoThe teenager said he was taken to a centre for unaccompanied minors after he crossed, but there were no places available, so he ended up back on the streets. According to a soldier who asked to remain anonymous, the current protocol for the authorities – including the military, the police and the Guardia Civil – is to treat unaccompanied minors as regular migrants and return them to Morocco.Said and the other teenagers with him said no one would sell them food or allow them into shops and restaurants because they did not speak Spanish.Three days after the mass influx, Ceuta is slowly trying to recover a sense of normality. By early evening on Saturday, cafe terraces were beginning to fill again and some businesses had reopened their doors. Many of the remaining arrivals are being tended to by Ceuta locals, who walk the streets handing out bottles of water, sandwiches, blankets and clothes. Others stop to ask if they need help or to offer to call a relative.Such shows of solidarity have been threatened by the arrival of far-right politicians and a neo-Nazi group, all keen to use the humanitarian crisis for their own ends.“They’re going to exploit our feelings to claim the credit and say they defended Ceuta,” said a local woman called Malika. “We don’t want them here. If they want to defend something, they should go somewhere else.”View image in fullscreenPeople who crossed into Ceuta this week are escorted back to Morocco by the Spanish army on Saturday.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/APMalika, who was born in Ceuta to a soldier who served in the Spanish army, rejected the notion that the city should be defined solely by the political confrontation that followed this week’s mass arrival. But she also acknowledged the pressure on a city of just over 80,000 people. “It would have been an impossible situation for any city,” she said.Fatima Hamed Hossain, a member of Ceuta’s assembly, fears that the strain created by the crisis has deepened divisions within the city. “Everything we’ve lived through has created tensions between neighbours,” she said. “That’s exactly what feeds the far right.”As a caravan of people returned back over the border, Said’s mind was on the future. His goal is simple: get a place in a protection centre, spend the next year learning Spanish and, once he turns 18, find work as a barber. What he fears most is ending up without legal documentation and seeing that plan collapse before it has even begun.Leaving is not on his agenda, however. “All I need,” he said, “is a chance.”Explore more on these topicsSpainMoroccoMigrationAfricaEuropeMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Anti-LGBTQ+ laws are on the rise across west Africa, campaigners warn | LGBTQ+ rights | The Guardian
description: Activists in the region say politicians regard LGBTQ+ people as ‘the easiest scapegoats to maintain their power’
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Activists in the region say politicians regard LGBTQ+ people as ‘the easiest scapegoats to maintain their power’
Content: African leaders who are toughening anti-LGBTQ+ laws have been accused of ‘political opportunism’ by campaigners.Photograph: Ben Curtis/APView image in fullscreenAfrican leaders who are toughening anti-LGBTQ+ laws have been accused of ‘political opportunism’ by campaigners.Photograph: Ben Curtis/APLGBTQ+ rightsAnti-LGBTQ+ laws are on the rise across west Africa, campaigners warnActivists in the region say politicians regard LGBTQ+ people as ‘the easiest scapegoats to maintain their power’Rachel Savagein JohannesburgSun 2 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA growing number of west African countries are implementing or strengthening anti-LGBTQ+ laws, amid local political pressures and a global pushback against LGBTQ+ rights.In March, Senegaldoubled the maximum prison sentencefor gay sex to 10 years and criminalised the “promotion” of homosexuality. Niger criminalised“sexual relations with a person of the same sex”in February, the first time same-sex intimacy had been outlawed in the country.MaliandBurkina Faso, which neighbours Niger, also criminalised same-sex relations for the first time in the last two years. All three are ruled by military juntas.In June, Ghana, which already outlaws gay sex, passed a lawcriminalising LGBTQ+ “activities”. The bill, which hasn’t been signed into law by the president, is the latest iteration of a bill that wasfirst introduced in 2021.“What I see in all of them is a political opportunism,” said Anthony Oluoch of PanAfricaILGA, a continental LGBT+ rights campaign group.In some countries, he said, the new or harsher laws had been backed by religious groups and campaigns for “family values”, while inBurkina Faso, whose population is predominantly Muslim, the law was framed as boosting its sovereignty in opposition to the west. “Underneath that all, there’s a lot of transnational reinforcement,” Oluoch added.LGBTQ+ people “are the easiest scapegoats to maintain their power”, said an activist in Burkina Faso, who could not be named for her security.The impact on the community, even before the law was implemented, has been devastating, activists said. Thirteen transgender women were detained without trial from June to November last year, a HIV worker said, with the women reporting they had been beaten by a military unit that imprisoned them. After the law was passed, there have beenat least twosets of convictions.Police are entrapping LGBTQ+ people on social media and demanding they denounce other community members, said the HIV worker, who fled the country in May after he was named by someone who had been arrested.Despite military president Ibrahim Traoré’santi-western rhetoric, Burkina Faso has also caught the eye of anti-LGBTQ+ campaigners that include conservative, western Christian groups.View image in fullscreenIbrahim Traoré, the president of Burkina Faso, which has criminalised same-sex relations for the first time.Photograph: Stanislav Krasilnikov/APThe African Inter-Parliamentary Conference on Family Values and Sovereignty, a forum that many argue has influenced anti-LGBTQ+ laws on the continent, will be held in Burkina Faso and then Eswatini (formerly Swaziland) next year, it wasannouncedthis year.The first three conferences were held annually in Uganda, in east Africa, beginning in 2023. Ugandaimposed the death penaltyfor some same-sex sexual acts that year.According to US-based international reproductive rights organisation Ipas, the annual gatherings are supported byFamily Watch International(FWI), an Arizona-based Christian campaign group that opposes abortion and comprehensive sex education (CSE). Alsoin attendancehas been Dutch-founded lobby group Christian Council International, which promotes similar views.At this year’s conference, hosted by Ghana’s parliament in June, the draft African Charter on Family Sovereignty and Values treatywas drawn up. It condemns abortion and CSE, states that gender is either male or female, and asserts that parental rights supersede children’s. A draft copy was published onFWI’s website.The anti-LGBTQ+ bill passed by Ghana’s parliament is a “very effective political tool”, supported by powerful religious organisations in the country, said Amanda Odoi, a researcher at the University of Cape Coast.Nonetheless, Odoi added: “These international actors were very key in empowering, supporting, funding, financing and giving voice to the anti-LGBT campaign.”She noted the Ghana bill’s similarity to Uganda’s law, as well as its “alphabet soup” –the billuses the acronym “LGBTTQAP+” – that includes words like “questioning” not commonly used in Ghana.View image in fullscreenGhana has passed a law criminalising LGBTQ+ ‘activities’.Photograph: Eleventh Hour Photography/AlamyBringing this year’s African parliamentary conference to Ghana was a deliberate decision due to the country’s influence on the continent, said Ebenezer Peegah, executive director of Rightify Ghana, an NGO that supports LGBTQ+ people.“Ghana has a lot of credentials thatUgandadoes not have … some clout that other countries in Africa do not have,” said Peegah, listing Ghana’s stable democracy, free and fair elections and relative press freedom.Across west Africa, LGBTQ+ people are suffering the consequences of the new and harsher laws. In Senegal, the law is alsohindering HIV preventionfor men who have sex with men and transgender women, who have higher rates of HIV prevalence, as well as lawyers representing LGBTQ+ people, said Marame Kane, a French-Senegalese activist based in Paris.Trump’s HIV funding cuts having ‘severe and devastating’ impact around the worldRead moreAbout 100 Senegalese people fled to the Gambia this year, although most had to return toSenegalas they had no money, according to a Gambian HIV worker.Same-sex relations are alreadypunishablewith up to life in prison in the Gambia, while transgender women are criminalised by a cross-dressing ban. However, the HIV worker worried that the government could strengthen the laws, making HIV services even harder to provide.The crackdown in Senegal had also increased homophobia in the Gambia, he said, adding, “Gambia and Senegal share the same culture, the same religion, literally everything.”Explore more on these topicsLGBTQ+ rightsAfricaBurkina FasoSenegalNigerNigeriaUgandanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Stop all outdoor activities’: South Korea records its highest ever temperature | South Korea | The Guardian
description: Authorities issue alert saying indoor spaces without airconditioning are ‘dangerous’ as temperatures pass 40C for fifth straight day
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Authorities issue alert saying indoor spaces without airconditioning are ‘dangerous’ as temperatures pass 40C for fifth straight day
Content: Women use portable fans to cool off at the Gyeongbokgung Palace in Seoul in July. South Korea has recorded its hottest temperature and issued a heat alert.Photograph: Jade Gao/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWomen use portable fans to cool off at the Gyeongbokgung Palace in Seoul in July. South Korea has recorded its hottest temperature and issued a heat alert.Photograph: Jade Gao/AFP/Getty ImagesSouth Korea‘Stop all outdoor activities’: South Korea records its highest ever temperatureAuthorities issue alert saying indoor spaces without airconditioning are ‘dangerous’ as temperatures pass 40C for fifth straight dayAgence France-PresseSun 2 Aug 2026 19.54 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 19.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSouth Korea has registered its highest temperature since records began more than a century ago, as authorities warned people to “immediately” stop all outdoor activities in affected areas.The south-eastern city of Yangsan saw the temperature reach 42.5C on Sunday afternoon, the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) said, the highest temperature reported since modern weather observation began in 1904.Yangsan has been the centre of an ongoing heatwave, where temperatures exceeded 40C for a fifth consecutive day on Sunday, while many other cities including Daegu and Busan are seeing temperatures climb into the high 30s.Will brutal wildfires force French leaders to take climate crisis seriously?Read morePeople gathered in airconditioned shopping malls or cafes to escape the blistering temperatures. Ju Dong-yeol, 27, took refuge from the heat in a Starbucks in Seoul along with his parents and told AFP “it is too hot to be outside doing anything”.“I can’t think of anything else to do other than stay in airconditioned places like home, shopping malls and cafes,” the office worker said.More than 20 localities were under emergency heatwave alerts on Sunday – a new warning category introduced this year to better address rising temperatures. An emergency alert is issued when areas experiencing a heatwave are forecast to hit perceived temperatures of 38C or an actual temperature of 39C for the day.View image in fullscreenWorkers harvest strawberries under parasols to protect against the scorching sun in Miryang, South Gyeongsang Province, South Korea.Photograph: YONHAP/EPAIssuing a heat warning, the weather agency urged people to “immediately stop all outdoor activities”, adding that “indoor spaces without air conditioning are dangerous”.“Move immediately to a cool place, such as a designated cooling centre or a shaded area, and stay hydrated while resting,” it advised.KMA data show the average annual number of heatwave days in the country has more than doubled to 19 in the past five years.A heatwave day is defined as one with a maximum temperature of at least 33C.South Korea’s professional baseball league was forced to cancel one game in Changwon after the city’s temperature climbed to 39.5C, marking the second consecutive game cancellation in the city.“The decision was made with the safety and health of spectators and players as the top priority, as a severe heatwave warning remains in effect for the Changwon area,” said the Korea Baseball Organization in a statement.Scientists warn that extreme weather events such as heatwaves are becoming more frequent and intense as a result of human-induced climate change.Adding to theextreme weather is the return this year of El Niño– a natural climate phenomenon that warms Pacific Ocean surface temperatures and typically occurs every two to seven years.Explore more on these topicsSouth KoreaAsia PacificClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alan Jones trial on indecent assault and sexual touching charges begins in Sydney | Alan Jones | The Guardian
description: The 85-year-old former broadcaster faces 22 charges from six different complainants in what is expected to be a four-month trial
Author: Amanda Meade
Headline: The 85-year-old former broadcaster faces 22 charges from six different complainants in what is expected to be a four-month trial
Content: Former radio broadcaster Alan Jones faces 22 charges of sexual assault between 2003 and 2020.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPView image in fullscreenFormer radio broadcaster Alan Jones faces 22 charges of sexual assault between 2003 and 2020.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPAlan JonesAlan Jones trial on indecent assault and sexual touching charges begins in SydneyThe 85-year-old former broadcaster faces 22 charges from six different complainants in what is expected to be a four-month trialAlan Jones trial live updatesAmanda MeadeandJordyn BeazleySun 2 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 19.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe high-profile trial of former broadcasterAlan Jonesfor indecent assault and sexual touching charges begins on Monday in Sydney’s Downing Centre local court and is expected to run for four months and hear from 76 witnesses.Judge Glenn Walsh will hear from six complainants who were allegedly indecently assaulted by the 85-year-old between 2003 and 2020.Jones is facing 22 charges at his judge-alone trial. They include 20 indecent assault and two sexual touching charges, the court was told in pre-trial hearings last month. In 2018 the offence of indecent assault was replaced by sexual touching, carrying a maximum penalty of five years’ imprisonment.The youngest complainant, who was 17 at the time of the alleged offending, is giving evidence in camera – presented in a closed courtroom – on Monday after the delivery of opening statements by the prosecution and the defence.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailOn Friday, Walsh knocked back an attempt by the defence to prevent media reporting the evidence of complainants.Jones’s barrister, Claire O’Neill, argued that under the Criminal Procedure Act, in-camera evidence was not permitted to be published.But Walsh did not agree, saying he wasn’t satisfied in-camera meant “a non-publication or suppression order”.He also said Complainant J was not “fussed” by media reporting his evidence.“The Complainant J doesn’t seem to be jumping up for the crown to say no, but the defendant is.”Complainant J is anonymised in line with the right of all alleged victims of sexual offences to maintain their privacy. The court heard in pre-trial arguments Complainant J, whose case accounts for nine of the 22 charges, told police he met Jones as a young man and was given a mobile phone by the then 2GB breakfast host, who invited him to visit his Macquarie Street apartment.Jones is alleged to have put his arms around Complainant J at the apartment, and given him a “squeeze” and a “peck” on the mouth while saying “I love you mate”.The court has heard that Jones allegedly touched Complainant J’s penis while he was driving him to Fitzroy Falls in the New South Wales southern highlands.The prosecution case is that there is a pattern of alleged behaviour by Jones involving the targeting of “significantly younger men” in his professional and social circle.Prosecutors told the court last month in pre-trial that it is “improbable” that two similar accounts of Jones allegedly touching a complainant’s penis while driving would be “untrue”. Each complainant was driving a car and there was “no reciprocity prior to the touching”, the court heard.Two of the six complainants told police they were assaulted on the first occasion they met Jones: one at a fashion show and one at a fundraising meeting.Jones has denied all wrongdoing and said the allegations are all either baseless or they distort the truth.“I have never indecently assaulted these people,” he said outside court in December 2024. “The law assumes that I am not guilty, and I am not guilty.”NSW police formed Taskforce Bonnefin after alleged victims came forward after a report in the Sydney Morning Herald and the Age.Explore more on these topicsAlan JonesCrime - AustralianewsShareReuse this content

title: A record number of First Nations people died in NSW prison custody last year. Advocates fear this year will be worse | Indigenous Australians | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Karlene Whitton says her son Matthew Roberts took his own life three months into his jail term. ‘I keep picturing it every night’
Author: Jordyn Beazley
Headline: Exclusive: Karlene Whitton says her son Matthew Roberts took his own life three months into his jail term. ‘I keep picturing it every night’
Content: Matthew Roberts, a 27-year-old Bundjalung, Yaegl and Gamilaroi man, took his life inside Lithgow correctional centre on 7 July after being remanded in custody in March.Composite: Guardian Design/SuppliedView image in fullscreenMatthew Roberts, a 27-year-old Bundjalung, Yaegl and Gamilaroi man, took his life inside Lithgow correctional centre on 7 July after being remanded in custody in March.Composite: Guardian Design/SuppliedIndigenous AustraliansA record number of First Nations people died in NSW prison custody last year. Advocates fear this year will be worseExclusive:Karlene Whitton says her son Matthew Roberts took his own life three months into his jail term. ‘I keep picturing it every night’Warning: This article contains images and names of Indigenous Australians who have diedFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJordyn BeazleySun 2 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirst Nations advocates warn that prisons in New South Wales couldexceed the record number of Indigenous deaths in custody set last year, after two men died this month.Matthew Roberts, a 27-year-old Bundjalung, Yaegl and Gamilaroi man and father of two young boys, took his life inside Lithgow correctional centre on 7 July after he was remanded in custody in March. Another First Nations man, 21, died a week later at Clarence correctional centre.“I’m in shock, I keep picturing it every night,” Roberts’ mother, Karlene Whitton, said.Whitton said Roberts had been on suicide watch during a previous period he spent in prison some years ago. On the night he died, she said he told her over the phone that he wanted to end his life.“He hung up and said ‘I love you, Mum’, and I started crying and thinking, ‘Oh, please don’t!’” she said.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailAsked what preventive measures were taken to support Roberts, a spokesperson for Corrective Services NSW said: “The intersection between mental health and the justice system is complex.“Many individuals enter custody with significant and longstanding needs. Corrective Services NSW works with Justice Health to deliver mental health care to people in custody, with a strong focus on safety for those in our care, our staff and the broader community.“Given this matter is being investigated and will be considered by the coroner, we can’t provide further comment at this stage.”The Roberts family are being supported by the Dhadjowa Foundation, which is helping them fundraise for his funeral. The foundation was started by April Day, whose mother, Tanya, a Yorta Yorta woman, died in custody in Victoria 2017.Man dies in Sydney prison unit that watchdog wanted shut down because it ‘cannot provide a safe environment’Read more“Right now, our focus has been supporting the family to lay Matthew to rest and helping them navigate a system that no grieving family should have to face alone,” Day said.“No family should have to fundraise to bury their loved one, especially when they have died in the care of the state.”Whitton said her son was “a real joy”. “He was always happy, he loved his babies, he loved his niece, he loved all of his three nephews,” she said.“He played football, he was into sports, I’ve got trophies of his, he played rugby union. He had a lot of friends.”‘Shameful’ recordClarence correctional centre, which is privately run by British multinational Serco, issued a statement extending its sympathies to the family of the man who died there on 15 July, and to “the wider Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community”, but has not released information about his cause of death.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLast Monday an 18-year-old womandied at Dame Phyllis Frost centrein Victoria.At least seven First Nations people have died in NSW custody so far in 2026 amid a record number of people in prison, despite crime rateslargely remaining stable over the past two years.Twelve First Nations people died in New South Wales prisons in 2025, a new record for the state. Of the 39 total deaths in Corrective Services custody, almostone in four were described as self-harm.The prison population – which is correlated to the number of deaths in custody – grew more in the four months to March 2026 than in the previous four years, Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research (Bocsar) data released in May showed.Some 41% of those who entered prison during this period were First Nations people and more than one-third of the prison population at the time of the Boscar report in March were Indigenous, the highest proportion on record.Sharif Deen, the acting chief executive of the NSW and ACT Aboriginal Legal Service, said the state was in the middle of “a deaths in custody crisis” and she worried it may exceed the “shameful” record set last year.“This tragedy is being fuelled by an unprecedented increase in the number of Aboriginal adults being forced into prisons and police cells,” she said.“We are terrified about the consequences for our clients.”Indigenous Australians can call13YARNon 13 92 76 for information and crisis support; or call Lifeline on 13 11 14, Mensline on 1300 789 978 or Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636Explore more on these topicsIndigenous AustraliansDeaths in custodyNew South WalesPrisonsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Man arrested after Scottish woman found dead inside suitcase in Athens | Greece | The Guardian
description: Greek police say 26-year-old Afghan national is believed to have left Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s body in derelict building
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Greek police say 26-year-old Afghan national is believed to have left Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s body in derelict building
Content: Elisabeth-Jane Ross is believed to have died between five and seven days before her body was found on 18 July.View image in fullscreenElisabeth-Jane Ross is believed to have died between five and seven days before her body was found on 18 July.GreeceMan arrested after Scottish woman found dead inside suitcase in AthensGreek police say 26-year-old Afghan national is believed to have left Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s body in derelict buildingHelena Smithin AthensSun 2 Aug 2026 14.29 EDTFirst published on Sun 2 Aug 2026 10.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreek authorities have arrested an Afghan national in connection with the death of a Scottish woman whose body was found in a suitcase in an abandoned building in central Athens.Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, a charity worker described as an “angel full of innocence and goodness” by friends, had been in Greece for almost three weeks when she is believed to have died.Police sources said the suspect was a 26-year-old Afghan citizen who had allegedly confessed to the crime. He had been brought in for questioning by Greece’s homicide division last Thursday, two days after Ross’s body was publicly identified.A statement released by police on Sunday said: “A criminal file has been opened against a 26-year-old foreign national for intentional homicide, robbery and violation of the law [regarding] weapons.”Explaining the accusation of ownership of illegal weapons, security officials said “various arms – some real, some fake” had been discovered in the suspect’s home, also thought to be in the downtown area of Kypseli where the body was discovered.He is expected to be charged on Monday.Throughout the investigation, Greek authorities had worked closely with the UK’s National Crime Agency (NCA) and Police Scotland, according to the statement.Ross, who had strong links with the charity sector in Greece, is the daughter of a prominent lawyer in Edinburgh, where she also lived.She was reported to have friends in Kypseli, where her body was discovered on 18 July by a homeless man in what had once been a car park. Wrapped in cloth, it had been placed in a suitcase left in a decrepit, rubbish-strewn building at the site.Sources told the Guardian that the suspect’s alleged use of credit cards that belonged to Ross had contributed to police identifying him.“He was caught on camera withdrawing money with the cards from various ATMs,” one said. “The credit cards belonged to Ms Ross. That played a big role in leading us to him.”For days, investigators were unable to make headway, citing the lack of fingerprints or DNA on the suitcase. Adding to the mystery was the discovery that her mobile phone had been used until the time when the body was publicly identified last week.Police had described text messages sent to her father and other members of her family as deliberately misleading. The messages had spoken of her “need to be alone”.The Briton’s “dispersed movements” in the days leading up to her death had made the quest to track her killer even harder.After leaving the home of close friends in Keratsini, a suburb close to the port of Piraeus, where she had stayed for two weeks after flying to Greece, she had gone her own way, renting an apartment in the district of Exarchia in downtown Athens.Greek media outlets reported the suspect had been found in possession of the keys to the rental apartment and that he was “the partner” of one of the Briton’s friends.“As confirmed, the victim arrived in the country on June 26 and stayed at the home of friends until July 10, from where she departed to an unknown [address],” the police statement said.The homicide division said it had made the announcement after amassing evidence that proved the Afghan had “placed the body in the case and carried it to the abandoned car park” in Kypseli.Analysis of CCTV footage had played a role.“The subsequent preliminary investigation … using investigative material and digital analysis of video footage, proved the involvement of the 26-year-old foreign national in the incident. [He] was brought in [for questioning] on 30 July and confessed to his actions,” the statement said.It remains unknown how Ross died. Media reports quoted the suspect as telling police that when he visited the flat in Exarchia he had discovered her lifeless body in the bathroom.An initial on-site postmortem showed there were no evident signs of injury or struggle on the Briton’s body but proved inconclusive because of advanced decomposition. Authorities have fast-tracked toxicological tests and analysis of vital organ tissues to determine the cause of death.Grigoris Leon, who heads the Hellenic Society of Forensic Medicine, told the Guardian that examination of the lungs and eyes would help provide answers and determine “whether she had died a natural death”.As tributes have poured in, flowers have been left beside the abandoned lot in Kypseli. One note read: “Here lies an angel.”One friend in Edinburgh agreed with that, saying: “We have lost an angel, an angel full of innocence and goodness who only wanted to help people wherever she went.”The UK Foreign Office previously said: “Our thoughts are with Elisabeth’s family during this difficult time. We are providing consular support and are in contact with the local authorities.”A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We are aware of the death of a Scottish woman in Athens and are liaising with authorities in Greece. Officers are providing support to her family in Scotland.”Explore more on these topicsGreeceScotlandEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Two helicopters collide outside Athens as Greece battles to control wildfires | Greece | The Guardian
description: Fire department says two-person crew of one aircraft killed in incident during gale-force winds to west of capital
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Fire department says two-person crew of one aircraft killed in incident during gale-force winds to west of capital
Content: Wreckage of a firefighting helicopter lies on a road after two helicopters collided while battling a major wildfire near Psatha, Greece.Photograph: Hellenic Red Cross/ReutersView image in fullscreenWreckage of a firefighting helicopter lies on a road after two helicopters collided while battling a major wildfire near Psatha, Greece.Photograph: Hellenic Red Cross/ReutersGreeceTwo helicopters collide outside Athens as Greece battles to control wildfiresFire department says two-person crew of one aircraft killed in incident during gale-force winds to west of capitalHelena Smithin Athens and agenciesSun 2 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTFirst published on Sun 2 Aug 2026 09.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo firefighting helicopters have collided west of Athens, killing the two-person crew of one of the aircraft, as efforts to control a massive wildfire barrelling towards the outskirts of the Greek capital intensified.Footage showed one of the helicopters losing control in the face of gale-force winds that have pushed flames towards settlements on Athens’ western fringes.“The pilots … were taken unconscious to hospital, where their death was confirmed,” said the fire department’s director of communications, Vassilis Vathrakogiannis.The Greek prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis said the two dead were a Dane and a Greek. The two crew members of the second helicopter were rescued.The helicopters had been leased from Australia’s McDermott Aviation, part of a fleet of 15. The company has said it has supported operations inGreecefor the past seven years.As Europe’s wildfire crisis fractured along different routes, and in further proof of the destructive force of climate-driven wildfires across the continent, the blazes ripped through Greece’s tinder-dry landscape, up mountain slopes and down to the sea, before encroaching on the capital.Warning of “extremely difficult” days ahead, Mitsotakis underlined the threat posed by gusts that in recent days have exceeded 78mph (125km/h).“When the winds blow with such force, even the dozens of aircraft we have at our disposal cannot operate safely,” he wrote on social media.More than 100 homes were destroyed overnight in fires that broke out around the popular coastal village of Porto Germeno, about 45 miles (70km) north-west of Athens. By Sunday, more than 500 firefighters and forest commandos had been dispatched to keep the flames at bay.View image in fullscreenA firefighting helicopter drops water over a forest near Porto Germeno, north-west of Athens, on Sunday.Photograph: Michael Varaklas/APThe eastern Mediterranean, no stranger to wildfires, has had a relatively calm summer to date, leaving Greeks to watch in horror as the blazes have hit farther west.As the advance of wildfires in Spain was finally curbed and officials inFranceannounced that a mega-fire – four times the size of Paris – had begun to be contained, the blazes in Greece have prompted mass evacuations and devastated huge swathes of land from Crete to the southern Peloponnese, the Ionian isle of Cephalonia and islands across the Aegean.Last week three Greek firefighters died from injuries sustained while they fought blazes.Extreme winds have been a blessing – in bringing down summer temperatures – but also a curse, with their-gale force strength obstructing firefighting efforts.Greece’s civil protection minister, Evangelos Tournas, a retired air force general, said at the weekend that the fire department had been “pushed to its limits”. He said high winds had created “extremely difficult conditions resulting in many cases where aircraft either cannot draw water or cannot carry out drops due to extreme turbulence”.View image in fullscreenPeople using olive branches to beat back the flames in the Megara valley, in western Attica, Greece, on Sunday.Photograph: Louisa Gouliamaki/ReutersFrance’s largest wildfireremained contained after 224,000 people wereforced to fleein what may have been the largest peacetime evacuation in French history. But active pockets still burned across 160 sq miles (420 sq km) of devastated forest.Thousands remained unable to return home, and nearly 3,000 firefighters were deployed against the Gironde mega-fire and a second blaze in Provence that had stopped advancing but remained uncontained.“The fire is now fixed, which does not mean that the fire is extinguished,” the Gironde prefecture said on Sunday, using the French firefighting term for a blaze whose advance has been stopped and whose perimeter has been contained.The region remained under France’s highest red forest fire alert. Dry conditions and soaring temperatures around Bordeaux, combined with afternoon winds, created a continued risk of renewed flames.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA deer in the forest in Le Temple, Gironde.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersAdditional firefighters from Ukraine, Lithuania and French Polynesia were expected on Sunday and Monday to reinforce the operation.Weather tracker: Why Europe’s wildfires are proving so fierce and difficult to stopRead moreHundreds of miles away, nearly 1,500 firefighters were battling a separate fire in the south-eastern Var department that tore through roughly 7 sq miles in little more than a day.Authorities said the fire in the Gros Bessillon hills was stabilised on Sunday morning, meaning its perimeter had not expanded overnight. But unlike the Gironde fire, it had not yet been declared contained.Firefighting aircraft supported crews working to keep the flames away from villages among the vineyards, olive groves and wooded hills of the region known as Green Provence. About 2,500 people were evacuated as the fire threatened communities.The blaze was the fourth major fire to strike the central Var since 19 July. A separate, smaller fire near Brignoles earlier in the week forced the Hollywood actor George Clooney and his family,along with about 700 other residents, to evacuate before it was brought under control.View image in fullscreenSmoke above Montfort-sur-Argens, near Correns, in Var, on Saturday.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersThe prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said France’s wildfires were generally under control but cautioned that conditions remained highly changeable.He announced that a national coordinator attached to the prime minister’s office would oversee reconstruction in fire-ravaged areas. More than 450 sq miles have burned across France since the beginning of the year.Fires in France andSpainalone have driven roughly a third of a million people from homes and holiday sites, emptied communities at the height of the summer and stretched firefighters, aircraft and emergency services across simultaneous disasters.The crisis is unfolding on the world’s fastest-warming continent.Europehas heated at more than twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service.Higher temperatures and prolonged drought leave forests and scrubland drier and more combustible, allowing fires to spread faster and burn more intensely. Human-caused climate breakdown doubled the likelihood of the extreme fire conditions that fuelled the French blazes, scientists at World Weather Attribution calculated in a rapid analysis on Thursday while the fires were still burning.The Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsGreeceWildfiresSpainFranceExtreme heatExtreme weatherEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Moscow bomb kills at least three as device carried by woman explodes | Russia | The Guardian
description: More than 20 people injured in blast near Italian restaurant Balzi Rossi in centre of Russian capital on Saturday night
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: More than 20 people injured in blast near Italian restaurant Balzi Rossi in centre of Russian capital on Saturday night
Content: Police and ambulance crews at the site where an improvised explosive device was detonated in central Moscow.Photograph: Pavel Bednyakov/APView image in fullscreenPolice and ambulance crews at the site where an improvised explosive device was detonated in central Moscow.Photograph: Pavel Bednyakov/APRussiaMoscow bomb kills at least three as device carried by woman explodesMore than 20 people injured in blast near Italian restaurant Balzi Rossi in centre of Russian capital on Saturday nightReuters in MoscowSun 2 Aug 2026 09.51 EDTFirst published on Sat 1 Aug 2026 20.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA homemade bomb carried by a woman killed three people and injured at least 21 in ⁠an explosion near a restaurant in central Moscow on Saturday evening, prompting speculation on social media that the attack may have been linked to the war in Ukraine.The explosion occurred just before 8pm local time (6pm UK time) close to an Italian restaurant in one of Moscow’s seven Stalin-era skyscrapers at Kudrinskaya ​Square, police said.Russia’s anti-terrorism ‌committee said an ‌unidentified woman carrying ​an improvised explosive device had tried to get into the restaurant but was stopped by a security ‌guard, the state RIA news agency reported.View image in fullscreenOfficers stand guard at the Balzi Rossi restaurant.Photograph: Anastasia Barashkova/ReutersIt said the woman, the security guard and a customer at the Balzi Rossi restaurant were killed in the blast.REN TV cited a source on Sunday as saying that two people who had been taken to hospital had later died of their wounds, bringing the death toll to five, but there was no official confirmation. The channel said six people were in a serious condition.Moscow’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, offered his condolences to the families of those killed and said those responsible would be punished. “A brutal terrorist ‌attack was carried out in Moscow yesterday,” he said in a statement on Sunday.mapHeavily armed law enforcement officers sealed off the scene of the attack. The authorities did not name those killed or injured ​or any suspects. Unverified social media reports suggested a senior Russian military commander had been the intended target but had been unharmed.More than four years into a full-scale war with Ukraine, Russia promised better protection for high-ranking military officials this year after a series of assassinations and attempted killings, which it blamed on Kyiv. Russian war bloggers, without citing any evidence, were quick to blame Ukraine for ⁠the latest attack. Kyiv did not immediately comment.The Kommersant daily suggested the woman carrying ​the bomb may not have known about ​it, and that it had been set ​off remotely by someone else.View image in fullscreenThe scene in central Moscow after the blast.Photograph: Anastasia Barashkova/ReutersThe restaurant’s website said the venue had been closed on Saturday for a ​private event. The nature of ‌the attack recalled a ​bombing carried out in ​2023 that killed the Russian pro-war blogger Vladlen Tatarsky. A young woman, Darya Trepova, was jailed for 27 years for delivering a bomb concealed inside a statuette that exploded in his hands. She said she had been acting under instruction from a man in Ukraine who had sent her money.Senior Ukrainian officials at the time neither claimed responsibility nor denied involvement.Explore more on these topicsRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: EU citizens in UK get letters telling them post-Brexit residency rights were given ‘in error’ | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: After years of building lives in UK, potentially thousands of EU citizens could be told they have no right to remain
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: After years of building lives in UK, potentially thousands of EU citizens could be told they have no right to remain
Content: A van driving around central London in June 2021 to remind EU citizens living in the UK to register for settled status.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA van driving around central London in June 2021 to remind EU citizens living in the UK to register for settled status.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockImmigration and asylumEU citizens in UK get letters telling them post-Brexit residency rights were given ‘in error’After years of building lives in UK, potentially thousands of EU citizens could be told they have no right to remainLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentSun 2 Aug 2026 08.42 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UKHome Officehas started stripping some EU citizens of their post-Brexit residency rights, in a move that has raised concerns about Britain’s compliance with its withdrawal agreement with Europe.The UK internal affairs authority has told at least 100 people that they were given residency rights “in error”, disrupting their lives just as they come to the end of their five-year “pre-settled status” and prepare to upgrade to the permanent “settled status”.A Portuguese woman working in the NHS and researching a PhD in Britain says her life has been turned upside down after being told by the Home Office she was granted post-Brexit rights to live in the country “in error”.She was granted pre-settled status under the EU settlement scheme, similar to 1.3 million others who had been in the country for fewer than five years before the UK left the EU.She had expected that this would be upgraded to settled status without issue and was dismayed when the Home Office told her her status was a mistake.“I feel so overwhelmed, because this is going to influence so many spheres of my life,” said Gabriela, whose name has been changed to protect her identity. She said she was fearful of the hostile environment that may kick in if her legal right to stay in the UK expired.“I can lose my job, I maybe don’t have the right even to rent the property that I’m living in now, because of course I have to prove my right to live here to the landlord to rent a place.“My bank account might also be affected. I work in the NHS as well, I work with other surgeries as well, so I have three different contracts in different places and I don’t know how it’s going to be if this happens, It’s just very stressful.”Gabriela is one of more than 1 million EU citizens who were granted “pre-settled status” to remain legally in the UK because they had been in the country for fewer than five years before Brexit.The Home Office is now reviewing the cases of those who are required to apply to have their status upgraded to full “settled status”, including children, non-European Economic Area (EEA) citizens and anyone who arrived after 31 December 2020.It declined to say how many people it had written to, but through a freedom of information request the3million campaign group has been told that 95 people were contacted in March alone.Gabriela is Brazilian-Portuguese, however she did not have a Portuguese passport at the time of her application, something that is now being questioned by the Home Office.In a five-page letter, the Home Office said: “It has come to our attention that you were granted pre-settled status without the evidence required to confirm that you meet the definition of ‘relevant EEA citizen’ before midnight 31 December 2020, when the UK legally cut ties with the EU.“On the basis of the information and evidence that is currently available, it is therefore considered that your pre-settled status was granted in error,” it added.Gabriela said she had been totally open with the Home Office and had “not excluded anything” including the fact that her father is Portuguese, making her an EU citizen by birth.“Citizenship is by blood so it is not something I have changed since I was born,” she said.Monique Hawkins, the acting chief executive of the3million, said the impact of the Home Office’s retrospective review was devastating for many.The group has knowledge of dozens of cases but fears there may be hundreds or thousands like Gabriela who will be hit by similar letters threatening removal from the country.“People applied to the EU settlement scheme in good faith and were granted status by the Home Office years ago. They acted on those decisions in good faith by building their lives in the UK and putting down roots.“We hear from people who are progressing in their jobs, from those whose children are in schools and have known no other country, and now, five years on, when they apply for settled status, they are being told that it was all a mistake. Imagine building a life somewhere and having it ripped out from under you like this.”Gabriela is appealing against the Home Office decision but the issue of “in error” cases has raised alarm bells at the Independent Monitoring Authority (IMA), the statutory body set up to monitor the implementation of the EU citizens chapter of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement (WA).In a statement, it said it “has raised concerns with the Home Office that the policy may be incompatible with the EU withdrawal agreement”.Hawkins said that under the WA, status “should only be removed if it is genuinely proportionate to do so”, but said “the Home Office is simply side-stepping that … entirely”.She said the approach was “completely unacceptable” and called on the Home Office to reconsider its policy.The Home Office said it had a longstanding policy not to routinely comment on individual cases.It said people who it judged had been granted status in error could apply to remain through other inmigration routes such as visa stays.It added that it would allow people to stay until their pre-settled status had expired, during which time they could seek alternative arrangements. They could also apply for full settled status, and if that was refused, legally they could appeal.The subheading and main text of this article were amended on 2 August 2026. A reference to “hundreds of thousands” of people potentially receiving letters threatening removal should have been to “hundredsorthousands”.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeBrexitForeign policyEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Italy says it’s temporarily suspending EU Schengen arrangement with Spain after 60,000 migrants reach Ceuta – as it happened | Spain | The Guardian
description: The measure will impact people travelling by plane or boat between the two countries
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: The measure will impact people travelling by plane or boat between the two countries
Content: 13.27 EDTClosing summaryJakub KrupaAnd, on that note,we will be closing the blog for today.At least 57 people have died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after as many as 60,000 migrants entered the tiny territory from Morocco(17:33).At least 57 people die as tens of thousands cross to Spanish enclave of Ceuta from MoroccoRead moreSpain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, called it a “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”(12:51) and blamed on misleading narratives spread by human traffickers (12:54,13:17).In response,Italy has moved to suspend its free-travel Schengen arrangements with Spain by sea and air(18:26), claiming it was necessary to safeguard the security of its citizens (19:02,19:07).
