title: The rich get richer as Dodgers land ace Tarik Skubal in blockbuster trade | MLB | The Guardian
description: The Los Angeles Dodgers have acquired the biggest prize on the trade deadline market, getting two-time reigning AL Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal from the Detroit Tigers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Los Angeles Dodgers have acquired the biggest prize on the trade deadline market, getting two-time reigning AL Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal from the Detroit Tigers
Content: Tarik Skubal is a two-time AL Cy Young award winner and will be joining the two-time defending World Series championsPhotograph: Paul Sancya/APView image in fullscreenTarik Skubal is a two-time AL Cy Young award winner and will be joining the two-time defending World Series championsPhotograph: Paul Sancya/APMLBThe rich get richer as Dodgers land ace Tarik Skubal in blockbuster tradeDefending champions send prospects to TigersCy Young-winning Skubal joins stacked rotation in LAAssociated PressSun 2 Aug 2026 10.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Los Angeles Dodgers have acquired the biggest prize on the trade deadline market, getting two-time reigning AL Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal from the Detroit Tigers on Saturday night.Skubal got the news during the Tigers’ 8-6 win over the Athletics and was emotional after the game as he prepared to leave the team that drafted him in 2018 and developed him into a star to join the two-time defending World Series champions.“I’m excited to be a Dodger,” he said. “I’m excited to get down there and meet all those guys and chase three championships in a row. That’s hard to do, so I’m so excited to a part of that. But it’s a lot of different emotions. Definitely kind of a rollercoaster a little bit.”‘Like pulling a tractor trailer’: what it’s like to play on an awful MLB teamRead moreSkubal is the latest star to join the high-priced roster for the Dodgers that already has big-name players like Shohei Ohtani, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Mookie Betts. If everyone is healthy, he could be part of a rotation with Ohtani, reigning World Series MVP Yamamoto, fellow two-time Cy Young Award winner Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. The Dodgers lead the majors with a 3.36 ERA from their starting pitchers and now add Skubal to the mix.The Dodgers are in first place in the NL West and were already the favorites to become the first team to three-peat since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000 before adding Skubal. They began the season with a $323.3m opening-day payroll for their 40-man roster and a $163.7m tax for a $487.1m total . They will pay Skubal about $9.5m for the remainder of the season.ESPN first reported the deal and said the Tigers would receive three minor league prospects in return: right-handers River Ryan and Brady Smith and outfielder Zyhir Hope.Skubal is eligible for free agency after the World Series. He has a $32m salary, a record total in arbitration , after the team offered $19m, and is expected to sign a massive contract in the off season.The 29-year-old lefty said in July that it was his preference to finish the season with the Tigers and to compete for a World Series championship, which has eluded the franchise since 1984. Skubal took the loss in the decisive Game 5 of the division series against Cleveland in 2024 and then got a no-decision in a 15-inning loss to Seattle in Game 5 of the division series last year.He said it was “very tough” to leave the Tigers having fallen short of the goal of winning a title.“Ever since that ’24 Game 5, the failure that I experienced on the mound, I’ve used that as fuel to try and bring a World Series to the city of Detroit. I truly did,” he said. “That whole off season I’ve never been more motivated and then go in and we lose Game 5 again. That failure kind of sparks some more motivation, just to dig deeper and see how good you can truly be. The goal was always to win a World Series for the city, for the organization that took a chance on me. It’s tough. I love all those guys in there. They’re some of my best friends.”View image in fullscreenSkubal could join a rotation featuring two-way player Shohei Ohtani.Photograph: Harry How/Getty ImagesDetroit planned to contend again this season, bolstering the Skubal-led rotation by giving two-time All-Star pitcher Framber Valdez a $115m, three-year contract in free agency and retaining three-time All-Star infielder Gleyber Torres with a $22m deal.The Tigers, though, got off to a rough start and are now two and a half games out of the last wild-card spot in the American League.“It’s crazy. Going into the season, this isn’t what I planned on doing,” Skubal said. “But circumstances change, situations change, and I’m very appreciative of everything the Tigers have done for me.”They bounced back in June and most of July to get into playoff contention with Skubal leading a rotation and three All-Stars in the lineup: rookie infielder Kevin McGonigle , catcher Dillon Dingler and outfielder Riley Greene.With a chance to possibly persuade management to keep Skubal by improving its playoff positioning, Detroit lost ground by dropping four of its last five games at home, including Skubal’s last start that was made even more memorable by a late-inning collapse.The Tigers led Baltimore 7-0 after six innings Wednesday and lost 10-9 in 12 innings. Skubal started the game, recorded his 1,000th career strikeout and was cheered at every opportunity by a crowd of 34,406.“I’ve watched this guy rise to the top of the sport,” manager AJ Hinch said. “He’s carried us a lot. I’ll forever be grateful that our paths crossed and the things that he did for this organization and for a couple of playoff teams. His presence, his work ethic, his example, his dominance. There’s so much to go through, it’s hard to capture in one quote or kind of one setting. But I’m very grateful that I was able to manage him for the time that I did.”Skubal is 7-5 this season with a 2.79 ERA and 116 strikeouts in 96 2/3 innings. He is 61-42 with a 3.04 ERA over seven seasons, all in Detroit. In two postseasons, Skubal is 2-1 with a 2.04 ERA in six starts.Skubal had a minimally invasive surgery on 6 May to remove a loose body from his pitching elbow and returned to pitch on 13 June.“The way the surgery went is exactly how it was supposed to go,” he said in July.Explore more on these topicsMLBBaseballUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Robert Lewandowski strikes twice for Chicago Fire in MLS win over Charlotte | MLS | The Guardian
description: Robert Lewandowski scored two goals on his home debut for Chicago while Lionel Messi returned as Inter Miami drew 2-2 with Columbus
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Robert Lewandowski scored two goals on his home debut for Chicago while Lionel Messi returned as Inter Miami drew 2-2 with Columbus
Content: Robert Lewandowski celebrates his second goal against Charlotte at Soldier Field.Photograph: Harry Figiel/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRobert Lewandowski celebrates his second goal against Charlotte at Soldier Field.Photograph: Harry Figiel/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesMLSRobert Lewandowski strikes twice for Chicago Fire in MLS win over CharlottePoland striker scores double on his home MLS debutMessi returns as Inter Miami draw 2-2 with ColumbusReutersSun 2 Aug 2026 07.02 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 09.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRobert Lewandowski scored two goals on his home debut as the Chicago Fire eked out a 2-1 victory over Charlotte FC on ⁠Saturday. The win is Chicago’s first in Major League Soccer since the end of the international break.Lewandowski, signed in late June as a free agent, produced a vintage performance to help the Fire (9-6-2, 29 points) close an ever-narrowing gap with the Eastern Conference’s top three clubs. Charlotte (7-7-4, 25pts) has now lost four of its last five road matches.Pep ⁠Biel opened the scoring in the 18th minute for Charlotte. After playing a one-two with Idan ​Toklomati at the top of the box, ‌the Spanish attacker sped past his marker and ‌rifled his shot past Chicago goalkeeper Chris Brady into the top right corner. The goal was Biel’s ‌team-leading ninth of the season.Lewandowski responded just two minutes later, scoring his first goal in a Chicago uniform. Jonathan Bamba lofted a through-ball to Philip Zinckernagel, who headed it to an incoming Lewandowski. After faking a shot, Lewandowski put the ball on his right foot and slotted into the bottom ‌left corner, past goalkeeper Kristijan Kahlina.The Fire almost took the lead when Zinckernagel found Robin Lod open in the box. However, the Finnish midfielder couldn’t steer his shot on ​target at such a steep angle, and Lewandowski could not connect with the ball at the far post.In the 56th minute, Lewandowski played a pinpoint through-ball to a streaking Zinckernagel, setting him ⁠up for a one-on-one with Kahlina. Zinckernagel took one too many touches ​as he neared the keeper, who deflected his tight-angle shot away.Chicago found the go-ahead goal in the 68th minute ​when Andrew Gutman found Lod ‌just outside the ​box in transition. Lod ​played Lewandowski in with a through ball, and the former Dortmund, Bayern Munich and Barcelona striker beat Kahlina at close range for his second goal of the game.Lionel Messi returned to MLS action on Saturday, coming on in the second half as hisInter Miamiside drew 2-2 withColumbus Crew. The Argentina star could not mark his return with a goal, though, twice shooting wide.View image in fullscreenLuis Suárez celebrates after opening the scoring for Inter Miami.Photograph: Marta Lavandier/APLuis Suárez scored his seventh goal in his last four games to put Miami 1-0 up in the 16th minute, but Casemiro scored an own goal to draw Columbus level. Suárez then set up Noah Allen to head the hosts back in fronts, but midfielder Brais Méndez levelled again with a late free-kick on his debut for the Crew.Tai Baribo scored in the 77th minute to cap a second-half rally from two goals down asDC Unitedearned ⁠a 2-2 home draw against Eastern Conference leadersNashville SC.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSam Surridge’s penalty and Shakur Mohammed’s strike came eight minutes apart in the first half for Nashville, but Silvan Hefti volleyed in from a corner to make it 2-1 in the 56th minute. Baribo levelled for DC United when his shot from out wide beat Nashville keeper Brian Schwake.Quick GuideMLS resultsShowNew York City 1-1 Toronto; DC United 2-2 Nashville; Inter Miami 2-2 Columbus; Montréal 2-2 New England; New York Red Bulls 3-2 Orlando; Philadelphia Union 3-2 Atlanta United; Vancouver Whitecaps 1-1 LAFC; Chicago 2-1 Charlotte; Sporting KC 0-2 Houston Dynamo; Minnesota United 1-1 San Diego; St Louis City 1-1 Real Salt Lake; Colorado Rapids 1-0 Austin; Cincinnati 4-2 Sane Jose; LA Galaxy 0-0 Dallas; Portland Timbers 2-1 Seattle Sounders.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Thomas Müller’s penalty secured a 1-1 draw for theVancouver WhitecapsagainstLAFCon the team’s return to BC Place Stadium. Son Heung-min had fired the visitors ahead with a neat turn and shot, but Müller won and converted a 76th-minute spot-kick after he was hauled down in the box by defender Yevhen Cheberko.Brandon Bye scored the winning goal in the 82nd minute as thePortland Timbershanded theSeattle Sounderstheir sixth straight loss. Kevin Kelsey also scored for the Timbers, who are undefeated in four games after this 2-1 win. Kalani Kossa-Rienzi scored for the Sounders, who are dealing with a spate of injuries.Explore more on these topicsMLSChicago FireRobert LewandowskiUS sportsInter MiamiPortland TimbersShareReuse this content

title: It’s double Dutch as Lorena Wiebes wins second stage of Tour de France Femmes | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: The Dutch sprinter Lorena Wiebes took her second win in this year’s Tour de France Femmes in Geneva, further extending her overall lead in the nine-day race
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: The Dutch sprinter Lorena Wiebes took her second win in this year’s Tour de France Femmes in Geneva, further extending her overall lead in the nine-day race
Content: Lorena Wiebes of SD Worx Protime celebrates crossing the finish line to win the second stage of the Tour de France FemmesPhotograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenLorena Wiebes of SD Worx Protime celebrates crossing the finish line to win the second stage of the Tour de France FemmesPhotograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersTour de France FemmesIt’s double Dutch as Lorena Wiebes wins second stage of Tour de France FemmesDutch sprinter makes it two from two in GenevaHer team still intend to sue UCI over Giro disqualificationJeremy Whittlein GenevaSun 2 Aug 2026 14.24 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Dutch sprinter Lorena Wiebes took her second win in this year’sTour de France Femmesin Geneva, further extending her overall lead in the nine-day race. Wiebes is proving untouchable in the sprint finishes and her turn of speed in the final 250 metres, on the lakeside finish of the Quai du Mont-Blanc, reduced her rivals to onlookers.Lone breakaway Riejanne Markus had led by more than half a minute on the flat approach to Geneva and maintained that advantage into the final 5km, even with the whole peloton giving chase. But as the kilometres clicked down, the peloton clawed its way back, eclipsing Markus in the last 500 metres, before Wiebes made her inevitable surge to take yet another sprint win.Tour de France Femmes: Lorena Wiebes wins stage two as Markus’ brave bid falls short – as it happenedRead more“The girls were chasing full gas to bring back Riejanne,” Wiebes said of her teammates. “It’s even more beautiful to finish it off in yellow.” She now leads the Tour overall by 14 seconds from Kim Le Court and by 16 seconds from the 2023 winner, Demi Vollering.Despite her success in the Femmes, Wiebes remains set to sue the UCI over her disqualification from the women’s Giro in May when, after she won the opening stage, her bike was ruled underweight and she was stripped of the race leader’s pink jersey.There is no indication that either Wiebes or her SD Worx Protime team intend to back down from their threat of legal action over what they consider to be a flawed weighing process, conducted in a gusting wind.After herstage win in Lausanne on the opening day, Wiebes’ team manager, Erwin Janssen, made sure there was no repeat of the Giro debacle.“I wanted to see how it all worked, how they actually did it,” he told the media at the start of stage two in Aigle. “I took some videos of the process. There was a four-person jury, and the whole setup was fairly enclosed. It took place in a tent, so there was no wind, and the installation looked solid. One of the four was someone who had handled the weigh-ins at the Giro. I think even he was feeling a bit nervous.”Wiebes’ bike, Janssen said, came in within the rules at “a solid seven kilos”. “I could really sense a certain tension among the jury. I got the impression they were thinking, ‘I hope everything goes smoothly.’ Everything was recorded, and then you get a brief report,” he said. “If you agree with it, you have to sign it.”But Janssen said that neither he nor any of his staff had signed ­paperwork at the Giro. “Our lawyers are currently exchanging questions with the other side, including questions about the procedure. We’ve received answers, but they’re too vague. There will be further developments on that front in the coming months.”Janssen insisted that Wiebes was “unfairly expelled from the Giro” and that theTour de Franceleader suffered both financial and reputational losses. “The stakes are incredibly high. Lorena could have secured three, perhaps even four, [stage] victories there. We are looking into whether we can be compensated for this. We have sponsorship contracts stipulating financial bonuses for achieving specific results – bonuses we missed out on because of this incident.”Janssen insisted that the issue will be resolved, but through “a court case or arbitration” and added that “we expect that to happen”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe UCI president, David Lappartient, however, was defiant when he was asked if the sport’s governing body was prepared for a suit from Wiebes and her team. “We have very good relationships with the teams,” he said, “but you can’t be friends with everybody, otherwise we’d never decide anything.View image in fullscreenThe peloton passes through the village of Bougy-Villars during the second stage.Photograph: Jean-Christophe Bott/EPA“Sometimes we take decisions that are not 100% supported, but that’s the reality about anything in the world. We have some tensions with some teams, but even if we have tensions, we keep the dialogue. It’s not a personal conflict.”Wiebes is thought unlikely to make it a hat-trick of wins on the hilly third stage on Monday, through the Jura to Poligny, even if her improved climbing still makes her an outside bet. The first-category climb of the Col de la Faucille, however, after just 24km of the stage, followed by three more categorised climbs, may well make a third success beyond her.The defending champion, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, has so far been a discreet presence. Currently in ninth place overall, the Olympic gold medallist is awaiting Tuesday’s individual time trial and the bigger climbs of the final weekend. “As soon as we knew there was a time trial, we made sure to put me in a better position on the time-trial bike, and do quite a few aerodynamic tests on the track,” Ferrand-Prévot said. “I’ve spent a lot of time on the time-trial bike these last months. So I will try to give my best and to limit the damage on the fourth stage.”Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingTour de FrancenewsShareReuse this content

title: UCI president backs night-time drug testing after Tour de France controversy | Tour de France | The Guardian
description: The UCI president, David Lappartient, has given his support to night-time testing, as happened at the Tour de France, in ‘exceptional cases’
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: The UCI president, David Lappartient, has given his support to night-time testing, as happened at the Tour de France, in ‘exceptional cases’
Content: David Lappartient said transparency is paramount in the UCI.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenDavid Lappartient said transparency is paramount in the UCI.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersTour de FranceUCI president backs night-time drug testing after Tour de France controversyDavid Lappartient says selective night testing is justified‘We always have suspicion in cycling, due to our past’Jeremy Whittlein GenevaSun 2 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UCI president, David Lappartient, has said there will “always be suspicion in cycling” and insisted this year’s men’sTour de Francewas clean. Lappartient, speaking at the start of stage two of the Tour de France Femmes in Aigle, also said he supported night-time testing during races in “exceptional cases”.Lappartient added that the absence of any positive test announcements by the International Testing Agency (ITA) indicated that last month’s men’s Tour was drug free. “The ITA never make a press release about negative results, only about positive results,” said Lappartient. “We didn’t see any press release in the Tour de France, so it seems there was nothing in the Tour.”It’s double Dutch as Lorena Wiebes wins second stage of Tour de France FemmesRead moreTadej Pogacar, the five-time champion, and his rival Jonas Vingegaard were subjected to night-time tests,at 5am and 2am respectively, by the ITA midway through this year’s race. “We will not support something they do every night on the riders. The normal hours [of testing] are not in the night,” said the head of cycling’s governing body.“However, we support the ITA if they have to do some specific test, because we know that, with micro-dosing EPO, that’s something you can’t detect six or seven hours after. So, for the riders to know that the ITA may come, that’s always a fear.“We always have suspicion in cycling, due to our past. I know what has been done to fight against doping. Night testing is a tool in this fight, but it is not a tool to use every day. You must use it very exceptionally. It’s not suspicion about any rider, but it’s a global message to the bunch.”View image in fullscreenNight-time testing is a deterrent that sends ‘a global message to the bunch’, said David Lappartient.Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPALappartient is an International Olympic Committee member alongsidethe besieged Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, and was re-elected UCI president unopposed for a third term in September last year. He believes involving stakeholders is key to successful reform of sports governance. “I will not interfere in Fifa’s matters, but I can tell you that in the UCI transparency is important,” Lappartient said.“When we want to make a reform of professional cycling, we will first make a presentation to the teams, the riders and the organisers. We have consultation with the stakeholders.“I will not give advice to Fifa, but I think it’s important to work with this kind of transparency.”Explore more on these topicsTour de FranceCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: The five big beasts are gone: who will be the Premier League’s next alpha manager? | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Arsenal’s Mikel Arteta is perhaps best placed to fill the void but the coaching contenders are legion as another season looms
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: Arsenal’s Mikel Arteta is perhaps best placed to fill the void but the coaching contenders are legion as another season looms
Content: The big beasts of the Premier League and the possible contenders to join their realm this season.Composite: Getty Images, ReutersView image in fullscreenThe big beasts of the Premier League and the possible contenders to join their realm this season.Composite: Getty Images, ReutersInside footballArsenalThe five big beasts are gone: who will be the Premier League’s next alpha manager?Jonathan WilsonArsenal’s Mikel Arteta is perhaps best placed to fill the void but the coaching contenders are legion as another season loomsSun 2 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareThis used to be a land of giants. This used to be a land where big men fought. This used to be a land where Sir Alex Ferguson and Arsène Wenger tussled, then José Mourinho joined the fray. This used to be a land where Jürgen Klopp made Pep Guardiola reconsider, and he changed his style and won anyway.Not any more. Next season will be the first since the inauguralPremier Leaguein 1992 not to feature any of the five big managerial beasts – not Ferguson, not Wenger, not Mourinho, not Klopp and not Guardiola.Who should win the men’s Ballon d’Or?Read moreWhat’s come over our great land? The Premier League is still our home, but where have all the heroes gone? Where’s the man who ruled by fury? Or the man who made virtues of broccoli and sobriety? Where’s the man who made the conference room the pitch? Where’s the gegenpressingmeister, or the cold philosopher of the positional game? Now they take a man who instigated some interesting pressing patterns and they call him a regular hero. Where are the men who are willing to play the game?You don’t have to be a nostalgist in the vein ofBill Andersonto think that the Premier League looks a little diminished. Régis Le Bris took over at Sunderland two summers ago and already he is the fourth longest-serving manager currently at a Premier League club. While his quiet authority impressed last season, the understated Breton is no one’s idea of a main character. And it’ll take a while before the meeting of the two longest-servers, Mikel Arteta and Unai Emery, looks like a clash of the titans, even with the twist that Emery was Arteta’s predecessor at Arsenal.Tottenhamappointed Roberto De Zerbiin March and, the promoted sides excepted, he has already been a Premier League manager longer than 11 of his rivals. All long-running dramas go through this process. Major characters move on, new ones arise. At least they are easier to tell apart than in House of the Dragon: they don’t all have the same hair, and they are not all bafflingly interrelated. Still, it will take time for the new breed to become familiar. Quirks have to be learned, strengths and weaknesses understood.View image in fullscreenRoberto De Zerbi has the charisma of a leading figure.Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/PAThe result is that this season looks as hard to call as any in living memory. Perhaps the Premier League has entered its Arsenal era and Arteta will soon squat like a giant toad across English football. But retaining the league is difficult, particularly given the emotional outpouring that inevitably comes with ending a lengthy drought. Neither Declan Rice nor Bukayo Saka looked especially fresh at the World Cup, whileWilliam Saliba damaged his back. It would be no great surprise if Arsenal started the season slowly.But who is equipped to take advantage? The previous two league title winners are under new management.Enzo Maresca– Guardiola’s replacement at Manchester City – is a curious manager in that his record is rather better than the experience of watching his teams play. Although his reputation was enhanced by Chelsea’s decline after his departure, it shouldn’t be forgotten just how frustrated Leicester and Chelsea fans became at times with the cautious nature of his football. Arne Slot showed at Liverpool that it is, at least in the short term, possible to thrive when following one of the big beasts but it remains an enormous challenge to succeed somebody who has defined the personality of a club.Andoni Iraola impressed at Rayo Vallecano and Bournemouth, but the truth is that it’s impossible to know how anybody will adapt to the greater scrutiny of a club such as Liverpool, no matter how composed they may previously have appeared.There’s a lingering doubt about his Bournemouth’s propensity to concede late goals. It may be thata deeper bench offersan immediate solution but equally that could indicate a problem with load management – and that is not going to be made any easier by involvement in the Champions League. Iraola has always relied on extremely physical training sessions, but they will have to be tempered, at least to an extent, by the demands of European football, in which Iraola has little experience.Similar questions can be asked of Michael Carrick at Manchester United. He did enough last season that United effectivelyhad to appoint him, without doing enough to offer overwhelming proof of his abilities. Signings so far seem to have addressed the right areas in the squad, but the big issue is whether he can handle the demands of playing in multiple competitions. United finished third last season without ever playing a team who had played fewer matches than them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhere all 20 Premier League clubs should strengthen before the seasonRead moreSo demanding is the modern calendar that fatigue may end up being a bigger factor than any manager. If you are a superclub, the key to having a bad season, as United have demonstrated, is to have one so bad that you don’t qualify for any form of European competition.View image in fullscreenXabi Alonso endured an awkward few months at Real Madrid but has the time to impose his ideas at Chelsea.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersWhich is extremely good news for Chelsea. Not only do they have, in Xabi Alonso, one of Europe’s most promising young managers but he has timeto impose his ideasand his side will be fresher than their opponents in almost every game this season.Emery’s domination of the Europa League has paradoxically given him a reputation of not quite being of the highest tier, but if Aston Villa can find a way ofwinning games beyond Morgan Rogersthrashing long-range efforts into the top corner, he has a great opportunity to impose himself. De Zerbi, who has the charisma of a leading figure, should also find himself in the Champions League qualification shake-up given Tottenham’s summer signings and their lack of European football.The big beasts may have gone but that simply means the Premier League is entering a new phase. What matters now is the battle to be the next alpha. Arteta is perhaps best placed, but the contenders are legion. The land awaits its next giant.Explore more on these topicsArsenalInside footballMikel ArtetaMichael CarrickRoberto De ZerbiUnai EmeryAndoni IraolaEnzo MarescacommentShareReuse this content

title: Leeds stage thrilling comeback to sink Liverpool in Chicago friendly | Friendlies | The Guardian
description: Leeds came from two goals down to beat Liverpool 4-2 in a pre-season friendly at Soldier Field, Chicago
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Leeds came from two goals down to beat Liverpool 4-2 in a pre-season friendly at Soldier Field, Chicago
Content: Liverpool’s Ifeanyi Ndukwe and Lukas Nmecha of Leeds tussle for possession.Photograph: Daniel Bartel/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLiverpool’s Ifeanyi Ndukwe and Lukas Nmecha of Leeds tussle for possession.Photograph: Daniel Bartel/Getty ImagesFriendliesLeeds stage thrilling comeback to sink Liverpool in Chicago friendlyLiverpool 2-4 LeedsCalvert-Lewin scores twice as Leeds come back from 2-0 downAndy Hunterat Soldier FieldSun 2 Aug 2026 18.40 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter 45 minutes at Soldier Field the tale of Liverpool’s pre-season tour of the US was of three straight wins and Andoni Iraola’s ideas taking shape thanks in no small part to Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak. After 90, with Liverpool’s expensive duo off the scene, it centred on a stirring Leeds fightback and the recurrence of a fragility that Iraola could well do without.Daniel Farke’s team staged a convincing comeback to inflict a first defeat of pre-season on the new ­Liverpool head coach. Dominic ­Calvert-Lewin, twice, Brenden Aaronson and Sean Longstaff all scored in the space 25 minutes as Liverpool failed to deal with Leeds’ strength at set-pieces and the disruption caused by a series of half-times changes. The drop-off from Liverpool, who led 2-0 at half-time, following the departures of Wirtz, Isak, Trey Nyoni and Rio Ngumoha was drastic.“Why are there so many fans?” an incredulous Chicago police officer asked his colleague as the crowds descended on Soldier Field, a stadium as impressive in design and location as the skyline that towers behind it. More than 32,000 had been present the previous night to see Robert Lewandowski mark his home debut for Chicago Fire with both goals in a 2-1 win over Dean Smith’s Charlotte FC. The lure of Liverpool and Leeds, even for a friendly, attracted an eye-catching 49,128 to the edge of Lake Michigan.Wirtz and Isak had missed the midweek win over Wrexham in New York having started pre-season training only on Monday. Ring-rusty or not, they both brought an immediate improvement to Liverpool’s performance level and displayed a rapport that will be crucial to realising Iraola’s vision next season.Isak looked sharper, more aware of his teammates and more involved in a Liverpool performance than he did during a first season hindered by fitness and injury problems. The Sweden international played all four of his country’s games at the World Cup and, Liverpool will hope, may not need too much time to get back up to speed as a result. That appeared the case here.It was Isak who instigated the counterattack that led to Liverpool winning a corner having weathered early set-piece pressure. Dominik Szoboszlai took it, Milos Kerkez deftly flicked it across the six-yard box and Luke Chambers lashed in the finishing touch. Isak also led Liverpool’s pressing game with an aggression and relentlessness that augurs well.Wirtz was involved in much of Liverpool’s best work during his 45 minutes on the pitch. His instinctive link-up play with Isak and Ngumoha, who gave James Justin a torrid time at right back, caused Leeds frequent problems. Liverpool’s second goal five minutes before the break was a delight. Nyoni, who has enjoyed a fine tour at the heart of Iraola’s midfield, floated an inch-perfect cross into Jeremie Frimpong’s run down the right. Frimpong hooked the ball back across goal first time and Wirtz stole in between three Leeds players to slide home. On the touchline Farke berated the officials over an offside call that went ignored in the buildup.Nyoni, Ngumoha, Wirtz and Isak were replaced as planned at the interval by Ryan Gravenberch, making his first appearance under Iraola, Lewis Koumas, Federico Chiesa and Curtis Jones respectively. Farke also made four half-time changes and the introduction of Calvert-Lewin, the new signing Harry Wilson, Longstaff and Aaronson brought the necessary improvement. The contest was completely transformed.The Leeds comeback commenced with a mistake by Kerkez. His over-elaborate back-heel was seized on by Ethan Ampadu, who released Aaronson in space on the left of the Liverpool penalty area. The USA international beat Giorgi Mamardashvili with a confident low finish. Calvert-Lewin levelled from close range after Joe Rodon flicked on a long throw from Ampadu and, just two minutes later, a third of Farke’s half-time substitutes put Leeds ahead in slapstick fashion. Jones attempted to sweep away Aaronson’s low cross into the Liverpool area and succeeded only in turning the ball against Longstaff. The Leeds midfielder looked sheepish after the rebound trickled beyond a stunned Mamardashvili.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLeeds were not done there. Worryingly for Iraola, his team were undone by an identical routine to Calvert-Lewin’s first goal. Another Ampadu long throw, another flick on, this time by the commanding new recruit Tarik Muharemovic, and the former Everton striker inflicted more punishment on Liverpool by converting a towering header off the underside of the crossbar.Explore more on these topicsFriendliesLiverpoolLeeds UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: Chelsea sign Argentina international Valentín Barco from Strasbourg | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: Chelsea have handed a seven-year deal to Valentín Barco, a left-back from their sister club Strasbourg
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Chelsea have handed a seven-year deal to Valentín Barco, a left-back from their sister club Strasbourg
Content: Jude Bellingham argues with Valentín Barco after the World Cup semi-final.Photograph: Jacob Kupferman/APView image in fullscreenJude Bellingham argues with Valentín Barco after the World Cup semi-final.Photograph: Jacob Kupferman/APTransfer windowChelsea sign Argentina international Valentín Barco from StrasbourgBarco a left-back who can also play in midfieldPlayer had spell at Brighton before move to FrancePA MediaSun 2 Aug 2026 17.28 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 18.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChelsea have signed the Argentina international Valentín Barco from their sister clubStrasbourgon a seven-year deal.The 22-year-old, who played seven times for Brighton including six Premier League appearances during the 2023-24 season, becomes the eighth arrival of new manager Xabi Alonso’s reign.Pressure on Gianni Infantino increases as Uefa members prepare to oppose re-electionRead moreA versatile player who can be used in central midfield as well as his regular position of left-back, Barco was in theArgentinasquad that finished as runners-up at the World Cup, winning his fifth cap in the 3-1 group-stage win over Jordan.He moved to Strasbourg initially on loan from Brighton in 2025 and signed permanently later that year having helped the club to qualify for the Conference League. In all he made 54 appearances for the Ligue 1 side.He was involved in a heated exchange with England’s Jude Bellingham immediately after his side’s 2-1 World Cup semi-final win in Atlanta, with Bellingham appearing to clip Barco around the head. The Argentinian, who was an unused substitute, had earlier run on to the pitch to celebrate after Enzo Fernández had equalised. He is expected to join up shortly with his new teammates on their tour of Australia and Hong Kong.It continues a busy summer in the transfer market forChelseaas they look to remodel under Alonso. On Saturday they confirmed the signing of the veteran striker Danny Welbeck from Brighton, following the signings of Crystal Palace’s Maxence Lacroix and Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa. Denner, Marco Palestra, Emmanuel Emegha and Geovany Quenda have also been signed.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowChelseaStrasbourgEuropean club footballArgentinanewsShareReuse this content

title: Scottish Premiership: Aberdeen’s late double stuns Hearts, St Johnstone edge thriller | Scottish Premiership | The Guardian
description: Stoppage-time goals secured Aberdeen a 2-1 win against Hearts, while St Johnstone began their campaign with a see-saw 4-3 win over Kilmarnock
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Stoppage-time goals secured Aberdeen a 2-1 win against Hearts, while St Johnstone began their campaign with a see-saw 4-3 win over Kilmarnock
Content: Kevin Nisbet plays to the crowd after scoring Aberdeen’s 95th-minute winner.Photograph: Mark Scates/SNS GroupView image in fullscreenKevin Nisbet plays to the crowd after scoring Aberdeen’s 95th-minute winner.Photograph: Mark Scates/SNS GroupScottish PremiershipScottish Premiership: Aberdeen’s late double stuns Hearts, St Johnstone edge thrillerTwo stoppage-time goals secure 2-1 win at PittodrieSt Johnstone fight back to beat Kilmarnock 4-3PA MediaSun 2 Aug 2026 12.21 EDTFirst published on Sat 1 Aug 2026 15.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHearts’ miserable summer continued as they conceded two late goals to lose 2-1 toAberdeenin their Premiership opener at Pittodrie.Wouter Vrancken andHeartslooked on course for a much-needed victory after a turbulent few months as they led through Oisin McEntee’s first-half goal. But just as they looked to be closing out a first win at Pittodrie for more than a decade, Lewis Mayo equalised in the 90th minute before Kevin Nisbet won it for Aberdeen with a stoppage-time penalty after Stuart Findlay was sent off for denying a goal-scoring opportunity.Rangers held by Dundee United to kick off McInnes era and Scottish PremiershipRead moreIt was a third consecutive defeat for Vrancken, who has endured a chastening start since replacing Derek McInnes in June. There were five changes to the side that lost Wednesday’s Champions League qualifier at home to Sturm Graz, with the goalkeeper Beau Reus and Laurent Mendy handed their debuts.In what was their first league match since beingpipped to the title by Celticin May, the 1,600-strong travelling support could be regularly heard singing anti-SFA songs in protest at the contentious calls from officials in the closing matches of last season. There was also a sense of trepidation about the prospect of kicking off the new season at Pittodrie, where Hearts had not won in their previous 14 visits.Hearts took the lead in the 35th minute after some pinball in the penalty area. Ba-Sy’s cutback from the left broke to Blair Spittal, whose shot was blocked by Nesta Guinness-Walker on the edge of the six-yard box. Dan Happe’s attempt to clear ran into the path of McEntee, who shot low into the net from seven yards.Aberdeen levelled in the 90th minute when Mayo bundled in from close range after Happe headed Ronan’s free-kick back into the danger area. The dramatic turnaround was completed in stoppage time when Toyosi Olusanya was hauled down by Findlay, who saw red, and Nisbet despatched the spot-kick.Ibrahim Said netted a late winner asMotherwellstarted their league season as they left off by beatingHibernianat Easter Road. Said finished off an excellent counter-attack in the 85th minute to secure a 2-1 victory.The Motherwell midfielder Oscar Priestman had earlier won and conceded a penalty. Lukas Fadinger put the visitors ahead five minutes before the end of a largely uneventful first half. Regan Charles-Cook missed a glorious chance to double the lead before Martin Boyle levelled in the 56th minute after being bundled over by Priestman.Hibs had two efforts cleared off the line by Martin Moorman before Said slotted home his fourth goal for the club.St Johnstonetwice gave up the lead before storming back to edge a seven-goal thriller at home toKilmarnockon Sunday.Josh Fowler gave the home side a 16th-minute lead but Greg Kiltie equalised against the run of play. Cheick Diabate’s header put the home side back in front after 47 minutes but two quick goals from Joe Hugill and Jason Holt – into his own net – somehow saw the visitors lead.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMichael Schjønning-Larsen put through his own net and Kai Fotheringham grabbed a late winner.“That was a test of character,” said Valakari, whose side came up as Championship winners last term. “Would we be this team who plays nice football in the Premiership but concedes goals and loses?”TheSt Mirrenmanager, Craig McLeish, believes his team’s 2-0 win atFalkirkaugurs well for a successful campaign.McLeish is convinced his squad will improve on last season’s struggles before he steered Saints to safety when the interim head coach. He has set a high bar of the top six and a European qualification bid this term, and a double from Killian Phillips helped St Mirren get off to a fine start atFalkirkStadium.“I thought the performance was excellent and if we can build on that we can go and achieve something as a group,” McLeish said. “I’m delighted for the group. We got the result our performance deserved. I thought we were excellent.”Explore more on these topicsScottish PremiershipAberdeenHeartsHibernianMotherwellSt JohnstoneKilmarnockShareReuse this content

title: ‘Plenty of challenges’: Laurie Daley steps down as NSW Blues State of Origin coach | State of Origin | The Guardian
description: Laurie Daley has stepped down as NSW State of Origin coach after a successful but tumultuous 2026 campaign
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Laurie Daley has stepped down as NSW State of Origin coach after a successful but tumultuous 2026 campaign
Content: Blues head coach Laurie Daley, who has now quit, hugs Nathan Cleary after NSW’s State of Origin game three win over Queensland at Suncorp Stadium.Photograph: Dave Hunt/AAPView image in fullscreenBlues head coach Laurie Daley, who has now quit, hugs Nathan Cleary after NSW’s State of Origin game three win over Queensland at Suncorp Stadium.Photograph: Dave Hunt/AAPState of Origin‘Plenty of challenges’: Laurie Daley steps down as NSW Blues State of Origin coachDaley resigns after leading NSW to famous 2026 series victoryCoach finishes with two series wins from six during two stintsAustralian Associated PressSun 2 Aug 2026 19.24 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 19.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLaurie Daley has ended months of speculation by officially quitting his role as NSWState of Origincoach.The NSWRL on Monday paid tribute to “true blue” Daley while announcing he would be stepping down after NSW successfully won back the shield from Queensland following a turbulent 2026 campaign.The Blues claimed the series 2-1 after becoming only the fourth team in Origin history to win a decider at Suncorp Stadium in Brisbane.In doing so, Daley became the only NSW representative to win a series decider in Brisbane as both a captain (1992, 1994) and a coach (2026).NSW silence Queensland and claim State of Origin shield with boilover for the agesRead moreBut the Blues legend endured relentless criticism for his coaching style and selections throughout the series, raising serious doubts about his desire to carry on in 2027.“NSWRL owes a massive debt of gratitude to Laurie for the service he has given to his state as both a player and a coach,” NSWRL chief executive David Trodden said.“He is widely regarded as one of the greatest players to have ever pulled on a sky blue jumper, becoming the first NSW captain to lead his state to three consecutive series wins in 1992-94.“He has also led NSW to arguably two of the greatest Origin series wins of all time as a coach, after ending Queensland’s eight-year winning streak in 2014 and overcoming adversity to steer the Blues home in 2026.“Those wins transcended football. They lifted and reinvigorated the whole state. He deserves to leave the NSW Origin arena as the hero that he is.”Overall, Daley finished with two series wins from seven during two stints at the helm.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toAustralia SportGet a daily roundup of the latest sports news, features and comment from our Australian sports deskPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I’ve always considered it an absolute honour and privilege to be involved with the NSW Blues State of Origin team, whether that was as a player or a coach, and I’ve always been ready to answer the call for my state whenever they needed me,” he said.“We faced plenty of challenges in the 2026 series and I’m proud of the way the players banded together to overcome them and save their best performance for game three in Brisbane to secure a memorable series win.“I thank the fans for their passion and their support, and I can’t think of a better way to move on with the Shield back where it belongs in NSW.”Explore more on these topicsState of OriginRugby leagueNRLAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australia’s cyclists complete mammoth medal haul at end of Commonwealth Games | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Australia has completed its domination of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games with 70 gold – more than double England’s tally – and 171 medals in total
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Australia has completed its domination of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games with 70 gold – more than double England’s tally – and 171 medals in total
Content: Alyssa Polites celebrates winning the women’s elimination race gold medal with Sophie Edwards at Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAlyssa Polites celebrates winning the women’s elimination race gold medal with Sophie Edwards at Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/ShutterstockCommonwealth Games 2026Australia’s cyclists complete mammoth medal haul at end of Commonwealth GamesAustralia end Games with 171 medals all up, including 70 goldCycling squad contributes 10 gold medals and 28 in totalAustralian Associated PressSun 2 Aug 2026 18.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia’s track cyclists have transformed pure pain, near-retirement and woefully-timed ill health into a dominatingCommonwealth Gamescampaign.Georgia Baker’s history-equalling exploits earned her the honour of carrying the flag at the closing ceremony. She was stunned when team chef de mission Petria Thomas broke the news to her in the middle of the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome, moments after finishing runner-up to teammate Alyssa Polites in the women’s elimination race.Australia’s Louise Hoskins, 76, wins historic Commonwealth Games gold medalRead moreBaker had wondered whether any of this would be possible, given she was sick for a crucial training camp only days out from the Games. Polites was emotional, given she nearly retired from the sport and took time off because of ill health. Instead, she and Baker are key members of the women’s track endurance group that won the team pursuit in Glasgow and are targeting the Los Angeles Olympics with growing confidence.Also on day four of Games cycling, Leigh Hoffman won the 1km time trial with a Games-record time. Just as Baker joined the select company of Anna Meares, Matt Glaetzer and Brad McGee as Australian cycling’s five-time Commonwealth Games gold medallists, Hoffman also made history. His three gold and one silver made him the first Australian cyclist to win four medals at a Commonwealth Games.View image in fullscreenEngland’s silver medalist Joseph Truman with Leigh Hoffman and Tayte Ryan of Australia.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPTara Neyland won her second gold of the Games in the women’s C4-C5 1km time trial as fellow Australian Erin Normoyle took bronze. Oli Bleddyn won silver in the men’s points race – the last event of the Games – and Kristina Clonan took bronze in the women’s keirin.All up, Australia won 171 medals, featuring 70 gold, that easily topped the Glasgow standings. England were a distant second with 29 gold and 110 medals. The Australian cycling squad’s solid campaign contributed 10 gold and 28 medals in total.Thomas said the emotional hugs from Polites and fellow elimination rider Sophie Edwards after she broke the flag bearer news was a good indication of why Baker was given the honour.“You can at least see from her the way her teammates reacted how respected she is within this group of cyclists, so I think we we made a good choice there,” Thomas said.Given how much her teammates backed her in for the team pursuit and then the scratch race gold medal, despite the illness, it was fitting that Baker ended up with a medal. The two Australians worked over Canadian Maggie Coles-Lyster at the end of the race, with Polites dashing clear as Baker ensured their quinella.Commonwealth Games 2026 medal tableRead more“She deserves this gold medal so much,” Baker said. “Alyssa’s worked so hard for me this week - it’s the least I can do, to repay the favour. I don’t want to take that away from her at all. The girls really backed me [for the team pursuit], my experience I suppose – ‘you can do it, G’ – I levelled up and did it.”Then came Thomas’s news. “I felt like I was in a bit of a dream, with Alyssa winning the gold and this on top of it. It was a really emotional moment,” Baker said. “I’m just really proud, one of the biggest honours of my career.”For Polites, gold in the team pursuit and elimination was proof perfect that her comeback from illness had been worth it. “I thought I was going to quit. These girls kept me on the pedals. I can’t thank them enough,” she said through tears.Hoffman reflected on the brutality of the “kilo” after clocking 58.530 seconds to break the Games record. Teammate Tayte Ryan won the bronze medal. “You don’t feel human. My legs are still burning ... 58 seconds of pure pain,” Hoffman said. I’m proud I didn’t spew.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesAustralia sportCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kuwaki wins Women’s Open after Henseleit’s unlucky break off marshal’s leg in playoff | Women's Open | The Guardian
description: The 23-year-old wins her first major championship as Japan now has back-to-back Women’s Open victories
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: The 23-year-old wins her first major championship as Japan now has back-to-back Women’s Open victories
Content: Shiho Kuwaki of Japan won the AIG Women's Open 2026 at Royal Lytham & St Annes.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenShiho Kuwaki of Japan won the AIG Women's Open 2026 at Royal Lytham & St Annes.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAWomen's OpenKuwaki wins Women’s Open after Henseleit’s unlucky break off marshal’s leg in playoffJapanese 23-year-old wins her first major championshipEngland’s Charley Hull and Lottie Woad finish tied sixthEwan Murrayat Royal Lytham & St AnnesSun 2 Aug 2026 16.41 EDTFirst published on Sun 2 Aug 2026 15.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was no surprise that an extraordinary Sunday at the Women’s Open ended in such circumstances. Has the ankle of a marshal ever before played a crucial role in the outcome of a major championship? A competition that looked for so long as if no one wanted to win rumbled on at Royal Lytham & St Annes until fate played its hand.Glory for Shiho Kuwaki, pain for Esther Henseleit. That barely explains the half of it. Henseleit had forced a playoff with a stunning birdie from 45ft on the final hole of regulation play. On the first visit back to the 18th, Kuwaki played a glorious approach to secure her four and the extension of the tournament.Clicky Ponting and ‘known cheats’ on the golf course: the crisis in UK sportsmanshipRead moreWhat happened next was beyond anyone’s comprehension. Kuwaki found the fairway with a perfect drive. Henseleit cut her tee shot to the right, where it looked in enough bother before hitting the lower leg of a volunteer. The ball ricocheted to the bottom of a gorse bush. Henseleit did exceptionally well to advance the ball up the fairway but the clear advantage was with Kuwaki. Her four secured the trophy. Henseleit has legitimate cause to bemoan horrible fortune.Earlier, this was a tournament where the nerves associated with the pursuit of a major championship were writ large across the faces of those looking to win the Women’s Open’s 50th edition.View image in fullscreenShiho Kuwaki celebrates victory on the 18th green at Royal Lytham & St Annes.Photograph: Luke Walker/Getty ImagesKuwaki’s is the most unlikely of triumphs. Perhaps her lack of experience in this domain actually helped the 23-year-old as those around her wilted. Kuwaki had played in only one Women’s Open before, missing the cut at Royal Porthcawl last year. Lytham provided such a contrasting storyline and Japan now has back-to-back Women’s Open victories.Henseleit needed a birdie three at the last to halt Kuwaki. She sat 45ft from the hole in two, with the odds firmly stacked against her. The ball was 5ft from the hole when Henseleit knew its destination. Kuwaki surely feared the worst but she need not have worried.Henseleit earlier offered a snapshot of what played out on this major Sunday. The German tied Kuwaki’s minus five with a tap-in birdie at the 15th. From the very next tee, Henseleit hooked a three wood into long grass. A bogey ensued. It was as if anyone who earned a proper view of the Women’s Open trophy was immediately blinded by the light.View image in fullscreenEsther Henseleit misses her crucial putt in the playoff.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAYealimi Noh held a three-shot lead after 54 holes. She even increased that advantage by one before wobbles started at the 4th. Noh posted a 74 before admitting it “stung” to fall short in this manner. She was one shy of the playoff mark of five under.On the final hole, in the final group, Henseleit and Noh had the opportunity to force Kuwaki into extra time. Both missed the fairway, with approaches leaving only the remote chances of birdies. Noh left her attempt short, moments after her playing partner had stunned the crowd.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRyu Hae-ran, seeking a third major win in as many starts, carded a three over par 74. Jeeno Thitikul? 73. Nelly Korda closed in the manner of a world No 1 with a 68 – the lowest round among the top 13 names on the leaderboard – catapulting her into a share of fourth.Charley Hull and Lottie Woad never seriously looked like delivering a British winner for the third time in a row at Lytham. Hull’s 72 left her at minus one. Woad’s putter was colder than a winter’s morning in Siberia during her 73, which meant the same aggregate. Neither undertook media duties, which given their standing here was less than impressive. Tied sixth is hardly the stuff of disaster.Anna Nordqvist signed off with a 68 before admitting the stresses and strains associated with her European Solheim Cup captaincy. Nordqvist will name her four captain’s selections on Monday for the clash against the United States, which takes place in the Netherlands in September. Intrigue surrounds whether Ireland’s Leona Maguire will keep her place in team Europe despite indifferent form. Nordqvist made some calls to players during Women’s Open week, which she conceded affected her own performance at Lytham.“I think it’s hard to put it in words how hard it has been,” Nordqvist said. “I felt like as soon as I came off the course, it was just so much stuff about Solheim Cup, which has been hard because I really wanted to go and enjoy this week.“I felt really off the first day but managed to battle through. I played really well the second day and then yesterday, I didn’t really play that badly, but mentally I was just exhausted. I think it [the size of the job] has been a lot more than I expected. There has been a lot more practical stuff to deal with. Maybe looking back, it was going to be a tough task to do both [play and be a captain], but I’m very proud of myself for how I’ve done it.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's OpenGolfnewsShareReuse this content

title: Emma Finucane lands keirin to claim historic fourth Commonwealth gold | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Emma Finucane picked up a fourth gold medal in Glasgow on the final day of a Commonwealth Games dominated by Australia
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Emma Finucane picked up a fourth gold medal in Glasgow on the final day of a Commonwealth Games dominated by Australia
Content: Emma Finucane on the velodrome podium. ‘To stand here and have four golds, I have no words,’ she said.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEmma Finucane on the velodrome podium. ‘To stand here and have four golds, I have no words,’ she said.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026Emma Finucane lands keirin to claim historic fourth Commonwealth goldWelsh cyclist had won in two sprints and time trialAustralia dominate Games with 171 medals, 70 goldSean Inglein GlasgowSun 2 Aug 2026 15.06 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Welsh cyclist Emma Finucane wrote her name into the history books on the final day of theCommonwealth Games, but Glasgow 2026 will be remembered most for Australia’s dominance.Before the Games, the Australia swimmer Sam Short had told reporters: “I’m so pumped – I can’t wait to go over there and smash those Pommies up.” And the whole Australia team seemed to get the memo as they finished with 171 medals, of them 70 gold. That put them a staggering 61 clear of England, who won 110 medals, with Canada third after winning 62.‘Ready for next 100 years’: Glasgow 2026 chief hails revamped Commonwealth GamesRead moreDespite the medal gap to Australia, Team England chef de mission, Jonathon Riall, issued a bullish assessment of the performance. “To finish the Games with 110 medals and second place on the medal table is an incredible achievement, one that every athlete, coach, support staff member and national governing body should be immensely proud of,” he said.“For Team England, success is about more than medals. It can mean achieving a lifetime best, overcoming adversity simply to reach the start line, or standing on the podium with a medal around your neck. We have seen all those different ways of winning throughout these Games.“We won medals across nine sports, saw established champions deliver once again on the biggest stage and watched a new generation announce themselves on the Commonwealth stage. This team has embodied everything Team England stands for, and it has been an immense privilege to lead them.”Finucane will certainly go down as one of the athletes of the Games after becoming the first sprint cyclist to win four track gold medals at the same Commonwealth Games.The Welsh cyclist added to the golds she had already won in the team and individual sprints and 1,000m time trial, with a bravuro victory in the keirin.Finucane, who won Olympic gold as part of the Great Britain sprint team at Paris 2024, moved to the front with two laps to go, daring others to get past her. None of them could as she won by half a bike length ahead of the Olympic champion, Ellesse Andrews of New Zealand.“I was convinced they would come round me,” admitted Finucane. “Honestly it is hard to put into words. I could have easily gone out in the semis.“After Paris, everything was a huge learning curve for me emotionally,” she added. “That week was really tough, and what I came away with was hard to process. But going into these Games I’ve learned to handle pressure better and regulate my emotions more.”Finucane now plans to take a holiday with her sister before shifting her focus towards the track world championships in Shanghai in October.View image in fullscreenEmma Finucane of Wales sprints down the home straight to win the women’s keirin final.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian“I definitely did feel the pressure but throughout the week I just rode my own race,” she added. “The team sprint was a big aim. The last time we rode it was four years ago and we got a bronze medal.“To come back as the same team and win gold was iconic. Singing on the podium with the team was insane. I just rode each race as it came. I went out there and left everything on the track. To stand here and have four golds, I have no words.She added: “I don’t think I’ll ever believe that I’ve made history here. I can’t believe little me has done this. Ten-year-old Emma is screaming inside, like, ‘What is going on?’ I hope I’ve inspired the nation to get on to a bike and get into a velodrome. I can’t believe I found this sport and this sport found me.”Earlier on the last day, Leigh Hoffman became the first Australian cyclist to win four medals at one Games by winning the 1km men’s time trial, ensuring he took home three gold and one silver.And there was more success for Australia in the para bowls as 76-year-old Louise Hoskins became theoldest athlete to win goldin Glasgow.Hoskins and her partner, Serena Bonnell, secured a 6-3, 4-4 win, leaving Hoskins delighted. “It is incredible. I’m still pinching myself,” she said. “I never thought I’d ever get gold at my age. Get out there and have a go, and never give up.”Elsewhere Jamaica fell short of pulling off another epic Commonwealth Games upset as they went down 56-48 to New Zealand in the women’s netball final. However England missed out on bronze after being thrashed 68-50 by Australia, who recovered from ashock one-point defeat to Jamaicaon Saturday.“Fourth place is agonising,” admitted the England captain, Fran Williams. “It’s the position nobody really wants to finish in when you’re just outside the medals. We just weren’t clinical enough today, and credit has to go to the Diamonds.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“Australia managed to show up stronger than us on the day it mattered most. It hurts at the moment, but there are so many lessons to take from this experience.”At least England were able to win three more gold medals on the final day. Emma Reid successfully defended her women’s 78kg judo title, Katherine Rednall triumphed in the women’s bowls singles final and Matthew Robertson defeated the home favourite Fin Graham in the velodrome to win the C1-C3 3,000m individual pursuit.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Stock market turmoil sheds stark light on the opaque AI economy | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Investors scramble to make sense of a shock Chinese challenge to the dominance of western chipmakers
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Investors scramble to make sense of a shock Chinese challenge to the dominance of western chipmakers
Content: A lithography machine at ASML in Veldhoven, the Netherlands. The Chinese have broken the Dutch company’s hold over deep-ultraviolet lithography, a technique essential to the computer chip supply chain.Photograph: Bart van Overbeeke Fotografie/AS/ReutersView image in fullscreenA lithography machine at ASML in Veldhoven, the Netherlands. The Chinese have broken the Dutch company’s hold over deep-ultraviolet lithography, a technique essential to the computer chip supply chain.Photograph: Bart van Overbeeke Fotografie/AS/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)AnalysisStock market turmoil sheds stark light on the opaque AI economyAisha Down,Dan MilmoandGraeme WeardenInvestors scramble to make sense of a shock Chinese challenge to the dominance of western chipmakersSun 2 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTShareEven for the rollercoaster world of AI, last week was particularly volatile as investors scrambled to keep up with developments that threatened the dominance of the largest western chipmakers.It began with a double whammy. On Monday, the Chinese memory chipmaker CXMT floated on the Shanghai stock market, soaring by 466% in value to 3.3tn yuan (£365bn).That same day, it was reported thatChinahad developed its own tools to carry out deep-ultraviolet lithography, a technique essential to the computer chip supply chain over which the Dutch company ASML had held a monopoly.AI-linked shares, particularly chipmakers, dropped around the world, sending many indices sliding. South Korea’s main share index, the Kospi,fell 11.5% on Tuesdayand a further6% on Wednesday, dragged down by its two biggest companies – the semiconductor maker SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics.On Thursday, the main US tech index, the Nasdaq, fell into correction territory at one point after dropping more than 10% from its recent high, before easing back. Nvidia lost more than 5% by Thursday evening, by which time it had beenovertaken by Apple as the world’s largest listed company.The next day there was a big rebound, when strong financial results from Amazon and Microsoft calmed traders’ nerves. The Kospi jumped nearly 20% – although the week’s slump still means it recorded its worst month since the height of the global financial crisis in October 2008.So, what exactly do these advances mean, and why have they got western investors so jittery?CXMT’s debut is impressive. But the company is arguably more of a boon to the global AI economy than a threat. It makes dynamic random-access memory (Dram) chips, which store the data that other AI chips draw on for their calculations.There is a global shortage of Dram chips, which is why phones and computers are expected to getfar more expensive. Crucially, they are not graphics processing units (GPUs) – which are the key chips and the “brains” in an AI system.This means, put simply, that CXMT is not a threat to GPU maker Nvidia, the biggest company in the AI economy and the only onemaking a profiton AI. They produce complementary, not competing goods.View image in fullscreenChina’s president, Xi Jinping, speaks at the opening of the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Beijing. China is making rapid advances in the semiconductors used to drive AI.Photograph: Greg Baker/AFP/Getty ImagesThe Chinese company could be a threat to SK Hynix and Micron, which do make memory chips. However, Alvin Nguyen, an analyst at the research firm Forrester, said the sell-off in these shares was an “overreaction” given that the global memory chip shortage is likely to continue until 2030.“SK Hynix, Micron, others, they can’t produce enough memory chips to begin with … the demand keeps growing even higher,” Nguyen said.A more serious concern could be the news that China can make the lithography tools. These are essentially extremely precise lasers that allow chipmakers to etch the thinnest lines in the world into wafers of silicon.Until now, only ASML could manufacture such machines. If this week’s reports are correct, Beijing could – in theory – produce GPUs that rival Nvidia’s. This would spell trouble for the world’s biggest company, and therefore Wall Street. But a serious competitor is still years away.“Fabs [semiconductor fabrication plants], as I know them, still take years to develop,” said Nguyen.Mark Boost, the chief executive of the UK cloud company Civo, agreed. “Investors are overreacting to the short-term threat,” he said. “Manufacturing a handful of [deep-ultraviolet] machines is a massive symbolic victory, but not a commercial replacement for ASML overnight.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Fabs run on efficiency and yield, and until these Chinese tools can match western reliability, ASML’s global dominance remains structurally safe outside mainland China.”Long term, this week’s advances are gamechanging for the AI economy, although in many ways they should have been predictable. Given US export controls,China has had little choice but to develop domestic capabilities.Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at IG, an online share trading company, said: “These Chinese chip companies appear poised to do to the big chipmakers what they have done to steel, automobiles and a host of other industries, namely undercut them and outcompete them on price.”It may be that last week’s correction is an overreaction – but also a reasonable response to a circular and extremely opaque AI economy that rests heavily on the fate of a single company, Nvidia.Its shares are gradually creeping up again, although they are still below what they were last week. A contributing factor to the investor skittishness appears to be yet another circular, opaque deal.Last Sunday, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia was considering providing a $250bn (£186bn)backstopto OpenAI for a large datacentre project. This comes roughly half a year after a $100bn deal between the two companiesfell apart.It was a significant factor in Nvidia’s decline over the week, according toMorningstar. The anxiety that underlies this is that the company has become the “central bank of AI” – holding up vast parts of the economy, and the global stock market, in ways that most people, investors included, do not understand.Many believe that it cannot last. What is on the other side is less clear.“Nvidia knows the gravy train’s going to run out,” Nguyen said. “Everybody’s waiting for them to fall apart. I don’t know that they will because what they do still has value … at some point in the future, they’ll no longer be one of the most valuable companies in the world. Maybe … they’ll be worth only $2tn. It’s still pretty good.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ChinaNvidiaStock marketsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘The language of Pokémon is universal’: why fans are still catching ‘em all after 30 years | Pokémon | The Guardian
description: As Pokémon Go celebrates its 10th anniversary, its devoted players explain how the game has created a vibrant intergenerational community spanning the globe
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: As Pokémon Go celebrates its 10th anniversary, its devoted players explain how the game has created a vibrant intergenerational community spanning the globe
Content: One Pokémon fan says the game appeals because it ‘brings people back to a happy place, no matter how bad the world is’.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOne Pokémon fan says the game appeals because it ‘brings people back to a happy place, no matter how bad the world is’.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianPokémon‘The language of Pokémon is universal’: why fans are still catching ‘em all after 30 yearsAs Pokémon Go celebrates its 10th anniversary, its devoted players explain how the game has created a vibrant intergenerational community spanning the globeSammy GecsoylerSun 2 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMostPokémonobsessives count rare, absurdly expensive playing cards or pristine, fully boxed game cartridges that have survived decades in the attic among their most prized possessions. But for Mairead Ralph, her Pokémon-related crown jewel is a bit different. “Technically, it’s my husband!” she says.The pair first locked eyes amid decks of Pokémon playing cards and Pokéballs at a fan event 16 years ago and the rest is history.Ralph was among hundreds of Pokémon fans who flocked to Shoreditch, east London, on Saturday afternoon for a pop-up celebrating the 10th anniversary ofPokémon Go, the massively successful augmented reality smartphone game that has seen millions of players physically venture to all corners of the earth to catch ’em all in person. In that spirit, the surrounding area was full of Pokéheads wandering the streets, their heads in their phones, seeking to catch exclusive Pokémon that had been released.Ralph, 42, is an OG Pokémon fan, getting into Pokémon Red when the game (and franchise) debuted 30 years ago. “I’ve been in love with it ever since,” she says. Months after Pokémon Red released in Japan in February 1996, the now-famous playing cards were released, some of which have since soared in value to thousands or even millions of pounds. Earlier this year, the world’s only Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA) 10-graded Pikachu Illustrator card was sold for a staggering £12m.The franchise, which spans video games, playing cards, TV shows, films and merchandise, has become so big that the Pokémon company, which celebrated its 30th birthday in March, is now the world’s biggest media franchise, with total revenues of $147bn (£110bn), according to Guinness World Records.View image in fullscreenPokémon GO’s 10th anniversary Summer Quest celebration in Shoreditch, London.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianThis is far from the first Pokémon-related event Ralph has attended. She has travelled to Japan, the US and France to mingle with fellow fans. Despite often not sharing the same language, this hasn’t been a challenge for Ralph. “The language of Pokémon is universal,” she says.Ralph even met her husband at one event. “I was at an event doing Pokémon stuff and he was working in a different area, and then we ran into each other at the local nerdy shop,” she says. Their love of the franchise extended to their wedding. Instead of having numbered tables, they had Pokémon. “If you were told to join Pikachu’s friends, you had to find the table with his face on it,” she says.She thinks Pokémon has remained popular because it “brings people back to a happy place, no matter how bad the world is”, especially during these tricky times where issues such as the cost of living are hitting hard. It helps that most Pokémon are “happy and smiley” apart from a few “grumpy” outliers. “I’m looking at you, Mewtwo,” she says.View image in fullscreenRumeysa Usca and her pomeranian at the event.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianAlso at the pop-up was Rumeysa Usca and her animated pomeranian Boomi. The 34-year-old engineer travelled from Leamington to attend the event. For her, the appeal of Pokémon Go is simple. “I can entertain my dog, entertain myself and lose weight,” she says. Usca has been playing the smartphone game for four years and has been a lifelong fan of the franchise, which she attributes to it “never having a break”, with new products being regularly released.She also says Pokémon taps into nostalgia and a desire to return to simpler times. “As kids, we were so happy watching and playing it. It just brings back those good emotions,” Usca says.Summer Till, 24, says it’s a good way to connect with younger relatives. “There’s a generation gap between me and my niece and nephew, but Pokémon is common ground for us,” she says.View image in fullscreenPokémon Go has helped Summer Till connect with younger relatives.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianThose who wanted a free coffee with a branded Pokémon Go cup needed to complete a challenge on the game along the surrounding streets. Among those taking part was Stacie Smith and her son Rupert. They travelled in from Southend in Essex. “She’s been getting all the luck,” says Rupert, referring to his mum catching better Pokémon than him on her phone. Smith remembers collecting Pokémon cards when she was growing up. “We would buy them along with panini stickers and Spice Girls postcards,” she says. And she then became fond of the cartoon, which was a staple on children’s TV in the late 1990s. Rupert enjoys the playing cards aspect more, but the pair have found a “shared love” of the franchise through Pokémon Go.View image in fullscreenStacie Smith with her son Rupert, 12.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianRupert has autism, which means he “doesn’t like leaving the house very much”, says Smith, but the game has encouraged him to start venturing outside more, and the pair spend more time together. This, she says, is “really important for his mental health and trying to get him integrated into communities so he can talk to other people”.At school, he’s made friends through his enthusiasm for Pokémon. He’s been handed down some Pokémon cards from family, including a first-edition holo Mewtwo from his dad. If kept in pristine, PSA 10-graded condition, the card could fetch about £18,000, but with a few bends and tears Rupert’s has been well-loved and is sadly less valuable.But for many in attendance, their love of the franchise is hardly material. Ralph’s love of Pokémon will be enduring. “It doesn’t matter if it’s your first Pokémon or your thousandth Pokémon, that little click of the Pokéball will always bring you joy.”Explore more on these topicsPokémonPokémon GoLondonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on global corporate tax: a $500bn prize that states must seize | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Donald Trump may reject the negotiations, but he cannot veto a global effort to make multinational companies answer to governments
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Donald Trump may reject the negotiations, but he cannot veto a global effort to make multinational companies answer to governments
Content: ‘Donald Trump’s US walked out last year and urged others to follow. None did.’Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Donald Trump’s US walked out last year and urged others to follow.
