None did.’Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesOpinionUnited NationsThe Guardian view on global corporate tax: a $500bn prize that states must seizeEditorialDonald Trump may reject the negotiations, but he cannot veto a global effort to make multinational companies answer to governmentsSun 2 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareGovernments are told that public services must shrink because money is tight. Yet a new Tax Justice Networkreportsays that countries could capture an extra $500bn a year without raising corporate tax rates. The answer is to tax multinational profits where real economic activity happens – known asunitary taxation. No new profit is created. Revenue simply shifts from tax havens where profits are “booked” to the countries where workers produce and customers spend.Making that principle a global tax standard depends on UN talks opening inNew Yorkon Monday. Modelled on the UN climate regime, a fiscal framework convention would create the governing body and procedures, with protocols providing detailed rules. The UN wants agreement by late 2027. Donald Trump’sUSwalked out last year and urged others to follow. None did.Rich countries gain most when firms pay tax where people work, not where profits vanish in havens, because their economies are the largest. Britain would collect about £13bn extra a year in tax receipts – two‑thirds of thecost of an NHS-style social care system. EU governments could raise enough to quadrupleclimate-adaptation spending. Poorer countries also benefit. The report calculates that the global south would receive $156bn in one year – more than the International Monetary Fund has outstanding in loans to those nations.For the first time in decades, multinationals could be taxed where they actually do business. Rules built for the corporate world of the 1920s – when national industrial giants dominated – would finally confront today’s companies organised around intangible assets and global supply chains, as well as profits of an altogether different scale. In 1929, General Motors made the equivalent of $4.7bn. Apple’s profit last year was $112bn. What the report calls “diversified” tax havens such asSwitzerlandand theNetherlandscould offset losses by raising rates. Pure booking centres such as the Cayman Islands could not.The talks suggest states are beginning to reclaim powers surrendered under globalisation to corporate lawyers and private tribunals. One protocol would let countries tax digital and other cross-border services without waiting for firms to establish domestic offices, blunting Mr Trump’strade threats. A second could go further, shifting tax disputes fromsecretive investor-state arbitrationinto a more open, publicly accountable UN-led system.The direction is unmistakable. Ireland, which is facing an estimated $11bn annual tax loss, has already begun putting aside part of its “windfall corporate tax receipts” in a new fund – an admission that the revenue won’t last.IndiaandNigeriahave legislated so that companies profiting from their economies should not escape the tax net just because they operate across borders.Britain has belatedly backed a UN-led shift towards taxing real activity. Defending rules entwined with its offshore network was politically indefensible and economically perverse. The US can sit out the negotiations, but it cannotshieldAmerican companies from others’ rules. The success of these talks has largely been down toAfrican nationsinsisting on consensus where possible and majority rule where necessary. That denies the US and any rich-country bloc an effective veto. Backed by India, Brazil and other developing powers, an African-led coalition can now press a simple claim: countries should be free to tax value created within their economies. Britain should help them prevail.Explore more on these topicsUnited NationsOpinionTax and spendingCorporate governanceTax avoidanceDonald TrumpAfricaGlobal economyeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Trump is determined to pursue his trade war – and he may be difficult to stop | Eduardo Porter | The Guardian
description: The president’s minions have trawled the statutes to restore roadblocks to trade. The invocation of Smoot-Hawley looks especially dangerous
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: The president’s minions have trawled the statutes to restore roadblocks to trade. The invocation of Smoot-Hawley looks especially dangerous
Content: President Donald Trump greets supporters after speaking at General Motors’ Milford Proving Grounds on July 27, 2026 in Milford, Michigan.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPresident Donald Trump greets supporters after speaking at General Motors’ Milford Proving Grounds on July 27, 2026 in Milford, Michigan.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesTrump tariffsTrump is determined to pursue his trade war – and he may be difficult to stopEduardo PorterThe president’s minions have trawled the statutes to restore roadblocks to trade. The invocation of Smoot-Hawley looks especially dangerousSun 2 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTShareDonald Trump may have found the killer weapon to punish countries at will: by imposing tariffs on their exports to the United States.The president has been looking for a new tool since February, when the supreme courtstruck down tariffshe slapped on virtually all of America’s trading partners based on the International Economic Emergency Powers Act, or IEEPA, on the spurious grounds that the US faced a variety of national emergencies. It’s become a parlor game among policy wonks to predict what new legal justification he would deploy to replace them.Well, it’s probably not what you think. The round-robin tariffs imposed on everybody last Friday, under the argument that America’s trading partners unfairly undercut US companies by importing things made with forced labor, has drawn a lot of attention. The blatantly specious accusation, sitting uneasily alongside America’s own state-sanctionedabuse of forced labor, underscored how low Trump will stoop to get his way on trade.But those tariffs, imposed under section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974,do not provide the carte blancheTrump wants. Tariffs under this section are meant to retaliate against specific “acts, policies and practices” that are “unreasonable” and “burden or restrict” US companies. A blanket charge that every foreign country is enabling forced labor and thus hurting American business isunlikely to fly in court. The whole strategy can be challenged as “arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law” or as “unsupported by substantial evidence”.The truly menacing precedent comes from Trump’s decision, made the Monday before the worldwide forced labor tariffs came into play, to foist a 50% tariff on imports from Canada.The White House’s pretext is Canadian discrimination against American dairy, booze and cars, which, paradoxically, came about as retaliation against Trump’s original barrage of tariffs last year. Sly observers, however, have pointed to Trump’s threat to punish Canada for the forest-fire smoke that wafted into the US. Maybe the new duties are meant to soften Canada as talks get under way to renew the USMCA North American trade pact, or to convince Canadians to become America’s 51st state. Or just because “tariff” isa pretty word.The authority Trump invoked to attack Canada is ominous: section 338 of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930, which is the law that choked global trade in the 1930s and helped sink the world into the Great Depression. Section 338 is particularly dangerous because it offers cover for the president to slap trade levies on whatever country he wants under some fairly hazy arguments.Specifically, it grants the president authority to retaliate against countries that do anything to put the United States “at a disadvantage compared with the commerce of any foreign country”. As soon as the president decides this is going on, he is authorized to “declare such new or additional rate or rates of duty as he shall determine will offset such burden or disadvantage”.Until Trump, section 338 was never invoked to impose tariffs. It was mostly used as leverage, to guarantee that other countries treated American products the same as imports from anywhere else. If some country offered preferential access to a neighbor or ally, the US could demand the same terms, or else.This principle is now called “most favored nation treatment,” which is central to multinational trade rules enforced by the World Trade Organization. Trump doesn’t care about such niceties, though. He has a more destructive agenda in mind. And the statute appears to give him semantic wiggle room. He is determined to pursue his trade war. With such a sprawling mandate, he may be difficult to stop.America’s trading partners were elated in February when a 6-3 majority on the court, including two justices appointed by Trump, ruled against his use of the 1977 IEEPA to impose tariffs at will. It was close, though.The court has shown an almost unbelievable deference to the president. It didn’t object to Trump’s spurious invocation of national emergencies – a “public health crisis” due to illegal drugs from Canada, Mexico and China; trade deficits that “led to the hollowing out” of American manufacturing; something something because Brazil jailed its ex-president Jair Bolsonaro for plotting a coup. The justices merely objected to his use of the statute to impose taxes, which are the preserve of Congress.The executive has gotten away with similarly spurious arguments before. In 1975 President Richard Nixon was allowed to invoke the Trading with the Enemy Act of 1917 to slap tariffs on a zipper company from Japan, a country with which the US was not at war. Trump’s lawyers, in fact, argued before the supreme court that this precedent supported the president’s emergency powers to raise tariffs on anybody under IEEPA.Though Trump lost, his menace to the world remains. Since February his minions have trawled through legal statutes across American history to restore roadblocks to trade.Balance of payments crises don’t exist any more. Still, fresh from his supreme court loss, Trump imposed a 10% tariff on everybody by invoking section 122 of the 1974 act, which allows for tariffs to prevent such imbalances. The use of the law is so ridiculous that Trump’s own lawyers, in the IEEPA case, argued before the supreme court justices that section 122 could not be used as a substitute.In 1974, when the dollar’s exchange rate was fixed, a balance of payments crisis could happen when inflows of money from abroad couldn’t cover the trade deficit, forcing the government to sell foreign assets to plug the gap and preserve the exchange rate. These days the dollar floats. If too little money is coming in, it falls, making it cheaper and thus more attractive for foreigners to buy dollar assets, bringing things back into balance.Fortunately, the balance of payments tariffs had a statutory limit of 150 days. But Trump has tried other stuff too. Section 301 has been used many times before, including by Trump against China in his first term to penalize it for its industrial subsidies, which give its producers an unfair leg up. Trump has also relied on section 232 of the 1962 Trade Expansion Act to put levies on steel, aluminum, lumber, semiconductors and autos on specific grounds about protecting national security.None of these authorities, however, grant him the unrestrained blanket power that could be his under section 338. Let’s see what he does with it.Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on SubstackExplore more on these topicsTrump tariffsTariffsDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: For most US small businesses, Trump’s tariffs aren’t the big issue they were | Gene Marks | The Guardian
description: Tariffs are annoying and disruptive, but this round is less impactful – and business owners are taking them in their stride
Author: Gene Marks
Headline: Tariffs are annoying and disruptive, but this round is less impactful – and business owners are taking them in their stride
Content: Chef Sunny Bertsch at work last year at his sushi restaurant in Houston.Photograph: Houston Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChef Sunny Bertsch at work last year at his sushi restaurant in Houston.Photograph: Houston Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesUS small businessFor most US small businesses, Trump’s tariffs aren’t the big issue they wereGene MarksTariffs are annoying and disruptive, but this round is less impactful – and business owners are taking them in their strideSun 2 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTShareRebounding from his defeat at the supreme court in February, Donald Trump has recently announced a new round of tariffs, invoking sections ofvarious trade actsto levy amounts on industries and countries based on reasons ranging from “forced labor” to “excess capacity”.And how are small and medium-sized businesses in the US reacting? One word: snoozefest.For context, my firm has hundreds of clients who are small and medium-sized. I’m also a professional speaker and present to literally thousands of business owners across many industries at associations and conference events. Last year I was frequently asked to discuss tariffs to these groups. This year that topic is not even on the agenda. People don’t care. Why?For starters, the new tariffs announced aren’t as big as before.Remember “liberation day”, when tariff rates ranging anywhere from 10% to 50% were being ultimately assessed? Remember how products coming from China were subject to rates as high as 145% at one point. As recently as February, tariff rates on Indian goods were as much as 50%.Corporate America may be using AI to cut jobs, but small businesses are using it to keep them | Gene MarksRead moreThose numbers were significant and had an impact on many of my clients. But the new rates are much lower, generally ranging from 10% to 12.5% (although higher rates are being assessed on certain products and countries). Already the administration is carving out exemptions. It’s not nothing. But they’re way below previous attempts and more manageable.And refunds from the last tariff attempt are helping.As I write this, approximately$122bnin refunds have been accepted and are due to be paid. I wasskepticalthat this was ever going to happen, but it’s happening. The process is bureaucratic and doesn’t include all the tariffs paid (yet), but a number of my clients have seen money returned to them through their original customs brokers.Now their biggest problem is making sure they’ve estimated enough taxes to be paid on this unexpected windfall. The experience not only has helped many companies’ bank accounts, but also gives them confidence that there is a process for overturning these actions.Which brings me to the next reason why tariffs aren’t as big a deal this time: lawsuits. They’re inevitable. In fact, afew small businessesalready filed suits contesting the president’s latest round of levies. We’ve learned that the court system works. The appeals process is reliable. The supreme court actually cares about the law. And – despite the protests and marches – our “king” actually behaves more like a president and complies with the courts when he loses a case there.Given the way the administration has handled so many other big challenges (Hello, Iran? Immigration enforcement?) I – and a number of my clients – have confidence that the plaintiffs’ attorneys will find many holes in how these new tariffs were implemented and the likelihood of repeal is pretty strong.One thing that can’t be denied about American entrepreneurs: they’re innovative. I’ve seen this in practice over the past two years as a number of them dodged, danced and navigated their way around the many tariff bombs hurled their way. They moved products to bonded warehouses. They leveraged their data and got better at targeting their pricing. They pivoted to technology for cost savings elsewhere in their business. They scrambled to find alternative suppliers and to do more domestic assembly and manufacturing. New tariffs will simply be another incentive to exercise these options and explore others, and businesses are less fearful of the impact than they were in the past.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMost of the businesses I know, regardless of industry, have seen their production, delivery and operating costs increase anywhere from 20% to 40% since Covid. It’s been a massive change. Energy prices are contributing to this. Inflation caused by government spending is another. Supply chain issues aren’t helping. But the fact is that tariffs are just a small part of that. When small businesses are asked if tariffs are hurting their margins they’re likely to say yes. But not as much as some other factors, which mutes their overall impact.Back when he first took office it seemed like the president was announcing new tariffs, changing his mind, increasing them, decreasing them, removing them – it all got a bit much.Yes, more tariffs will be announced. But there’s a process required by the trade acts he’s invoking to get these tariffs approved. That provides time to figure out a response. Things are still relatively uncertain because … well, Trump. But the uncertainty caused by his behavior has muted a bit. That’s good news for any business owner making their plans.When the president announced his initial round of tariffs, the media was wringing its hands over the countless small businesses that would be affected. I remember the bike shop owner who bought all of his supplies from India, the wine merchant who specialized in French products and the woman who ran a specialty shoe site online using shoes from China. Yeah, they were screwed. Hopefully they received refunds and – more important – diversified their supply chains. But most small businesses don’t buy their products overseas. These are pizza shops, auto mechanics, dry cleaners, architects, accountants, healthcare providers.Tariffsdidn’t affect them very much or at all. Same for this time.Tariffs are annoying, disruptive and in many cases unnecessary. But the latest round won’t be as impactful, if they happen at all. US business owners are just taking them in stride.Explore more on these topicsUS small businessTrump tariffsTariffsDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Decades on from the US’s disastrous campaign in Afghanistan, Trump is making all the same mistakes | Simon Tisdall | The Guardian
description: The president has blundered into a ‘forever war’ with Iran he can’t win, but refuses to end. Such hubris has a long history, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Author: Simon Tisdall
Headline: The president has blundered into a ‘forever war’ with Iran he can’t win, but refuses to end. Such hubris has a long history, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Content: A woman walks past rubble in southern Tehran after Israeli/US airstrikes in April 2026.Photograph: Majid Saeedi/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA woman walks past rubble in southern Tehran after Israeli/US airstrikes in April 2026.Photograph: Majid Saeedi/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpDecades on from the US’s disastrous campaign in Afghanistan, Trump is making all the same mistakesSimon TisdallThe president has blundered into a ‘forever war’ with Iran he can’t win, but refuses to end. Such hubris has a long historySun 2 Aug 2026 07.31 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIt’s five years this month since the chaotic retreat of US forces from Kabul. The Nato-backed invasion and occupation of Afghanistan, launched after the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks on New York City and Washington DC, is now widely regarded as a failure. It cost the lives of more than 2,400 US and 450 British troops, and tens of thousands of civilians (the exact number is unknown). Although al-Qaida terrorists were routed, their Taliban hostsreimposed repressive, misogynistic Islamist ruleafter regaining power in 2021. Afghanistan became a byword forill-considered western interventionismand nation-building. It was the archetypal “forever war”, a phrase firstcoined during Vietnam.If this cautionary tale had any lasting value, it was as a deterrent to politicians and generals tempted to rashly embark on open-ended conflicts without just cause, defined, achievable aims, and an exit strategy. Dismayingly, the forever war lesson had to be learned all over again in Iraq, which the US and UK invaded in 2003 and departed, having caused huge harm for scant benefit, in 2011. “Never again!” was the passionate cry at the time and since. And yet, it seems, the same disastrous pattern is now repeating after Donald Trump’s incomprehensibly foolish decision to attack Iran. A war he termed a “little excursion” is entering its sixth month andhas been escalating rapidly. It, too, has a forever feel.That this nightmare is happening again defies all reason. How can it be? Immediate causes of the war aside, answers may be found in persistent US exaggerations and misconceptions about the level and extent of external threats, mixed up with political dishonesty, national hubris, naivety and misplaced idealism. Recalling the harrowing US experience in Afghanistan, Carter Malkasian, a National War College professor who served as a civilian adviser to US forces in Helmand and Kabul,suggeststhe basic premise for keeping troops in Afghanistan for 20 years – a belief the country would otherwise revert to being a safe haven for international terrorism – was fatally flawed.“Nothing of the sort occurred. Over the past five years, not a single act of terrorism against the US was carried out by a group based inAfghanistan,” Malkasian wrote. “Washington spent roughly $1tn on the war. More than 775,000 American service members were deployed … all to defend against a threat that turned out to have been exaggerated.“Five years on, the greatest danger is not that a terrorist safe haven might once again emerge in Afghanistan. A graver threat comes from the risk of collective forgetting.” In short, “fears of the moment” should not cloud memories of the dreadful long-term costs – human, financial, geopolitical – of endless forever war.View image in fullscreenA US military Chinook helicopter lands on a field in Afghanistan in 2019.Photograph: Thomas Watkins/AFP/Getty ImagesIf the Afghan war was prosecuted on the basis of a false assumption, so much more so was the invasion of oil-rich Iraq. George W Bush’s claim in 2002 that Saddam Hussein’s regime possessed stockpiles of readily usable chemical and biological weapons and was seeking a nuclear bombproved untrue. Untrue, too, was the claim from the then vice-president, Dick Cheney, that Iraq “aids and protects” al-Qaida. The subsequent occupation and insurgency became part of an even larger forever war – Bush’s “global war on terror”.According to Brown University’s Costs of War project, an estimated 940,000 people were killed in direct post-9/11 violence in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, Yemen and Pakistan between 2001 and 2023. Up to 3.8 million died indirectly in post-9/11 war zones.It’s easy to second-guess decisions about war and peace taken under the pressure of horrific events. The disingenuous pursuit of political, military and commercial agendas, and the manipulation of intelligence and public opinion, is harder to excuse. Yet was any war ever launched without ulterior motives? The much-discussed new film of Homer’s epic poem, the Odyssey, concerns the aftermath of the 10-year-long Trojan war, which was ostensibly triggered by the abduction of the beautiful Helen of Sparta. Yet, prosaically, the warmay have been more about fair tradethan a fair maiden. The US maintained it fought the Vietnam war to support democracy and halt the spread of communism – the discredited “domino theory”. But it was also very much about US exceptionalism and global hegemony. In that sense, little has changed.What else makes American politicians risk costly entanglements in foreign wars they can’t control and usually lose? Insecurity – meaning fear – is a common denominator. Like Bush before him, Trump and Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, have greatly and knowingly exaggerated the immediacy and existential nature of the Iranian threat. Like Iraq in 2003,Iran possesses no nuclear weaponsand there is zero firm evidence it is trying, or has recently tried, to acquire them. There is a recurring paradox here: it’s the spectacle of the world’s most powerful country once again fearfully tilting at shadows.Trump’s overbearing hostility to weaker neighbours such as Venezuela, Cuba, Colombia, Panama and Greenland has a forever aspect, too. It is rooted in the foundational myth that the US has a unique mission – and right – to oversee the western hemisphere, a view it later extended to the rest of the world. Likewise, greed is forever.Abandoning altruistic ideas of democracy promotion, Trump seeks to exercise economic as well as geopolitical dominance. He has tried to monetise the wars inUkraineandGaza. His focus on the strait of Hormuz shows how security policy and financial and commercial interests invariably intersect.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion33:00Is Iran a ‘forever war’? – Stateside with Kai and CarterLack of effective UN mediation and peacekeeping, the hollowing out of US diplomacy, which has accelerated under Trump’s lickspittle secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and astubborn refusal to accept the militarily inevitableall play a role in turning US-led conflicts into intractable quagmires. In Trump’s case, ego is also a factor. It seems he would rather kill thousands more civilians, risk committing war crimes, set the Middle East ablaze and destroy Republicans’ electoral chances than admit he was wrong over Iran. Such extreme behaviour illuminates another pernicious aspect of the forever war phenomenon. Its utter pointlessness is fundamentally immoral. In its sheer un-reason, itoffends against the laws of God and man. War without end is the death of hope.As he frantically twists and turns over Iran, it’s plain that Trump perceives the bottomless pit on the edge of which, thanks to him, the US totters – and has no idea how to avoid it. One day, he talks about talks. The next, he hits out with massive, murderous violence. Careless of their people’s suffering, implacable Iranianhardliners relish his dilemmaand turn the screw, mounting widening regional militia attacks and global economy-spooking drone and missile strikes. Lost in a maze of denial, Trump tries in vain to bomb his way out of trouble while desperate for a deal that can somehow be sold as a victory.Neither option is going to work. This abysmal Iranian catastrophe is already defining Trump’s presidency. The bloody stain, the blame and the shame, if not the war, will last forever.Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentatorExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionIranUS foreign policyAfghanistanIraqMiddle East and north AfricaSouth and central AsiacommentShareReuse this content

title: As retired US judges, we’re not used to speaking out. But we cannot be silent | Michael P Donnelly and Robert F Orr | The Guardian
description: We joined a recent bus tour of 30 judges, lawyers and advocates fighting not for any partisan aim, but for the rule of law itself
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: We joined a recent bus tour of 30 judges, lawyers and advocates fighting not for any partisan aim, but for the rule of law itself
Content: ‘Restraint should not be confused with silence about the survival of the institution itself.’Photograph: Brian Jackson/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Restraint should not be confused with silence about the survival of the institution itself.’Photograph: Brian Jackson/AlamyOpinionUS newsAs retired US judges, we’re not used to speaking out. But we cannot be silentMichael P Donnelly and Robert F OrrWe joined a recent bus tour of 30 judges, lawyers and advocates fighting not for any partisan aim, but for the rule of law itselfSun 2 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 16.41 EDTShareLast October, US lawyers, judges and rule-of-law advocates traveled to Warsaw as guests of the Carter Center. Neither of us was among them. But when our colleagues returned, their stories inspired us.They told us about judges and lawyers across central Europe who had been surveilled, smeared, prosecuted and sometimes jailed for standing between political power and courts meant to remain independent.And they kept going.Poland’s example was especially compelling. When its government sought greater control over the judiciary, Polish judges put on their robes and marched through Warsaw. Judges from across Europe joined them in what became the March of 1,000 Robes.Then they left their courthouses and traveled through towns and villages, explaining what an independent judiciary means to a farmer, shopkeeper, parent or business owner. They talked about law not as an abstraction, but as protection against arbitrary power.How do we defeat authoritarianism? By building a sense of belonging | Julie Fernandes and Katrina GambleRead moreThey understood a truth Americans can no longer overlook: judicial independence cannot survive merely because judges believe in it. The public must understand why it matters.That lesson brought us on to a bus.Last month, shortly after the United States celebrated its 250th birthday, the Justice in Motion tour traveled from western Pennsylvania through Ohio and into Michigan. Thirty sitting and retired judges, lawyers and advocates handed out pocket constitutions, met students and asked a question Americans do not consider often enough: what does the rule of law mean in everyday life, and what happens when we take it for granted?In Columbus, we did something neither of us imagined during our years on the bench. We put on our robes and marched from the federal courthouse toward the supreme court of Ohio, carrying purple flowers, an international symbol of judicial independence.American judges do not ordinarily march in the streets. Nor should they. The judiciary derives much of its legitimacy from restraint. Judges do not campaign for particular outcomes or answer criticism with press conferences. They speak through their decisions. But these are no ordinary times.And our Polish colleagues taught us that silence can carry its own risk.Our march was not about Democrats or Republicans, nor about defending particular judges or decisions. It was about defending the system that allows legal disagreements to be resolved according to law rather than political power.One of us was elected to the supreme court of Ohio as a Democrat. The other was elected to the supreme court of North Carolina as a Republican and is now an independent. Through two long careers, we have disagreed about plenty.That is precisely the point.The rule of law is not a partisan possession.Both sides enter a courtroom with the right to be heard. Judges must apply the law to the facts without regard to which party is more powerful, popular or politically useful.Sometimes judges get it wrong. That is why we have appellate courts. Sometimes courts issue decisions that elected officials or citizens strongly dislike. That is unavoidable in a constitutional democracy.The answer is appeal, legislation where constitutionally permissible, or constitutional amendment. It cannot be intimidation, retaliation for unpopular rulings or the suggestion that compliance with lawful court orders is optional.Once adherence to judicial decisions depends upon whether the politically powerful agree with them, we have left the rule of law behind.In Wooster, Ohio, about 150 people gathered across from the historic courthouse. The discussion was not about red America or blue America. It was about ordinary life.The rule of law is why you can deposit money in a bank and expect it to be there tomorrow. It is why contracts mean something, property can be protected and an individual citizen can enter a courthouse and challenge the government.These protections seem ordinary only because generations before us built institutions strong enough to make them ordinary. When the rule of law works, it is almost invisible.Judges are trained – rightly – to exercise restraint. During our years on the bench, we spoke through our rulings. That tradition is essential to maintaining confidence in an impartial judiciary.But restraint should not be confused with silence about the survival of the institution itself.When judges are threatened because of their rulings; when an adverse decision is answered not with an appeal but with demands for retaliation; when courts are judged legitimate only when they produce politically desired outcomes, those who understand the system have an obligation to explain what is being lost.Our Polish friends understood this before we did. Their circumstances differ from ours, and comparisons should be made carefully. But the lesson travels well.The rule of law does not defend itself. Neither does an independent judiciary. Constitutions are pieces of paper unless citizens and public officials possess the courage and habits necessary to honor them.Division is a threat to resistance. Here’s how to build a stronger coalition | David C Turner III and Eric Morrison-SmithRead moreFour days on a bus will not persuade a nation. The purpose was more modest: to begin conversations, one community and one citizen at a time, about institutions Americans have been fortunate enough to take for granted.That work belongs not only to judges and lawyers, but to all of us.The rule of law is not something judges possess. It is something citizens inherit.And every generation must decide whether to preserve it.What’s giving us hope nowJustice Robert F Orr (retired):What gives me hope is the scope of individuals and groups now focusing and talking about the rule of law and the independence of our judiciary. Our bus trip had a great mix of backgrounds and experience both in the judges participating and meeting us at stops as well as the young people who amplified the message across various media platforms. It’s genuinely a national movement.Justice Michael P Donnelly (retired):What gives me hope is the genuine appreciation we encountered during the bus tour for the role of an independent judiciary in protecting individual rights and civil liberties. The people we met understood that these freedoms, defended at great sacrifice throughout our history, cannot be taken for granted – and that each generation must be willing to stand up for them.Michael P Donnelly is a retired justice of the supreme court of OhioRobert F Orr is a retired justice of the supreme court of North Carolina. Both participated in the Justice in Motion tour organized by the Democracy Rising Collaborative and Keep Our RepublicExplore more on these topicsUS newsOpinionLaw (US)ActivismPolandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Annie thought perimenopause symptoms were keeping her awake. Alcohol was playing a role too | Diane Young | The Guardian
description: Hot flushes, anxiety, poor sleep and mood swings are common during perimenopause. But the very thing Annie was using to manage her symptoms had become an even bigger problem
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Hot flushes, anxiety, poor sleep and mood swings are common during perimenopause. But the very thing Annie was using to manage her symptoms had become an even bigger problem
Content: ‘For women already experiencing sleep disruption because of perimenopause, alcohol can make an already challenging situation significantly worse,’ writes Diane Young.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘For women already experiencing sleep disruption because of perimenopause, alcohol can make an already challenging situation significantly worse,’ writes Diane Young.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesThe modern mindMenopauseAnnie thought perimenopause symptoms were keeping her awake. Alcohol was playing a role tooDiane YoungHot flushes, anxiety, poor sleep and mood swings are common during perimenopause. But the very thing Annie was using to manage her symptoms had become an even bigger problemThe modern mindis a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their workSun 2 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 19.28 EDTShareWhen Annie* started pacing around her house at 3am and struggling to find words during work meetings, she put it down to stress and perimenopause. She wasn’t entirely wrong. But it wasn’t the whole story.At 43, she was juggling a full-time job as a hospitality HR manager, three teenage children and the endless demands of family life. Like many women in midlife, she felt stretched in every direction. “I was doing long hours at work, running around with kids’ activities and household chores. I wasn’t sleeping well. Then I’d get up feeling exhausted and spend the day dealing with headaches, mood swings, hot flushes and brain fog. I went around in circles for six months feeling like my world was imploding.”After speaking with friends and reading about the symptoms online, Annie became convinced she was in the depths of perimenopause. One friend’s advice seemed particularly appealing. “She said, ‘When the kids are in bed, run yourself a bath, pour yourself a glass of wine and then get into bed.’ At the time, it sounded like the perfect way to end the day.”How do I know when I’ve hit perimenopause?Read moreAt first, Annie felt it was helping. She would often have a glass of wine with dinner to unwind after a stressful day. But the glass before bed soon became two. Then three. What had started as a way to relax gradually became a nightly ritual. “It seemed to quiet the racing thoughts I was having at that time of night and make it easier to fall asleep.”While alcohol can initially make people feel sleepy, it often disrupts sleep later in the night, leading to poorer sleep quality and early waking with increased fatigue the following day. For women already experiencing sleep disruption because of perimenopause, alcohol can make an already challenging situation significantly worse.Annie confessed that over a few short weeks her consumption increased. “I didn’t really think it was a problem – I told myself I was simply helping myself fall asleep. My husband had no idea as he was in bed before I was and up at 5am for work.”It wasn’t until Annie slept through her alarm and was too sleepy to drive to work that she began to question herself. “I’d always been reliable. I remember sitting in my car later that day thinking, ‘This isn’t me.’”Annie’s experience reflects what many of us therapists and clinicians see during perimenopause. Fluctuating hormone levels can affect the brain, contributing to memory lapses, poor concentration, anxiety and “brain fog”. These symptoms coincide with the stage of life when career pressures, family responsibilities and relationship stress are at their peak.Mood changes, sleep disruption and emotional overwhelm can place enormous strain on women during midlife. For some women, like Annie, perimenopause also marks the first time they experience significant anxiety symptoms.While women can experience all the usual signs of anxiety disorders such as excessive worry and physical signs (sweating, heart racing and shaking), there can be specific anxiety-related signs that can be more common in women. These include difficulty making decisions, increased crying, irritability, mood swings and feelings of guilt or shame.By the time Annie sought help from her local doctor for her symptoms, she was drinking most nights and feeling paralysed with anxiety. “I still thought perimenopause was the real culprit,” she said. “I didn’t really question the wine because many of my friends seemed to be doing the same thing.”What Annie didn’t realise was that the very thing she was using to manage her symptoms had become an even bigger problem. The challenge is that many symptoms of perimenopause overlap with the effects of alcohol itself.Annie’s doctor recommended a residential treatment program after completing an online alcohol addictionself-assessmentthat can help identify key indicators of alcoholic behaviour. The program gave her something she hadn’t had for months: the time and space to understand what was really happening. Through individual therapy, group counselling and a comprehensive mental health assessment, Annie began to see the pattern clearly. What had started as a way to cope with anxiety, insomnia and stress had evolved into a cycle that was worsening her sleep, anxiety, cognitive functioning and emotional wellbeing.Why does alcohol make us both happy and miserable – and what else does it do to our minds and bodies?Read moreTreatment focused on both her alcohol use and the anxiety that had been driving it. Annie learned practical strategies to manage racing thoughts, regulate stress and improve her sleep without relying on wine. Over several weeks, Annie learned to meditate, took up yoga and pilates, and began beach walks to relax and reconnect with something she enjoyed. And while she still enjoys the occasional bath at the end of a busy day, she no longer reaches for wine.Anxiety treatment for women should be personalised and consider specific symptoms and life circumstances. Annie’s treatment plan also included medical support, ongoing psychological therapy and lifestyle changes tailored to her individual needs.Today, Annie’s sleep is improving. She still experiences hot flushes from time to time, and there are days when the brain fog returns. But the symptoms are no longer as relentless as they once were. She is sleeping more consistently, her anxiety has eased and she feels clearer, more energetic and better equipped to manage the changes that come with perimenopause.Perimenopause was part of Annie’s story. But it wasn’t the whole story. Many women like Annie can actually find themselves treating symptoms that alcohol is quietly making worse. While sometimes hormones are the explanation, other times they’re only one piece of a much bigger puzzle. It is essential for women to seek professional help to explore the best treatment options for their needs.*All clients discussed are fictional amalgamsDiane Young is a trauma specialist and psychotherapist withSouth Pacific Private, a trauma, addiction and mental health treatment centreExplore more on these topicsMenopauseThe modern mindAlcoholSleepMental healthWomen's healthPsychologyAnxietycommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m all for the nanny state – but we should abolish fines for holidays in term time | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett | The Guardian
description: Some parents are sticklers for the rules, yet mass civil disobedience by parents in England and Wales suggests many agree with me, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: Some parents are sticklers for the rules, yet mass civil disobedience by parents in England and Wales suggests many agree with me, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Content: ‘Value to taxpayers is often mentioned in these discussions, but the wellbeing and mental health benefits for children can be economic as well as holistic.’Photograph: MBI/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Value to taxpayers is often mentioned in these discussions, but the wellbeing and mental health benefits for children can be economic as well as holistic.’Photograph: MBI/AlamyOpinionSchool holidaysI’m all for the nanny state – but we should abolish fines for holidays in term timeRhiannon Lucy CosslettSome parents are sticklers for the rules, yet mass civil disobedience by parents in England and Wales suggests many agree with meSun 2 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePerhaps it’s my stage of parenthood, or the fact that I’ve been lying awake at night, but I think I have an idea that could secure the electoral future of the Labour party. All Andy Burnham needs to do to win a landslide at the next general election is abolish fines for parents who take their children on term-time holidays.More than 2 million– around a fifth–have taken their children out of school because they could not afford to travelduring holidays, according to a national survey released this month. A record459,288 fines were issuedto parents last year.This issue has recently become relevant to me because my son starts school in September, so this year will be the last in which we will be allowed to take term-time trips. Obviously, as I contemplate the preposterous costs for summer holidays, I have developed a new and vested interest in being able to get away with my family. It’s deeper than that, though: I didn’t get many childhood holidays, for financial and circumstantial reasons. As a result I feel very passionately that all small people need leisure time away. Without wanting to turn this into a big sob story, I was so desperate to go on holiday like my friends that I used to collect brochures from high street travel agents andspend hours poring over the different hotels, with kids’ clubs, beaches, swimming pools and waterslides that I could only dream of.Living in a wealthy middle-class area has further radicalised me. I have heard enough parents casually admit that they simply incorporate the fine into their budget to understand that a two-tier system exists. Fines for term-time holidays discriminate unfairly against low-income and Send families, who for the aforementioned financial and circumstantial reasons (too expensive, too crowded for children with sensory or mobility issues) will struggle to take their children away at peak times or cover the fines for doing so in term time. Handing out fines also discriminates against people who work in certain professions, such as farmers, members of the military or people who work in the leisure and tourism industry, and those who have family living a great distance away.Also, fines don’t even work. Taking your child out of school for a holiday is an ongoing act of mass civil disobedience on the part of the public inEnglandand Wales (Scotland and Northern Ireland do not have automatic fines). Considering how law-abiding we generally are, I find this quite extraordinary. It implies there is a passionate and significant proportion of the public who believe in the importance and the value of a family holiday to the extent that they are willing to break the law to give their kids one. I also suspect many find the rules off-puttingly paternalistic (even as a socialist who loves the “nanny state”, I consider it a huge overreach).Of course, there are inevitably people who get very exercised about everyone following the rules. These objectors think you should simply plan your holidays around the school calendar, and if you can’t afford to go anywhere, tough. I have met people in real life who have said this in conversation, and they are always the sorts who take their children on gastronomic cycling tours of the Dordogne every summer. In other words, they have a certain level of privilege and don’t seem able to make the imaginative leap to barely being able to scrape together enough cash for a few rainy days in a caravan near Prestatyn.Don’t get me wrong: there are reasonable objections to my proposition. School attendance and its impact on education is an important issue – I fundamentally believe that. What I don’t believe is that schools should be such a high-pressure environmentthat one term-time holiday a year – which would still need to be authorised at the headteacher’s discretion – will always have a disastrous impact on learning. With school refusals at record highs and a crumbling Send system, term-time holidays are clearly not the most urgent cause of poor educational outcomes. The coalition government did much to damage the state education system. It also, incidentally, made the system for unauthorised absences at state schools muchmore punitive. Many of the politicians responsible were privately educated and went on to send their children to fee-paying schools where parents are free to take their kids on term-time holidays.If I’ve managed to convince you, perhaps I will risk losing you when I say that I don’t believe these trips even necessarily need to be “educational”. On the few holidays I was taken on, we went to museums and old workhouses and castles and ruins, and yes, it’s beneficial to do that. It’s also good for children to see the worried frowns on their parents’ faces melt away – to socialise, to practise their swimming and eat new foods. Memories of fun and togetherness can last a lifetime, sustaining us through tough times. Value to taxpayers is often mentioned in these discussions, but the wellbeing and mental health benefits for children can be economic as well as holistic.By all means, also look at other measures, such as penalising travel companies that engage in unreasonable profiteering, and staggering or shortening the summer holidays – and providing proper childcare during them. But this should be an open goal forBurnham. He says he cares about alleviating the cost of living pressures on families, allowing them to enjoy life. Abolishing fines would be one effective way of doing that, while correcting a source of social inequality. And it’s a vote winner.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsSchool holidaysOpinionSchoolsChildrenEnglandWalescommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s Glastonbury on wheels’: Welsh eisteddfod cultural event celebrates 850th year  | Festivals | The Guardian
description: This year’s edition, Eisteddfod y Garreg Las, has gone back to its roots at the castle where a prince first held it in 1176
Author: Bethan McKernan
Headline: This year’s edition, Eisteddfod y Garreg Las, has gone back to its roots at the castle where a prince first held it in 1176
Content: The puppet of Lord Rhys at Eisteddfod y Garreg Las, which begins on Saturday near Cardigan in Pembrokeshire.Photograph: Joann Randles/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe puppet of Lord Rhys at Eisteddfod y Garreg Las, which begins on Saturday near Cardigan in Pembrokeshire.Photograph: Joann Randles/The GuardianFestivals‘It’s Glastonbury on wheels’: Welsh eisteddfod cultural event celebrates 850th yearThis year’s edition, Eisteddfod y Garreg Las, has gone back to its roots at the castle where a prince first held it in 1176Bethan McKernanWales correspondentSun 2 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 11.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy 1176, Lord Rhys ap Gruffydd, a medieval Welsh prince, had become one of the most powerful rulers the country had ever known. He’d successfully banished Norman invaders from his lands, made peace with King Henry and rebuilt Cardigan castle in stone.Prosperous and secure, he threw a grand holiday tournament, inviting bards and musicians to play and compete under his patronage in the first recorded eisteddfod, roughly, a “sitting together” – a tradition that still lives on today. This year’s national eisteddfod, a celebration of Welsh language, culture and creativity, has returned to its roots near Lord Rhys’s castle for its 850th birthday.The eisteddfod is the oldest and one of the largest touring cultural events in Europe, moving between north and south Wales each year.This year’s Eisteddfod y Garreg Las– meaning blue rock, after the celebrated bluestone in the nearby Preseli hills that was used to construct the inner circle of Stonehenge – features more than 1,000 events and activities between 1 and 8 August and is expected to attract 150,000 visitors.View image in fullscreenThe crown and chair of the Eisteddfod y Garreg Las, the traditional prizes for the best free-verse poem.Photograph: Joann Randles/The Guardian“The eisteddfod is Glastonbury on wheels, basically, so I don’t know why it goes so under the radar in the rest of the UK,” says Marc Rees, the creative director who has brought Lord Rhys back to life as a 5-metre puppet for this year’s event.“It’s this massive festival of music and poetry and dancing and some incredible bands: the Super Furry Animals are playing this year. It has a different character every year and it’s always so joyful.”double quotation markIt is amazing that the eisteddfod is still developing and evolving every year and is a dynamic and modern festivalJohn Davies, eisteddfod chairLord Rhys, created with input from the community by Cardigan’s Theatr Byd Bach, has been touring the area after being “awoken” from his deep sleep in St David’s Cathedral, visiting towns and villages around the area in the run-up to the eisteddfod’s opening on Saturday. Travelling with him have been this year’s crown and chair – the traditional prizes for the best free-verse poem, since Lord Rhys awarded a chair at his table to the first winner – as well as Teifi, his faithful hunting dog.Since this year’s location was announced in 2024, local fundraising committees have raised £400,000 for staging the event, and hundreds of volunteers have prepared the site near the village of Llantwdfor this week’s festivities.View image in fullscreenThe Wilyman family, visiting from Haverfordwest. Mum Elliw is taking part in several competitions throughout the week.Photograph: Joann Randles/The GuardianJohn Davies, chair of Eisteddfod y Garreg Las’s executive committee, says: “I hope that Lord Rhys himself would have enjoyed the trip … 850 years is a long time, and it is amazing that the eisteddfod is still developing and evolving every year and is a dynamic and modern festival that offers something for everyone.”After Lord Rhys’s time, bardic schools inWaleswere closed during the Edwardian conquest, and eisteddfodau to some extent fell into abeyance.The tradition enjoyed a revival in the 18th century thanks to London-based Welsh literary and cultural societies, and the modern iterationowes much to the Gorsedd Cymru– at the time a secret society of poets, writers and musicians, heavily influenced by druidism and mysticism.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenNaomi Chiffi from Tenby.Photograph: Joann Randles/The GuardianIolo Morganwg, an eccentric antiquarianand poet who founded the Gorsedd, came up with much of what he said was the modern eisteddfod’s ancient lore and history while high on laudanum – but his colourful and imaginative creation proved enormously popular, and lives on in the pageantry today.“It’s like the eisteddfod has had a homecoming,” says Naomi Chiffi, 45, from Tenby. “My kids are all in Welsh-medium education; the first Welsh school in Tenby opened a decade ago now. Events like this on our doorstep show them that the language is a living, fun thing.”The Wilyman family, visiting from Haverfordwest, said they were delighted to be close to the festival this year; mum Elliw, 48, is taking part in several competitions throughout the week.“We’ve been fundraising since February,” she says. “It’s so nice to see it all come together.”Explore more on these topicsFestivalsHeritageWalesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I loved the Police from the get-go’: Elaine Paige’s honest playlist | Music | The Guardian
description: The singer and actor is partial to Mozart and once did Édith Piaf at karaoke, but to which musical showstopper does she owe everything?
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The singer and actor is partial to Mozart and once did Édith Piaf at karaoke, but to which musical showstopper does she owe everything?
Content: Diva patrol … Elaine Paige, who loves her crooners, too.View image in fullscreenDiva patrol … Elaine Paige, who loves her crooners, too.Honest playlistMusic‘I loved the Police from the get-go’: Elaine Paige’s honest playlistThe singer and actor is partial to Mozart and once did Édith Piaf at karaoke, but to which musical showstopper does she owe everything?As told toRich PelleySun 2 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withI used to sing All I Have to Do Is Dream by the Everly Brothers with my schoolfriend who lived over the road, when I was 11 or 12. I sang the harmony and she sang the melody.The song I do at karaokeThe only time was on holiday in Nice with a friend. We’d been out for a lovely supper and had far too much rosé, and I was about to play Édith Piaf in the West End. I ended up singing Hymne à l’amour, and he did Fools Rush In.The first single I boughtMagic Moments by Perry Como from the record shop in Barnet High Street, for my mother’s birthday. She loved Perry Como, Andy Williams, Matt Monro – all those crooners.The song I know every lyric toWhen I was in Hair in 1968, we were in the pub having a snifter before the show when the company manager came in and said: “Jeanie’s off – and so are her understudies. Paige, you’re up.” I was terrified. Jeanie comes up through a trapdoor, covered in beads, singing Air. Somehow I knew every word.The best song to play at a partyRoxanne. I’ve loved the Police from the get-go.The song I can no longer listen toShall We Dance? from The King and I. My co-star Jason Scott Lee pulled out after three months. After that I had to dance with a catalogue of different kings in a huge crinoline dress, wearing thick stockings, suspenders, corsets and layers of underwear.The best song to have sex toI do have a bit of a penchant for Wicked Game by Chris Isaak. But I’m not saying I’ve tried it!The song that gets me up in the morningI wake up to Radio 4, then switch to Radio 3. I’m a big Mozart fan – one of the first things I ever sang in public was a Mozart aria: Deh vieni, non tardar from The Marriage of Figaro.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPaige, Perón … Elaine sings Evita in 1980.The song that changed my lifeDon’t Cry for Me Argentina, because without it, I probably wouldn’t be talking to you today.The song that makes me cryEv’ry Time We Say Goodbye by Cole Porter, because it reminds me of my mum. My dad was an estate agent, but he also had a band, the Arcadians, and would go out gigging. Mum and I would wave him off, then listen to records on the radiogram.The song I’d like played at my funeralOh God, I don’t want to think about it. Maybe George Michael’s cover of The Long and Winding Road – I was a huge fan, he had the most beautiful voice, and it’s a lovely song.Elaine Paige’s new album Miscellaneous Paige is out now.Explore more on these topicsMusicHonest playlistfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Could a couch-to-5k for books get you back into reading?  | Books | The Guardian
description: With smartphones stealing our attention, we’re picking up fewer books than ever. A novelist shares her eight-week scheme to get you back into the habit
Author: Naomi Alderman
Headline: With smartphones stealing our attention, we’re picking up fewer books than ever. A novelist shares her eight-week scheme to get you back into the habit
Content: Get with the programme … is the books couch-to-5k for you?Photograph: Alina Rudya/Bell Collective/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGet with the programme … is the books couch-to-5k for you?Photograph: Alina Rudya/Bell Collective/Getty ImagesBooksCould a couch-to-5k for books get you back into reading?With smartphones stealing our attention, we’re picking up fewer books than ever. A novelist shares her eight-week scheme to get you back into the habitNaomi AldermanSun 2 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDo you feel that it’s harder to read than it used to be? Not harder to read emails, texts and social media posts, of course. We’re reading those all day long. Harder to sit down and lose yourself in a book? How long is it since you even sat down with a weekend newspaper and read it cover to cover? Do you feel that you used to have a life-sustaining reading habit, everything from fun popcorn novels to serious nonfiction, classic and contemporary, many genres and writers, but somehow it’s gone away? It doesn’t feel like a decision that you made. It just happened.I feel like that. At least more like that than I’m comfortable with. I’m a novelist and I present programs about thinking on the BBC, and yet even I am finding that I’m reading less than I used to. It seems more of an effort and less of a consistent, persistent habit than it was. I hate this feeling. I still have the habit of acquiring books, buying them, getting them from libraries, being sent them. And I do still read. Compared with many people, I probably read an enormous amount, but I know it’s not as much as I used to read. And I know where the time has gone.It is, of course, the damn phones.The other day I was sitting with a friend who is a doctor and an expert in public health – that is, large-scale interventions that might improve the health of millions of people by a tiny bit. I found myself saying: “I don’t think it’s a coincidence that smartphones are about the same size and shape as a packet of cigarettes.” We talked about how the really massive public health crisis from tobacco was caused by the arrival of cheap mass-market cigarettes, which you could smoke endlessly without having to do the ritual of emptying, cleaning and refilling your pipe, and which were not as expensive as cigars. We talked about how people didn’t know, when they started smoking those cheap mass-market cigarettes during the first world war, how deadly they would be. We talked about how it’s not our fault.My friend said that he too misses his regular reading habit. I think of him as an avid reader, but we’re remembering each other from a few years ago. In the trenches in the first world war, men smoked cigarettes to steady their nerves. During the pandemic, when we couldn’t speak to each other in person or give each other a hug, we all got glued to our smartphones. It’s not our fault, but we are going to have to fix it now. My friend said that he wished someone would do a couch to 5k-style training program for reading. And then I couldn’t stop thinking about it.double quotation markDo you feel that you used to have a life-sustaining reading habit but somehow it’s gone away?The problems of people not reading are well documented. Students are apparently arriving at university unable to read a whole book. A2024 reportby the OECD has found that literacy has declined or stagnated in most developed countries. In his forthcoming book, The New Dark Ages, James Marriott traces the problems for society that are increasingly coming out of a lack of literacy. Marriott argues that when we’re not reading, we’re increasingly unable to follow complex arguments and find the problems with them. We tend to be more swayed by cartoonish figures with simple slogans we can repeat. We will believe gossip and treat it seriously rather than thinking through the intellectual ideas behind politics or business.It’s a public health crisis of intellectual health, and most governments don’t seem minded to do anything about it. It’s the damn phones, but dealing with the phones means tussling with the massively wealthy American technology companies that are protected by Donald Trump. It would be straightforward to force technology companies to give us ways to use the useful services on the phones with all the pernicious features turned off. But it would take political will to do it.While we’re waiting, if nobody is going to do it for us, for now, we’re going to need to do what we can for ourselves.View image in fullscreenNaomi Alderman.Photograph: Pål Hansen/The ObserverSo I thought about the couch to 5k for reading, how you could do it. I worked on designing the couch to 5k for my running app Zombies, Run several years ago, so I know the theory. When I mentioned the idea on mySubstack newsletter, Whatever Works, readers bit my hand off with excitement (much like a zombie). It suddenly seemed very urgent. There is no more time to wait.We used to live in a world where the only way to get information, or to be entertained, or to simply pass the time when you were waiting, or queueing, or on a bus, was reading. Well, we also used to live in a world where the only way to get places was to walk. Then we invented technologies that are very useful in some ways, but we had to take on exercise programs to help us get enough movement in our lives. That’s where we are with reading now.We just need to accept that and get on with it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSo I’ve designed a program. Eight weeks, with three separate tracks. It’s mostly for people like me, who remember that they had a life-sustaining reading habit once but feel that it has somehow fallen away. Over eight weeks, we are working ourselves back to reading half an hour every day, with two or three longer sessions during the week. There are also tracks for people who are really time-limited and just want to be reading 20 minutes a day, and people who feel that they’re basically still reading, but know that they are shying away from the more challenging stuff they want to be tackling.The response has been extraordinary. After the first week of the program, people are already saying that they’re finding their morning routine goes more quickly now they’re not brain-fogged from scrolling first thing, that reading in stressful times is making them feel calmer and not more anxious as scrolling did, that they can watch a long film without being tempted to look at their phone. They are rediscovering the simple joy of being gripped by a great book after as few as two or three days of working on this together. Fans have put together homemade digital and printable trackers to keep themselves motivated. Teachers are already asking me how to introduce this idea into schools.Try these habits to reinvigorate your reading | LettersRead moreIt’s really exciting to find out how easy it is to put this right. The program is running right now, and if you’re reading this, you’re not too late to join. Just start from the beginning. All you have to do is put down your phone, pick up a book, and read for 10 minutes. That’s day one.There is so much joy in books, and it’s all still there waiting for us. All we have to do is take it back from the technology billionaires, one day of reading at a time.Seenaomialderman.substack.comfor further detailsExplore more on these topicsBooksLiteracyHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From The Wizard of Oz to Trainspotting: 25 films to watch before you turn 25 | Movies | The Guardian
description: As AI slop takes over our screens, what better antidote for enquiring minds than a magical film? We ask directors, producers and critics to pick one must-see movie for each year – from infancy to young adulthood
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As AI slop takes over our screens, what better antidote for enquiring minds than a magical film? We ask directors, producers and critics to pick one must-see movie for each year – from infancy to young adulthood
Content: Illustration: Yuewei Nino Li/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Yuewei Nino Li/The GuardianMoviesFrom The Wizard of Oz to Trainspotting: 25 films to watch before you turn 25As AI slop takes over our screens, what better antidote for enquiring minds than a magical film? We ask directors, producers and critics to pick one must-see movie for each year from infancy to early adulthoodSun 2 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 16.40 EDTShareScreentime has a bad rep these days: it’s allegedly at the root of everything from the collapse of media literacy to the rise of the far right. For parents, and indeed anyone who cares about the future of the planet, the relationship children have to their screens is a particular hot potato.Orson Welles’ advice to young people to be selective about your viewing – “Don’t be marinated, don’t soak yourself in films” – has never been more relevant in the era of AI slop and doom-scrolling. So we asked film-makers, critics and industry names for the joyful, imaginative and thought-provoking films that every child and young adult should see. Here is their curated list of just 25 screen experiences worth having.Catherine BrayAt the age of …1Fantasia(1940)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Disney/Cinetext/AllstarMy first child is due in autumn and it’s made me think about what I’d like to share with them in their journey into the magical world of movies (I know they will be asleep or crying, but allow a man to dream). Disney’s Fantasia holds some of my own earliest film memories: the music; the dancing ostriches; Mickey Mouse just trying to have a rest. If cinema is the fusion of sound and image into something greater than the sum of its parts, then Fantasia is truly visceral and joyous cinema. I hope my wee one will feel the same.Tom Nicoll, director2The Snowman(1982)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Channel 4/AllstarWith its winsome, crayon textures, The Snowman is a dream. Young James delights in showing his miraculous visitor around his domestic domain, but it’s the Snowman who expands the kid’s horizons, as they soar above the Sussex countryside. In the morning, the snow has melted, but the magic remains.Michael Leader, author of The Animation Atlas3My Neighbour Totoro(1988)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Studio Ghibli/Tokuma-Shoten/Nibariki/Kobal/ShutterstockHayao Miyazaki’s animation is a beautiful, meditative film about illness, grief and the power of nature. My daughter was three when she first watched it and was totally mesmerised. It is a real shift in tone from the usual American fare and offers something different for kids to connect with.Imran Perretta, director4Muppets Take Manhattan(1984)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Tri Star/Kobal/Rex/ShutterstockComing at the tail end of “peak Muppets”, and directed by Frank Oz (also at his creative apex, having just done The Dark Crystal), this film sees Kermit and friends take their ensemble play to the Big Apple with the dream of opening on Broadway. Things are not as easy as they seem and they encounter hardships and learn life lessons. The film is full of laughs and inspired cameos (including Joan Rivers inflicting her version of an extravagant makeover on a permed Miss Piggy). It’s a deserving entry in the canon of great 1980s New York City films.Michelle Carey, founder of Red Balloonalliance5Chicken Run(2000)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Cinetext/Dreamworks Skg/AllstarA masterclass in stop-motion, I’d choose this for every five-year-old, mainly having seen the effect it had on mine. Drawing heavily from classic second world war adventure films, this tale of plucky chickens who dream of a life outside their electric-fenced egg farm is filled with slapstick, action and gags that hit kids and grownups alike, all wrapped around a message about the fundamental right to freedom. It’s The Great Escape – with chickens.Briony Hanson,director offilm, British Council6The Wizard of Oz(1939)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Allstar/AlamyThe Wizard of Oz changed my life when I was six years old. It is a visual delight that expands imaginations and every six-year-old should see it.Prano Bailey-Bond, director7Scooby-Doo(2002)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Warner Bros/AllstarMy younger self thought Scooby-Doo was a masterpiece. My current self agrees. It has everything you need from a film: a compelling story, an incredible cast of characters, mystery, thrills and laughs. It’s pure pop spectacle. Rewatching it as an adult, I could see that this was also a film with big ideas: it’s an autopsy of the American project post-9/11, an examination of gender relations and performance at the beginning of a new century, and a deeply felt exploration of the value of friendship under late capitalism. The exact kind of film a seven-year-old should be watching.Naqqash Khalid, director8Labyrinth(1986)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Tristar Pictures/AllstarDavid Bowie may have been the Thin White Duke but he was also Jareth the Goblin King in Jim Henson’s charming family fantasy adventure. A ludicrously bewigged Bowie taunts and tantalises Jennifer Connelly’s Sarah as she undergoes a perilous journey to find her kidnapped baby brother.Alex Larman, author of Lazarus: The Second Coming of David Bowie9The Amazing Mr Blunden(1972; remade in 2021)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Hemdale Film Corporation/AllstarI can’t remember exactly how old I was when I saw this ghost story, directed by Lionel Jeffries, but it affected the smaller me deeply, mainly by introducing me to a kind of exhilarating dread. I saw two kids in 1918 find themselves in a lonely country house haunted by two other kids who died in a fire 100 years earlier (instigated by, of all people, Diana Dors in a Regency bonnet); they head to 1818, save the kids, do in the baddies and inherit the lovely house. The estimable Mark Gatiss’s remake should really be the gateway drug to the source – your nine-year-olds may never be the same again.Andrew Pulver, associate editor, film, the Guardian10The Princess Bride(1987)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Landmark Media/AlamyIt’s whimsical fun for a kid, but also has a bunch of jokes for the grownups that go over your head until you revisit it in a fit of nostalgia as, say, a hungover 24-year-old looking for a comfort watch. Rob Reiner, what a talent you were.Julia Jackman, director11Mulan(1998)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Everett Collection/AlamyBrilliant songs, sweeping romance and a great way to introduce younger audiences to the comic brilliance of Eddie Murphy as Mushu the dragon. Based on the Chinese legend of Hua Mulan, this fun adventure about identity follows a girl who disguises herself as a boy, because people won’t let her do what she wants when she’s a girl. They’re furious when they find out!Rhianna Dhillon, critic12The Witches(1990)View image in fullscreenPhotograph:  Alamy/Once you hit your preteens, it’s time to cue up this dark and delightful adaptation of Roald Dahl’s book. Anjelica Huston goes from glam to gruesome when she transforms into the bald, child-hating Grand High Witch, determined to wipe out the kiddos of the world with a new magic potion. Young viewers will root for Luke (who is turned into a mouse) and his grandmother, who use cleverness, bravery and trust in each other to triumph over the witless witches.Rebecca Fons, Barbicanhead ofcinema13Princess Mononoke(1997)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Everett Collection/AlamySpeaking as a fully grown adult, The Wind Rises sits high atop my list of favourite Miyazaki films, but I’m not sure I’d feel that way had I not grown up alongside the reverence for nature instilled in me by this earlier classic. It is a film so beautiful, frightening, hardcore, playful and prescient about the pained relationship between nature and technology – and a child can grasp its profundity as easily as an adult. In Miyazaki’s films, children are often more capable of achieving wisdom than the rigid adults trying to make the old ways endure. That seems about right.David Osit, director14Ferris Bueller’s Day Off(1986)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Paramount/AllstarYou would not have caught me watching a John Hughes film for love nor money in my youth. It was my assistant who got me into the film about 10 years ago – she declared one day on a set that she was a big Hughes fan and this was one she held close. I watched it and thought it waspretty damn funny– with all its un-PC flaws ignored.Elizabeth Karlsen, producer15Run Lola Run(1998)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Warner Home/AllstarSince I was young, plenty of films have made me yearn to be a director, but I left a matinee of this in the summer of 1999 both completely envious and fizzing with excitement, desperate to make a movie that very day. It’s a brisk but profound film about how your whole life can change in the next 20 minutes, and how true destiny and blind chance may not be as far apart as we imagine. It’s also propelled by a pulse-quickening techno score, so I defy you not to be moved – both literally and figuratively.Edgar Wright, director16The Umbrellas of Cherbourg(1964)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: AlamyWhen I was a teenager, most of my favourite films involved guns and swearing. So a film shot in bright pastels about young lovers in a French port where everyone singsall the way through the moviewas a hard sell. But there was nothing else on and iPhones didn’t exist yet, so I went and it changed me. It’s a musical about how disappointing life is – a lesson best learned early – and one of the most beautiful films ever made.Gareth Tunley, director17Get Out(2017)View image in fullscreenPhotograph:  Blumhouse/AllstarJordan Peele’s film, in which a young photographer realises something isn’t quite right while meeting his girlfriend’s family, is the perfect gateway for a young cinephile – so much fun you barely notice it’s teaching you how to watch.Farhana Bhula,director of Film418Gaza: Doctors Under Attack (2025); Louis Theroux: The Settlers(2025)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: BBCThese films depict Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and the ethnic cleansing of the West Bank. The images are heartbreaking and unforgettable: there are horribly mutilated children facing death; medics in wrecked hospitals knowing they themselves are targets. Theroux’s documentary shows the chilling smile of a settler woman who knows she has the power to drive Palestinians from their homes. Pictures seen when young stay in the mind for a lifetime. Never was the need for such films so urgent. Remember Martin Luther King: “The ultimate tragedy is not the oppression and cruelty by the bad people but the silence over that by the good people.”Ken Loach, director19Trainspotting(1996)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Channel Four Films/AllstarIt has been 30 years since we made Trainspotting, and the film Danny Boyle put together fromIrvine Welsh’s brilliant bookhas taken on a life of its own. Its iconography still seems to be everywhere, which is gratifying if a little overwhelming. We are immensely proud of the film we made and what it has to say about being young and pushing back on what’s expected. The good people at the BBFC insist that you have to be 18 to see the film and we must abide by the law. But if you are old enough, I highly recommend the film.
